Privilege-Speaker's Ruling
FRIDAY, 15 SEPTEMBER 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 12.30 p.m.
Prayers.
PRIVILEGE-SPEAKER'S RULING
Mr SPEAKER: I have to rule on a matter of privilege involving the honourable member
for Mt. Albert. I have to decide whether the honourable member misled the House
deliberately or inadvertently when giving the source of a quotation he used in a speech he
made last evening. I have studied the unrevised Hansard report and I have listened to the
recording of the debate.
The incident started when the member for Mt. Albert said, "This is the man who in the
1978 Budget debate and I refer to Hansard at page 1287". I then interrupted him to point
out that he could not allude to a previous debate of the same session. He then proceeded to
say, "I am reminded of the fact that the Prime Minister is on record as saying in 1976 how
proud he was that the National Government had been able to spend some 2 or 3 weeks
working out"-and he was interrupted again, when the Prime Minister raised a point of
order to ask for the source of his quotation.
The honourable member for Mt. Albert then said, "I was interrupted before I could
quote the source. I am quoting from 1976 Hansard, not this year's debate." After I had ruled
that that was in order and had answered his query about how much time he had still to speak,
he said, "I wanted to quote from Hansard 1976 at page 1287", and then he proceeded with
his quotation. A few minutes later the member for Franklin, the Chief Government Whip,
raised a point of order to say that the Prime Minister was not recorded on that page of
Hansard as having said anything. The honourable member for Mt. Albert then said, "I am
very happy to speak to the point of order. The member for Franklin has quite correctly
stated the position. I regret that in the confusion of all the interruptions I have had in trying
to make a 20-minute speech-I have now been going for more than half an hour-I misread
my notes, for which I apologise." In short, the honourable member misattributed the
quotation and then apologised for having done so.
The question is, was the misattribution a breach of privilege? For that to have been the
case it would have had to be deliberate. If it were, then the apology was phoney, because he
would have been trying to cover up his earlier infringement. The Prime Minister asserted
that it was inconceivable and illogical that the honourable member for Mt. Albert could have
said he was quoting from the 1978 Budget debate, and then, shortly afterwards, say it was
from the 1976 Hansard.
It would appear strange that such an experienced member would have made such a
mistake, but, as I have said, I have studied the unrevised Hansard report and listened very
carefully to the tape recording of the debate, and I make the following observations. First,
he was not, I believe, following his notes very carefully. Secondly, between the reference to
1978 and the quotation there was a lapse of nearly 2 minutes and there were four
interruptions. Thirdly, it is therefore reasonable to assume that there was some confusion in
his mind and that the apology was offered genuinely. On a close examination of all the facts
available to me--both given to me in the House and available to me as Speaker in consulting
the Hansard records-I cannot find justification for saying that he deliberately misled the
House. Therefore the error must have been inadvertent, and I find that no prima facie
breach of privilege exists.
DOMINION HEADLINE
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I
draw your attention to the Dominion of today's date, and particularly to the banner headline
on the front page about an incident involving a member of the House. I believe that that
headline is sensationalism of the worst possible kind. It reflects not only on the member in
question but also on Parliament generally. In view of the degree of irresponsibility shown in
the publication of the article, would it not be proper for you, as our president in effect, to
take up the matter with the chairman of the press gallery with a view to ensuring that this

kind of journalism in relation to events in the House does not recur?
Mr SPEAKER: The right honourable gentleman is not raising a matter of privilege. It is
simply a suggestion that I take up the matter with the chairman of the press gallery. I take up
various matters with the chairman when I believe the rights of Parliament are being infringed
in some way. I shall look at the article. I saw merely the headlines this morning. I have not
read that paper much lately, and I did not get round to reading it properly this morning. I
shall look at the headline, and consider what it would be appropriate for me to do. The
honourable member will appreciate my reluctance to interfere with the right of the press to
publish what it wants to so long as there is no breach of privilege.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): On Tuesday, Wednesday, and
Friday I propose that we proceed with the legislation on the Order Paper. I shall probably
move the tax Bills up. On Thursday we shall take local Bills, if any, followed by legislation
on the Order Paper.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-URGENCY
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): I move, That urgency be accorded
the introduction and the passing of the Imprest Supply Bill (No. 2). As honourable members
know, it is the normal practice to take urgency for the debate on the Imprest Supply Bill. It is
done for quite obvious reasons, and it gives the Opposition the opportunity to go beyond the
normal time.
Motion agreed to.
IMPREST SUPPLY BILL (No. 2)
A message was received from His Excellency the Governor-General recommending the
House to make an appropriation of public money for the purposes of the Imprest Supply Bill

Bill presented and read a first time.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The Opposition wants to
debate the Government's mishandling, by its own caucus, of the prosecution of freezing
workers in Southland, and of other industrial relations matters. The Government said it
would restore the legal framework to industrial relations. The member for Wairarapa, the
member for Invercargill, and the member for Awarua have all made provocative speeches.
All three are on record as saying that, if the Government did not stand its ground, they
would resign.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: Not quite-I didn't mention resigning.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: The member for Invercargill is taking one step backwards and two
steps sideways, because he knows he has to hang on to his superannuation rights. The
principles of industrial relations do not really matter. I want to concentrate on an article
published in an Invercargill newspaper on Tuesday, 18 July, which contained one step
sideways, because it stated, "Invercargill M.P. Mr N. P. H. Jones would seriously consider
standing down if the Government withdrew the prosecutions of 192 Ocean Beach freezing
workers." The Government did not want the debate to take place after it had arrived at a
decision, so it has been putting pressure on Federated Farmers and trying to put pressure on
other groups in an attempt to slide out of the responsibilities it had taken upon itself
gratuitously. Everyone knows that industrial relations in the last 2 years 9 months have been
deplorable, and everyone knows the main reason—the man who holds the office of Prime
Minister. Fifty-three other reasons are scattered around the House like debris, because at
different times they have backed him up.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: A point of order, Mr Speaker. To say that 53 members are scattered
around the House like debris is more or less suggesting that honourable members are akin to
debris. That is a pretty obnoxious word, and I take exception to it.
Mr SPEAKER: The Deputy Leader of the Opposition was using a figure of speech that

was fairly mild, and to one that I do not think I should take too much exception. I am sorry

Hon. R. J. TIZARD: Thank you for your ruling, Mr Speaker. I assure the member that,

Hon. J. B. Bolger: That's a smart trick.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: I do not need smart tricks in dealing with the Minister of Fisheries;
the plain truth will do. The Government, backing up the Prime Minister, is now scattering in
diverse directions. Some members want to see the resumption of freezing works activity on
the due date; others want to uphold the law, whatever the law might be; others want to
uphold their own principles, whatever they might be; and yet others believe that we should
return to the principle of law as enshrined in our democracy. There is a very wide range of
difference between those four viewpoints.
I wonder whether any back-bench members opposite would care to comment, because
they do have the opportunity to do so on the air, on what has been going on in the
Government caucus. Whose arm is furthest up his back about coming down from their
pronouncements? I get a very happy smile from the member for Whangarei. He has been
away on public business and perhaps he has not suffered quite as much pain as some of the
others may have. I would hate to see the member suffer at all, but I assure him it will be only
short lived-it will end on 25 November, when the poll is declared about 9 o'clock that night.
It is very clear that members opposite are torn between different courses of action. They are
all on record as saying publicly that they will hold the line. They were quite sure of the line
they were on. Some of them come from areas where the railway lines have been ripped up,
and it has left them with only ballast to balance on. That is the sort of difficulty a lot of them
face. They are finding it difficult to decide the line they will follow.
They know that, unless they can convince the public in some way before the election,
the only record they will leave for public scrutiny before the votes are cast is their
confrontation tactics, the damage that has been caused to New Zealand and, specifically, the
damage that has been caused to the farming industry. We have not had a clear statement
from any of them about what they will do. Only 2 days ago further prosecutions were
instituted in the court. A union connected with the freezing industry, but not directly
involved in the way the meat workers or the freezing workers themselves are, had two of its
officials charged before the courts. At the same time, the Government is attempting to
assure the meat workers that there will be at least a stay of prosecution or some sort of
deferment while the gentlemen get together and work it out.
On television, however, we saw the president of Federated Farmers being backed into a
corner, but carefully trying to step out of the corner. Oh no, Federated Farmers has not
promised to withdraw the charges, the Government has not given any undertaking that it will
withdraw the charges, and the Attorney-General, who has done such a good job in sweeping
charges under the rug so far, is unfortunately absent ill. I do not know whether they cannot
find anyone else to do the sweeping under the rug, or whether they do not want anyone to do
it, but we want some answers in the House. The member for Awarua is looking very
thoughtful. He knows the risk he ran and, like some others, he is mindful of the old adage
that quite a few people have been hanged for what they did say, but many fewer for things
they did not say. I expect we shall find him very silent in the debate. The same cannot be said
of the member for Invercargill.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: I shall be quite happy to keep going.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: He will be happy to keep going. I draw him back to his statement
that he would seriously consider standing down if the Government withdrew the
prosecutions.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: It has not done it yet.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: The member is hanging on to the last shred of hope. When the
Government leads with prosecutions of officials of other unions, what conclusions must the
meat workers or the freezing workers come to? Do they conclude that this is just a play to get
them back into conciliation? The members of those unions have made it absolutely clear that
the slate must be wiped completely clean. They do not want to be left with someone with a
cloth poised over the slate, which will be wiped clean if they are good boys for 3 months or 6
months.
Members have seen how the Government works. At one stage the law operated in
Auckland on an alphabetical system. It was all right for the Tizards of this world, but not so

good for the Arthurs. At other times mass appeal motivates the Government's decisions.
The courts are clogged. The court in Invercargill will be seriously clogged with 192
prosecutions. It will be more clogged than Auckland's court was, with about 200
prosecutions in the Bastion Point dispute. Members opposite do not understand what is
happening to justice in the country. Either we have a law that is enforced, or we have no law.
We then would have anarchy. Members opposite will not face that realisation.
The problem is the law passed by the Government. Its members have an abysmal
ignorance of industrial relations. The member who has jumped 24 places into the
crossbenches knows all about industrial law. He is the chairman of the Government's caucus
committee. I wonder whether any member opposite would quote what Tom Skinner said
about the member for Eden. He said the member had an abysmal ignorance of anything to
do with industrial relations. The problem with the Government's relations with the court
comes back to its relations with the people. The Government does not understand the
people. Government members think they can develop a confrontation and win.
In a democracy government depends on the consent of the Government. It is time
members opposite, including the Minister of Justice, realised that. He has the least
administrative responsibility in the Government. He has used his position to make trouble
rather than to make law. I thought he was a troubleshooter, but he is a troublemaker.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: We had it before.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: When it is effective, it will be used over and over again. Members
opposite have become so smug in their ways they do not consider the views of the people
outside. The industrial problems are not the result of confrontation sought by union
members, but the result of the abysmal ignorance of members opposite about the feelings of
working people, their aspirations, and their means. Government members are backing off,
because they know they must get the freezing industry working under an agreement shortly
after 1 October. They are prepared to sing the principles of law, to resort to expediency, and
to blame everyone but themselves for the position they are in.
I want to emphasise the Government's position. The problems are the Government's
responsibility. No principles that Government members can enunciate will get them out of
this difficulty. This is to be found in all walks of our society. The Minister of Justice has a
charade about the electoral rolls. The Minister of Customs interfered with the courts. He
was also Attorney-General, but did not really know what he was doing when he blocked the
action that was properly taken against the Prime Minister in the court. The abortion debate,
an issue of major interest, was forced through the House under urgency at all hours of the
night. The issue of the Repeal petition did not even get to the House. Whatever the merits of
their case, citizens have the right to take it to Parliament.
Industrial law and the way the Government has failed miserably to give any indication
of its policy are what we are really concerned about at the moment. The Government is
resorting to its old policy of divide and, hopefully, rule. What has Federated Farmers agreed
to? It was pretty clear on television that Federated Farmers had agreed to discuss the matter,
but not to go along with what the Government wanted. After the Government caucus
meeting it was very clear that it did not know the way it wanted to go. It is very clear that the
union is sticking to its principles that until the threat of prosecution is removed-
[Interruption.] That is what I am saying about the abysmal ignorance of the members
opposite. As soon as unions are mentioned, the members for Invercargill and Awarua ask,
what principles?
Mr N. P. H. Jones: That's right.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: They have the principles that they will defend the interests of their
members, but they will meet other interested groups on an equal footing. If they do not meet
those other interested groups on an equal footing they reserve the right to withdraw their
labour. That is the only weapon left to them.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: All they did last year was to work out of season.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: The member for Invercargill cannot understand that this is not a
dictatorship. He tells us what he went to fight against, but cannot tell us what he is fighting
for here. That is the problem. Many members on both sides of the House believe that they
fought for democracy. However, the only ones who are democrats today are on this side of
the House. That is what we are debating.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! That is a somewhat offensive remark, and I think the
honourable member should withdraw it.

can get the co-operation of Federated Farmers and get caucus to go along with it, we will do
what the Labour Pary said was right in the first place." I wonder if any Government member
is prepared to admit that.
Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora): I had the misfortune recently to follow the Deputy Leader
of the Opposition. I wonder why a junior back-bencher has to match that particular person?
I noted that the Deputy Leader of the Opposition-and I hope I quote him correctly-said
that democracy depended on the consent of the people. Could I remind the Deputy Leader
of the Opposition that it also carries with it an obligation to govern, and that means you do
not run away from issues, as did the Labour Government during its period in office from
1972 to 1975.
I refer particularly to the penalty provisions that were in a draft Bill that Labour
inherited from the previous National Government, but that Labour removed from the
Industrial Relations Act. Those penalty provisions were put back in the legislation by the
National Government, because the National Government believes that the rule of law and
the law should apply to all sections of the community; one section of the community should
not be excluded and treated differently.
I can recall a recent Labour Party conference at which there was a discussion about the
use of injunctions in the industrial relations field. What was the outcome of it? There was

Some of the changes in industrial relations introduced by the National Government
were designed to overcome the disruption that was being caused to the economy. There were
rolling strikes, in which small sections of the work force withdrew their labour and put others
out of work. Because the legislation in force, emanating from the Labour Government, was
weak-kneed, with a requirement to give 7 days' notice before a person could be suspended,
striking workers had gone back to work long before the notice period had elapsed. Then, a
few weeks later, another section would withdraw its labour and throw others out of work. So
the National Government-and this was one of the very early changes it introduced—
changed the Industrial Relations Act to provide for suspension without notice. As a result of
that change, the rolling strike stoppage virtually disappeared. That is an illustration of the
difference between the National Government and the Labour Government-the latter ran
away from such issues.
Another change was the creation once again of the Arbitration Court and the
reintroduction of the general wage order. Changes to the Commerce Act were introduced
also, and it is interesting to note that the amendments to that Act were used recently by the
freezing companies to bring the unions and the employers round the table to resolve the
interpretation of an award. Those provisions were recognised as a means of solving that
particular difficulty.
The changes to the Commerce Act also brought about an opportunity for persons to
take proceedings for political strikes, and we have seen illustrations of the activity involved
in that sphere. I have already mentioned the ban on export trade to Chile. There was also the
incident of the submarine, Pintado. The changes to the Commerce Act also covered a failure
to resume work in cases in which the public interest was affected and the matter was of
importance to the economy. A provision relating to particular industries was incorporated.

Recently, many examples have come to light of employers seeking labour; some
requiring only minor skills, but have been unable to fill the job vacancies. When I was in
Dunedin 10 days ago I spoke to the manufacturer of a product that required only basic
processing. He told me that he had had six vacancies. About 700 people are registered as
unemployed in Dunedin. The manufacturer sought the assistance of the Department of
Labour and advertised extensively, but he was able to fill only two of the six positions—and I
repeat that he did not require skilled labour. He has been able to obtain only two people

The member for Birkenhead made a particularly good point. Earlier, when the subject

employed. In fact, the figures for the middle of the year show that, in the case of working
proprietors and full-time employees, the number of employed males has increased by 0.7
percent since 1975. Despite those registered as unemployed, or on special work, the absolute
number of males gainfully employed has increased in the past 3 years. The number of
working females has increased considerably, by almost 3.5 percent, and the total work force
has increased by 1.5 percent.
Opposition members often say that we exclude part-time employees from the registered
unemployed, and that we do not take them into account. The number of people in the work
force engaged in gainful part-time employment is considerably higher than it was 3 years.
ago. In the case of men it is up 2.3 percent; in the case of women it has increased by more
than 14 percent in 3 years, and the average across the whole work force is up more than 11
percent. That gives the lie to the charge that the employment situation has drifted with this
Government. In fact, it has strengthened. The real problem that lies behind the growth
factor in the economy originated with the economic damage done by the previous Labour
Government. On the hustings in 1975 we said that our first responsibility was to restore the
shattered economy, and we have been constructively and effectively engaged in that in the
last 3 years. The task is incomplete, but we have made substantial progress. Although
unemployment figures are not pleasing I remind our opponents that unemployment figure,
as a percentage of the work force, are vastly better in New Zealand than in any other major

In 1972 we bequeathed a $1,000 million nest egg of overseas exchange reserves to the
incoming Labour Government. In 1975 Labour had spent it all, and had borrowed New
Zealand into a very considerable hole. The National Government has since been repairing
that damage, and the deficit of $1,000 million for the trading year 1975 has been virtually
halved in the latest 12-month period. The overseas exchange deficit as a percentage of gross
national product tells an even better story. The member for Rangitikei should listen very
carefully to this and brush away "funny money” ideas so that he can consider the real facts.
In 1975, the last year of the previous and last Labour Government, the deficit in overseas
exchange as a percentage of gross national product was 9.5—a quite unacceptably high rate.
By 1976 the National Government had brought it down to 5.2, by 1977 to 4.3, and by last
July to 3.4. That proves that the Government is making substantial progress in the very
important area of overseas exchange earnings from imports and exports. The country will
have no future, unless we rearrange the balance of exports and imports so that we are on the
winning side, not on the losing side as we were during the term of the Labour Government.
In 1975 the value of imports was $2,300 million, compared with exports of $1,600 million,
but by 1978 the value of exports had increased to $3,400 million and imports had decreased
to $3,000 million. Therefore, the balance of trade had improved from minus $600 million to
plus $420 million. Including invisibles and the total current account balance, the deficit left
by the Labour Government has been halved to about $500 million.

STATE SERVICES AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): I move, That the State Services
Amendment Bill be introduced. The purpose of this Bill is to introduce a preferential right of
re-entry into the Public Service, for any person who has resigned to care for one or more
dependent pre-school children. These provisions were negotiated in the State services as part
of an overall package aimed at further promoting the concept of equal career opportunities
for men and women. Preferential re-entry rights to the Public Service will be given under
these provisions at any time up to 4 years after resignation, or up to 5 years in the case of a
woman who is also entitled to maternity leave. Where a person returns to a position in the
same department in which he or she was employed at the time of resignation, and that
position involves substantially similar duties at no higher grading than that previously held,
there will be no right of appeal against reappointment. Where a person is appointed to a
higher grade, or to a graded level in a different class of work, there will be a right of appeal.
However, a person being reappointed will be treated as if he or she is already an officer
in the Public Service at the time of the reappointment. This will place the onus of appeal on
the appellant, rather than the appointing department, as would otherwise be the case with an
appointment made from outside the Public Service. These provisions represent a further step
by this Government to remove any discrimination against a person who remains at home for
a period to care for dependent pre-school children. It is expected that the new provisions
will, in the main, be used by women who want to make a career for themselves in the Public
Service. But I repeat my earlier statement that the provisions will apply equally to both men
and women in the case of solo parents. Other clauses in the Bill are purely machinery
amendments to update and clarify existing provisions in the State Services Act. Both the
State Services Commission and the Public Service Association have recommended minor
amendments as a result of their everyday dealings with the State Services Act in the SSCC.

mean that fundamentally we would have to keep lists of all women who, presumably, having
their first child, would be kept on the records for a period of 5 years, with the right to ask for
their jobs back; but they might not want their jobs back because they might subsequently
have a second child. The resignation and re-entry provisions in the Bill would achieve exactly
the same objectives, but without the need to keep lists. The question of who has the right to
appeal against re-entry is spelt out quite clearly. If a person, male or female, is going back to
the same position he or she held, there is no right of appeal. If he or she is applying for a
position with a change of grading or status then there is a right of appeal under the normal
State Services appeal arrangements. It is quite clear and it is spelt out precisely in the Bill.

HOWARD ESTATE BILL
Introduction
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): I move, That
the Howard Estate Bill be introduced. This Bill consolidates and amends the Howard Estate
Act 1919. The purpose of the 1919 Act was to give effect to the intentions of the late Josiah
Howard who died in 1919 leaving his estate to the Crown as a foundation or endowment for
agricultural education. Today, the estate comprises a large sheep and cattle station at
Tikokino in Hawkes Bay, including a training farm for boys known as Smedley Boys
Training Farm. Currently, there are 16 cadets-8 first year and 8 second year. The basic
purpose of the existing legislation has been carefully preserved in the Bill, but the experience
of almost 60 years gained since the original Act was enacted has shown that a number of
changes to detail in the administration of the estate will enable the intentions of the donor to
be more effectively attuned to modern conditions.
There are three main changes proposed in the Bill. The first is that whilst the existing
very successful scheme of both practical and theoretical farm training conducted on the
estate property will be continued, the opportunity is being taken to give males and females
the right to undertake training. At present, only males are entitled to enrol for the training
programmes conducted on the estate.
The second main change is to transfer the overall responsibility for the estate to the
Public Trust Office. Under the existing legislation responsibility for the estate rests with the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, although the assets are vested in the Public Trustee,
and the day-to-day administration of the estate and the conduct of the training scheme are
conducted by that office, assisted by the valuable guidance and advice of an advisory board
!


## p. 3570 (#50) ############################################

3570
19 September
Howard Estate Bill
representing a wide range of local interests. Retention of overall control by the Ministry of
Agriculture and Fisheries was a valid approach in 1919 when the training farm had then to be
established, and it was also desirable in its formative years. This divided control is, however,
no longer thought to be necessary, partly because of the greatly improved financial position
of the estate, and partly by reason of the high calibre and wide experience of the persons who
have been appointed to membership of the advisory board. The functions of the advisory
board are more clearly set out in the Bill, and its members will have an increasingly
important role to play in the administration of the Howard estate.
The third main change is to define and extend the powers of the Public Trustee. Some of
these alterations are necessary to bring those powers more into line with modern standards
and practices of trustees, and the balance reflect the increased responsibility the Public
Trustee will have under the Bill, and the wider role the advisory board will have to play in
future. Pursuant to Standing Order 223 I will be moving that this Bill be referred to the
Lands and Agriculture Committee.

similar to Smedley Boys Training Farm, in that it is a bequeathed farm, and local people,
especially the farming community, have taken a great deal of interest in it. Telford now has a
training scheme for young people, with the idea of them obtaining a trade certificate and
later having an opportunity to qualify for land settlement blocks. Some time ago it was
transferred with some difficulty to the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries to enable the
ministry to run courses at Telford. Will transferring Smedley Boys Training Farm from the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries to the Public Trustee deny young people in the future

Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): The member

The effect of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries on what is essentially a private

be in any difficulty in that respect.

LOCAL LEGISLATION BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Local


## p. 3572 (#52) ############################################

3572
19 September
Local Legislation Bill
Legislation Bill be introduced. This is the usual measure that is brought down each year
containing provisions affecting particular local authorities or other public bodies. Each
clause has been promoted by the local authority concerned, and deals with matters of a
relatively minor non-contentious nature. This year there are 15 operative clauses. Some
clauses validate irregularities in actions already taken by local authorities; others authorise
specific proposals to be carried out where no provision is made in existing general legislation.
Government departments having an interest in particular clauses have been consulted. All
members of Parliament whose constituents are or may be affected by individual clauses have
been advised by the local authority or public body concerned, as required by the Standing
Orders. I have not received objections to any clauses in the Bill. Standing Order 272 requires
that the Bill be referred to the Local Bills Committee, where each clause may be examined in
detail.

satisfy this side of the House that that is not a contentious matter. Members will know that
this is the same locality from which contentious suggestions were made about the Local

question of reserve funds, which for many years have been used by local bodies under

that was collected for public reserves has been paid to the Paraparaumu College for the
construction of a gymnasium.

on the introduction of Government Bills. I do this because the Bill is a washing-up one. It is
the annual Bill introduced by the Government every year. It does not matter whether the
Government is a Labour Government or a National Government, an annual washing-up Bill
has been introduced.
The committee set down what should guide us on relevancy: "There was general
agreement that the introduction of a Bill, except in exceptional cases, need not be a lengthy
process and that in general, all that is necessary is a brief explanation from the Minister
followed by a limited period of questions. It is unnecessary for the Minister at this stage to
give a detailed analysis of the Bill as this material is contained in the printed explanatory
note attached to the Bill and it is also not the appropriate time for members to make
impromptu speeches that would be more suitable on the second reading after they had had
an opportunity to study the legislation."
That decision was not varied by the 1974 committee, which laid down that the total
debating time would be 2 hours. That procedure is important. The Minister is not obligated
to give a detailed analysis of the Bill when it is introduced. It has been suggested that the
Standing Orders have been changed. The Standing Orders have not been changed since they
were studied in 1972 and 1974.

by a Labour Government. The Bill now before the House has 16 clauses. So much for the
nonsense that the National Government encourages local authorities to commit
irregularities.
Finally, to put everything into the right perspective I shall read the Standing Order
referring to local legislation bills. Standing Order 270 reads: “Application in writing may be
made to the Minister of Local Government, . . . by any local authority or public body, for
preliminary consideration and provisional approval of a clause or clauses to be included in
the local legislation Bill. Every such application shall be accompanied by a draft of the
proposed clause or clauses, and by a certificate signed by some responsible officer of such
local authority or public body that members of the House (stating the names) whose
constituents may or are likely to be affected by such proposed legislation have been
furnished..." I make the point that every member likely to be affected has had a copy of the
clause and been asked, if he disagreed with the clause, to refer it to the Minister. I have not
received one objection from any member.
The legislation will be referred to the Local Bills Committee, on which the Opposition
has representatives. It is over to those representatives to decide whether the Bill is of a
contentious nature. If they still consider the matter to be contentious it will be withdrawn
during the Committee stage and the local authorities will have to introduce a local Bill. I
hope that sets the record straight.

Electricity Bulk Price
3. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram), on behalf of Hon. F. M. COLMAN
(Petone), to the Minister of Energy: What factors, other than the increase in interest charges
from 0.7429c per unit, will have to be taken into account in fixing the bulk price per unit of
electricity sold by the ministry in the financial year 1979-80?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Energy. "The bulk price of electricity for the 1979-80 year should be at least sufficient to
maintain the financial situation of N.Z. Electricity and avoid operation at a loss. Interest has
increased with the escalation in the cost of capital works and with a proportion of NZE's
existing loan debt being converted to the new interest rate. Interest charges will also increase
as a fraction of the total of estimated working expenses, because operating and maintenance
are forecast to fall from 0.651c per unit in 1977-78 to 0.605c per unit in 1978-79. Increased
plant capacity reduces the need for more expensive thermal generation. The other part of
working expenses, which is depreciation, naturally increases with the additional capital
investment in new plant and equipment over the 1977-78 year".
Hon. Michael Connelly: What will the charge be after taking those factors into account?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That is an impossible supplementary question.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I cannot give the answer. However, I am sure that the
member will be able to work it out with his calculator.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Will any increase, already predicted, be substantially because of
the permitted increase in the interest rate both on current and previous Government works
and loans?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No. The change in interest rate is relatively gradual and is
being rolled over at 10 percent of the loans. That will take several years, but is a relatively
small part in the increase in electricity costs. The whole basis of the system is to try to get rid
of the subsidised system we inherited from the Labour Government. That is now being done.
There is a realistic charge for energy, which every other Western country is entitled to

RATES REBATE AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. When I introduced the Bill, members opposite endeavoured to raise an
outcry by constantly suggesting that the Government was taking something away from
pensioners and others on low incomes. They did their loudest and best to have the House
believe and to have the country believe the nonsensical idea that the Government is
determined to do away with the rates rebate scheme, and that this Bill was the start of the
process. [Interruption.] They are admitting that was their idea: to get this over to the public.
They abandoned all sense of proportion, and endeavoured to read something into the Bill
that is just not there.
Let me take a few minutes to explain to the House what the Bill does. First of all, clause
3 makes no difference whatsoever to the qualifying income limit below which a ratepayer is


## p. 3589 (#69) ############################################

19 September
3589
Rates Rebate Amendment Bill
entitled to a full rates rebate. Since 1 April last, the limit has been $4,235 plus $156 in respect
of each dependant. The limit includes, and always has included, even in the Labour
Government's time, the income of the spouse, although members tried to fool the public that
it was not so. The Bill does not alter this one iota: $4,235 is the sum a national
superannuitant and his wife would have received during the year ended 31 March 1978, so no
national superannuitant is affected by the Bill solely by reason of the income limit.
Further, $4,235 is substantially in excess of the benefit a sickness beneficiary or anyone
else on a social welfare means-tested benefit would have received during the year ended 31
March 1978. A married sickness or unemployment beneficiary with two children and no
other income during the year ended March last would have received $3,787, or $448 less than
the income limit. So let me stress once again that the income limit in the Bill takes nothing
away from any sickness beneficiary, national superannuitant, or anyone else on a low
income. To suggest that it does so is just so much nonsense.
Let me assure the House, and honourable members opposite, that the Government
keeps its promises. Our last election manifesto said that rates concessions would continue for
the same categories of beneficiaries, using the same means test, and at the same rates as were
applicable when the National Government assumed office. We have kept that promise.
Mr Prebble: Rubbish!
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: We will continue to keep that promise.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: That's why the taxpayers are up in arms.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Listen to members opposite. They cannot think of anything else
but rubbish. In fact, we have done better. In addition to the rates rebate, ratepayers who are
liable for income tax will in future receive an additional income tax rebate, initially of $25 a
year. The Bill enables the income limit to be adjusted by Orders in Council, as has been the
case in the past. So far as I am concerned, that practice will continue to be followed in the
future. The maximum limit will be adjusted from time to time, having regard to changes in
national supernnuation and social welfare benefit rates generally.
Mr Prebble: Oh yes?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Yes, we have done that all the time under our legislation affecting
superannuitants and old age beneficiaries. We have kept the benefits up with the rate of
inflation at all times, and members opposite know that. It is no good their trying to fool the
public as they are. Let me repeat that the maximum limit will be adjusted from time to time,
having regard to changes in national superannuation and social welfare benefit rates
generally. So much for the income limit. The Bill does not change it at all.
The Bill goes on to provide in clause 3 that, as from 1 April next, the maximum rebate
that may be paid in any individual case will be $200. That amount can be altered from time to
time by Order in Council. Along with the income limit, the maximum rebate figure stated in
the Bill, which is based very largely on information about last year's rates and incomes, will
be reviewed in the light of later trends before 1 April next. There is nothing inconsistent in
that approach. If circumstances change, the Government will move to meet the change. We
could just as easily have left out of the Bill the figures for income limits and the proposed
maximum rebate, but that would not have been in keeping with the Government's
philosophy of open government.
Mr Prebble: Ha, ha! How can you say that?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: It is very difficult to speak over the jackasses who keep on
interrupting, but I shall endeavour to do so. Let us consider for a moment what the
maximum rebate is designed to achieve. Undoubtedly there have been some cases in which
individual rebates paid at taxpayers' expense have been excessive. My officers have quoted
to me one case of a $1,100 rebate. Cases of rebates amounting to hundreds of dollars are not
unusual.
To some degree that state of affairs has arisen because some local authorities have
deliberately ceased to encourage their ratepayers to obtain other concessions that are
available. The mayor of one major city is reported to have said recently that his council had,
to all intents and purposes, abandoned the rates postponement scheme. The rates rebate
scheme was never intended to be a substitute for rates postponement or remission of rates
when residential ratepayers are occupying land in industrial areas or when they suffer
hardship, and so on; yet that is occurring. It should not occur.
A check of 6000 rates rebate applications for last year, taken at random, revealed that
only about 1 percent of ratepayers would be affected by the proposed $200 maximum limit;
and even then the extent to which each one would be affected would vary substantially from


## p. 3590 (#70) ############################################

3590
19 September
Rates Rebate Amendment Bill
$1 to $2 to hundreds of dollars.
Admittedly, the situation can vary according to rating levels in various districts, and it is
possible to quote statistics showing different percentages for those who might be affected.
For instance, we took out another sample of 1080 applications processed during 1977-78 and
960 processed during 1978-79. In that case we restricted the sample to applications from
borough and city dwellers, where residential rates generally are higher than elsewhere. In
that sample of 2040 we found 32, or only about 1.5 percent, who had been granted refunds
exceeding $200. That sample contained examples of refunds ranging from $669 in one case in
Takapuna down to $208.
Mr Prebble: That is not in Auckland, though.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: That was in Takapuna. Is that not in Auckland? If the member for
Auckland Central would listen instead of just opening his mouth and letting something come
out he might do better. That example certainly was taken in Takapuna.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: You're rubbishing your dignity.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I am sorry, but I realise that the member for Auckland Central
upsets the member for Roskill as much as he does me. He gets under everyone's skin.
Mr Prebble: Have a drink of water.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I shall. All those people will still receive a rebate of $200, which is
surely not an insignificant sum. The proposed maximum will not affect the great majority of
eligible ratepayers. Let me repeat that it will affect only about 1 percent of those who are
entitled to a rates rebate.
Mr T. J. Young: Why should it affect that 1 percent?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: After all I have said, the member for Hutt has asked that
question. The answer is that it will do so because that 1 percent of ratepayers are getting far
more than the Government ever believed they should get. Does the member for Hutt
suggest that, under the rates rebate scheme, someone should be entitled to a rebate of
$1,080?
Mr T. J. Young: If it works out that way, yes.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Well, I don't. Let me repeat that the proposed maximum will not

The reasoning of the member for Porirua as to the effect of the $200 limit is fallible. In
the last day or two we have found cases of rates rebates amounting to over $1,600. The
member for Porirua referred to the old family home in the centre of a city. Invariably in such
a case other forms of assistance are available-rates postponement, as I mentioned earlier,
and sometimes a reduction in the rateable value may be applied. The $200 limit is based on
1977-78 figures and will be reviewed on 1 April 1979 in the light of the 1978-79 figures. No
limit applies until that date.
The member for Porirua also mentioned the desperately hard-up family who, so he said,
would obtain no rates relief. That person can and will always be able to get rates relief. He
can also obtain a rebate on what he actually has to pay. I shall set out the other means by
which a person can obtain rates relief.
The rates rebate scheme was never intended to be a substitute for but rather a
supplenient to other forms of rates relief, the first of which is a special rateable value. Under
section 25C of the Valuation of Land Act a rural or residential property which is located in an
area zoned for commercial or industrial purposes may have a special rateable value
determined on the basis that the actual use is a permitted use under the district planning
scheme. The special rateable value lowers the rateable value of the property and therefore
reduces the amount of rates to be paid. Under section 25D of the Valuation of Land Act a
special rateable value may also be placed on single-unit or double-unit dwellings in areas
where values are influenced by the demand for multi-unit housing. Any ratepayer who
comes within that category will get rates relief. He will not have to depend on a rates rebate.
Let us turn to remission of rates. Under section 114 of the Rating Act, if a local
authority is satisfied that extreme financial hardship on any individual exists or would be
caused by requirement of the whole or part of the rates, and that the circumstances giving
rise to hardship arise from accident or continued illness or other cause beyond the control of
the occupier, it may remit the whole or any part of the rates due. Any person suffering in
that way may go to his city council or county council and have all his rates, or part of those
rates, as the case may be, remitted.
We also have postponement of rates. Under section 145 of the Rating Act, if a local
authority is satisfied that hardship exists-and this is what members opposite have been
talking about—or would be caused by non-postponement of the whole or part of the rates, it
may postpone the payment of the whole or part of those rates due. Postponement may be
until the death of the occupier or until a change of occupancy or until a date specified by the
local authority. If a local authority remits part of the rates due to it, it may postpone the
balance of the rates or any part of that balance. Then we have the rates postponement value
in special cases, which I shall not go into at this stage. The point I am making here is that the
rates rebate scheme is a last resort after all other relief made available from city councils.
Members opposite have been endeavouring to suggest that the Government is taking away
something from pensioners and others on low incomes. They continue to try to make the
House and the country believe that the Government is determined to do away with the rates
rebate scheme. Nothing could be further from the truth.

entitled to a full rates rebate. Since 1 April 1978 the limit has been $4,235, plus $156 in
respect of each dependant. This limit has always included, even in the Labour Government's
time, the income of the spouse. The Bill does not alter that one iota.
I am sorry the member for New Lynn is not here because he kept repeating, "What
about the married superannuitant?" The amount a national superannuitant and his wife
would have received during the year ended 31 March 1978 is $4,235, and so no national

Once again I stress that the income limit in the Bill takes nothing away from any
sickness beneficiary, national superannuitant, or anyone else on a low income. To suggest
that it does is a pathetic and cruel attempt to hoodwink people, particularly national
superannuitants, into believing that they will lose their rates rebate. Let me once again
assure the House, particularly members opposite, that this Government keeps its promises.
Our last election manifesto said that rates concessions would continue for the same
categories of beneficiaries, using the same means test, and at the same rates as were
applicable when the National Government assumed office. We have kept that promise.
Mr Prebble: Oh, come on.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: In spite of what the member for Auckland Central says, we have
kept our promise. He has overlooked the fact that all benefits, including superannuation,
have increased substantially since we took office. The maximum limit will be adjusted from
time to time, having regard to changes in national superannuation and social welfare benefits
generally, which will increase to keep pace with the cost of living index.
The Bill states that as from 1 April next the maximum rebate which may be paid in any
individual case will be $200. This amount can and will be altered from time to time by Order
in Council. Along with the income limit, the maximum rebate figure stated in the Bill, which
is based very largely on information about last year's rates and incomes, will be reviewed in
the light of later trends before 1 April next. On 1 April next we will look at the whole
situation to see whether we should alter income limits and whether we should also extend or
increase the amount of rebate that will be available. If circumstances change, this
Government will move to meet those changes.
The member for Porirua saw something suspicious in including the figures in the Bill.
We could just as easily have left out of the Bill the figures referring to the income limit and
the proposed maximum rebate. There is nothing unusual in putting in the amount, but as I
said earlier that would not have been in keeping with the Government's philosophy of open
government. Let us consider what the maximum rebate is designed to achieve. There have
been some cases in which individual rebates paid at the taxpayers' expenses have been
excessive. I mentioned one case of $1,600 for a rebate. When he introduced his Bill, Henry
May never intended that anyone would receive a rebate beyond $1,000.
Mr T. J. Young: You should talk to him. That is not what he said.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I will make a point of talking to him before the Committee stage,
to get his confirmation. I said that in my opinion Henry May would never have thought of
anyone receiving a rebate of over $1,000. I am sure he never dreamed of it. To some
degree-and he would not have thought of this- this state of affairs has arisen because some
local authorities have deliberately ceased to encourage their ratepayers to obtain other
concessions. It is in the interests of some local bodies to let the Government pay. Some local
authorities-only a very few--are not reminding their ratepayers of other avenues which are
available to them for rates relief.
The rates rebate scheme was never intended to be a substitute for rates postponement,
or the remission of rates where residential ratepayers are occupying land in industrial areas,
or where they suffer hardship, and so on. This is occurring. It should not occur, and that is
why the Government has introduced this Bill. I repeat that a check of 6000 rates rebate
applications for last year, taken at random, revealed that only about 1 percent of ratepayers
would be affected by the proposed $200 maximum limit. In another case we restricted the
sample to applications from borough and city dwellers, where residential rates generally are
higher than elsewhere. The member for Auckland Central rightly said that a very good case
could be made for Auckland.

CO-OPERATIVE DAIRY COMPANIES AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill reviews the definition of a co-operative dairy company, amends certain
provisions relating to the Co-operative Dairy Companies Tribunal, and increases the fines
payable in respect of offences under the Co-operative Dairy Companies Act 1949.
Clause 2 extends the definition of co-operative dairy company to include a company that
sells to another co-operative dairy company or to the New Zealand Dairy Board the milk,
cream, or butterfat supplied to the company by its shareholders. The clause makes it clear
that a co-operative dairy company may carry on its business through the agency of another
co-operative dairy company. These amendments arise from the decision last year of the Co-
operative Dairy Companies Tribunal that a company had ceased to be a co-operative dairy
company because it did not operate a dairy factory, but, instead, had its shareholders' milk
processed and marketed by another co-operative dairy company. I am circulating a
Supplementary Order Paper to provide that the Companies Act 1955 referred to will also
have added after it, "or under any former Companies Act".


## p. 3606 (#86) ############################################

3606
Co-operative Dairy Companies Amendment Bill 19 September
In clause 3 we provide that the Co-operative Dairy Companies Tribunal can hear
submissions from a wider class of persons when deciding whether a company has ceased to
be a co-operative dairy company. We make it clear that, when the tribunal makes a decision
adverse to the company, the duty of the Registrar of Companies to cancel the company's
registration as a co-operative dairy company would depend on the determination of any
appeal against the decision.
Clause 4 inserts in the Co-operative Dairy Companies Act 1949, without amendment, a
provision in the Finance Act (No. 3) 1944 allowing the Minister of Finance to subscribe for
shares in a co-operative dairy company. I understand that this power has not been exercised,
and this amendment is made merely to repeal an old Finance Act provision.
Penalties under the Act are increased by clauses 5 and 6. The penalty for the offence of
failing to comply with a direction of the Registrar of Companies to a company to change its
name when it is no longer entitled to remain registered as a co-operative dairy company is
increased from $20 a day to $50 a day. Similarly, the penalty for breaching the restrictions on
the extent to which shares in a co-operative dairy company may be surrendered is increased
from $100 a share to $200 a share.
Clause 7 increases the membership of the Co-operative Dairy Companies Tribunal from
three to five by increasing from one to two in each case the members to be appointed on the
nomination of the Minister of Agriculture and the New Zealand Dairy Board. As a result of
the increase in membership of the tribunal, clause 8 provides for a quorum of three,
including the chairman and one of the members nominated by the New Zealand Dairy
Board. The clause also provides for the Commissions of Inquiry Act 1908 to apply to any
referral by the Registrar of Companies to the tribunal of grounds for believing that a
company has ceased to be a co-operative dairy company.
Under clause 9 the tribunal is empowered to state a case for the opinion of the Supreme
Court. Clause 10 widens the grounds for an appeal against a decision of the tribunal, from
lack of jurisdiction to error of law, and, in respect of any subsisting appeal not yet heard,
provides that the appeal may be heard on the ground of error of law. Clause 11 reviews the
penalties that may be prescribed in regulations for offences against such regulations; and, in
the Supplementary Order Paper I have already referred to, I propose that the sentence of
imprisonment provided should be omitted.
In the preparation of the Bill the New Zealand Dairy Board has been consulted, as I
indicated to the House on the introduction of the Bill; and the board has now considered the
terms of the Bill and, through its Chairman, Mr Friis, has expressed to me its agreement with
the Bill. I commend the Bill to the House.
Mr BELL (Gisborne): I support the Bill, particularly on behalf of the Gisborne Co-
operative Dairy Company. Problems faced by that company before the introduction of this
amending legislation played an important part in the preparation of the Bill. The company
was faced with a problem in that suppliers, because of the fertility of the land and the
alternative uses it could be put to, changed their land use from dairying to horticulture and
cash cropping. The dairy farmers remaining were producing whole milk for Gisborne Milk
Industries Ltd., a company supplying whole milk for Gisborne and Wairoa, and surrounding
townships. The dairy company was not a manufacturer. Its suppliers supplied milk to the
Opotiki Dairy Company, which is a co-operative dairy company. It does not make butter.
Under the previous legislation the company could not be classed as a co-operative dairy
company.
The tribunal's decision referred to by the Minister was about the Gisborne Dairy
Company. The tribunal found that, under the legislation, the company could not appeal to
the Supreme Court, and the company sought amending legislation on behalf of the few
suppliers still producing milk for dairy production rather than whole milk. Whole milk
suppliers have seasonal surpluses for butter, cheese, or casein making. They sought
protection through the amendment.
I have discussed the Bill with the spokesman for the Gisborne Co-operative Dairy
Company, who supports it. Clause 2 provides that a company may remain in being as a co-
operative dairy company while it sells the suppliers' milk to another company. That clause
will adequately solve the problems of the Gisborne Co-operative Dairy Company. The
company is very pleased with clauses 9 and 10, which give it the opportunity to appeal on
matters of law and not just on the grounds of lack of jurisdiction on any adverse decision
made by the tribunal. I strongly support the Bill. It will solve the problems of my
constituents and the dairy company. I trust that the House will support the legislation

Department of Social Welfare
Social Welfare, $86,170,000.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) said the vote revealed the Government's
pathetic approach to social welfare. Under the National Government expenditure had
rocketed to $1,800 million. Means-tested beneficiaries and national superannuitants would
receive further increases in January and February. The increased staff had dealt with
unemployment-which the country could do without-rather than with social problems, for
which they were needed. Partly as a result of the vote, the department was employing 280
people to pay people to do nothing. It was evident to all but the Government that its policy
of promoting unemployment had had a multiplier effect. If more people were deprived of
their jobs, more administrators would have to be employed by the Department of Social
Welfare.
The vote provided another $11 million for unemployment benefits, in addition to the
$45 million provided in the main estimates, making a total of $56 million, with another $100
million for employment promotion and $5 million for domestic purposes benefits. That
revealed that the Government was placing an unnecessary burden on the Social Welfare
vote. If the Government had followed sound economic and social policies, much additional
expenditure would have been avoided. A prominent National Party spokesman had called
social welfare "applied lunacy". There could be no greater applied lunacy than to follow a
policy that precipitated unemployment and then called on the taxpayer to pay people for
doing nothing. The only way New Zealand could overcome its economic problems was by
increasing output and economic performance. Although the National Government had left
the impression that it would reduce the payout to solo mothers, the supplementary estimates
had provided nearly three times the amount that had been provided by the Labour
Government.

precluded the hassle of going through the courts had been entered into.

Welfare, and if they proved satisfactory they were given full-time jobs when vacancies
occurred. The total vote of $86 million included $2.5 million for family benefit capitalisation,
allowance for increases in income-tested benefits in line with the consumer price index, and
increases in national superannuation in line with the average ordinary-time wage as surveyed
by the Department of Labour.

Standing Order 47(2), which is becoming well known to honourable members, states: “If

p.m. Those hours are set down in Standing Order 39, and have come and gone. If no other
arrangements are made by the Leader of the House, broadcasting will take place only on
Tuesday, the sitting day.

Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): We have asked you to come back, Mr Acting

It is not now midnight on Tuesday, 19 September. That is not the official parliamentary
time, because the Clerk of the House would have to record the time of an amendment, and
he cannot pretend the time of that amendment. If he put in a fictitious time the amendment
would be wrong, because the member who moved it might not, under that time, have been in

regret to say--and I can understand his position; I would have been in a similar position had

I bring you back to Standing Order 49, which is the Standing Order that your authority
requires you to uphold. Nobody individually, or even a majority of members, has a right in a
parliamentary democracy to bend the Standing Orders. Their interpretation, of course, is
your responsibility. That Standing Order is quite clear. It states that the proceedings of
Parliament shall be broadcast during the hours of sitting prescribed by Standing Order 39.
The extension beyond that is at the will of the Leader of the House, but all hours of sitting
are prescribed by Standing Order 39.
I then refer you to Standing Order 39, which states that, unless otherwise ordered, the
House shall meet at 2.30 p.m. on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. We are either in
Tuesday or Wednesday; we are certainly not yet in Thursday. However, we are in the
normal sitting hours of the House as described by Standing Order 39.
Standing Order 49 prescribes the broadcasting hours. The two questions-whether it is
Tuesday or whether it is Wednesday-are totally reconciled, and one would need the
imagination of an odd Minister or two whom I know to decide anything other than that this is
the time when Parliament should be broadcast. I do not consider there is any way out of it,
and the public will not be able to see any way out of it. The Standing Orders require you, Sir,
to decide, not the whim of the majority. Until that majority changes the Standing Order or
sets it aside, in my view you must rule in that way.
During the discussion in the Committee of the Whole, the Chairman referred to
Standing Order 47(2), which states: "If urgency be so accorded any such Bill, matter, or
other proceeding may be proceeded with, and proceedings thereon completed at the same
sitting of the House, notwithstanding any Standing Order or rule of the House to the
contrary; and any time fixed by the Standing Orders or by any other order of the House for
the conclusion of the sitting then in progress shall (where necessary) be deemed to have been
extended accordingly."
There is nothing wrong with that, but nowhere does it state that, when we reach a
normal broadcasting time as set out in Standing Order 49, and as provided for in Standing
Order 39, any individual or group of individuals in the House can deny to the House and to
our masters the capacity to hear what is happening in their Parliament. If that is not so, Sir,
and if you rule against that, we are in a position of great difficulty in taking representations
from, and replying to representations by the people we represent. They will consider it a
serious erosion of a long-held right of every New Zealander to hear what is happening in
Parliament during those hours. Although it may be inconvenient for members to have their
position revealed, the reason for the broadcasting of the proceedings of the House is that it is
an open democracy, and not operated as some facade to suit some other philosophy.
I do not want to go any further. To the best of my memory over the past 20 years, it is
clear that the normal sitting hours, regardless of what day it is considered to be in the House,
have always been broadcast; the normal sitting hours as provided in Standing Order 39 have

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The argument of the member for
Roskill contains fallacies that I must draw to your attention, Mr Acting Speaker. The House
is now sitting under urgency as provided for in Standing Order 47, and Standing Order 47(2)
is relevant to the matter you are being asked to rule on, but I do not want to begin there. I
want to begin with Standing Order 49, which states: "Proceedings of Parliament shall be
broadcast during all hours of sitting prescribed by Standing Order 39 and during such other
periods as may be determined by the Leader of the House." That means we have to look at
Standing Order 39, because it will be during the hours of sitting prescribed therein.
The member for Roskill did not point out to you, Sir, that Standing Order 39 is not
definitive on the hours of meeting, because it states: "Unless otherwise ordered, and subject
to the provisions hereinafter contained, the House shall meet at 2.30 p.m. on Tuesday,
Wednesday, and Thursday, and shall (unless previously adjourned) continue to sit until 5.30
p.m. when Mr Speaker or the Chairman of Committees shall interrupt the business then
proceeding and the sitting shall be suspended until 7.30 p.m., and the House shall (unless
previously adjourned) then continue to sit until 10.30 p.m. and no longer."
I emphasise that that applies only "unless otherwise ordered". In fact, the House has
otherwise ordered. It did so when it gave urgency last night to the consideration of the
supplementary estimates. It is traditional for urgency to be given to allow the Opposition,
the minority, more time than usual in the sitting hours of the House to examine the
estimates. Usually the consideration of the supplementary estimates takes about 5 or 6
hours. We are in the position we are now because the Opposition wanted to take more time
to discuss the supplementary estimates, and more time has been granted.
Therefore we must abide by Standing Order 47 on urgency, which indicates what
happens when that qualifying clause at the beginning of Standing Order 39—“unless
otherwise ordered"-applies. Standing Order 47(2) states: "If urgency be so accorded any
such Bill, matter, or other proceeding may be proceeded with, and proceedings thereon
completed at the same sitting of the House, notwithstanding any Standing Order or rule of
the House to the contrary." In other words, Standing Order 47(2) specifically states
"Notwithstanding any Standing Order or rule of the House to the contrary; and any time
fixed by the Standing Orders or by any other order of the House”—and obviously in this case
it refers to Standing Order 39-"for the conclusion of the sitting then in progress shall
(where necessary) be deemed to be extended accordingly." The words in brackets, "(where
necessary)", mean when the House sits beyond the normal time of 10.30 p.m.
We are still sitting under the order of urgency given on Tuesday, 19 September, and we
are meeting to consider the supplementary estimates. Because Opposition members have
wanted additional time to discuss them, we are still sitting. I suppose that if we had a clock
that was not divided into 12 hours but into an unlimited number of hours, we could say that
we are now sitting on Tuesday at 39.13 hours, to allow Opposition members to take all the
time they want to examine the supplementary estimates.
The point has already been ruled on by Mr Speaker, and I am certain that it was ruled
on in a similar way by the Speaker of the former Labour Government, which used to apply
the same sort of rules to the National Party when it was in Opposition. At that time the
Labour Government did not broadcast the proceedings of the House in similar
circumstances. Everyone in New Zealand knows that this happens. We have to take urgency
when one Order of the Day has to be completed before the House rises. That is really the
reason for taking urgency; we must have time to consider the Order of the Day, and it must
be completed that day. Undoubtedly the people expect Parliament to get on with its business
and get it done, and the Standing Orders provide for that.
