PENAL INSTITUTIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Pre-release hostels play an important function in bridging the inevitable gap
between the regimented life in a penal institution on the one hand and the normal freedoms
of our society on the other. The Bill makes proper provision for pre-release hostels by
establishing them as separate entities from prisons. Hostels are now either part of a prison or
separate prisons in themselves. Given the nature of these hostels, as I outlined it when
introducing the Bill, it is now inappropriate for all the rules and regulations applicable to
prisons to apply to the hostels. Accordingly, the Bill provides for rules and regulations that
are appropriate to pre-release hostels, while recognising that hostel residents are
nevertheless still subject to sentences of imprisonment.
Clause 1 provides in effect for the Act to come into force upon a date to be appointed by
the Governor-General by Order in Council. I expect that this will be early next year, once
the necessary accompanying regulations have been prepared. As borstal training has yet to
be abolished and the new sentences of corrective training implemented, clause 1 also
provides for the necessary consequential amendments when this changeover occurs.
Clauses 3, 4, 5, and 6 are basically machinery provisions providing for the establishment
and staffing of these hostels. Clauses 7, 8, 9, and 10 provide for the transfer of inmates from
prisons, borstals, and corrective training institutions to hostels of the appropriate type. For
example, a borstal trainee can be transferred only to a borstal pre-release hostel, and a
prison inmate must go to a prison pre-release hostel. The general thrust of these clauses is
that the inmate would be transferred to a hostel catering specifically for inmates from his
type of institution. The only exception to this rule is that female inmates may be transferred
to a hostel of any type. This is necessary to ensure that hostels for females can be
maintained. The small number of female inmates means that it is impractical to maintain
separate hostels for adult and youthful offenders.
Before an inmate is eligible for transfer to a hostel he must have been approved by the
Release to Work Committee, and the Secretary for Justice must have given a direction,
under the principal Act, for release to work. The transfer of an inmate is a matter for
agreement between the hostel warden and the prison superintendent. This, however, is
subject to the control of the secretary, who may direct that a certain inmate or certain type of
offender is not eligible for transfer to a hostel.
Clauses 11, 12, 13, and 14 deal with the transfer of a hostel resident back to a penal
institution. Clause 11 permits such a transfer at the request of the resident, and requires the
resident to be transferred if his release to work direction has been revoked by the secretary.
In such cases the resident will be transferred to an institution similar to that from which he
was originally transferred to the hostel. Under subclause (3) of clause 11, the secretary, is
required to direct the return of a resident to prison if the resident becomes a risk to the


## p. 3641 (#121) ###########################################

20 September
3641
Penal Institutions Amendment Bill
community at large or to the safety of the staff or other residents of the hostel. A hostel
resident transferred under this provision will go to the nearest penal institution of whatever
kind and be returned to the appropriate institution by the prison service.
Subclauses (4) and (5) of clause 11 permit the return of a hostel resident to prison if he
has escaped or refused to work. Such a resident will be transferred to an institution similar to
that from which he was originally transferred to the hostel. Clause 12 provides for the
temporary transfer of the hostel resident in the event of his incapacity or inability to get
work. In those circumstances, the resident will be transferred to the nearest penal institution
and may be returned to the hostel once he has recovered or work is available.
Clause 13 allows the transfer of residents during the temporary closure of the hostel.
That is to enable a hostel to be closed for the Christmas holidays. Residents would be
transferred to another hostel or to the nearest prison while the hostel was closed. The
machinery provisions for the actual transfer of residents in the situations I have outlined are
set out in clause 14. Clause 15 deals with the effect of the imposition of any further sentences
upon the offender's residence in a pre-release hostel. If a resident commits an offence after
his transfer to the hostel and receives a further custodial sentence he will automatically be
returned to prison. If an offence has been committed before the offender's transfer to a
hostel, he will, generally speaking, continue to be detained in the hostel if his current term is
not extended by the new sentence. If his current term is extended he will be returned to
prison.
Clause 16 provides for hostel residents to be in the legal custody of the warden. The
clause also provides that a resident who is absent from the hostel with the warden's
permission for no longer than 30 minutes at any one time shall continue to be in the warden's
custody. That will allow residents to go to the corner dairy or nearest phone box, for
example, without the necessity of being formally granted parole for such a trivial purpose.
Clause 17 authorises the temporary release of residents from custody for such things as
home leave, and reflects to some extent the current provision in the principal Act. Under
that clause wardens will be entitled to fix the actual period of release within the criteria set
out by myself as Minister. Because of the nature of the hostels, I shall be setting more
generous guidelines for hostels than those currently prevailing for prisons. In addition,
clause 17 provides for the automatic suspension of parole privileges for a week when the
warden is satisfied that the resident failed, without reasonable excuse, to return by the
specified time or was at any place other than that approved by the warden. There is a right of
appeal to a visiting justice against such a suspension.
Clauses 18 and 19 are disciplinary provisions specifying offences and the manner of
dealing with them. All breaches of discipline will be dealt with by a visiting justice appointed
under the principal Act. If a disciplinary charge is proved, the visiting justice may, in effect,
prohibit release on parole for up to 14 days, dock up to 14 days' remission, or order the
return of the resident to prison. Clause 20 and the schedule to the Act apply the appropriate
provisions of the principal Act to pre-release hostels with the necessary modifications, and
clause 21 makes the usual provision for making appropriate regulations.
Clause 22 relates to borstal trainees and removes the current power of a superintendent
of a borstal institution to revoke release to work directions in respect of borstal trainees
transferred to pre-release hostels. In such cases the exercise of that power is restricted to the
Secretary for Justice, as a borstal superintendent will no longer have any legal control over
trainees in hostels. Provision is made in clause 23 for the repeal of the provisions in the Bill
relating to borstal training once borstal training is abolished and corrective training is
brought into force.
Clause 24 is an amendment to the principal Act designed to clarify doubts about the
position of inmates transferred for treatment for psychiatric or alcoholic problems, in respect
of their eligibility for remission. The clause makes it quite clear that such inmates will still be
eligible for remission, notwithstanding their transfer. A minor amendment to the provisions
relating to compensation for property damage caused by escaping inmates is proposed in
clause 25. At present compensation claims may be dealt with only by magistrates' courts
designated for the purpose. The clause allows these claims to be dealt with by any
magistrate's court exercising civil jurisdiction.
When I introduced the Bill I undertook to send copies to all those who made
submissions on the Penal Institutions Amendment Act 1975. That has been done, and to
date a number of submissions have been received by the legislation committee of the New
Zealand Law Society and from the Prisoners Aid and Rehabilitation Society. Basically,


## p. 3642 (#122) ###########################################

3642
20 September
Penal Institutions Amendment Bill
there was no objection to the present Bill, which, after all, is primarily a machinery measure.
Some matters of principle were raised, but these relate to the policy contained in the
principal Act, not the proposed amendment, and will be looked at when the principal Act is
reviewed. I commend the Bill to the House.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): The Opposition welcomes the Bill, in broad terms, and would
not detract from that. Of course, not having seen the submissions from the societies to which
the Minister referred, I do not know the matter of principle that was raised in relation to the
Act to which he referred.
Hon. David Thomson: There was no objection to the Bill.
Mr LANGE: I raise with the Minister and the House the issue as to whether the Bill, the
intention of which is excellent in the sense that it tries to grapple with the standing of pre-
release hostels, is perhaps thwarted a little by the fact that a person must be in a prison
before he can be transferred to what is called a pre-release hostel. The Criminal Justice Act
provides for pre-release hostels, and the wording of that Act does not preclude the
possibility of a person, on being sentenced to imprisonment, being directed to serve out that
term in a hostel while continuing to work and not therefore being a charge on the taxpayer.
The Bill precludes the possibility of that becoming the practice, as it could have been, under
the administrative direction of the Department of Justice. The Bill states that a person must
come from a prison, a borstal, a corrective youth centre, or a youth prison before he can be a
resident in a pre-release hostel. This is unfortunate, and I look to the Minister, in
promulgating the sort of regulations that will be effective in pre-release hostels, to ensure
also that the policy of the penal service will allow for people who have been sentenced to
short terms of imprisonment to be moved as swiftly as possible from total incarceration to
that form of residence where they can actually earn money and carry on their work, so that
they will not necessarily lose their employment and their families will not become a total
charge on the State.
Ambiguity appears in clause 24. It is quite clear that a person who is serving a sentence
of imprisonment may be remanded to a psychiatric hospital pursuant to section 42 of the
Mental Health Act or subject to some of the provisions of the Alcoholism and Drug
Addiction Act 1966. Is it the Government's intention that those persons, while there, should
be deemed to be in the custody of the warden of the pre-release hostel from whence they
came? If that is the intention, it is inconsistent with the provisions of the Criminal Justice Act
whereby, pursuant to the terms of section 47 of that Act, persons are deemed to be in the
custody of the superintendent of the penal institution notwithstanding their physical
presence in a psychiatric hospital or other unit for the purposes of section 47A of the Mental
Health Act. It becomes a matter of some importance for people who live close to psychiatric
hospitals because, if those persons are deemed to be in the care of the superintendent of the
psychiatric hospital only, the occupants of houses adjoining psychiatric hospitals will not
have the benefit of compensation if damage is done to their property by escapees who are
considered to be inmates under the Penal Institutions Act. Before this matter comes to the
Committee stage I should like the Minister to consider whether it might be appropriate to
examine the position, and, if necessary, bring in a Supplementary Order Paper to deal with
it. I am sure the Department of Justice does not intend that it should escape liability for
damage done by escaping inmates merely because they happen to be in the physical care of
the superintendent of a psychiatric hospital. It is quite clear that the Bill deems that those
persons will be serving terms of imprisonment while they are under therapeutic care. If that
be so, and if remission can be allowed for the period that they are there, I ask the Minister to
clarify the situation.
The third matter is simple and relates to the fact that 3 years after the passing of the
Criminal Justice Amendment Act 1975, borstal sentences have still not been phased out and
corrective youth sentences have not been introduced. This matter has been of concern to the
Government, which has, I know, been concerned to see that the provisions of the 1975
amendment Act should be made to work. I appreciate also that there has been difficulty in
the provision of buildings. I am told that the stage is fast approaching when it will be possible
to use one such establishment. I should like the Minister to tell the House when it will be
likely that we will not need to make provision for four types of pre-release hostels. The Bill
does that, and I look to the day when there will be a prison pre-release hostel, a youth prison
pre-release hostel, and a corrective training pre-release hostel with a fourth arm of pre-
release hostel-a hostel that is not in fact pre-release, but a place to which a person on being
sentenced to imprisonment is directed so that during the period of the sentence he or she


## p. 3643 (#123) ###########################################

20 September
3643
Penal Institutions Amendment Bill
may be subject to restraint on his or her liberty or leisure, but may none the less remain
profitable members of the community, socially and economically.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I thank the member for Mangere for his
general support of the Bill. I shall deal with the points he raised in reverse order. He asked
when the 1975 Act, which was supported by both sides, will become effective. That will be
when the buildings are ready. That is the problem. The member might know that work on
the Manawatu youth prison is proceeding in quite good time, and that construction of the
institution inland from Rangipo was completed some time ago. We ran into problems at
Otatara in Southland, and I have been very much obliged to the member for Awarua for his
great assistance in sorting out the problems there. Rearrangements are to be made in other
institutions in the South Island. The problem is totally irrelevant to the building programme.
It has not arisen because of lack of money, but because of other problems. I hope that the
1975 Act will be brought into force next year, and that corrective training will take over from
the detention and borstal system.
The next question the member raised related to clause 24, which deals with release after
serving part of a sentence. I am sure the member will appreciate that the express purpose of
this amendment is to make sure that the inmate does not lose remission. Clause 25 deals with
compensation for property damage by escapers, but, before the Committee stage, I will
certainly look into the matter raised by the member and satisfy myself that everything is
shipshape in that area.
Pre-release hostels have been very close to my heart, and were, I believe, instituted by
me. I have always referred to those establishments as halfway houses, which is perhaps not a
good name, because other people call other places halfway houses. The Bill provides for the
court to administer a type of custodial sentence to those who need not, for the sake of
society, be isolated entirely and locked away in a medium or top security prison. They will be
able to continue at their ordinary occupation within the community, maintain their families,
pay their fines, pay board to the institution, and live a disciplined life when not at work.
That, together with the discipline of work, will mean that they will be in a disciplined
environment for 24 hours a day. Wrongdoers who are sent to prison do not have much
difficulty adapting to that life, because they do nothing but obey orders, and accept no
responsibility. They face the greatest difficulty when they return to the "jungle of
temptation". This is being worked on by the Department of Justice, and I hope I shall be
able to establish a pilot scheme, which would give the courts the option of dealing with young
offenders in this manner, and which would be developed along the lines of the development
of periodic detention centres.
Bill read a second time.
The House adjourned at 11.53 p.m.

Food Price Increases
4. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: In view of
Government claims that the rate of price increases for food is slowing, how does he, as
Minister in charge of price control, adjust this to the fact that in the week ended 25 August
there were 49 grocery price increases, that in the week ended 1 September there were 85
grocery price increases, and that in the week ended 8 September there were 161 grocery
price increases?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The rate of price
increases as measured by the consumer price index is on a statistically sound basis and
reflects the extent of price increases as well as the quantity of each item typically purchased
by consumers. The number of price increases during particular weeks is not in itself of
statistical significance, particularly bearing in mind that in many instances two or more sizes
of the same product have been included in the number of price increases quoted.
Hon. W. W. Freer: How can the Minister reconcile his answer in view of the fact that
the latest week's figures show an increase in price to 187 items, a large number of which have
increased individually by 20c each?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The statement I made can be reconciled by the fact
that economic statistics are produced by the Government Statistician, and his statistics have
been accepted by members of both sides of the House, by successive Governments, by
economists, and by other people over the years. An illustration of that is that the food price
index has dropped by half, from 18.3 percent to 9.1 percent in the past year, and the
consumer price index is running at single figure rates for the first 6 months this year,
compared with 15.7 percent under the last Labour Government.

Electoral Office-State Services Commission Responsibility

departmental operations rests with permanent heads. Section 25 of the Act, and regulation
64 of the Public Service Regulations 1964, give emphasis to this point. The commission has a
supportive and reviewing role. The commission has been closely associated with the
Department of Justice during the preparation of the electoral rolls. It appreciates the special
problems encountered in having them prepared centrally for the first time, and has readily
agreed to additional staff when the need has been apparent. Its computer services division
has participated in the development of the system in use, and is very familiar with all aspects
of the process. The commission is satisfied that the department is taking all proper steps to
ensure that the rolls will be in as complete a state as is normally achieved by election date.

Balance of Payments Deficit
9. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) to the Minister of Statistics: What percentage
of gross national product did the balance of payments deficit represent as at 31 March 1973,
1974, 1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): New Zealand had a surplus on
current account for the 1972-73 year of 2.2 percent of gross national product. Thereafter it
faced deficits. The deficit in 1973-74 was 1.3 percent; in 1974-75, 14.5 percent, in 1975-76,
9.3 percent; in 1976-77, 7 percent, and in 1977-78, 5.7 percent. These percentages are based
on the official national income and expenditure aggregates, except for the 1978 year
percentage, which uses estimates prepared by the New Zealand Institute of Economic
Research.

indicates a reduction of approximately two-thirds since the Labour Government was in
power?

statement of fact on the evidence given.
Natural Gas
10. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Is it correct, as asserted
by the energy reporter of the New Zealand Herald in that newspaper on 7 September 1978,
that "the New Zealand taxpayer will have to foot a bill of millions of dollars for massive
quantities of natural gas left in the ground through cancellation of thermal power station
projects"?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): No. Any need to advance money to meet the
take-or-pay is not money wasted. It is merely a question of pre-paying for the gas, and this
can be drawn, without further payment, at any time during the 30-year period of the
contract. Where any money required to meet any shortfall in the early years of the take-or-
pay might come from would not be decided until the need to make such an advance was
established. The recent decision to provide for Maui gas to make ammonia-urea and liquid
fuels will lessen and may even eliminate the deficit in take-or-pay.
Hon. F. M. Colman: What is the gap between the contracted arrangements made with
the consortium and the arrangements for the industries that the Minister mentioned, and
how will the cost of any delay in setting up those industries affect the taxpayer?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The inference in the question is that the taxpayer must meet the
deficit. There are other ways in which this could, if necessary, be financed. I am not in a
position to give specific figures for the years ahead until some of the planning for the
ammonia-urea timetable and the methanol timetable is a little more definite. A deficit is
possible in the first few years, but, until the platform is built, the take-or-pay quantities are
very much smaller than the substantial take-or-pay plateau quantities that would be available
from the late 1980s onwards.

Deer Farming-Yersinia
23. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Health: Is the diagnosis of yersinia,
an infection contracted from deer, likely to create any difficulty for the deer-farming
industry?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Yersiniosis, which can be caused by Yersinia
pseudotuberculosis, is primarily a zoonotic disease of wild and domesticated birds and
mammals, with man as an accidental host. It occurs throughout the world and is not
associated with any particular species of animal. There is, therefore, no special danger to
those engaged in deer farming. However, it may be that deer in poor condition and confined
on farms in large numbers may give rise to some increase in the incidence of this disease, but
the likelihood of this is directly related to the hygiene of the farm and its operators.
Infant Mortality Rate
24. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Health: What was the recorded
infant mortality rate for 1976-the latest year for which data are available--and how does
this compare with other comparable countries?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): New Zealand's infant death rate for 1976 was
14.0 per 1000 live births. This is the lowest ever recorded in New Zealand. By way of
comparison, the latest available rates for some other countries against which New Zealand
customarily measures its performance were: Sweden (1975), 8.3; Finland (1974), 10.3;
Norway (1974), 10.5; Denmark (1974), 10.7; New Zealand comes in here at 14.0; Canada
(1974), 15.0; England and Wales (1975), 16.0; and Australia (1974), 16.1.

Electoral Enrolment Cards—Porirua
Dr WALL (Porirua) to the Minister of Justice: Is he aware that the officer reputed to act
for the electorate officer in the Porirua Post Office refused to give enrolment cards to a
Labour Party official when she requested those cards for the purpose of canvassing for
enrolments, and, if he is aware, would he inform the House if this action is in accordance
with Government policy, and, if not, what does he intend to do about it?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Justice.
"A refusal to provide electoral enrolment cards in response to a bona fide and reasonable
request, as for instance by an official of a political party, is certainly not part of the
Government's policy, nor of the practice of the electoral office. In the incident referred to by
the honourable member a request was made to a staff member at the Porirua Post Office, at
a time when the electorate officer was not present, for a bulk supply of enrolment cards. The
person seeking the bulk supply, I am informed, gave no indication of her association with a
political party, and the request was wrongly declined on the basis that it could have resulted
in adding to the number of duplicate applications for enrolment that had to be processed.
The electorate officer has been instructed that this policy is not to be followed, and that any
person requiring supplies of cards should be issued with them.”

LOCAL AUTHORITIES LOANS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Local
Authorities Loans Amendment Bill. The Bill is very important, because it embraces some
important democratic principles. One purpose is to widen the franchise of those eligible to
demand a poll on a local body loan. The second purpose is to widen the voting rights of those
eligible to vote in a poll to raise a local authority loan. The third purpose is to change the
number of people who can successfully demand a poll on a local body loan back to 5 percent
of those qualifying. The fourth purpose is to establish a reasonable time in which people can
organise a demand for a poll, recognising that the greater the number of people involved the
longer it takes to get the required number of signatures.


## p. 3661 (#141) ###########################################

21 September
3661
Local Authorities Loans Amendment Bill
The Bill tidies up and clearly defines the particulars required of people when they
petition to demand a poll on a local authority loan, and also requires the Wellington City
Council to conduct a poll in respect of the proposal to raise the Town Hall Construction
Loan 1978 of $5 million.
The principle behind the Bill is important. It involves the strengthening of participatory
democracy. The ideal motivating the Bill is that decision making should not be further
removed than is necessary from people involved and affected by that decision. Nowhere
does this apply to a greater degree at present than in local authority affairs, in which a
decision to raise a loan has an immediate effect on the burden of rates, that eventually every
resident must pay in one form or another.
The question of whether the people of Wellington want a town hall is not for me to say.
What is relevant to me, because it affects all regional and local authority amenities built with
loan money, is that people must have a say in whether or not they will pay an outrageous
amount of money for a regional or local amenity. The Bill provides that all affected do and
will have a say. I suspect that the Wellington Town Hall loan could become the issue that
symbolises the great injustice being done at present, because of the way in which all local
authorities are required to finance their loans. The burden of high interest as it moves into
rate costs affects everyone.
Let us take the Wellington Town Hall loan as an example. The amount of money
needed to get the project under way is $5 million. If the loan is for 35 years at 10.5 percent
per annum, the interest charges alone will be 367.5 percent of the principal, which, with its
repayment, will be 467.5 percent of the $5 million needed. Present financial policy will
require the people of Wellington to repay over $23 million for the $5 million loan.
One purpose of the Bill is to ensure that all those affected by the Wellington Town Hall
loan have a say as to whether or not they are prepared to accept the injustice of an additional
burden on their rates.
It is my belief that the Wellington Town Hall loan could well become an issue that will
be a significant part of the rate revolt that is now evident in Auckland. People should have a
say as to whether they are prepared to continue to tolerate a situation where $5 million of the
cost of the town hall, which is funded by loan, is paid to those actually doing the job, whilst
more than $18 million is paid to moneylenders and others who provide the loan money, in
addition to getting their money back.
Clause 3 repeals the existing section 34 and substitutes new sections 34 to 34H. The
existing section 34 makes no provision for full names, addresses, or other particulars of
persons making demands for a poll to be given. The Bill specifies particulars that should be
stated in demands or in communications accompanying them, but does not invalidate a
demand that is without such particulars. However, for all cases in which particulars are given
the Bill provides for the enrolment of electors who are not already on the appropriate
electoral rolls, and for the amendment of such rolls if any particulars supplied are different
from those that appear on the rolls in respect of electors already enrolled. Those who
become enrolled under this requirement are to be counted among the numbers making the
demands and the numbers on the rolls for the purpose of ascertaining whether a sufficient
proportion of electors has demanded a poll.
The Bill provides for a scrutiny of demands and enrolments, as well as prescribing
phases in the scrutiny. Any 10 or more electors are given the right to appoint scrutineers for
the scrutiny. The principal Act at present contains no provisions on these matters. Those
making demands have no rights to ensure that the checking is accurately done. While this is a
serious deficiency in the present Act, the complete integrity of those who made the check in
the recent Wellington City case is accepted without question.
If experience is any guide, the procedures outlined in the Bill for local and regional
authorities could become a model for cleaning up the main electoral rolls. The necessity for
clean rolls is fundamental to a healthy democracy, and I await with some interest the
comments of the Labour Party on the proposal, because I share with it concern about
present problems involving the right to vote. I am particularly interested in the Bill that
stands in the name of the member for Porirua.
The new section 34F requires that 5 percent of qualified electors can succeed in
demanding a poll, which would take us back to the position before the 15 percent
amendment of 1976. Clause 5 of the Bill outlines the problems arising from the Wellington
Town Hall construction loan 1978. In that case the demand for a poll allowed only 25 days
for the organising of the required number of signatures--and who fixed that number of days


## p. 3662 (#142) ###########################################

3662
21 September
Local Authorities Loans Amendment Bill
still remains a mystery. Clause 3 amends the principal Act and corrects this rather
unreasonable time, bearing in mind the number of people in the district involved.
A further unsatisfactory feature of the Wellington Town Hall issue was that by one
calculation 12.75 percent of ratepayers were eligible to demand a poll, whereas by another
calculation only 10.36 percent qualified. This difficulty in interpreting eligibility is obviated
under clause 3 of the Bill, containing new sections 34B and 34F, because all residents will
become eligible.
The practice of treating only one co-owner of a property as a ratepayer is yet another
unsatisfactory feature at present. The law has been applied so that the first name registered
as the joint owner of a family home is the only one that qualifies as a ratepayer. In most cases
it is the husband, and the wife is disfranchised, which amounts to sex discrimination. The
position concerns me, because the problem of rising rates probably affects women more than
men, as women have to manage home finances. The same problem arises with owners of
flats and other premises under a company system. I do not accept that all residents do not
eventually have to pay their share of rising rates, but co-owners should have an equal
franchise with present ratepayers, because, in reality, they pay rates directly, even if through
a company.
In proposing that the Bill be introduced I reiterate that fundamental principles of both
democracy and economic justice are involved. The Wellington Town Hall loan issue is a
symbolic one, and has underlined many existing problems. The Bill is intended to correct
most of them, and I believe it would. It will apply to other local authorities throughout the
country as well, and for that reason I commend it to the House.

Let us have a look at the position relating to eligibility to sign valid demands for loan
polls as provided in the Local Authorities Loans Act. The eligibility to vote in such polls also
is clear. The Local Authorities Loans Act provides that a valid demand for a poll requires
the signature of 15 percent of the ratepayers on the ratepayers' roll. This is interpreted as
meaning in effect 15 percent of the names on the valuation roll or rate records, including the
names of joint occupiers or owners where these are shown.
Voting eligibility, however, is determined under the Local Government Act 1974, and
in section 110 of the Local Election and Polls Act 1976. The practical effect of the latter
section is that only one person can exercise a ratepayer's vote in any election or poll in
respect of any one property. That person is the nominee of company, partners, or joint
owners, as the case may be, or, if there is no nominee, the person whose name appears first
on the roll in respect of that property. The number who may vote in a loan poll will therefore
invariably be less than the number who can validly sign a statutory demand for a loan poll.

If one includes all who are potentially financially disadvantaged by a loan proposal, one
must include not just ratepayers, but anyone who is to receive any benefit from the facilities
provided by the local body concerned. The extra financial burden taken on by that body will
not be carried straight through to the rates-it never is. Instead, budgeting arrangements of
that local body take into account the increased burden of capital and interest repayments
involved in the loan from then on. Some of these obligations may be restricted to particular
types of funds within the council's control, but the overall effect is to diminish the amount of
finance available for the other purposes of the council.
It is not just those whose rates are likely to be increased who are affected by the
increased financial burden of a new loan. It is because this broader financial impact has not
been duly considered over the years that we still have, in this method of voting, this remnant
of class privilege, which really died at the end of last century, and continues only in this field.

to vote has been dead for nearly 100 years.

POLICE AMENDMENT BILL
Second reading
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 defines the terms "date of settlement",
"Higher Salaries Commission", "Police Gazette”, and “public sector tribunal", which are
relevant to the amendment. Clause 3 adds a new subsection (4) to section 12 of the principal
Act that will enable a temporary member to be permanently appointed. This will entitle
those members serving in positions such as radio technicians and carpenters to be eligible for
permanent appointment. A consequential amendment to the Police Regulations will be
required.
Clause 4 amends section 14 by substituting a new subsection (3) and adding a subsection
(4). At present, section 14 provides that a successful appellant against a recommendation for
promotion must be appointed to the position to which the appeal relates, and the original


## p. 3671 (#151) ###########################################

21 September
3671
Police Amendment Bill
recommendation is automatically cancelled. This provides a problem of seniority where the
person appealed against is also worthy of promotion, and of administration where the
position is of a specialised nature. The new subsection (3) enables the successful appellant to
be appointed to the rank without cancelling the original recommendation. The Minister or
the commissioner, depending on whether the position relates to a commissioned or a non-
commissioned officer, is given a discretionary power to cancel the original recommendation.
Clause 5 inserts a proviso to section 32 (1) to enable the commissioner to modify a
decision concerning the suspension of a member pending the hearing of a charge. Under the
amendment the commissioner will be able to take account of changing circumstances that
arise after the original suspension is imposed. Clause 6 increases the maximum penalties that
may be imposed on members found guilty of breaches of duty following an inquiry under
section 33.
Clause 7 substitutes a new section 61 for the present section 61, and inserts a new section
61A. The present section 61 declares the Police Gazette to be a confidential State document
and sets out the offence of unlawful possession of a copy of the Police Gazette. The present
section also declares that the Police Gazette shall not be produced in court without the
written permission of the commissioner; nor shall civil or criminal proceedings be brought
based on anything contained in the Police Gazette. The new sections 61 and 61A restate
provisions relating to the Police Gazette, and also specifically apply the protection to the
police notices, police circulars, and other similar publications containing information
relating to crime, criminal offenders, or suspected offenders.
I must emphasise that the protection will apply to a limited class of police documents
only. It will apply only to documents as described which are intended for circulation to
members of the police only. Therefore, the protection will apply to such documents as
specialised crime circulars dealing with, for example, drug pushers or persons currently
believed to be committing robberies and large burglaries. Such documents are published by
police intelligence sections and circulated to police enforcing the law in those fields. That is
the type of publication which the amendment quite properly, aims to protect.
It should be noted that such details could legally be included in the Police Gazette and
then would have the protection section 61 presently affords. However, in the interests of
greater efficiency and indeed in the interests of maintaining greater confidentiality of the
information, this information is contained in specialised publications with more restricted
circulation than the actual Police Gazette.
The new provisions will not apply to documents outside the defined class. The
provisions will not apply, for example, to statements from offenders, as obviously they are
not documents intended solely for circulation to members of the police; they are intended for
production in court. Similarly, the new provisions will not apply to general police files
relating to investigation of offences. Such files are intended for ultimate referral to persons
outside the police, such as Crown solicitors, should this be necessary for the prosecution of
offenders.
It has been suggested that the new provision is designed to overcome a judgment of the
Court of Appeal delivered in March of this year. I can be quite emphatic that this was not
intended, nor, in my view, will the amendment have that effect. The document involved in
those proceedings was a statement of admission from an offender which referred to another
person allegedly involved. Obviously, as a statement of admission, the primary purpose of
this statement was for subsequent production in court. In no way could it be described as a
document for circulation to members of the Police only. Therefore, the availability of that
document for production in court will not in my view be affected by this amendment.
Some concern has been expressed that the words "or other document" in the proposed
new section 61A(1) are too wide. I should therefore point out that the term "other
document" applies only to a document which satisfies four criteria. The first is the one I have
already explained—that is, the document must be one intended for circulation “only to
members of the Police". Secondly, the document must be one "published" by a member of
the Police. The word "published" must, in the context of the Police Act, be given its
common meaning, which is "to make generally known". It would not be given the specific
meaning it has acquired in another context-namely, the law relating to defamation.
Thirdly, the document must be one "containing information relating to crime, criminal
offenders, or suspected offenders". Again, these words narrow the meaning of the term
"other documents". For example, the term would seldom include documents relating to
disciplinary offences committed by a member of the Police. Only rarely would such a


## p. 3672 (#152) ###########################################

3672
21 September
Police Amendment Bill
document contain information relating to crime or criminal offending. Fourthly, the term
"other document" must not be read alone. It must be read in the context of the section in
which it appears. In particular, the term follows the specific words in the section—namely,
"Police Gazette", "Police Notice", and "Police Circular". Therefore, this is clearly a case for
the application of the “ejusdem generis" rule. This is a rule of statutory interpretation which
applies when general words follow particular and specific words. The meaning of the general
words must in such cases be confined to things of the same kind as those specified in the
particular words. Applying that rule here, it is obvious that the term "other document"
would be given a narrow interpretation by a court and apply only to a document similar in
kind to the "Police Gazette", "Police Notice", and "Police Circular". Therefore, in my view,
the new provisions could not be applied to the documents involved in two recent court
decisions, as has been suggested in some quarters.
I have been advised that the police have discussed the proposals with the Crown Law
Office, and the view of that office also is that the term "any other document" would receive
the narrow interpretation I have described. This is also the view of the New Zealand Law
Society, who have written to me about the proposal. That society has said that it sees nothing
insidious about the clause.
However, it has made a suggestion which would remove any genuine concern. I
therefore intend to move an amendment to this clause by way of a Supplementary Order
Paper in the Committee stage. This amendment will insert after the words "or other
document" in the proposed new section 61A subsection (1) the words "of a like nature". This
is what was intended, and is the way I am sure the new provisions would have been
interpreted. The amendment will make that clear.
I should also make the point that the amendment in no way interferes with the wide
studies to be carried out by the Committee on Official Information chaired by Sir Allan
Danks, which has been set up to examine, among other things, legislation affecting the
confidentiality of official information. The police will be reporting to that committee in due
course, but the committee's recommendations will not be available until 1979.
The amendment recognises the need to clarify the status of specialised circulars, and the
like, published for police circulation. The new provisions will raise the penalty for offences
under the section from a maximum $100 fine to a maximum $500 fine, or up to 3 months
imprisonment. This is necessary to preserve the confidentiality of such documents and to
prevent their circulation among persons outside the police.
Clause 8 provides the general rule that the commissioner's determination on salaries,
allowances, and expenses be in force for at least 12 months. Clause 9 requires the
commissioner to consult the Higher Salaries Commission in appropriate cases. Clause 10
reduces from 10 months to 6 months the time a service organisation must wait before seeking
the review of a determination made by the commissioner. Clauses 11 and 12 make
consequential amendments by inserting reference to the yearly general review of
remuneration, which replaces the former half yearly surveys.
Clause 13 makes a further consequential amendment by substituting reference to
section 20 of the State Services Conditions of Employment Act for the corresponding
provision in the previous legislation. Clause 14 makes several consequential amendments
involving the constitution of the Police Staff Tribunal following the replacement of the State
Services Tribunal by the Public Sector Tribunal. Clause 15 provides for the appointment of
assessors to assist the Police Staff Tribunal. Clause 16 authorises the Police Staff Tribunal to
make recommendations to the Higher Salaries Commission or to the Minister on increases in
salaries exceeding the amount prescribed in the Order in Council.

However, the Opposition does not accept the Minister's explanation that the words

words in that way, because it is used disjunctively, and the words are "Police Notice or
Police Circular or other document". Even though the words "of a like nature" are included,
it should not be the desire of a Government to take away from judicial review matters that
could affect the livelihood of individual policemen and matters that could be at issue in
litigation between the citizen and the State, or matters that could have been examined
hitherto by a judge of the Supreme Court using the principle of Crown privilege--which the
Police can always claim—and letting the judge determine whether it is in the public interest,
after weighing up the interest of the parties to the litigation against the broader public
interest. Why must we now take away from a judge the power to review that and have a
judge competent and skilled in determining Crown privilege make his decision? We now let
judges review a Crown claim to privilege on a whole range of litigation, which could involve
millions of dollars or only a few cents. We are content to let that review remain vested in a
judge of the Supreme Court.
The Bill gives the Commissioner of Police the right to have that material kept from the
sight of the court and the notice of a judge, which is wrong. The Government should protect
the interests of the police to ensure that necessary documents are kept confidential, but
should not place a blanket over the activities of the police when it comes to litigation
between citizens or between employees of the Police Department and the department itself.
Did the Police Association ask for this law? I do not believe it did, because serving
members of the Police would know that it is possible at the moment to endorse a piece of
paper "Supplement to the Police Gazette", and that piece of paper then becomes part of the
Police Gazette and is protected. The Police Gazette consists not only of that which is printed
and bound, but also of material that is clearly designated to form part of the Gazette, and
when that designation is given that material does form part of the Gazette. The penalty
offences and the right to review by a judge will depend on the intention of the police officer
at the time the document was made. I suggest that there should be no confusion about that at
all, and that the Bill should contain a formula whereby matters come within the protection
the Minister alleges is there. If the Minister is correct in his explanation, and if any document
not intended for public distribution but intended only for publication within the police force
is to be covered, let there be a procedure at the time the document is compiled to state that
intention clearly on the face of it. Then no one could fall into committing an offence
punishable by 3 months imprisonment or a fine of $200 without knowing instinctively what
was in the mind of the person who drew up the document.
How is a serving officer of the police force to know the state of mind of another officer
in respect of a particular document? If that other officer's mind is clear and he intends the
document to be restricted to circulation within the police, then let that officer say so. Do not
let the other officer be at risk. What happens in the case of serving officers who have come to
retirement and who have in their possession, as many police officers have, material which,
quite appropriately, they have retained as memoirs, relics of their job, things to remember
places or cases by, and which now have come, under this Bill, to be subject to the penalty of
imprisonment or a fine if the documents they have in their possession fall within the
particular sweep of the legislation?

function, later the subject of a liquor investigation-any form of innocuous material could in
fact be within the scope of the Bill. That would render serving police officers and retired
police officers liable to the penalties set out in the Bill, and would be an unsatisfactory state
of affairs for the morale of the police force. It does nothing to enhance crime-breaking

Fishing Industry Board Amendment Bill
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): A point of order, Mr Acting Speaker. The Minister, when

FISHING INDUSTRY BOARD AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Bill provides for the reconstitution of the Fishing Industry Board, which was
established in 1963, and also for a new fish levy to be paid by fishermen to provide finance
for fishermen's organisations. As I outlined during the introduction of the Bill, the
reconstituted board will ensure the more direct involvement on the board of the catching,
processing, and exporting sectors of the fishing industry. This, I believe, is desirable at a time
when the fishing industry is expanding and diversifying at a very rapid rate. This growth is
illustrated by the fact that in 1963, when the Fishing Industry Board was established, there
were only 1727 licensed fishing vessels in New Zealand. Today, there are approximately
5000. Likewise, exports of fish in 1963 were worth approximately $3 million. This year it is
confidently expected that the value of fish exports from New Zealand will exceed $60
million. This illustrates the tremendous growth of the industry since the Fishing Industry
Board was first established.
Because of that, it is logical that we should look again at the constitution of the board.
The reconstitution proposed in the Bill was recommended by a fishing industry review group
set up in August 1976 to recommend on the institutional structure that would best serve the
needs of the developing fishing industry. The review group, made up of representatives from
all parts of the industry, concluded that the paramount concern was to have an authoritative
body that could, first, present a strong and single voice on all major issues-and that is
important; secondly, be representative of the industry; and, thirdly, play a major role in
shaping the future of the industry and the further development of its export potential. I
emphasise the major role that I envisage the board will play in the future development of the
industry.
The review group concluded that the most effective and practical method of achieving
this would be to reconstitute the Fishing Industry Board. I make the point strongly that the
decision to change the Fishing Industry Board is no reflection whatever on the calibre or
capability of those who have served on the board. The tremendous expansion that has taken
place over recent years in the New Zealand fishing industry is due, in no small part, to the
efforts of all board members, and those efforts are properly acknowledged at this stage. The
members, both individually and collectively, have served the board and the industry
extremely well since it was established in 1963. I want to place on record my thanks to those
members, past and present, who have served on the board.
The other major proposal in the Bill involves the insertion of a new section 14A to
impose a new levy on fish, payable only by fishermen, which will be paid to an organisation
or organisations representing fishermen, as directed by the Minister. The levy will provide
finance for the administration costs of these organisations. Let me be clear that the levy will
be in addition to the levy actually paid by fishermen, wholesalers, and retailers, and used to
fund the Fishing Industry Board. The levy will be similar to the levy collected by Federated
Farmers to finance its activities. The exact rate of the levy and the organisations to which it
will be paid will be set by regulations made under the Act.
When I introduced the Bill I expressed my understanding at the time, which was that the
levy proposals had the almost unanimous support of the fishing industry. For example, the
Commercial Fishermen's Association assured me that its members supported it 100 percent.
However, within the last 48 hours, some reservations on the levy proposals have been
expressed to me, and I intend to have discussions with the groups involved in the next few
days. If it is necessary to make any changes in the Bill, I will propose suitable amendments
during the Committee stage. The proposal to reconstitute the board has been discussed
widely within the industry and has received widespread support.
I shall now refer to the provisions of the Bill. Clause 1 is the short title and includes the
commencement date-members will note that the Act comes into force on 1 January 1979.


## p. 3679 (#159) ###########################################

21 September
3679
Fishing Industry Board Amendment Bill
Clause 2 inserts into the principal Act definitions of the terms "exported" and "exporter".
This makes it clear that the levy payable under the Fish Levy Regulations 1976 is payable on
all fish caught by New Zealand fishing craft within the exclusive economic zone, even if the
fish is not landed in New Zealand. It is necessary to make that clear, because the joint
venture proposals at present being studied, and ventures that have been in operation over
the last couple of years, sometimes do not land their fish in New Zealand, although we do
require them to pay a levy to the Fishing Industry Board.
Clauses 3 to 7 amend the constitution of the board. Clause 3 changes the name of the
board to the New Zealand Fishing Industry Board. There are a number of fishing industry
boards throughout the world, and the board sought the addition of "New Zealand" to give it
international recognition. The present board comprises the chairman and three other
members nominated by the Minister. The Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries is a
member but does not have a vote. He cannot be counted for quorum purposes. There are
three other members representing the fishermen, the fish wholesalers and processors, and
fish retailers. Clearly the industry is in a majority position on the board. Under the Bill, the
board will comprise the chairman and one other member nominated by the Minister, the
Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries, who will now be a full member of the board
with full voting rights, and five other members representing various sections of the industry.
Those five members will include one member nominated by the New Zealand Federation of
Commercial Fishermen, one member nominated by the New Zealand Sharefishermen's
Association, two members nominated by the Seafood Processors Association, and one
member nominated by an organisation recognised by the Minister as representing fish
retailers. This gives clear industry representation on the board, and majority representation
to those directly involved in the industry. Members are now to be appointed directly by the
Minister rather than by the Governor-General on the Minister's recommendation, as has
been the position until now.
Clause 4 consequentially amends the provisions relating to the term of office of board
members. Clause 5 provides for the appointment of deputies of members of the board.
Clause 6 consequentially amends the provisions relating to extraordinary vacancies. Clause 7
provides for the appointment of a deputy chairman, and consequentially alters the quorum
provisions of the board. Clause 8 amends section 14(3) of the principal Act to make it clear
that the levy payable by wholesalers and recovered by them from fishermen and retailers
should be paid only once by any person. Clause 9 provides for the imposition of a levy on
fish, payable to an organisation or organisations representing fishermen, as directed by the
Minister. Clause 10 is a transitional provision. All the existing appointed members of the
board will go out of office but may be reappointed. When the board has been reconstituted,
the first members will be appointed for varying terms to provide for an initial rotation.
Thereafter the normal 3-year term will apply.
The changes provided for in the Bill will be welcomed by the industry. They are another
positive indication of Government support for the industry, and another important step in
the development of the growing fishing industry. I welcome also the opportunity to restate
the Government's commitment to the expansion of the New Zealand fishing industry, a
commitment that is obvious in the wide range of measures introduced, far surpassing
anything introduced by previous governments. One of the first undertakings given by the
National Government was to ensure that the Fishing Industry Board would have sufficient
funds to carry out the functions entrusted to it under its Act. Previously it had had
inadequate funds. In the last year of the Labour Government's term of office, the grant to
the Fishing Industry Board was a miserable $95,000-an increase of $10,000 on the year
before. I quote from the board's report of that year: "This increase is only a portion of what
is necessary to enable the board to play a fuller part in the development of the industry." I
believe it is important, when setting up statutory boards, to ensure that those boards have
the financial strength to carry out the responsibility entrusted to them. It is sad to note that
until the advent of this Government the Fishing Industry Board was hamstrung. In the last
year of the former Government it received $95,000; this year the Fishing Industry Board will
receive a Government grant of more than $400,000.
Mr Rogers: And the people who buy the fish will pay for it.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: The member for Onehunga prattles away in the background. He
would not know a fish it he tripped over one. The new level of funding will enable the board
to expand its activities in disseminating information to fishermen, and will enable it also to
become more involved in providing marketing advice to exporters. It is important that the

HIVE LEVY BILL
Second Reading
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The purpose of the Bill is to transfer from the Honey Marketing
Authority to the National Beekeepers Association the responsibility for collecting the
compulsory hive levy-at present 15c per hive-payable in respect of each hive by
beekeepers with 50 or more hives. The reason for transferring the responsibility for
collection is that the association is the main recipient of the funds collected, and the industry
feels that it should be the body to collect the levy. No other substantive changes have been
made to the principles behind the collection of the levy and the method by which it is fixed,
assessed, and the dates of collection.
Clause 1 relates to the short title and the commencement date; and the Bill is to come
into force on 1 October 1978. Clause 2 defines the various terms used in the Bill. These are
similar to the definitions in the Honey Marketing Authority Regulations 1975, under which
the hive levy is presently imposed. For the purposes of the Bill, a "beekeeper" is defined as a
person who keeps 50 or more hives. Clause 3 imposes an obligation on every beekeeper to
pay to the association an annual levy at such rate per hive kept by him on 1 January each year
as may be fixed by the Minister by notice in the Gazette. The rate of levy is to be fixed by 30
November each year, after the Minister has received the joint recommendations of the
association and of the authority; so the Minister operates on the joint recommendations of
those two bodies. If no recommendations are made, the rate continues the same as for the
previous year. Under clause 15, which makes transitional provisions, the levy for 1979 will be
15c if no recommendations are made to the Minister. That is the rate of hive levy currently
payable to the authority pursuant to the Honey Marketing Regulations 1975.
Clause 4 provides that everyone who is a beekeeper on 1 January each year must
complete a form declaring the number of hives he is keeping, and containing such other
information as may be required by the association. Those forms must be delivered to the
association by 20 February, along with the amount of hive levy due. The association has the
power, if it wishes, to require the forms to be verified by way of a statutory declaration.
Clause 5 gives the association discretion to defer the date by which the hive levy is required


## p. 3691 (#171) ###########################################

21 September
3691
Hive Levy Bill
to be paid. Clause 6 provides for a penalty payment of an additional 10 percent on the levy,
to be imposed if the levy is not paid by 31 March or such other date as may have been set by
the association under clause 5. Once again the association has the discretion to remit the
penalty payment if it sees fit.
Clause 7 provides for an additional amount of levy, not exceeding 5c per hive, to be
imposed as a stabilisation reserve levy and paid into the authority's stabilisation reserve
account. The additional levy can be fixed by the Minister only after receiving the joint
recommendations of the authority and the association. As the stabilisation scheme operated
by the authority applies only to extracted honey, subclause (4) of clause 7 provides for
exemption from the levy for hives not producing extracted honey-that is, hives producing
comb honey or used for breeding queen bees. Clause 8 provides that any hive levy payable
under the Bill is a debt due to the association and may be recovered through court
proceedings. It is hoped that that will never be necessary. Clause 9 provides for the
operation of the hive levy account by the National Beekeepers Association.
When the Bill comes into force, money in the Honey Marketing Authority's hive levy
account will be transferred to the association's hive levy account, and from that day onwards
the association will operate the account. All hive levies received, including any stabilisation
reserve levy, will be paid into the account and the association can pay out of the account the
costs of collection and administration of the levy. The association must also pay to the
authority all amounts collected by way of stabilisation reserve levy, with the authority
accounting for those sums pursuant to the Honey Marketing Authority Regulations 1975,
which are amended by one of the later clauses of the Bill. The rest of the amount collected by
way of hive levy is used for funding the administrative expenses of the association and the
non-trading functions of the authority. The amounts to be applied for those purposes are
subject to approval by the Minister of Agriculture, and the practice under the present system
has been for both organisations to submit to the Minister their budgeted requirements for
the coming year at the time they present their recommendations for the rate of levy. The
Minister can then fix the levy and approve the payments from the account of the budgeted
requirements.
Subclauses (7) and (8) provide for a procedure in the event of the amount collected by
way of levy falling short of the amounts approved by the Minister for paying to the authority
and being used by the association. The intention is that any shortfall would be recouped by
an increase in the levy the following year. Clauses 10 and 11 are machinery provisions
requiring the association to prepare annual accounts and provide the Minister and any
members who so request with copies of the association's annual report and accounts. Clause
12 deals with offences and penalties. Clause 13 provides for the Hive Levy Act to be
administered by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. Clause 14 makes the necessary
consequential amendments to the Honey Marketing Authority Regulations 1975. Part II of
those regulations, which is being revoked, is the present legislation providing for the
imposition and collection of a hire levy. Regulation 25 is also amended to provide for the
handling by the authority of any stabilisation reserve levy collected under the provisions of
the Bill. Clause 15 contains some minor transitional provisions. One, to which I have already
alluded, fixes a rate of 15c for the 1979 hire levy unless there is a recommendation to the
contrary by the association and the authority.
The Bill before the House is to implement the levy procedures of the beekeeping
industry. It has been requested by the producers, and is to fund the operations of the
industry and of the Beekeepers Association. I think I can say fairly that I do not expect that
the Bill will be controversial.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): We find ourselves in the very happy
position of the Opposition being in agreement with the Bill, and I shall not hold up
proceedings very long, but I do have one or two questions to put to the Minister. Clause 3
provides that the levy is to be fixed by the Minister of Agriculture by notice in the Gazette
after receiving the joint recommendation of the Beekeepers Association and the Honey

ACCIDENT COMPENSATION AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. As I indicated, when introducing the Bill, it is a short one comprising 13 relatively
minor amendments designed to improve the application and the effect of the Act, and to put
interpretation beyond doubt, pending the completion of the major surveys of the Act and its
schemes presently being conducted both by the commission and by others and which
probably will be the subject of a review in 1979. It may well be that as a result of these
surveys substantial amendments will be proposed for consideration next year or even the
year after.
Clause 2 introduces a definition of New Zealand for accident compensation purposes
only. It will exclude the Ross Dependency, the internal waters of the Ross Dependency, and
its territorial waters. In this respect the amendment clearly states Parliament's original
intention at the time the original Act came into force in 1974. In other respects the definition
is merely declaratory of the present legal position. The effect will be to make it absolutely
clear what cover exists for non-New Zealanders. It has never been the intention of the
legislation that American, Russian, or other foreign scientists or travellers visiting the Ross
Dependency or its territorial sea should have accident cover provided for them by the New
Zealand taxpayer or by the Government.


## p. 3693 (#173) ###########################################

21 September
3693
Accident Compensation Amendment Bill
Clause 3 corrects an anomaly in section 59(2) of the Act. If the present section were to
be read literally the full period of extension of cover of 13 weeks could not be given. The
proposed amendment will remedy this anomaly and give effect to what is understood to be
the intention of the legislation. I shall now deal with clause 4. Section 73 of the Act at present
would allow the commission to recognise good or bad safety records by adjusting the rates of
levy. The amendment will allow the commission to make adjustments, not only by adjusting
the rate of levy, but also by imposing cash penalties or awarding cash bonuses, whichever
system is considered to be more equitable or justifiable. In other words, it allows the
commission flexibility in introducing a satisfactory adjustment system. This has been
welcomed by most parties I have spoken to.
Clause 5 will incorporate into the principal Act the matters which have been dealt with
by Order in Council that were designed to ease the manner in which levy returns and tax
returns are to be made by self-employed persons. The amendment will benefit self-employed
persons and the many public and chartered accountants who prepare these returns on their
behalf. There has been agitation from professional accountants to have the self-employed
tax/levy forms combined. The proposal in relation to the combined tax/levy form is that the
self-employed persons who complete a financial year will in future file statements of earnings
within 1 month from 7 August, the date on which they are required to file tax returns for
provisional tax purposes. However, levy liability will not become payable until the time for
payment of terminal tax, namely, 7 March. In so far as the Accident Compensation
Commission levy payers are concerned, the date for delivering statements of earnings will be
advanced to 7 August, but the obligation to pay a levy will be postponed from 30 November
to 7 March.
The Commissioner of Inland Revenue is the statutory agent for the Accident
Compensation Commission in the collection of levies. It often happens that a tax defaulter is
also a defaulter in the payment of his Accident Compensation Commission levy. In seeking
to recover income tax arrears the Commissioner of Inland Revenue has power under the
Income Tax Act to attach moneys owing to the tax defaulter by a third party. At present the
Commissioner of Inland Revenue, acting as agent for the Accident Compensation
Commission, has no similar power. The proposed amendment, which closely follows section
400 of the Income Tax Act, will remedy this situation.
Clause 7 of the Bill deals with section 102c of the Act, which is unsatisfactory because it
does not adequately express the intended policy regarding cover for visitors to New Zealand.
The proposed amendment provides that if an overseas visitor or foreign seaman is injured
while on a ship or an aircraft he does not qualify for accident compensation cover.
Mr Lange: Can he sue in the New Zealand courts?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Not for accidents.
Mr Lange: What does he do?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: He should insure himself, as most of us do when we travel
overseas. Clause 8 of the Bill is one of the most complicated amendments. The existing
legislation is complex, and any simple change of policy involves the amendment of a number
of sections. However, the proposal is simple and straightforward. The Act at present
provides that earnings-related compensation shall not exceed $15,600. This has been
increased to $18,700 with effect from 1 April 1979. A person who suffers a partial loss of
earnings, but retains earnings above that limit, is not entitled to receive earnings-related
compensation. The amendment will enable such persons to receive earnings-related
compensation but with a maximum of $240 a week, or approximately $288 a week after 1
April next year. It is envisaged that the amendment will enable those who have earnings at a
higher level to receive some compensation when they suffer what may be a partial, but
nevertheless substantial, loss of earnings as a result of personal injury by accident. Clause 9
of the Bill is a consequential amendment since the territorial sea of New Zealand, now
extended to 12 miles, is and always has been part of New Zealand. Clause 10 introduces a
new section to deal with ambulance charges.
Mr Rogers: We'll be looking at that one.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I am quite happy to talk about the Auckland ambulance, the
Wellington Free Ambulance, or even my own west Otago ambulance. Without disturbing
the existing provisions of sections 107, 108, and 109 the proposed new section will provide
that the commission shall meet the reasonable costs of all necessary transportation of an
injured person by ambulance. The amendment further provides that in respect of such
transportation by an ambulance, provided by or under contract to a hospital board the

6. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Labour: In how many instances has it
been found that unemployed persons registered in one office have also registered in another,
and in how many cases have persons, having been given work, still remained registered as
unemployed?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I am not aware of any instances in which
unemployed persons have been registering in more than one office of my department at any
one time. Persons registered as seeking work with my department are enrolled on the basis
that they are willing and able to undertake employment. Should their circumstances change
the department cancels their registration, which is then renewed only when they satisfy an
employment officer that they are available for employment.
Mr Marshall: Can I take it from the Minister's answer, therefore, that there was no
evidence of the kind of abuse hinted at in the original question?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I cannot absolutely deny it. There has been speculation recently,
and the member may know that the Department of Labour has caught up with some abuse
and miscalculation in other areas, so I cannot be categorical.
Mr Schultz: In view of the large number registered in Auckland, would there be
anything to prevent any member of the Labour Party registering as unemployed whether or
not he had a job?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Frankly I cannot answer that question, but having read the back
page of yesterday's New Zealand Herald I begin to wonder myself.
Mr Hunt: Despite the Minister's statement that he cannot say categorically that there
has been no evidence of this happening, are the chances less than 100 to 1 that this sort of
offence would occur?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I am not a betting man, and I will not take chances at 100 to 1.
The member must remember that the large number of people handling the applications and
doing the checking are temporary workers, and that was the subject of criticism by the
Opposition this week.

Compressed Natural Gas
7. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What proposals are
contemplated to use "compressed natural gas" as a transport fuel, and how does the fuel
compare economically with LPG as a transport fuel?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The New Zealand Energy Research and
Development Committee has let a contract to evaluate compressed natural gas, or CNG, as
a transport fuel. The contract is due for completion in March 1979. The need for, and
desirability of, encouraging CNG should then be able to be assessed appropriately. Whether
a fleet operator would be attracted to CNG or LPG would depend on the nature of his
vehicle use.
Hon. F. M. Colman: As the two fuels are in competition, will the Ministry of Energy
publicise their benefits and attractions so that those contemplating their use may properly
judge their value?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The ministry will certainly co-operate. The time of the House would
not permit me, but I could give a number of details that identify the attractiveness or
disadvantages of the respective fuels. Operators should have all the information available to
make a choice to suit their needs.

14. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson) to the Minister of Fisheries: What is the growth of rock

tonnes valued at $700,000 this year.

Migration Statistics
18. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North), on behalf of Miss DEWE (Lyttelton), to the
Minister of Immigration: Has he seen a publication entitled Lyttelton '78 issued by the
Labour Party and dated August 1978, and, if so, has he seen a statement in that which states
"New Zealand had a permanent and long-term migration loss of over 42,000 for the year

current financial year", and, if so, (i) is this correct, and, if not (ii) what are the correct
figures; and (iii) can he explain where the Labour Party may have got the figures quoted?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Immigration. "No, I have not seen the publication referred to, but the figure quoted is not
accurate. Official figures published by the Department of Statistics show that for the year
ended 31 March 1978 there was a net outflow, resulting from permanent and long-term
movements, of 26 708 persons. As I have previously informed the House, however, figures
relating to permanent movements are a more accurate reflection of the net effect of
migration on New Zealand's population. These show that in the year ended 31 March 1978
there was a loss to population of 4148 persons. I believe it is fruitless to speculate on how the
Labour Party arrived at the figures quoted by the honourable member."
Mr Lithgow: Would those figures be available to Labour Party members, and, if so,
could they use them?

14 188, and the total number of permanent departures of New Zealand residents was 18 336,
giving a net loss of 4148, as I have already stated.

that there was a net migration loss of 30 050 for the year ended 31 August 1978—a later

only fault with the figures given by the Labour Party in Lyttelton '78 is that they have been
understated?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The figures for permanent long-term movements include data
on people going overseas only temporarily, although for longer than 12 months--for
example, to gain wider work experience, or to undertake further studies. Figures relating to
permanent movements are a more accurate reflection of the net effect on New Zealand's
population. The Monthly Abstract of Statistics for August 1978 gives the following figures for
permanent movements for the year ended 31 March 1978, and they are the figures I have
quoted: total new permanent arrivals, 14 188; total permanent departures of New Zealand
residents, 18 336-giving a loss of people departing permanently of 4148.
Mr Lithgow: I again ask the Minister if those figures could be made available to Labour
Party members if they asked for them.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The figures are available to Labour Party members and, as
they well know, nothing lies like statistics. With the great ability of Labour Party members to
tell half truths and make innuendoes it is no wonder that they give unreliable statistics.
