Nuclear-powered Ships
20. Mr BELL (Gisborne), on behalf of Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of
Transport: To what degree has marine shipping moved towards nuclear power as a means of
propulsion?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Transport. "There are already more than 200 nuclear-powered warships in operation, some
of which have been in service for more than 20 years. A few nuclear-powered merchant ships
have been built, including an ice-breaker, a bulk-ore cargo carrier, and two general cargo
ships. Diesel engines are far and away the most popular and economic form of machinery in
merchant ships, but, as the price of oil fuel increases and its availability decreases, so other
forms of propulsion, including nuclear energy, could become very economically attractive.
Unless a smaller reactor system than at present envisaged can be developed, however, it is
unlikely that more than about 400 to 500 ships would require means of propulsion of
sufficient power to make nuclear energy economically feasible even if environmental, moral,
safety, and other considerations were satisfied."
Mr Bell: Could the acting Minister confirm that any political party that adopted a policy
of a complete ban on ships with nuclear propulsion coming into New Zealand waters would
seriously jeopardise the smooth flow of future exports from this country?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: That proposition, of course, is correct. If it were found necessary
in the future for a large number of trading ships-oil carriers, bulk carriers, and the like-to
have nuclear propulsion, clearly it would be against New Zealand's interests to refuse to
allow them to come here for trading purposes.

the magistrate's court in Invercargill revealed that certain aspects of the Industrial Relations
Act as amended in 1976, which the Government was warned at the time would be
unworkable, led to avoidable disruption and brought the law into disrepute. The
adjournment is both for the purpose of discussing the circumstances of the situation and

As Acting Speaker on Friday morning, 22 September 1978, I have four criteria on which
to establish whether I shall grant the adjournment of the House under Standing Orders 89
and 90. The first is that the statement shall not be framed in general terms. The statement of
the matter is not framed in general terms and meets the requirement.
The second is that the matter shall deal with a particular case of recent occurrence. I
must accept that this matter is of recent occurrence. Indeed, the Evening Post of yesterday
stated that only the first four of the 191 charges had been dealt with by the court. If that had
still been the case, debate on the matter would have offended against Standing Order 183
relating to matters awaiting judicial decision. However, the midnight radio report,
reinforced by this morning's Dominion, clearly indicates that all charges have been
withdrawn or dismissed. These factors enable me to accept the requirement of recent
occurrence and, in this case, of not offending under Standing Order 183.
The third criterion is that it requires the immediate attention of the House and the
Government. This is debatable, but, as this is a debating Chamber, I am persuaded that the
statement of the matter fulfils the requirement.
The fourth requirement is for the matter to involve administrative or ministerial
responsibility, which, of course, it does. As the written statement meets all requirements, I
shall allow it to proceed. Will members who approve of the proposed discussion rise in their
places.

PERSONAL EXPLANATION
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): With the leave of the House, I wish to make
a personal explanation. During the adjournment debate last Friday I indicated I was
requested by Sir Thomas Skinner to witness the signing of the agreement held in my office on
Thursday afternoon, 21 September 1978, for the killing out of stock at freezing works. I now
discover that the note passed into my office, from my secretary, conveying the request to
witness the signatures, was not from Sir Thomas Skinner, as I had presumed, and with whom
I had earlier spoken about the proceedings. I am now informed that it was Mr Allan Wright,
the President of Federated Farmers, who phoned my office, but no name was included in the
message passed to me. The mistake was compounded by the fact that it was Sir Thomas
Skinner who requested a deferment of the signatures until such time as I had obtained from
the Invercargill Magistrate's Court the decision covering the whole of the 192 workers. I
apologise for any misunderstanding that occurred in the House on Friday morning.

Food Price Index Increases
2. Dr. SHEARER (Hamilton East), on behalf of Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa), to

following July years-1972, 1975, 1978?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): The percentage increases in the all-
food group of the consumer price index for the year ended July 1972 was 5.1 percent; for the

Regulations 1974. My department had no objections to this increase of 4.5 percent on the

Electoral Rolls Special Votes
5. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Justice: Is it correct that the
checking of the declaration for special votes against the roll during the official count is
usually carried out by an official of the Post Office without the presence of the returning
officer or any scrutineers, and, if so, are any changes in the practice proposed because of the
high probability that many who have actually taken steps to enrol would not have their
names on either roll, yet have received an E2 form?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): There is no basis for the supposition
that anyone who has received an E2 card will not be able to cast a valid vote, and the
suggestion is irresponsible. The Electoral Act 1956-sections 95 and 112 to 115-provides
for scrutineers to be appointed by candidates to be present in polling booths during the
scrutiny of the rolls by the returning officer after the poll, and during the official count by the
returning officer, and this includes the counting of special votes. However, regulation 24 of
the Electoral Regulations 1975 provides for the declarations of special voters to be sent by
the returning officer to the electorate officer-an official of the Post Office-for checking
that the special voter is a qualified registered elector. After checking and endorsement by
the electorate officer, the special voters' declarations are returned to the returning officer for
the appropriate action. This has always been the practice, and there is no proposal for it to
be changed.
Hon. F. M. Colman: If a person who has received an E2 form is given a special vote on
election day because his name does not appear on either the main roll or the supplementary
roll, is that special vote then passed on to the electoral officer to check the voter's eligibility;

26 September

and will the electoral officer count or discount that vote because he has no record of the
person having enrolled, even though that person has an E2 form?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That is a long supplementary.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It is a long supplementary, and it is not in elucidation of the
question. The E2 card is an acknowledgement of the fact that a person has been registered as
being able to vote, and that is what the electorate officer needs to satisfy himself that the

Acts and amendments to Acts, which deal directly with improving the position of women in
our society. The Human Rights Commission Act 1977 prohibits discrimination on the
grounds of sex in a number of fields. The first schedule to that Act amends various statutes,
including the Sale of Liquor Act, by removing discriminatory provisions. The Matrimonial
Property Act 1976 is another obvious example. The Juries Amendment Act 1976 imposes
the same obligation on men and women in respect of jury service, and the Citizenship Act
1977 gives men and women the same right to pass on citizenship to their children. Other
relevant measures are the Domicile Act 1976-providing for the separate domicile of
married women-and the Equal Pay Amendment Act 1976. This is not necessarily a
complete list, because, in addition, many Acts benefit women in that they benefit the
community as a whole.

Education-Grants to Schools
11. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Education: What improvements to the
system of allocation of grants to schools has been made by this National Government?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Education. "When the National Government assumed office, I found that education
authorities were not informed of the increased levels of grants applicable for the current
school year in some cases until well into the third term. In 1976 the Government
acknowledged these difficulties in budgeting expenditure, and steps were taken to determine
the new rates of grant for announcement before the next academic year. As a result, in
December 1976 I announced the general level of increased grants for the 1977 school year,
and detailed grants were promulgated early in the new year. In 1977 I notified not only the
level of increase, but also the detailed rates to controlling authorities before Christmas 1977.
There is, I understand, real appreciation of the early notification of grants under a system
that now provides for sensible budgeting and financial management”.

Overseas Debt
14. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Finance: What sinking fund
arrangements are in existence to provide for the payment of the outstanding overseas loan
debt, which, according to Budget table No. 13, is $2,446,730,000?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): Table 13 in the 1978 Budget
shows total overseas public debt outstanding as at 31 March 1978 to be $2,446,730,000. The
total is made up by 97 loans in the form of direct loans, revolving credits, and capital
equipment credits. Approximately one-third of the direct loans are subject to sinking fund
requirements-that is, repayment of some part of the outstanding principal is required prior
to the date of final maturity. Sinking fund requirements in fact vary from loan to loan. The
majority of capital equipment credits are also subject to sinking funds. Details of sinking
fund provisions as they relate to individual direct loans can be found in the tables at the back
of each year's Budget, and I am sure the member will refer to those. The general provisions
relating to the repayment of outstanding overseas debt can be found in sections 40 and 87 of
the Public Finance Act 1977.

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I congratulate the member for Porirua on seeking leave to
introduce his Bill, because I see it providing for a fundamental reform if true democracy is to
apply in New Zealand. It is becoming increasingly apparent that the New Zealand electoral
system is descriminatory and is becoming progressively harder to administer. Voting in New
Zealand is governed by three statutes and part of a fourth statute: the Electoral Act, the
Licensing Act, the Local Elections and Polls Act, and Part III of the Local Government Act.
The member for Porirua's Bill is a first step towards consolidating arrangements for
enrolment, voting, and scrutineering into a fair, just, and understandable procedure.
In the 1870s Britain recognised the justice of a simple electoral system, with common
provisions for all types of voting to allow democracy to function in a fair and reasonable way.
The British assimilated electoral procedures into a series of statutes more than 90 years ago.
New Zealand has not yet reached that stage of democratic advance. The Minister of Local
Government has mentioned a 3-yearly review of the Local Elections and Polls Act. May I
suggest to him that, instead of continual patchwork solutions to the electoral problems of
local and regional authorities, it would be better to devote time to assembling the procedures
of local body elections and polls into a coherent code, based on democracy, embodying
principles that recognise human rights, and showing an understanding of the difficulties
people have when involved in complicated procedures, so that they can exercise their basic
right more effectively. The present shambles of the main electoral rolls, together with
problems in local body areas, particularly local body polls, have brought to a head the
necessity to humanise and simplify voting systems in New Zealand, so that everyone has an
equal opportunity to vote, in spite of technicalities.
I am convinced that we must move towards one source of enrolment for all voting
purposes, recognising that parts of a common roll could be used for various rolls in different
areas and for different purposes. The time has come when everyone eligible to vote in an
election should have the right to vote on issues of concern to them. I commend the member
for Porirua for recognising that we live in a computer age, and that provision must be made
to ensure that votes are computed fairly and justly, and I think that this new method of
voting can be clean and above board. I refer to clauses 5, 6, 7, and 8 in the Bill under
discussion. Increasingly, counting will be done with computers, and candidates must have an
opportunity to appoint scrutineers who can oversee computer counting elsewhere than at the
official place of counting. It is becoming apparent that if electoral fairness is to be seen to be
done the right of scrutiny must be available whenever any phase of official counting takes
place. I find it appalling that the Government seems to be blocking every attempt to give
people equal voting opportunities on all issues. It is well known that complicated and diverse
voting procedures tend to penalise the aged, the lesser educated, and even busy people, who
cannot cope with the growing complexities of voting procedures. The complexity of the
present system favours the National Party, which tends to be supported by people who have
the time to wend their way through present complicated procedures, allowing their votes to
qualify. I commend the Bill, and share the desire of the member for Porirua to see a fairer

Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
MISUSE OF DRUGS AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill. Pursuant to the
instruction given by the House when referring the Bill to the committee on 5 September
1978, the committee has divided it into two separate Bills. The committee has instructed me
to report the first of these Bills, consisting of the long title, clause 1, and Parts I to V
inclusive, together with the schedule, with the recommendation that it be allowed to proceed
with the amendments shown in the copy attached hereto. I move, That the report do lie upon
the table.
This important amendment to the Misuse of Drugs Act attracted 18 submissions. Of
these, those of the New Zealand Law Society, the National Society on Alcoholism and Drug
Dependence and the New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties were actually heard by the
committee, but all the others were carefully considered by the committee before its
deliberation. Before outlining the major recommendations made by the committee I should
make three points in relation to the submissions. First, for the benefit of those who made
submissions advocating the decriminalisation of marijuana, this Bill does not, except in a
very minor way, deal with class C drugs-for example, marijuana. Therefore, such
submissions were beyond our general terms of reference. Secondly, the Bill is concerned
basically with arming the Police, Customs, and other enforcement agencies with necessary
extra statutory powers to detect major drug trafficking, and to provide penalties that act as
deterrents to that activity. This legislative approach does not mean that the other aspects of
the drug problem-particularly treatment, rehabilitation, and education—are being ignored.
These are matters which are better dealt with by administrative decision, rather than by
legislative change. Thirdly, some members of the committee were concerned at certain
media reports on the submission made to the committee by the New Zealand Law Society.
With the exception of a criticism of clauses 37 to 40, and some other minor drafting changes,
the society was generally in support of the provisions of the Bill.
I turn now to those major provisions in the Bill that attracted attention, and will give a
brief indication of the committee's recommendation in respect of each. Clause 3 increases
the maximum penalty for dealing with class A drugs, such as heroin, from 14 years to life
imprisonment; and for class B drugs, such as LSD, from 10 to 14 years. The New Zealand
Law Society and the National Society for Alcoholism and Drug Dependence supported the
increased penalties. On the other hand, the New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties, the
New Zealand University Students Association, the General Practitioners Society, and others
took the view that, rather than increase penalties, a better approach would be to make
heroin and other drugs freely available to addicts, thereby depriving drug dealers of their
lucrative market. This might, very loosely, be described as the "heroin maintenance"
approach. Although the committee did not consider that it was within its brief to judge the
relative merits of the various methods of treating drug addicts—that is a matter for the
medical and related professions--we were satisfied, first, that most of the treatment methods
advocated were legally permissible within New Zealand—although, for the last 25 years, the
general policy has been against using heroin to treat addicts; but we concluded that the
"heroin maintenance" approach was inappropriate to the drug problem in New Zealand. We
therefore recommend that clause 3, which increases the penalties for drug dealing, should
proceed without amendment.
Clause 4 makes special provision to penalise those who conspire to commit specific drug
offences. Some of the witnesses argued that the provision was not really necessary and that,
in any event, it was inconsistent with section 310 of the Crimes Act. However, the committee
concluded that clause 4 is necessary if the penalty for conspiring is to be increased.
Furthermore, the clause effectively creates a new offence, and the provisions of the Crimes
Act are therefore not relevant. Clause 7 provides that the prosecution, in a magistrate's
court hearing on a drug offence, does not have to prove that the drug in question was in a
usable quantity, unless the defence puts that matter at issue. There was some criticism of this
clause from the Council for Civil Liberties, the NZUSA, and the Law Society. The criticism
differed in emphasis, from the view that the prosecution should not be enabled to repair its
case to the view that the magistrate should have a discretion to adjourn the hearing when the
issue of usability arises.
After carefully considering the submissions, the committee is of the view that the clause


## p. 3747 (#227) ###########################################

26 September
3747
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
is satisfactory as it stands. The provision is intended for use only in a summary trial—that is,
in the magistrate's court-and the question of usability is likely to arise in only a very few
cases. All that the clause really does is to provide that, where the defence puts the question
of usability at issue, and where the prosecution makes a request, there must be an
adjournment. No particular duration for that adjournment is specified, and it is in that
respect-that, if necessary, the magistrate is given considerable discretion.
In its original form clause 9 provided a defence for a police officer who committed a
drug offence in the performance of his duty. The New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties,
and others, while recognising the problems encountered by undercover policemen, criticised
the clause. After considering the matter carefully the committee believes the best approach
would be to provide that no undercover officer, or any officer directing or assisting him, can
be prosecuted under the Act, except with the leave of the Attorney-General. From the point
of view of the Police, and, for that matter, the other departments involved, this is, in fact, a
better solution to the problem, and, at the same time, should be more acceptable to those
opposed to the provision.
Clauses 14 to 18 provide a procedure for Supreme Court judges to issue warrants to the
Police enabling them to intercept private communications. Naturally, there were those
opposed to this provision, although others gave their support to it. The committee
recommends that these provisions should proceed, although we suggest a number of detailed
changes to give better effect to the warrant procedures. Clauses 29 to 36 provide stricter
rules relating to the granting of bail, and we recommend that these should proceed with only
two very minor amendments. There was some criticism of the details of bail provisions.
However, the committee points out that, except for the provision that bail can be granted
only by the Supreme Court in drug-dealing cases, clauses 29 to 36 follow the
recommendations of an interim report on bail prepared by the Criminal Law Reform
Committee.
In their original form, clauses 37 to 40 provided a procedure whereby, once a person has
been convicted of a drug-dealing offence, assets that he might have acquired in the course of
drug-dealing offences other than the offence in respect of which he has actually been
convicted could be taken into account in assessing any fine payable. Such fine would be
additional to, and not in derogation of, any term of imprisonment. In its original form the
provision attracted criticism-some resulting from a misunderstanding about whether the
burden of proof had been shifted to the accused. The select committee does not wish in any
way to depart from the principle that the fine imposed should reflect illicit gains, including
gains from other drug dealing, but does recommend an alternative or more acceptable
approach. In essence, when a person is convicted of a drug dealing offence, and the court is
satisfied on the balance of probability that any of his money or assets have been acquired
directly or indirectly from that offence, the court may, having regard to the value of those
assets, impose a greater fine than it would otherwise have imposed. When a person is
convicted of a drug-dealing offence, which I will refer to as the "primary offence", and the
court is satisfied, first, beyond reasonable doubt that before the commission of the primary
offence he had engaged in conduct other than that constituting the primary offence, that also
constituted drug dealing offences—
Mr Hunt: Members are listening to the chairman of a select committee reporting back

minutes available under the Standing Orders have expired. Secondly, on the balance of

probability that any money or assets owned by an offender had been acquired directly or
indirectly from drug dealing the court may have regard to the value of such assets in
imposing a greater fine. Furthermore, when the court is satisfied that the offender has
committed previous drug dealing offences and the offender fails to explain to the court's
satisfaction the source of the money or assets owned by him, the court may accept that
failure as evidence that the money or assets were derived by the offender from previous
drug-dealing offences, and could then take those assets into account in assessing the fine.
Part VI of the Bill inserts a new Part IXA in the Crimes Act 1961, to effectively outlaw
the use of listening devices, except as specifically allowed by the law. It is clear to the
committee that, whilst such a provision would be most desirable a blanket prohibition is not
without complications and would require detailed consideration. This was contemplated
when the Bill was introduced, and the select committee was instructed to divide the Bill into
parts if necessary; and this it has done. It has resolved to hold Part VI over for detailed
consideration during the parliamentary recess. The Bill, as now recommended by the select
committee, gives the Police and Customs vital means of detecting and enforcing the law
relating to drug trafficking, and the select committee commends it to the House. The
committee is grateful to the Department of Health and the Department of Justice--the two
departments involved in the preparation of the Bill-and also to the Police, Customs, and
the Post Office, for assisting the select committee in its deliberations. The committee is also
particularly grateful to parliamentary counsel, Mr Barker, for his work in preparing the
amendments that arose from the committee's decisions on the Bill.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 4)
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 4). The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table. The Bill was introduced late in the 1977 parliamentary session,
and was referred to the Local Bills Committee for recess study. It is the second part of the
legislation revising and amalgamating the Municipal Corporations Act 1954, the Counties
Act 1956, and the Local Government Act 1974.
The Bill is primarily concerned with procedures for the subdivision of land, and is a
complex technical measure. I think the fact that it has been before a select committee for the
best part of 10 months attests to that. Fifty-five formal submissions were made to the
committee, which heard and examined all those who wished to appear before it. In the
event, more than 20 parties, almost half those who made submissions, appeared before the
committee. It is understandable with a measure such as this that many people and
organisations would want to make submissions, resulting in the committee making a
substantial number of amendments. No other outcome could be expected, because of the
complexity of the Bill.
I do not propose to discuss the amendments in detail, because an opportunity will occur
during the Committee stage. However, it is appropriate to mention some of the more
important amendments. The proposed new section 260, in the Bill as introduced, provided
that before a united council undertook a function other than regional planning or civil
defence it had to have the agreement of all its constituent authorities. That has been
modified to provide that the acceptance of any new regional function by a united council will
be subject to resolutions of approval by those constituent authorities, being not less than
two, commanding a majority of the population, area, and adjusted net capital value of a
region. The majority would be the specified proportion as determined under the formula set
out in section 41(4) of the Local Government Amendment Act 1977, under which the
constituent authorities in a region may determine the form of a regional body to operate in
their region. That formula first appeared in the 1976 amending legislation.
Each constituent authority would be required to pass a resolution of either approval or
disapproval, and to advise the united council accordingly. A resolution of disapproval would
mean that the constituent local authority will not participate actually or financially in the
proposed function of the united council. It is important to remember that the constituent
local authorities will not participate actually or financially in the proposed function. That
would not prevent a territorial authority deciding at some future date to participate, subject
to the consent of a simple majority of members of that united council. I think it also bears
mentioning that the proposed amendment will not affect the position of ad hoc authorities,
such as electric power boards. The united council will assume the functions of such an
authority only if the authority agrees, or the appropriate Minister requests the Local
Government Commission to prepare a scheme to transfer the functions--and that is
provided in the law at the moment.
The reserve contributions on residential subdivisions have been altered from those
shown in the original Bill. That was the most keenly debated of the clauses in the legislation.
In the event, the Local Bills Committee has recommended that a territorial authority be
allowed to require a maximum of 130 m² per residential allotment or a maximum in cash or
land other than reserves of 7.5 percent of the sale value of the allotments. We had to decide
which of the two principles we should adhere to: should the reserve contributions be
essentially to provide land for reserves within the subdivision, or to meet the cost of projects


## p. 3756 (#236) ###########################################

3756
26 September
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 4)
beneficial to communities as a whole? I believe the formula sets it out and, as will be seen,
lays stress upon the former.
The Bill, as amended, also provides that a territorial authority may require a reserve
contribution of 20 m² or the cash equivalent for each household unit when no subdivision
occurs. That is a reduction from the 100 m² originally contained in the Bill. That particular
provision covers multiunit subdivision developments and the like. The contribution to
commercial and industrial development remains unchanged—that is, 0.5 percent of the value
of every development over $100,000.
The proposed new section 307 deals with the cancellation of agreements to purchase.
Here again the select committee made amendments, which I believe will largely meet the
objections raised during the course of the hearings. The 1-month cooling-off period has been
reduced to 14 days, and the withdrawal from the agreement will only be permitted 2 years
after the approval of the scheme plan or 1 year after the agreement to purchase, whichever is
the later.
The proposed new section 313 deals with the code of urban subdivision. Valid
submissions were made to the effect that the enforcement of the code by bylaw would be too
inflexible and would tend to defeat the purpose of the code as a guideline. To overcome that,
the committee has recommended that the proposed new section be amended to delete the
requirement that the code should be enforced by bylaw, and to make it clear that the code is
to be only a guide, or an explanatory document. In principle, those are the main changes to
the Bill as it was received by the Local Bills Committee.
In conclusion, I thank members on both sides of the House for their help, co-operation,
and courtesy during the many months of hearings, and through the deliberations on the Bill.
Members on both sides made many useful suggestions. I particularly thank the
Parliamentary Counsel, Mr McVeagh, and the departmental officers, led by Mr Williamson,
and including Mr Dench and Mr Tetley, who looked after the interests of the committee and
ensured that reports came in on time. I might add that many of the reports were voluminous,
as this is a very complex measure indeed. I believe that the Bill as reported back from the
select committee will stand close scrutiny, and that it is yet another move towards the day
that I believe both central government and local government look forward to, when we have
one Local Government Act covering all territorial local authorities in the country.

Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 4)
There was considerable disagreement among committee members when we considered
the problems of reorganising regional authorities, and particularly when considering the
further functions they might assume. I personally do not believe it is worth while straining to
find solutions to that particular problem, because of the badly organised reconstruction
provided for in the Local Government Amendment Act (No. 3). The provisions in that Act
make it almost impossible to promote the orderly development of regional authorities.
Under the National Government's legislation there is no point in creating a great fuss about
a very minor amendment. It appeared to be motivated entirely by political considerations.
Opposition members on the committee were much more concerned with the problem of
the reserves contribution. For at least 30 years, to my knowledge, and probably for a good
deal longer, the standard contribution has been up to 10 percent of the value of land involved
in a subdivision, payable to a reserve fund as required by the territorial local authority. That
has been variously interpreted, because the territorial local authority has always had power
to determine at what level payment or land contribution should be made, but the maximum
contribution was set at 10 percent. In general, the system has worked well, and has allowed
territorial local authorities, if so inclined, to go ahead with a progressive programme of
reserves development to benefit the public.
However, the Government, no doubt under pressure from its friends engaged in land
development or the financing of land development, has lowered the maximum contribution
to 7 percent. The argument put forward for that reduction was extremely weak. Land
developers, representatives of financial institutions interested in land development, and
surveyors, all of whom had a vested interest in keeping down the cost of land development,
though not the cost of sections, tried to get the committee to reduce the contribution in some
way, and the Government moved in their favour.
Evidence showed that, almost exclusively, section prices were determined by what the
market would bear, with no suggestion that the lowering of developers' costs would effect a
reduction in the prices of sections. However, considerable evidence showed that some
progressive local authorities, involved in comprehensive recreational reserve development
programmes, would be financially embarrassed because of the limitation of 74 percent put on
the contribution they might require from developers. This was the most contentious matter
considered by the committee. Labour members on the committee were uncomfortable at
being asked to support the interests of private developers against those of the public, and
were unhappy that the final report on the matter sided with the land developers.
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru): I support the reporting back of the Local Bills Committee
on the Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 4). The committee spent a great deal of
time on this detailed and complex measure, and there was a deal of unanimity on most
matters, largely due to the outstanding technical assistance given to the committee by
officers of the Department of Internal Affairs. The most important provision concerns
changes to what is known as the unanimity clause. The taking on by united councils of
functions, over and above the two mandatory functions of regional planning and civil
defence, has until now been by the unanimous vote of the united council. The suggestion for
change came from the new Local Government Commission, which, after discussion with
various local bodies around the country, discovered that, particularly in rural areas, local
authorities believed that it would hardly be worth while to form united councils only for
regional planning and civil defence.
After consulting the Counties Association and the Municipal Association, the
Government decided to proceed with the amendment to allow a majority of the local
authorities—the majority to be based on population, area, and rating value-to take on
extra functions, provided, of course, that an individual territorial authority that might wish
to opt out could do so by resolution. Response to this suggestion has been very favourable, a
significant majority of counties, boroughs, and municipalities responding well to the
proposal. Ad hoc authorities are not involved, and are still immune from the proposal that
united councils should take over functions at present enacted and administered by ad hoc
authorities, although by agreement extra functions at present administered by ad hoc
authorities could be taken over by a united council at the express wish of that ad hoc
authority. This amendment Bill is an important milestone in local government legislation,
and is part of a continuing process of amalgamation and revision of the Municipal
Corporations Act and the Counties Act.
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): The Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 4) is a complex
Bill. It deals not only with the establishment and the functions of regional united councils but

26 September
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 4)
also with subdivisions, redevelopment of land, reserves contributions, off-street parking,
general provisions on survey plans, operations on deposited plans, regional rates, and so on.
It would be impossible to report back on all matters considered by the committee, in view of
the hotchpotch of subjects covered by the Bill. I agree with the chairman of the Local Bills
Committee that we were greatly assisted by the technical advice given by officers of the
Department of Internal Affairs and parliamentary counsel, who attended the hearings.
The most contentious part of the committee's work, as the member for Porirua
intimated, concerned the reserves contributions provisions. I served on a local body for
many years, and was chairman of a town planning committee. Therefore, I know what
burden falls on ratepayers in providing adequately for open reserves, either for active or
passive recreation. The Bill, as reported back, provides for a substantial reduction in the
amount that local bodies have been able to claim for their reserves contribution. Most local
bodies expect a 10 percent contribution, either of land or the value of land. The Bill provides
that when any land is being taken by a local authority and other work is required, perhaps for
drainage or roading, that should be taken into consideration when finally costing the
reserves contribution. The new formula reduces the amount from 10 percent to 7.5 percent,
but that could place a greater burden on ratepayers, because subdividers can reasonably be
expected to provide land for reserves and other purposes. It is only right that when a
subdivider profits from the sale of land or from its settlement, an adequate amount of land
should be provided to give a better quality of life, and if that is not done a heavy burden will
be placed on the local bodies in developing reserves.
Difficulty has been experienced in getting access to sufficient loan money, and I know
that many local authorities will be financially embarrassed. They will suffer the cost of
providing roads and other facilities that will benefit the subdividers. The division of opinion
in the committee clearly showed those who were on the side of the subdividers and those
who were for the ratepayers. In any case, ratepayers have to contribute significantly towards
the development of facilities in new subdivisions that have been created by private
subdividers. There is perhaps good ground for saying that there should be a general
contribution from ratepayers, but the reduction in the reserves contribution provided for in
the Bill is quite unwarranted, and I shall have more to say on this matter as the Bill proceeds.
I remember being troubled 2 or 3 years ago by some people in Melling who had been
seeking to obtain access to land that they had bought from a company that had subdivided
the land on paper only. There was considerable delay, and those who had bought land off a
paper plan were not able to develop their sections as quickly as they would have liked. Many
purchasers and would-be purchasers were affected. I support the redrafted provision that
any purchaser who has suffered unnecessary delay may have his money refunded. It is vital
that people who have bought land from a paper plan only and before a subdivisional plan has
been approved by a local authority should have that right. I regret that such a course is
necessary, but there is no doubt that it is.
My only other comment relates to subdivisional land. Provision is being made to ensure
that local bodies can require subdividers to provide stable land for sections. I am thinking in
particular of the mischief that was caused at Himatangi Beach because of shifting sands. I
trust that the redrafted section 279 will provide the satisfaction that is required, and that
protection will be provided against subsidence, erosion, or inundation from any source for
land or any part thereof that does not form part of a subdivision. I shall develop this matter
further at a later stage.

Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The first of these Bills, of
course, makes major reference to the second, and it would be impossible to discuss it without
referring to the second. Therefore, it is quite reasonable to take the two together; but that is
the last reasonable point that can be taken from the discussion.
The Bills indicate the complete incompetence of the Government. The fact that we now
have to take urgency to get them through by 1 October is one factor, but that simply
illustrates that, until last week, the Government did not know what it wanted to do with the
country's tax legislation. It was holding up the legislation, and we got a Supplementary
Order Paper on 15 September, only one day after the Prime Minister had announced
Government policy outside the House at a meeting in Wellington.
That Government announcement involved major decisions for the business community
and for manufacturers. It amounted to a refusal to carry out an undertaking given by the
Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry. I presume that at the time, the
member for Tauranga was acting on behalf of the Government, but he gave a clear
indication at a public meeting that the proposals brought down last year in regard to the
valuation of stocks would be continued for a further year. After much investigation, the
Government has decided against that, obviously because of the size of the supplementary
estimates that it had to bring down 10 days ago. That illustrated what the Opposition has
been saying all along-that the Bills before the House are based on a very substantial deficit
and that the tax measures contained in them cannot last beyond the return of the National
Government; and that there is no intention on the part of members opposite to keep these
provisions in operation for more than the absolute minimum of time that might suffice to get
them through the election. That point was made over and over again during the Committee
stage of the Bills, but, in addition, quite a lot of time had to be spent on the Supplementary
Order Paper introduced, as I indicated, at very short notice. There was very little
opportunity for full discussion and, of course, because of the way things fell out with other
business of the House and the mismanagement of the Government, particularly over the
supplementary estimates, there was only about 4 hours' discussion on the very significant
clauses in the Bill.
I draw attention to two of them, because they illustrate the points the Opposition made
repeatedly in the second reading, points which it was laughed at for making. At that stage,
Opposition members said that a tax on persons on lower incomes was completely
unjustifiable. There have been three amendments to clause 20, two of which refer to the kind
of thing the Opposition was saying in the second reading. The proposed new paragraph (53)
in section 61 of the principal Act, inserted by clause 20, indicates that there is an exemption
for a small amount of income--it is defined as a nominal amount-derived by a disabled
person in respect of activities undertaken in a sheltered workshop. That refers specifically to
the money that is paid to residents of IHC workshops, who would have been brought within
the purview of the Income Tax Act by the Bill originally introduced into the House. It was
very strongly attacked by the Opposition, but, initially the Government pretended there was
no problem, and it was set right only at the last minute.
Another limited group had to be covered in the Supplementary Order Paper, and the
proposed new paragraph (54) of section 61 of the principal Act, inserted by clause 20,
contains an exemption of the value of the personal board and lodging and other personal
necessities received by unmarried members of religious societies whose sole occupation is in
the service of those bodies. So, although the Government has recognised an injustice done to
one section of the community, it has not recognised the injustice done to four very large
groups, and that is what the Opposition was fighting to remedy during the Committee stage.
They are: first, women who work seasonally, because no other work is available, and who, in
spite of a limited income, are now required to pay tax, and get no relief even in the Bill's
final form; secondly, all persons, specifically pensioners, who work part-time or limited time
to supplement their benefits and who are now paying tax; thirdly, students who work
whenever work is available, whether or not they have bursaries, and who are still paying tax;
and, fourthly, apprentices in their first couple of years of apprenticeship. We are supposed to
be encouraging apprentices to take on skilled jobs that will contribute to industry, but under
the Bill they come within the tax collector's net, and there is no escape for them.
In the Committee stage those matters were discussed widely by members on this side,

Bill-hardly a reduction in taxation. The third goal proposed in the Budget was a

Committee stage that a single-income family with three teenage children aged 13, 14, and 15,

teenage children is about $30 a week worse off just through having to provide food—but the
Government is asking that family to pay an extra $14 a week in tax.
The Bill means that a widow with three children aged 6, 8 and 10, who goes out to work
will pay the same amount of tax on a weekly income of $150 as the wife of an accountant who
is earning $32,000 a year; if his wife earns $150 a week, she will pay no more tax than the
widow with three teenage children. That is the justice of the National Government, and that
is what the Bill is trying to legislate for. A widow who has three teenage children and earns
$100 a week will pay as much tax under this Bill as a married man who has only one child,

$26.28." I still want to know what magic thing happens when a child turns 5.

all children equally, and any family with two children and a weekly income of $145 will pay

income of $214, the tax will be $30.85, the same as a family of six earning $162, which will
also pay tax of $30.85 a week.

overtime. I have already pointed out that a person who receives the young family rebate can
pay 58c in the dollar on any overtime worked. The Bill breaks every principle of taxation.

family responsibility. It should be fair and equitable. The Bill transgresses those principles.

The third point made by the Leader of the Opposition related to timing. He interpreted
that in the light of his own Labour Party philosophy. He said that bringing in tax changes on
1 October could only be seen as an election bribe. Every taxpayer knows that tax tables are
normally released on 1 April or 1 October. Any Government with its expenditure in mind
would avoid bringing out tax tables in say, July, August, or September, when the best time
to bring them out is halfway through the year. Every employer knows that that is easier for
him. It can hardly be done in a Budget announcement to take effect on 1 April. That is the
reason for the date 1 October, and if the Opposition insists that it is an election bribe, it is
demolishing all the arguments used in the Committee stage, because a bribe is something

or sometime, but within a very few days. If the Opposition wants to whinge about the timing,
let it, but I know the feeling about these tax reductions in my electorate.
The debate in the Committee stage came down to credibility. When New Zealanders
listen to taxation proposals they do not want to be immersed in masses of figures. I do not

credibility of the two parties they will look at past records.

Mr BIRCH: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The allegations were not of great substance, but I
felt that I should refer to them briefly. I emphasise that there have been substantial taxation
changes in the past 3 years-probably more so than in any other single 3-year period of a
previous Government. The changes have been criticised, canvassed, and debated during the
second reading and in the Committee stage of the Bill, almost ad nauseam.
I can add nothing new to the argument tonight. I want just to summarise what I consider
to be the most significant changes and to answer one or two criticisms that appear,
superficially at least, to have some validity. First, let me say that the Labour Opposition
tonight is opposing tax cuts for the largest single group of income earners—the middle
income earners. I emphasise that members of the socialist Opposition are opposing
reductions in taxation to those who contribute most to the country's productivity-those
earning between $4,500 and about $12,000 to $13,000 a year.
The first question asked, in a roundabout and oblique way, was why income tax
reductions should be directed to that group of people. Why should the largest income tax
reductions be for those in the centre, those earning about $8,000 per annum? People with a
feeling for the situation will know that such people contribute most to the gross national
product. They are in the centre of the productivity effort and must be, and are being, given
incentives to produce more. It has been said that income tax for middle income earners is a
disincentive. We had reached a stage where those in the middle income group were refusing
to work overtime or to accept greater responsibility because of high marginal rates of
taxation. If it does nothing else, the Bill will correct that, because it removes the high rates of
marginal taxation affecting such people as well as introducing substantial income tax
reductions as from this Sunday. It is no pie in the sky, as is the Labour Party's taxation
scheme-something that might be given if the Labour Party were to win the election.
The present marginal rates of taxation are implemented by a large number of steps-I
think about 17-between $3,500 and $22,000. They are being replaced by five steps, as set
out in the second schedule of the Income Tax Amendment Bill, starting at $4,500 and going
up to $10,000, and then to $16,000 and to $22,000. The first rate is for the lowest group, 14
1/2c in the dollar. Those in the middle-income group, between $4,500 and $10,000, will pay
38c in the dollar. If a taxpayer on $8,000 a year decides to work overtime and earns an extra
$1,000 or $1,500, his marginal rate of taxation does not increase-a point that seems to have
escaped the notice of Opposition members. If that same taxpayer accepts added
responsibility and is paid more, his tax rates will not increase-a fundamental improvement
surely.
Now I come to the question of benefits for certain family groups. The Opposition fails
or refuses to understand the recognition given to the young family or the single-income
family. The Government recognises that the family as a stable unit in society must be
encouraged. At the time that the rebate was introduced and recognition was given to the
family unit, families were being forced, through economic circumstances, to send the second
spouse out to work. The National Government said it wanted to encourage the second
spouse, the mother, to stay at home, if that were her wish, by granting income tax
concessions for mothers with chidren under the age of 5 years. That was the genesis of the
young family rebate. Its value has been recognised. It does not represent an increase in tax
when a child goes to school; it is a concession to families with children under 5 years of age, a
valuable and just recognition of economic help needed by that group.
The Government has also recognised the single-income earner. In thousands of families
the mother would prefer to stay at home, but economic pressures sometimes encourage or
put pressure on her to go out to work. If a Government, through fiscal or taxation measures,
can take some of the pressure off such a mother, then those measures are good and just—yet
they are being criticised by the Opposition. Its members have failed to recognise the
benefits.

## p. 3785 (#265) ###########################################

Income Tax Amendment Bill
amazing one. It cannot be called revolutionary, because it is an enormous step backwards, a
step backwards past the Victorian age, because we have a new principle of taxation from the

country is to pay tax from the first dollar he earns. That is a revolutionary concept, because
up to 1 October 1978 it was accepted in New Zealand that every taxpayer was entitled to a

Treasury, has been removed.

millionaire, he or she is entitled to a sum of money free of tax; that is quite simple, and is
what the Bill is all about. The effect of the Bill is simple. It means that people who would
normally expect to be completely free of tax because they do not earn enough under any
sensible definition to be able to get a living wage, will be dragged into the taxation net for the
first time.

Let us assume inflation will be 12 percent a year, and find out what this Bill will do to a
person on the average weekly wage. In October 1979 he can reasonably expect, at 12 percent
inflation, to have moved from $140 to $156.80. That means he will pay $22.37 a week in tax
next year, which means he has moved from paying 11.1 percent of his income in tax to paying
14.3 percent. But by October 1980 he can reasonably expect to be earning $175.62, and
under these scales he will then pay $31.42 in income tax, so within 2 years he will be paying
17.9 percent of his income in income tax. In other words, his tax will almost have doubled.
By October 1980, under the tax scales in this proposal, a person on the average wage will pay
$41.87, allowing for 12 percent inflation, and that is a massive 21.3 percent income tax rate.
The Government is planning to develop income tax at the present rate of inflation. The
tax will have gone up four times, and as a percentage of income it will have doubled.
Government members have not talked about that. They have not pointed out that Labour's
scheme is indexed against inflation, and that it will be adjusted automatically for inflation.
The Government's scheme is to continue the present system, whereby, because of inflation,
ordinary wage and salary earners find themselves driven into higher income tax brackets.
Their real incomes drop, and the Government's real income rises. Government members do
not talk about that. They do not want to talk about the fact that within 3 years at 12 percent
inflation a person on the average income of $140 paying $15.48, or 11.1 percent of his
income, in tax, will have moved to paying $41.87, or 21.3 percent of his income, in tax. That
is the clear difference between the Labour Party's proposals and the Government's
proposals. Can any member opposite deny that that is the principle contained in the Bill?

26 September The QE II Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill
3793
THE QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND ARTS COUNCIL OF NEW ZEALAND
AMENDMENT BILL
Third Reading
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): On behalf of the Minister of Internal
Affairs, I move, That this Bill be now read a third time.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): I support the third reading of the Bill setting up the
Council for Maori and South Pacific Arts, and remind the House that, when the Bill was
introduced, it was the Government's intention to expand opportunities for promoting the art
and cultural traditions of both the Maori and Pacific Island people of New Zealand. It did so
because it found an extra $50,000, and it was hoped that the Arts Council could undertake
this function. When the Committee of the Whole considered the Bill, it did not change the
basic principles referred to it by the select committee, which were that the Pacific people
were likely to be affected. The Arts Council is not the only body with the statutory
responsibility of undertaking such work. For many years, traditional art work by the Maori
people has been assisted by the Maori Purposes Fund Board, its ad hoc body, the New
Zealand Polynesian Festival Committee, and the New Zealand Arts and Crafts Institute of
Rotorua. All had important functions, and their basic functions are not altered.
The Government wished to include the South Pacific people who now reside
permanently in New Zealand. The contribution made by the member for Auckland Central
should be acknowledged. We have come to accept that many people who came from
Western Samoa, the Cook Islands, Niue, and the Tokelaus, as well as some from Fiji and
Tonga, now reside permanently in New Zealand. It has not been easy to identify them as a
group without offending their distinctive, specific identities and cultures. To overcome that
difficulty, it was suggested that the name of the council should include the words "South
Pacific", thus embracing the whole region, and acknowledging that they are now permanent
residents of New Zealand. A great deal of care has also been taken to ensure that no conflict
arises between the newly established council and existing statutory bodies with similar
functions. Moreover, I believe it will be the function of the new council to win the confidence
of both Maori and Island communities in New Zealand.
The $50,000 allocated to the council this year is not very much to enable it to initiate its
work. However, the Minister of Internal Affairs, during both the second reading and the
Committee stage of the Bill, gave an undertaking that the Government will ensure that
further funds are provided to assist the council to carry out its work. It is also worth
reminding ourselves that such a council can play a significant part in promoting the
distinctive cultures, traditions, and practices of different ethnic groups, both within New
Zealand and throughout the South Pacific.
Members on this side of the House recall with considerable pride the effort made by the
third Labour Government to establish and encourage the South Pacific Arts Festival. I
emphasise that that festival was promoted by the former Labour Government, through
various agencies, such as the South Pacific forum, and that the Government then handed it
to existing cultural boards and authorities. That task was carried out with distinction. I am
sure the next council will have a similar capacity for advising the Government. I understand
that the next South Pacific festival is to be held in Papua New Guinea. The new council will
probably be called upon to advise the Government on how New Zealand can best participate
in and support the festival, which was initiated in Fiji some years ago.
In the past the Government has been advised by the New Zealand Polynesian Festival
Committee, a body responsible for the Maori Purposes Fund Board. That it will continue its
good work is evidenced by its efforts to arrange a festival in Wellington early next year. Plans
are now well advanced, and the committee is looking forward to hosting a display of Maori
and Island art works and cultural activities in the Hutt Valley. The new council may add
greatly to the work already carried out by other groups.
Mr N. P. H. Jones: What are you talking about?

make it clear to him?

PRIVATE INVESTIGATORS AND SECURITY GUARDS AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I explained to the House in introducing this measure, the Private
Investigators and Security Guards Act makes provision for the control by a licensing and
disciplinary authority of both private investigators and security guards. Under that Act,
which was passed in 1974, a registrar is appointed to license those wanting to operate within
the definitions in the Act and to hear disciplinary proceedings brought against licensees or
those whom they employ.
Amendments to the principal Act are necessary to overcome some difficulties, or
potential difficulties, of a substantive nature and to make procedural changes. The principal
substantive amendment redefines "private investigator". Under section 3 of the 1974 Act a
private investigator is a person who undertakes any activity that is defined as gathering
information. As that definition is rather too wide, a number of activities that might fall
within it are specifically excluded, and there is a further provision that allows the Governor-
General to declare by Order in Council that persons in particular classes of business are not
private investigators. In the Bill that definition has been tidied up by retaining the present
definition of "private investigator" and by further providing that a person is not to be
considered to be carrying on the business of a private investigator when he carries on any
activity that involves some element of investigation if that is only a necessary, usual, or
reasonable incident of any undertaking that is not covered by the definition of private
investigator. Under the Act such a person would have to be excluded from its provisions by


## p. 3801 (#281) ###########################################

26 September Private Investigators and Security Guards Amendment Bill
3801
an Order in Council. The specific exclusions from the definition of "private investigator"
that I have just mentioned will obviate the need to make an Order in Council for every
situation that is unintentionally covered by the definition.
It has been urged on the Government that the provisions of the Act excluding debt
collectors and credit bureaus from the definition of "private investigator" should be
repealed, with the effect that those businesses would come within the definition of "private
investigator". Although it is true that those operating the businesses in question often seek
information on behalf of a client, the Government is not persuaded that this fact alone is
sufficient reason to license debt collectors and credit bureaus as private investigators. Such
businesses operate in a very much narrower field than licensed investigators do. If there is a
difficulty with these agencies, it arises not so much in the field of occupational licensing as in
the field of privacy. With respect to those who operate credit bureaus, it may well be
sufficient, on the need arising, if there is a general right for a person to learn of the
information held about him, but that matter is not in the Bill and can be taken no further in
the context of the Bill.
The Bill makes provision for the licence issued to security guards to be divided into
classes of business, a licensee being authorised to carry on all or some of those classes
depending on his suitability for each class. The classes of business follow the categories of
business defined in section 4 of the principal Act and differentiate between those who guard
property or install burglar alarms or other forms of electronic surveillance or who enter
premises for the purpose of selling or advising upon such systems.
Under the present provisions of the Act, a person who applies for and obtains a security
guard's licence for the purpose of guarding property may at some later stage go into the
business of installing electronic surveillance equipment. Neither the licensee nor his
employees may be suitable to carry on such a business, although his suitability to carry on the
business of guarding property remains unquestioned. The Bill provides that every person
who applies for a security guard's licence must do so in respect of each class of business that
he intends to undertake. His suitability will then be assessed in respect of each class of
business, and a licence may be issued for all classes of business or limited to a certain class or
classes.
Clause 3 amends the definition of "security guard" by adding another class of business
that requires the obtaining of a security guard's licence. For obvious reasons, those who
monitor burglar alarms or other detection equipment will require a security guard's licence.
Clauses 4 to 10 inclusive make amendments consequential upon the provisions relating
to the issuing of a security guard's licence for specified classes of business. Briefly, their
effect is that a person must apply for a licence in respect of each class of business he intends
to carry on, and any person objecting to the issue of a licence may object either generally or
in respect of a particular class of business. Before issuing a licence, the registrar must be
satisfied that the applicant is a suitable person to carry on each class of business specified in
his application. There is also a procedure by which a licensee will be able to add a new class
of business to his licence.
Clause 11 adds a crime involving dishonesty as a new ground upon which a security
guard's licence may be cancelled. This additional ground is necessary because of the gradual
movement of the security industry from mere guarding to the handling of money and
complex security systems.
Clauses 12 to 14 make some general amendments to the provisions of the Act relating to
licences. Under the present law an applicant for a licence must serve a copy of his application
on the Police. It was pointed out that the registrar can never be certain that this has been
done and, similarly, the Police have no way of knowing if the application, of which they have
a copy, has actually been made. Accordingly, clause 13 provides that an application for a
licence will be made to the registrar with the obligation on the registrar to serve a copy on the
Police. The provisions relating to the renewal of a licence have been changed because, rather
than endorsing the fact of renewal on a licence, which is impractical because licences are
sealed into plastic envelopes, it is intended that a renewal licence be issued.
Clauses 15 to 19 amend several provisions relating to the responsible employees of a
security guard. Clause 15 has a similar effect to clause 13. The provisions of clause 16 relating
to the renewal of a certificate of approval are necessary for the same reason as the provisions
relating to the renewal of a licence. This certificate, like a licence, is issued in a sealed plastic
envelope, and a renewed certificate must be issued each year.
Clause 17 overcomes a difficulty with certificates of approval, which currently bear the


## p. 3802 (#282) ###########################################

3802
Private Investigators and Security Guards Amendment Bill 26 September
name and registered office of the employer in whose name the certificate was sought. If an
employee takes up employment with another security firm, the name of his past employer
remains on the certificate, at least until the certificate of approval is renewed. The Bill
provides that, rather than bearing an employer's name and address, a certificate of approval
will bear words to the effect that the holder of such a certificate must give that information
on request.
Clause 18 places an obligation on a licensee to inform the registrar when an employee
who holds a certificate of approval leaves his employment, and when such a person is
employed by him. This will ensure that the registrar's records are kept up to date. Clause 19
gives an approved employee the same protection from a frivolous or vexatious complaint
now enjoyed by a licensee. Clauses 20 to 22 make minor amendments to the powers of the
Supreme Court on applications made to it under the Act, and give the registrar a discretion
to extend the time for filing any document or making any applications under the Act.

FENCING BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill amends and consolidates the Fencing Act 1908 following a review of
the Act by the Property Law and Equity Law Reform Committee, which reported in 1972.
The Bill has been considered by the Lands and Agriculture Committee, which received 10
submissions. Arising out of those submissions, some important changes have been made to
the Bill. Dealing as it does with the creation and the registration of fencing covenants and
agreements, the Bill has its complexities of a technical legal nature. The committee's task
was therefore unenviable, but the Bill as reported back indicates that the committee has
discharged it well, and I want to thank its members for that.
As I said, the new measure re-enacts existing legislation and I do not propose to tire
members with a recital of all the clauses-not that I want to suggest that members are tired. I
should, however, refer to the important changes. The most important is that the Crown,
subject to four important exceptions, is now to be bound by the provisions of the Bill and will
accordingly be liable to contribute to the cost of erecting or repairing a fence. This change
arose out of a proposal by Federated Farmers, and reverses the position of the Crown in the
Bill as introduced. It is, therefore, a notable and, I believe, a timely shift in liability. The
four exceptions are set out in clause 3; namely, roads, national parks, railways, and reserve
land along coasts, lakes, rivers, and creeks-sometimes known as riparian reserves.
In assuming liability it must also be remembered that the Crown gains corresponding
rights to claim contributions from neighbouring landowners, and to that extent the
imposition of liability on the Crown is not as one-sided as might appear at first sight.
Moreover, when the suggestion of imposing liability on the Crown was made, various
Government departments were canvassed to obtain their views on the proposal, and it
became quickly apparent that, although these departments had been under no statutory
liability to fence, most of them, as part of a good-neighbour policy, had made some
contribution to fencing by way of material, services, or financial contribution. To a large
extent therefore, this cushioned the contingent liability of the Crown. The proposal that the
Crown be bound by the provisions of the Fencing Bill is also consistent with trends in other
legislation, that before the law the Crown should have the same obligations as individuals.
The Bill as introduced was restrictive as to the type of fencing covenant that could be
registered. In the light of this, local bodies submitted that the traditional means of protecting
themselves from liability to contribute to the cost of fencing had been taken away. They
submitted that this was unreasonable. To understand why the Bill, as introduced, was
restrictive as to the type of covenant that could be registered, it is necessary to go back to the
report of the Property Law and Equity Reform Committee. One of the problems that
confronted the committee was the proliferation of fencing covenants registered on titles,
which eventually became spent. These spent covenants, unless removed under a rarely used
provision of the Land Transfer Act 1952, remained on the title with consequential
inconvenience to following dealings.
In attempting to overcome the problem of spent fencing covenants littering numerous
titles, the Property Law and Equity Reform Committee, as part of a two fold approach to
the problem, recommended restricting the type of fencing covenant that could be registered
to a covenant that was negative in effect and that would inure only for the benefit of the
transferor of the land, being the owner of the adjoining land. The other proposal was that


## p. 3810 (#290) ###########################################

3810
26 September
Fencing Bill
registered covenants should expire after 12 years. The effect of implementing this proposal
in the Bill precluded local bodies from registering fencing covenants unless they were the
actual transferors of the land, and, furthermore, as the New Zealand Law Society pointed
out, prevented the registration of other types of covenant relating to boundary division-for
example, a covenant not to fence in an "open lawn" type of subdivision.
The Lands and Agriculture Committee accepted the point made in both submissions on
the matter of fencing covenants, and the Bill as reported back introduces a new definition—
"fencing agreement”—and amends the definition of "fencing covenant”. The Bill introduces
new clauses 4A and 4B and clause 5 is amended and clause 6 is omitted. The effect of these
changes is that local bodies will be able to register covenants that will not expire after 12
years, and agreements relating to fencing, including an agreement not to fence, can be
registered.
Clause 6A is new and is intended to cover the situation when an adjoining owner intends
to erect a fence on the boundary, but does not intend to seek contribution from his
neighbour to cover the costs. In the Government's view an adjoining owner, particularly in
an urban area, should have some say on the type of fence that is to be erected on a boundary
but for which contribution is not being requested.
Another major change comes in clause 13. As it was introduced, a fencing notice given
under the Bill ran with the land. The Bill now provides that, if one of the parties ceases to be
an occupier, the notice or cross-notice shall cease to have effect and any new occupier must
be served with a fresh notice. This change preserves the principle that a purchaser who
acquires a property for value without notice of any outstanding interests affecting that
property takes it free of those interests. As the existing Fencing Act did not specifically cover
the point, it was important that the Bill clarified the position.
The other amendments in the Bill are of a minor and consequential nature and do not
require any further clarification. Finally, the reference in clause 3 to section 45 of the
Government Railways Act 1949 does not comprehensively cover all operational railway
land, and I intend to introduce a Supplementary Order Paper during the Committee stage to
clarify the land to which the Bill applies.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Opposition supports the Bill, but I want to make
one or two observations, particularly about clause 6A, which came about through
representations made by the member for Franklin. The explanatory note handed to the
Lands and Agriculture Committee stated that the proposal was put forward for the
committee's consideration by the member for Franklin, and that, under the present law, an
adjoining owner was free to erect a fence on a boundary without the consent of his
neighbour; so long as he did not intend to seek a contribution from his neighbour towards
the cost of the fence, he did not need to advise the neighbour of his intention or seek the
neighbour's consent.
The proposal of the member for Franklin would mean that the adjoining occupier could
proceed without his neighbour's consent or a court order if any part of the fence encroached
on the neighbour's land. If he went ahead, the neighbour could apply to the court for an
order for the fence to be removed. The Minister pointed out during his second reading
speech that the normal procedure in the past under the principal Act—and I think accepted
by everybody-was that there should be agreement between both parties. Under the
amendment notice is to be served to an owner when one of the adjoining owners wants to
build a fence right on the boundary and is not asking for some contribution to be made. The
amendment simply provides that the consent must first be received by the occupier of the
land or pursuant to a court order.
We in the committee felt that the matter was contentious, because really it is restricted
to urban areas. In rural areas we accept that, when boundaries have to be fenced, we bear
the cost accordingly. One of the messengers this afternoon pointed out to me the difficulties
he had experienced with four neighbours-two were co-operative, and two were not. He
suggested that the adjoining occupiers would all in fact benefit from the work he would
undertake in constructing a boundary fence.
As I said earlier, the committee had strong feelings about the amendment, and I am still
of the opinion that, in some respects, it encroaches upon and infringes the rights of
individuals. I wonder how far Parliament can go in infringing the rights of private individuals
in this way. It is fair to say that the committee was not unanimous in accepting the proposal.
However, it was pointed out by the member for Franklin that he knew of particular cases.
The Property Law and Equity Reform Committee made some reference to the matter,

as it has had experience over a number of years, particularly with the Law Society. I repeat

shall cease to have effect." That clears up the matter of the change of occupier.
I find the definition of “fence" intriguing. The interpretation in the principal Act was

Hon. J. B. BOLGER: When the ministry receives replies to its letters to the various

discussed further.

Food Price Increases
7. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: What was
the basis on which his departmental officers authorised the price of Gregg's 16oz food
colouring to be increased from $1.19 to $1.93, a jump of 74c?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The increase in the
price of Gregg's 16oz food colouring was not notified to my department. The manufacturer's
total annual sales of this product have a value of less than $50,000 and the manufacturer
considered no advice of the increase was necessary in terms of regulation 16(e) of the
Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974. My department is investigating this matter. The
prices quoted in the question are correct, but my department has yet to complete its
investigation into the reasons for the increase. I shall provide the honourable member with
further information when this has been done.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Minister confirm that, until such time as this question was
presented to him, his departmental officers had made no inquiry into the substantial
increase?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Under the terms of the regulations, which were
promulgated by the honourable member when he was the Minister, I understand that the
officers are not required to investigate when companies have a turnover of less than $1.5
million. Certainly, companies that increase prices are required under the regulation to keep
information so that increases can be picked up during the department's surveillance, which
takes place on a regular basis throughout the country. I am not in a position to tell the
honourable member how many investigations have been held into this particular matter. I
can only tell him that the price increase and the company's claim are being investigated.
Admittedly, the increase is 62 percent, but the price for the commodity went up by 72.5
percent in 1 year under the Labour administration.
