Unemployment Benefits
8. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) to the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he seen the statement
made by the Leader of the Opposition as quoted in the Evening Post of Tuesday, 19
September 1978, that "more than $150 million will be paid out this year in unemployment
benefits", and is this figure correct?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Yes, I have seen the statement
referred to, and it is not correct. The main estimates for 1978-79 provided $45.7 million for
unemployment benefits, and the supplementary estimates provided a further $11 million.
This amounts to a total estimated expenditure on unemployment benefits for 1978-79 of
$56.7 million.
Miss Dewe: What number of unemployed was taken into account in calculating the $45.7
million set out in the main estimates?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The assessment was made on an average of 18 000 unemployed.
Because of the increase in the number of unemployed this year, a new assessment, on the
basis of 22 000 was made for the supplementary estimates. The latest statistics available-for
15 September 1978-show that 18 035 people were in receipt of the unemployment benefit,
and that total is falling.
Mr Marshall: Will the Minister confirm that more than $150 million is budgeted for
expenditure on unemployment benefits and on subsidies for special relief work, and that a
further substantial amount could be included for taxation revenue lost from people who want
to work but are unable to obtain jobs?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That supplementary question is wide of the original question.
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I can confirm that the supplementary question represents more
woolly thinking by the Labour Opposition.
Mr Birch: As the total amount budgeted for unemployment benefits is $56 million, has
the Leader of the Opposition corrected his statement that more than $150 million would be
paid out this year in unemployment benefits?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I am not aware of the Leader of the Opposition having corrected
his statement, but I can confirm that the total amount budgeted for this year is $56.7 million
and not $150 million, the latter amount indicating more woolly thinking by the Labour Party.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Will the Minister confirm that when one considers that the words
used by the Leader of the Opposition were "unemployment relief" and not "unemployment
benefit", there is no case to answer, and the question becomes a typical mare's nest?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Those on special relief receive full award wages. We can only
conclude that this is a further deliberate attempt by the Labour Party to mislead the public.

Child Care, South Auckland
15. Mr WETERE (Western Maori), on behalf of Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn), to the
Minister of Social Welfare: What provision is there for after-school care for children of
working parents in south Auckland?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): There is no programme
administered by the Department of Social Welfare under which financial assistance can be
made available for organisations or individuals providing after-school care for children of
working parents. Priority has been given in this area to the care of pre-school children
through the child-care subsidy programme, under which capital and capitation subsidies are
made available to approved organisations providing child-care facilities. Most working
parents are, of course, able to make their own private arrangements for the after-school care
of their children.
Mr Birch: Can the Minister confirm that there is a child-care centre in Pukekohe that is
receiving the capital and capitation subsidies?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can confirm that. It is a particularly good day-care centre
in Pukekohe. It is well run, and is doing a tremendous job in that area.
Mr Wetere: Do I take it that the Minister and his department have some other projects
in mind?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No, we are emphasising pre-school child care. The child-care
subsidy programme is for the care of pre-school children—that is, children under 5 years of
age. The present level of the subsidy is 66 percent of the building cost and $7.80 a week
capitation subsidy for each qualifying child under care. I emphasise that there are over 40
child-care centres in the south Auckland area.

3822
27 September

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Education. "During the last 2 years my department has developed and put into practice a
comprehensive programme to reduce truancy. It involved regularly reviewing the level of
truancy; issuing a circular that gave guidance to principals; a national survey of absenteeism;
reviews of the teaching programmes for pupils at risk for truancy and of the procedures used
to check attendance and follow up unexplained absences; and a review of liaison with
parents and with other agencies that have responsibilities in this matter. A survey of
education board districts in May 1978 revealed that in the past year truancy has declined in
districts that had the greatest incidence. No increases are evident in any district."

22. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen a publication entitled

liquor and cigarettes, ostensibly for community health, only $2 million was paid out to
hospital boards. Of an estimated $26 million to be taken from the same source this year,

and, if not, what is the correct position regarding the expenditure of these community health
funds?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the publication referred to. I can say
that the statement in the publication on the additional tax on alcoholic liquor and tobacco is
quite incorrect and misleading. In 1977-78 the expected revenue from the additional lc tax
was $17.3 million, which was allocated to community health projects and included $3.369
million to hospital boards for specific projects. The estimated revenue from this source in
1978-79 is about $27 million, and of this sum $10.3 million has been allocated to hospital
boards for specific community care projects, including domiciliary care, family health
counselling centres, and health centres administered by hospital boards. The balance has
been allocated to other community care projects.
Miss Dewe: From where would the Labour Party have obtained the figures, and is there
any relationship between the figures quoted in the publication and the figures contained in
the estimates or any of the department's reports?
Hon. T. F. GILL: There is absolutely no explanation as to why these quite erroneous
figures, which are designed to mislead the public, were used by the Labour Party.

portfolios in the year ended 31 March 1978?

Expenditure by the Ministry of Defence that can be identified as having been
allocated to the Auckland area was $5,917,156 in 1978. This figure includes
capital expenditure on housing, buildings, and facilities, and the cost of mainten-
ance of defence establishments in Auckland, including Papakura. Expenditure on
equipment, wages, salaries, and the like cannot be allocated by location. The
Police accounting system does not provide means of ascertaining expenditure
solely within the Auckland metropolitan area. However, for the year ended 31
March 1978, expenditure in the 17 police districts (excluding amounts paid by
national headquarters) amounted to $61,591,000. Of this sum $14,757,000, or
27 percent of the total, was expended in the Auckland police district.

7.
Foreign Affairs Expenditure-Auckland
(7/9/78)
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: How
much expenditure was allocated to the Auckland metropolitan area for each of
his portfolios in the year ended 31 March 1978?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The only
formal allocation of funds that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs makes to the
Auckland metropolitan area is to meet the annual running costs of its Auckland
district office. These costs, mainly salaries, amounted to $105,000 in 1977-78.
As far as expenditure under the aid programme is concerned, the ministry does
not allocate expenditure by regions within New Zealand. The purchase of goods
and services for aid projects is on a competitive basis over the whole country.
Procurement of equipment is done through normal tendering procedures, but a
significant number of contracts goes to the Auckland metropolitan area, reflecting
that area's dominance in the New Zealand industrial and manufacturing sector.
Most consignments of aid equipment are dispatched from Auckland by sea or air
freight. In addition, a number of Auckland-based consultancy firms have obtained
substantial contracts for the supervision and implementation of individual. aid
projects. Further, a large number of aid-sponsored overseas students are attending
educational institutions in the Auckland area. Finally, I should mention that the
ministry subsidises, by means of grants from its vote, the shipping links between
New Zealand and various Pacific Island countries, particularly the Cook Islands
and Niue, for which Auckland is usually the New Zealand terminal.

Sales Tax on Wine
(7/9/78)

support would be given to the Wine Institute of New Zealand by the New Zealand
Wholesale Wine and Spirit Merchants Federation for any action the institute
might take to reduce the escalating sales tax on wine, and, if so, has the Govern-
ment plans to change the format of the tax or to reduce it?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied: I have seen the article

since 1942, and as wine prices have increased so has the tax content. This is the
position with all goods that are subject to sales tax on an ad valorem basis. I
recently received submissions from the Wine Institute for sales tax to be levied
at a specific rate, and discussions are currently being held with this organisation.

Twizel Project Site Allowance
(7/9/73)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of State Services: Which
groups working at Twizel qualify for a site allowance; which occupational
groups do not; and what is the reason for the difference?


## p. 3829 (#309) ###########################################

27 September
3829
Questions and Replies
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: 1. The State Services
Tribunal has approved payment of a project construction site allowance to the
following groups of State employees at Twizel: (a) all full-time employees whose
work is directly related to the construction undertaking; (b) any full-time State
itinerant workers who may be required to work periodically on any of the several
construction sites associated with this project; (c) transmission line construction
employees, should they be required to live in and work out from the Twizel project

and directly related to the project construction undertaking-this reflects private
sector practice; (b) other full-time State employees, including school teachers,
traffic officers, dental nurses, and police, whose work is not directly related to the
construction undertaking. In 1976 the Public Service Association made application
for payment of site allowance to be extended to these groups, but this was declined
by the tribunal.

Housing Corporation-Loan Repayment Rates
(8/9/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Housing: (1) What propor-
tion of Housing Corporation civilian clients had mortgage repayments (i) in
excess of $50 weekly, (ii) in excess of $60 weekly, (iii) in excess of $70 weekly,
(iv) in excess of $80 weekly, as indicated in (a) the 1975 loans survey, (b) the
1976 loans survey, (c) the 1977 loans survey; (2) what were the respective sample
sizes in each of the three surveys, how were the samples selected, and what were
the statistical limits of error in each case?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: (1) Information on
the weekly cash outgoings on mortgage payments is not available from the 1975
and 1976 housing loans surveys. In the 1977 survey, of civilian mortgagors for
whom this could be determined (75.3 percent of the sample), 26 percent were
paying in excess of $50 per week, 12 percent were paying in excess of $60 per
week, 4 percent were paying in excess of $70 per week, 1 percent were paying in
excess of $80 per week. (2) The sample size was 200 in 1975, 202 in 1976, and
200 in 1977. This represented, respectively, one-eighth, one-ninth, and one-eighth
of the population of loans authorised over the period of the surveys. Each of the
samples was taken systematically, with a quota from each Housing Corporation
branch set according to the number of loans it had authorised. The statistical
limits of error for the 1975 survey are not known. The statistical limits of error
are different for each variable. For example, for the mean age of the mortgagor
the sample mean ages in 1976 and 1977 were, respectively 30.10 years and 30.64
years, compared with population means of 30.60 years and 30.67 years. Analysing
the likely error in this figure, the sample mean for 1976 probably lies between
30.03 years and 31.17 years, and for 1977 29.53 years and 31.75 years (both
established at the 95 percent level of confidence). Accordingly, the sample is seen
as well based.

Middlemore and Epsom Day Hospitals
(8/9/78)
MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Health: Is he satisfied
that at Middlemore Hospital (full licence) and Epsom Day Hospital (limited
licence) "there are, in the institution, adequate surgical and other facilities and
adequate and competent staff for the safe performance of abortions" in accordance
with sections 21 (1) (b) and 21 (2) (b) of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and
Abortion Act, as there are no willing operators at Middlemore, and there have
been no operations or assessments at Epsom Day Hospital since 23 June, and, if
he is not satisfied that the above criteria are met, will he seek to have the licences
revoked by the Abortion Supervisory Committee?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The sections of the Contracep-
tion, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act referred to are matters for decision by the
Abortion Supervisory Committee. Parliament has specifically provided that it is
to be the task of the committee to determine whether an institution has adequate
accommodation, surgical, and other facilities and competent staff to ensure the
safe performance of abortions. Section 25 of the Act provides a procedure whereby
the committee, if it believes that an institution is no longer meeting the various
requirements laid down in section 21, may cancel the licence for that institution.

Waikokupu Harbour-Rebuilding Breakwater
(8/9/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Transport: Will he approve
the rebuilding of the 50-yard breakwater at Waikokupu Harbour, the formation
of which still remains, which will provide protection at the harbour mouth?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: The break-
water in question was established in 1930 or thereabouts to allow vessels to enter
and discharge steel and machinery at a wharf (not now existing) for power
projects such as Tuai or the Mohaka viaduct. If an economic proposal were to be
advanced which showed that rebuilding the breakwater was technically feasible
and could be financed and maintained by a responsible organisation, it could be
considered favourably for approval.

34.
LPG Supplies for Christchurch Gas Co.
(8/9/78)
Hon W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Energy: Has he seen
the report in the Mercantile Gazette of 10 July 1978 in which the chairman of
directors of the Christchurch Gas Co. asks a series of six questions of the Govern-
ment, and what is his reply to each of the questions, as set out below: (1) Will
our company at some time during the next 2, 3, 4 years, receive a supply of an
appropriately priced indigenous oil type feedstock such as LPG for reforming and
reticulation and for distribution in pressure vessels-or will it not? (2) Whether
the answer is yes or no, is the company required to keep operating and producing
gas in this 2, 3, 4 year period? (3) If it is to continue operating, will the Govern-
ment underwrite all of the extraordinary maintenance expense directly associated
with extending the life of the coal carbonising plant, or does it expect the share-
holders to meet the continuing losses? (4) Will the Ministry of Energy guarantee
to supply coal for carbonising in the correct quantities and blends to avoid further
damage to the plant, causing yet greater losses? (5) Will the Ministry of Energy
at once review subsidies as a means of funding the exceptional maintenance
expense and ensuring that the capital is adequately serviced? (6) Will the
Government recognise that the 5-year straight-line depreciation policy adopted
by the company is the correct policy in the circumstances and as such is to be
applied in the taxation accounts as well as the published accounts?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: (1) LPG from Maui is
expected to be available in Lyttelton in about 2 years' time, but the Govern-
ment is not in a position to give commercial assurances regarding price or supply.
Even though a maximum bulk supply price may be fixed in due course, the
company must be prepared to negotiate its own price arrangements within
such a maximum. (2) The Government is not responsible for deciding whether
the company should continue operating. This is a matter for the New Zealand
Gas Council pursuant to section 20A of the Gas Industry Act 1958. (3) The
Government will not underwrite the company's operating expenses, but the
New Zealand Gas Council could consider proposals for the upgrading of reformer
plant in terms of the provisions announced in the Budget. (4) The Minister of
Energy will endeavour to maintain adequate coal supplies to the company, but
cannot give an unconditional guarantee because of the limited availability of
coal to meet the company's specification. (5) Subsidies to the gas industry are
under review and substantial additional finance for subsidies has been approved
for the 1978-79 year. The actual subsidies payable to the company for this
financial year are currently being assessed. (6) The request that the 5-year
straight-line depreciation policy be adopted is in fact much too general. The
Commissioner of Inland Revenue can exercise his discretion in this matter and
it is for the company to demonstrate that it has a case for a special rate of
depreciation on plant and equipment that has a limited useful life.

37.
Geothermal and Hydro Power Costs
(8/9/78)
Mr LA VARIS (Taupo) to the Minister of Energy: Would he indicate
the cost of producing electricity by means of geothermal power, and, further,
would he produce figures comparing that cost with the cost of normal hydro
production and fuel production?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The current estimate of the
cost of power from the Ohaki (Broadlands) geothermal power station is about
2.4c/kWh at 80 percent plant factor, i.e. base-load operation. Huntly is also
expected to produce power at about 2.4c/kWh, from either coal or Maui gas, but
at 70 percent plant factor. The Clutha scheme is estimated to produce power at
between 2.1 and 2.3c/kWh at an intermediate-load plant factor of 35 percent.
Because of the difference in plant factors the costs/unit shown for cach develop-
ment are not directly comparable.

Human Relationships Publications in Schools
(13/9/78)
MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Education: Under
section 3 of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977, must the
prior approval of the principal of a school, in agreement with the board of
governors or committee of the school, be obtained before placing in the hands
of school pupils under the age of 16: Man and Society: Rigby Joy of Know-
ledge Library (article on birth control); Encyclopaedia Britannica: article on
birth control; Population, Resources, Environment: Erlich and Erlich Pub. Free-
man; Man, Medicine and Morality: A. E. Clark-Kennedy; Anatomy, Physiology
and Hygiene: Raeburn, et. al.; Biology and the Social Crisis: Brierley; and
Science Makes Sense, book 2 (standard text)?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: In terms of section 3
of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977 teachers are not named
as people who may give instruction in contraception. They could, therefore, be
at risk of prosecution under the Act unless they are protected by a prior decision of
their principal or head teacher given after agreement with the school committee
or board of governors, or (in the case of an integrated school) the school com-
mittee or board of governors and the proprietor, as set down in section 3 (3) (f)


## p. 3840 (#320) ###########################################

3840
27 September
Questions and Replies
of the Act. I am advised that all but two of the titles listed in the question would
seem to constitute materials for "instruction in the use of contraceptives" within
the terms of section 3 of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977.
The approval of the principal, with the agreement of the school committee or
board of governors, as provided in section 3 (3) (f) of the Act, would be required
to be given to any teacher, librarian, or school counsellor before the remaining
books listed could be used with pupils under the age of 16 years. The two possible
exceptions are: (a) the extract from Science Makes Sense, book 2, which describes
the effect of the contraceptive pill on the body, but does not give instructions
in the use of the pill; and (b) the extract from Anatomy, Physiology and Hygiene,
which does not mention contraception at all. Opinions may differ on interpreta-
tions of the provisions of section 3, as no ruling has yet been made in a court of
law. The member will know that the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion
Act was not a Government-sponsored Bill, but was enacted as a decision of
Parliament with each member acting on his or her own conscience. It has pro-
duced a number of administrative problems in the application of section 3 to the
work of teachers in schools.

55.
Primary Schools-Equipment Allocation
(13/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: How many
different categories are there in the basic equipment code for primary schools;
what number of pupils does each category apply to; and what arrangements are
made for schools with populations considerably above the last category?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The basic equipment code
for primary schools is divided into five different categories or equipment groups.
Each group is determined by the number of pupils in the school, i.e., group I:
9-28 pupils; group II: 29-120 pupils; group III: 121-230 pupils; group IV:
231-305 pupils; group V: 306 plus. The education boards are allocated finance
each year to equip new schools and progressively to upgrade the equipment in
existing schools to the standard of the basic list. Boards have some discretion
in the allocation of these funds to individual schools, and provision does exist to
enable very large schools to receive additional items of teaching equipment on the
recommendation of the district senior inspector. In addition to this, a special
grant of $80,000 was allocated to education boards in the 1975-76 financial year
to help meet the needs of large schools.
56.
Meat Levy to Federated Farmers
(13/9/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Agriculture:
What is the present levy on meat which is paid to Federated Farmers, and what
are the total amounts paid to them annually since 1972, and is there any
proposal to increase this levy, and, if so, by how much?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The present levy
payable to Federated Farmers on stock slaughtered is as follows: sheep and lambs,
0.25c per head, cattle, 4.5c per head; calves (under 27 kg), 3.0c per head; pigs,
0.5c per head. The levy has been charged on all stock slaughtered since 1 May
1973. The amount of levy received by Federated Farmers annually since the levy
was introduced has been: year ended 31 May 1974, $219,163; year ended 31 May
1975, $207.180; year ended 31 May 1976, $237,027; year ended 31 May 1977,
$234,115; year ended 31 May 1978, $226,913. The levy will be increased with
effect from 1 October 1978, and from that date the rates will be: sheep and lambs,
0.50c per head; cattle 9.0c per head; calves (under 27 kg), 5.0c per head; Pigs,
0.6c per head. At the new rates, levies are expected to amount to $425,000 per
annum.

Liquor Price Increases, 1972-75
(13/9/78)
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) to the Minister of Trade and
Industry: Will he give the various price increases for draught beer, bottled beer,
wines, and spirits sold through bottle stores and over the bar that have taken place
between 1972 and 1975, and state how they compare in percentage with the latest
increases?


## p. 3842 (#322) ###########################################

3842
27 September
Questions and Replies
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied:
In the 3 years 1972 to 1975 the following increases took place in public bar
prices: 12 oz (340 ml) glasses of draught beer increased by 2c to 19c a glass, an
increase of 12 percent compared with the recent increase of 12 percent on 340 ml
glasses; 8 oz (225 ml) glasses of draught beer increased by 3c to 15c a glass, an
increase of 25 percent compared with the recent increase of 10 percent on 225 ml
glasses; 5 oz (140 ml) glasses of draught beer increased by 2c to 10c a glass, an
increase of 25 percent compared with the recent increase of 13 percent on 140 ml
glasses; 35 oz (1 litre) jugs of draught beer increased by 9c to 55c a jug, an
increase of 20 percent compared with the recent increase of 11 percent on 1 litre
jugs; large bottles of beer (745 ml) increased by 13c to 55c a bottle in Wellington,
an increase of 31 percent compared with the recent increase of 9 percent; small
bottles of beer (340 ml) increased by 11c to 35c a bottle in Wellington, an increase
of 46 percent compared with the recent increase of 10 percent. The price of nips
of spirits increased as follows: Scotch whisky increased by 3c a nip to 26c a nip,
an increase of 13 percent compared with the recent increase of 11 percent; gin
increased by 3c a nip to 21c a nip, an increase of 17 percent compared with the
recent increase of 10 percent; brandy increased by 3c a nip to 24c a nip, an increase
of 14 percent compared with the recent increase of 9 percent. No wines are sold in
public bars. In the same period, bottle store prices increased as follows: flagons
of beer increased by 14c to $1 a flagon, an increase of 16 percent compared with
the recent increase of 11 percent; large bottles of beer increased by 13c to 42c a
bottle in Wellington, an increase of 45 percent compared with the recent increase
of 9 percent; small bottles of beer increased by 8c to 28c a bottle in Wellington,
an increase of 40 percent compared with the recent increase of 10 percent; bottles
of Scotch whisky increased by $1.29 to $7.88 a bottle, an increase of 20 percent
compared with the recent increase of 5 percent; bottles of gin increased by 40c to
$5.32 a bottle, an increase of 8 percent compared with the recent increase of 2
percent; bottles of brandy increased by 67c to $6.87 a bottle, an increase of 11
percent compared with the recent increase of 0.4 percent; bottles of bacardi
increased by 87c to $7.40 a bottle, an increase of 13 percent compared with the
recent increase of 0.4 percent; bottles of sherry increased by 56c to $1.55 a bottle,
an increase of 57 percent compared with the recent increase of 13 percent.

(13/9/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Finance: Does the Govern-
ment intend to introduce taxation concessions on plant and equipment used for
recycling waste material?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The Government extended
the energy conservation tax incentives in this year's Budget to include plant and

61.
Railcar Services
(13/9/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Railways: What
is the cost of running the following services, and what percentage of seats or
berths must be sold for the service to break even: Silver Fern; Northerner; Silver
Star; Southerner; Endeavour?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: The cost of
operating the services referred to for the year ended 31 March 1978 was
$8,925,000. This figure covers only expenditure directly attributable to the
services, Administration overheads and expenditure such as track maintenance
costs are excluded. The definition of a precise break-even point is difficult because
of the need to take into account weekend running and penal rates, revenue from
catering, train consist, and other factors. Load factors of the following order would
be necessary to reach regularly a financial break-even: Silver Fern, 70 percent;
Northerner, 90 percent; Silver Star, 100 percent; Southerner, 100 percent;
Endeavour, 100 percent.

St. Hilda's Secondary Schools, Dunedin
Effects on Integration
(14/9/78)
5. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) to the Minister of Education: (1)
What are the potential effects on the total State secondary educational places in
Dunedin of integrating St. Hilda's and any other non-Catholic single-sex school
in Dunedin, and, in particular, to what extent are parents who wish to send their
children to co-ed schools likely to be able to find places in the co-ed schools in
future if integration occurs; (2) what are the intakes in-zone and out-of-zone for
each Dunedin secondary school in 1978; (3) what progress has the department
made on the survey of secondary school preferences of parents in Dunedin, which
it undertook to carry out last year, and to what extent has or is forward planning


## p. 3846 (#326) ###########################################

27 September

for secondary school placements being conducted to prevent a recurrence of the
type of problems experienced under the zoning system in 1976 and 1977?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: As an agreement has
yet to be reached with the controlling authority of St. Hilda's, it would be
premature to assume the terms of a mutually acceptable integration agreement.
I have written to the controlling authorities of the local State secondary schools
and have assured them that I will not sign any agreement that will be detrimental
to the established pattern of schooling in Dunedin. In the particular case of
Dunedin schools there will be no change in the availability of co-educational
places through the integration of the existing single-sex private schools. The present
arrangements regarding zoning and enrolments in Dunedin State secondary schools
have been operating for the last 3 years. They divide the city into three natural
geographic districts. The northern and southern zones each contain a boys, a girls,
and a co-educational school, with freedom of enrolment at the type of school of
the parents' choice. The western zone contains only a co-educational school, but
arrangements are made for considerable movement into and out of this zone to
allow students reasonable access to the type of school their parents prefer. The
control of zoning is in the hands of a co-ordinating committee comprising repre-
sentatives of all schools and chaired by the regional superintendent of education.
This committee sets the boundaries of zones and recommends out-of-zone numbers,
which are later ratified by individual boards. The success of this arrangement can
be gauged by the fact that at the date of closing of enrolments for 1978 it was
possible for every school to accept all applications it had received. It is also an
indication that the distribution and type of secondary schools in Dunedin match
closely the wishes of the community. The intakes into individual schools in 1978

72.
Recycling Research Programme
(15/9/78)
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister for the Environment: What
research programmes are at present being undertaken to investigate the better
recycling of waste materials, and what contribution is the Government making
in this area?


## p. 3848 (#328) ###########################################

3848
27 September
Questions and Replies
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment) replied: Though recycling
of many waste materials is limited by logistic and economic factors rather than
by the need for research, there is a considerable research programme under way
in many institutions. The reports on "Liquid and Waterborne Wastes Research
in New Zealand" for 1976 and 1977 produced by the Water Resources Council
cover research on waste water treatment, and on industrial wastes. DSIR has
published a Guide to Land Application of Treated Sewage, bringing together the
factors governing success in this method of disposal. The Dairy Research Institute
has carried out a major research programme on the production of useful products
from what were previously dairy factory wastes, and the Meat Industry Research
Institute and private firms have undertaken research on recovery of protein from
meat works wastes. DSIR established an exchange of waste materials system in
the Auckland area, which is now being operated on a continuing basis under the
overview of the Department of Trade and Industry. The main department con-
cerned with co-ordination of recycling and practical encouragement to industry
is the Department of Trade and Industry, which maintains close liaison with
research agencies and fosters research contracts.
It is clear that, apart from the problem of marketing recycled products, an
important aspect affecting the financial viability of any process is cost of freight.
A freight subsidy has recently been announced to enable used oil to be brought
together for recycling. In order to ensure that practical programmes are achieved
with the backing of industry, an applied technology programme is operated by the
Development Finance Corporation. Some important programmes under active
investigation with trials under way or with local application already in train
involve plastics, used car bodies, and scrap steel paper and rubber.
73.

Kapiti Borough Area-Age Beneficiaries
(20/9/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Social Welfare: How many persons
in Paraparaumu, Waikanae, and Paekakariki respectively were in receipt of old
age pensions or universal superannuation in 1975?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: It is estimated
that, as at 30 June 1975, 1600 persons in the Kapiti Borough, incorporating Para-
paraumu, Raumati, and Paekakariki, were receiving age benefit and superannua-
tion benefit, and it is estimated that at the same date 900 persons in Waikanae
were receiving these benefits.

Railway Buildings Upgrading-Wanganui
(20/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Railways: What are the
Government's present plans for the upgrading of railway buildings in Wanganui,
apart from the Eastown workshops?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: Two new build-
ings are planned for Wanganui. A new road services terminal is to be provided
adjacent to the district offices in Taupo Quay. Sketch plans are currently being
prepared, and working drawings should be available next year. This will replace
the present station building. A new traffic foreman's office and shunters' amenity
in the Wanganui yard should be commenced in the new year. The old Aramoho
station building is being converted for use as a workshop for signals staff as well
as being used for the existing station staff.

Maui Gas-Alternative Uses
(20/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Energy: What plans are
being explored for alternative uses of Maui gas?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: Apart from the planned uses
in power stations, industry, commerce, and households, a decision has been made
to construct an ammonia/urea plant at Kapuni. Research work to be financed
by the Liquid Fuels Trust Board will investigate the production, distribution,
and use of methanol in blends with motor gasoline and automotive diesel fuel,
as well as the production of synthetic gasoline. An LPG feasibility study is nearing
completion, while research work on compressed natural gas is proceeding satisfac-
torily. Further analysis of possible petrochemical projects will take place from
time to time.
88.
Primary School Teachers-Permanent Appointments
(20/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: What con-
stitutes a permanent appointment to a primary school of an additional staff member
for special educational needs?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Two types of addi-
tional staffing are provided in primary schools where special educational needs
have been established. The first is additional staffing of a permanent nature
provided on the authority of the Minister of Education under regulation 23 (b)
of the Education (Salaries and Staffing) Regulations 1957. This is based on a
notional roll, which may be up to 20 percent above actual roll, and for which
the extra staff generated both in basic scale positions and senior teacher positions
are permanent appointments advertised and filled according to normal appointment
procedures. Schools designated in this category are confined to specific areas such
as Mangere, Otara, and Porirua. At the time this scheme was introduced some 87
additional teachers were apppointed.
The second type of additional staffing is appointed under regulation 31 (d) of
the Education (Salaries and Staffing) Regulations 1957, on an annual basis, under
the joint authority of the Ministers of Finance and Education. In 1978 there were
220 additional positions of this type in schools recommended by district senior
inspectors as having special educational needs. Because fresh authority must be
granted each year, these positions are not permanent ones. If schools remain
eligible for a further year, the teachers appointed often remain in the appoint-
ments for an additional year. Teachers appointed to regulation 31 (d) positions
are free to apply for permanent positions at any time.

money allocated to sport and recreation-$5,018,000 this year-benefits the
environment", and, if so, could he indicate what part?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment): Yes, I have seen the
article and can advise that funds are allocated under two schemes-a national scheme
through major organisations and a local scheme funded through local authorities.
Last year, grants to environmental organisations from both schemes totalled $15,060,
almost $13,000 being to the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society. In addition,
$46,000 was allocated to parks and reserves. These grants highlight allocations
specifically to environmentally orientated groups. However, the majority of the vote
can be said to be going towards the enhancement of the human environment as sport
and recreation facilities are improved.

Sheepmeats Agreement, EEC
(7/9/78)

Minister of Overseas Trade: What are the dangers to New Zealand in the


## p. 3859 (#339) ###########################################

27 September
3859
Questions and Replies
sheepmeats agreement proposed by the Common Market, if the safeguard clause is
adopted and implemented by the EEC?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply
on behalf of the Minister of Overseas Trade. "The implementation of a safeguard
clause, as in the case of beef, was used to exclude imports. The New Zealand sheep

stores to consumers that any interruption by a safeguard action could cause great
disorder. The New Zealand Government has expressed its concern to the EEC about
the proposed sheepmeat regulation, including the provision for a safeguard clause."

Voter Identification
(7/9/78)
Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Justice: What identification
ensures that a person claiming a vote against a name on the electoral roll is in fact
that person, and, in the event of plural voting, which vote is disallowed?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): No proof of identity is, or ever
has been, required of any voter. Our electoral system assumes the inherent honesty
and integrity of the people of New Zealand. The procedure is for an elector to attend
at a polling booth, state his name, address, and occupation, and, after the roll has
been checked, be issued with a ballot paper and licensing voting paper. When a
returning officer is satisfied that plural voting has occured both papers are withdrawn
and neither is counted.

the new rolling stock in south Auckland, the first of which will be entering the service
by mid-1980, an extensive programme of station upgrading is proposed. Most of the
platforms in the area need to be raised in height or rebuilt and completely resealed.
Attention will be given also to security fencing and access paths to stations. This work
is expected to begin later this year, and will be substantially completed by the time
the new rolling stock enters service.

Fish Exports
(8/9/78)
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Fisheries: What were the
tonnage and value of fish exports for the following years: 1973, 1974, 1975, 1976, and
1977, and has he an estimate for 1978?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): The figures requested are as
follows: 1973, 14 100 tonnes with a value of $20.1 million; 1974, 12 808 tonnes valued
at $20.3 million; 1975, 14 494 tonnes, with an export value of $25.7 million. It is
significant to note that those 3 years are almost identical, and were the 3 years under

$37.8 million. In 1977 it increased to 26 000 tonnes worth $50.3 million. For the first

estimate for the full 1978 year is between 35 000 and 40 000 tonnes, worth between
$60 million and $65 million.

Electoral Roll-Eligibility to Vote
(8/9/78)
Mr KIRK (Sydenham) to the Minister of Justice: If a person can prove that he
applied for enrolment in this year's election, and was qualified for enrolment, but his
name does not appear on the roll through no fault of his own, will the Minister
guarantee that person's right, none the less, to cast a valid vote in this year's election?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The right is guaranteed by the
statute. The matter is governed by section 99 of the Electoral Act, which defines those
who are qualified to vote. Under paragraph (d), any elector who has since the last
preceding election and before 6 o'clock in the afternoon of writ day applied for
registration as an elector of the district or, where a change of boundaries has
intervened, of some other district in which his then place of residence within the first-
mentioned district was then situated, is qualified to vote. If his name does not appear
on a printed roll, he will be accorded a special vote, which will be valid.

most recent figures available, as presented in the Reserve Bank monthly release New
Mortgage Registrations Interest Rates for March 1978, show that the weighted average
interest rate on all mortgages registered climbed to 10.77 percent in March 1978, and
can he further confirm that this rate represents the highest average rate ever in New
Zealand's recorded history?
DON
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): According to my

Rail Services-Availability of Alcohol
(12/9/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Railways: Why are
alcoholic beverages not available on the Endeavour express or rail ferries on Sunday, as
they are on the Northerner and Silver Star expresses?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Railways. "Alcoholic beverages are available on the Endeavour service on Sundays,
but may be consumed only in the dining car together with a meal purchased on the
train. This is in keeping with the generally accepted principle of confining liquor sales
on a Sunday to dining or house-bar areas. When the rail ferries were originally
licensed to sell liquor the service was provided in line with the normal trading hours
of most licensed hotels. Consequently, the liquor service on the ferries was provided
only on a 6-day-a-week basis, whioh is the position today."

Electoral Rolls

Lynn), to the Minister of Justice: Is he aware that the post office in Hamilton had
been giving stamped acknowledgments of the receipt of electoral enrolment cards
listed on a form, but the Chief Electoral Officer has since instructed that such receipts
can be given by each electorate officer only, and, as it has also been decided that in
future no form E2 acknowledgments will be issued despite the fact that section 49(2)

only after the registration card has been checked and the electorate officer is satisfied
that the application is in order and the elector is qualified. It is not correct that there
has been a decision not to issue acknowledgments of enrolments. All electors who
have completed a registration card will receive an E2 advice of registration card.

Housing Corporation-Refinancing Applications
(13/9/78)
Mr ROGERS(Onehunga), on behalf of Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda), to the
Minister of Housing: How many applications for assistance with refinance have
been turned down by the Housing Corporation to date in the current financial year,
and could he briefly outline the reasons for turning down these applications?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The answer is a little longer
than I would like, but I shall go through it quickly. I am unable to supply the figures
requested, as the number of refinance applications declined by the Housing
Corporation is not listed as a separate category. For the period 1 April 1978 to
22 August 1978, 242 refinance applications were not proceeded with for various
reasons. While the majority of these would have been declined by the Housing
Corporation, others would have been withdrawn or allowed to lapse by the
applicants. Housing Corporation refinance assistance is provided on a last resort
basis. Applicants have to show that suitable alternative finance is not available and
their home is in jeopardy and a forced sale is a definite prospect, or that there has
been a significant detrimental change in personal circumstances-for example,
incapacity of the sole wage earner- that renders initial arrangements incapable of
being maintained. The honourable member should not overlook the marked
improvement over the past 12 months in the availability of mortgage finance through
private and institutional sectors of the mortgage market, and the opportunity this
provides those facing difficulties to re-order their mortgage arrangements in a more
satisfactory form.

to reduce overseas oil imports into New Zealand?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I reply on behalf of the

when possible, advice and encouragement are extended to their authors. There are
some, however, that are not so practical, and on average I receive one proposition a
month on a new form of perpetual motion.”

Electoral Rolls-Mobile Voters
(14/9/78)
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of
Justice: Can a prospective elector who reaches the age of 18 years in the period
between the issue of the writs and the day before the election, and who has left home
to take up an apprenticeship or a job in another electorate 2 months before the
election, enrol as an elector and cast a valid vote, and, if so, in which electorate?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I refer the right honourable
gentleman to section 50 of the Electoral Act 1956, which provides for registrations to
close at 6 p.m. on writ day, but further provides “that this section shall not apply to
any applicant who satisfies the electorate officer that he has become qualified as an
elector of the district not earlier than 1 month before writ day". Section 99 (b) of the
Electoral Act makes such a person a qualified voter as long as he has applied for
registration before polling day. In the case mentioned by the right honourable
gentleman, the person would appear to be qualified to enrol for the electorate in
which his home address was situated, because that is where he would have last lived
for 3 months. If he was not in that electorate on polling day he would cast a special
vote.

Perch-Fishing Potential, Lake Rotoroa, Hamilton
(14/9/78)
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
to the Minister of Fisheries: Has any assessment been made of the potential for
perch fishing in Hamilton's Lake Rotoroa, what stocks are believed to be extant, and
has current angling pressure had any effect on these stocks?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Fisheries. "Over the past 2 years the fisheries research division and the
Auckland Acclimatisation Society have undertaken detailed studies into the fishing
potential and biology of perch in Hamilton Lake. The lake contains an abundant
stock of perch, and should be an excellent fishery in the future. However, at the
moment angling is prohibited by a Hamilton Lake Domain Board bylaw, and
therefore any current angling has no significant effect on the perch stocks."

Electoral Rolls Special Votes
(14/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Justice: As the Chief
Electoral Officer stated in the Dominion of 9 September that if the name of an
applicant for enrolment did not appear on the supplementary roll the person could
cast a special vote, can the Minister guarantee that such a vote would be valid, as far
as enrolment is concerned, and, if so, what procedure is to be introduced to ensure
this?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have seen the reported
statement. I must refer the honourable member to section 99 (d) of the Electoral Act.
This provides that a person who is qualified to be registered for an electorate, whose
name does not appear on the main or supplementary roll for that electorate, but who
has applied for registration there between the date of the last election and writ day, is
qualified to cast a valid vote. Such a person would vote as a special voter.

of those countries. Switzerland is another.

Electricity Bulk Price
(19/9/78)

price per unit of electricity sold by the ministry in the financial year 1979-80?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting: I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Energy. "The bulk price of electricity for the 1979-80 year should be at
least sufficient to maintain the financial situation of N.Z. Electricity and avoid
operation at a loss. Interest has increased with the escalation in the cost of capital
works and with a proportion of NZE's existing loan debt being converted to the new
interest rate. Interest charges will also increase as a fraction of the total of estimated
working expenses, because operating and maintenance are forecast to fall from 0.651c
per unit in 1977-78 to 0.605c per unit in 1978-79. Increased plant capacity reduces the
need for more expensive thermal generation. The other part of working expenses,
which is depreciation, naturally increases with the additional capital investment in
new plant and equipment over the 1977-78 year”.

(19/9/78)

payment refunded?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of

European quotas were reallocated to New Zealand. The Government has no
jurisdiction over the matter of prices paid by the Dairy Board to dairy companies for
products acquired for export, and does not propose to intervene.'

Environment-Contentious Chemical Sprays
(19/9/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister for the Environment: Has
he seen the article in the Evening Post of 22 August quoting him, and stating that
enormous amounts of money are devoted to environmental protection through
Government departments, such as $6,250,000 for pest control and $10,255,000 for
noxious weed control; and, if so, can he say how much of the $6,250,000 allocated for
pest control and the $10,255,000 for noxious weed control was associated with the
spraying of environmentally contentious chemicals?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the
Minister for the Environment. "I am unsure which chemicals the member for
Auckland Central refers to, but I assume he is referring to the use of the animal
poison 1080 and the herbicide 2,4,5-T. Of the $6.25 million in this year's estimates for
agricultural pest control, approximately $50,000 would be for expenditure on the
chemical cost of 1080. Of the $10.25 million for noxious weed eradication, about $8.5
million would consist of subsidies for farmers for 75 percent of the chemical cost of
approved spray programmes. Of the sum paid to farmers, possibly 60 percent or
about $5 million might be for 2,4,5-T compounds. I should say, in conclusion, that all
agricultural chemicals are environmentally contentious if applied recklessly, but they
are evaluated and all possible care is recommended to the users to use them with
safety and the environmental care in mind."

Rook Control, Hastings and Rangitikei
(15/9/78)
Mr COOPER (Otago Central) to the Minister of Science and Technology:
What methods has the DSIR established for the control of rooks in the Hastings and
Rangitikei areas?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology) replied: The
principal method of control is a poison known as DRC 1339, originally developed in
the USA. This poison is harmless to mammals, and deaths among birds of the few
other species susceptible to it have been kept to a minimum by use of appropriate
baiting methods. I should mention that DSIR, having conducted the initial
experiments with DRC 1339 in this country, is now involved with rook control in an
advisory capacity only. The actual job of control is done by the pest destruction
boards in conjunction with the Ministry of Agriculture. Methods used for minimising
damage to crops by rooks include scare guns and chemical repellants. It is very
difficult to trap or shoot rooks in sufficient numbers to have an effect on population
levels. The Agricultural Pest Destruction Council is currently reviewing this
country's policy on rook control, and the DSIR has contributed information to assist
it in this work.

give the Waitakere Labour candidate a street index of the electorate, and can he
confirm whether such a request was made to the Chief Electoral Officer?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: Yes, I have seen the
statement. The Chief Electoral Officer has no recollection of this specific request. The
electoral roll is an alphabetical list of all qualified registered electors of an electoral
district, and naturally the production of an accurate electoral roll is the first priority.

are not yet available; I am told that they will be printed by about mid-October. As I
have undertaken, they will be sold to any candidate or other interested person
wishing to have them. The street index showing the residences in order of house
number, together with the names of electors registered at each address, is another
matter. It is intended to produce such an index, but with priority given to the rolls
themselves this cannot be done before the rolls are closed.

Housing Corporation Loans on Existing Homes
(15/9/78)
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: How many
applications for assistance to purchase existing homes have been declined by the
Housing Corporation to date in the current financial year, and can he briefly outline
the reasons for declining to accept those applications?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: I am unable to supply
the figures requested, as the number of purchase applications declined by the
Housing Corporation is not listed as a separate category. However, for the period I
April 1978 to 22 August 1978, 990 purchase applications were not proceeded with for
various reasons. While the majority of these would have been declined by the
Housing Corporation, others would have been withdrawn or allowed to lapse by the
applicants. Housing Corporation assistance to purchase a previously occupied
property is currently restricted to the following priority groups: (a) families with three
or more children whether or not they can capitalise the family benefit-(previously
those with two children who capitalised family benefit also qualified); (b) those with a
special need-usually medical; (c) rehabilitation and defence borrowers; (d) married
depositors in a Post Office home ownership savings account with a proven saving
record; (e) public servants on transfer.
The decision of the Housing Corporation to decline a purchase application could
be because the applicant did not qualify under one of the headings listed above, or the
dwelling did not meet the corporation's lending requirements, or the applicant failed
to establish that he could complete-i.e. finance the transaction or meet the costs
involved in home ownership without causing himself and his family undue hardship.
The member should not overlook the fact that those who found that they did not
qualify for a loan for a used home could still apply to the corporation for a loan for a
new house. Furthermore, the Government has stimulated the involvement of the
institutional and private sectors in the housing mortgage market and those applicants
declined by the corporation for purchase funds have this source of finance to turn to.

East-West Centre, Hawaii
(15/9/78)
Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What
financial assistance is given at present to the East-West Centre in Hawaii, and is there
any intention to raise the level of assistance?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The New
Zealand Government believes the East-West Centre to be a worthy institution, which
assists the promotion of understanding and co-operation between the peoples of the
Pacific. We financially assist the centre in two ways: first, by meeting half the
operating costs of the centre's field office in Wellington, which amounted to $7,500 for
the 1978 financial year; and, secondly, by providing on an ad hoc basis Third
Country fellowships to enable Pacific Island students to attend East-West Centre
programmes. I discussed recently with Dr Jerry Chang, the centre's Vice-President
for Development and Public Affairs, the possibility of New Zealand's increasing its
contribution to the East-West Centre. Officials from my ministry and the Department
of Education are at present looking at this possibility.

Foreign Fishing Nations' Fees, NZ Economic Zone
(15/9/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Fisheries: What are the fees
to be paid by foreign fishing nations for access to New Zealand's 200-mile economic
management zone?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: The fees are prescribed in
the Exclusive Economic Zone (Licence Fees for Foreign Fishing Craft) Regulations
1978. They are as follows: jig or trawl caught squid, $80 per tonne of fish; fish (caught
by trawling), $17 per tonne of fish; fish caught by bottom-lining, $25 per tonne of fish;
licence to fish for albacore and yellow fin tuna by long-lining, $1,500 per year; licence
to fish for southern bluefin tuna by long-lining, $9,000 per year; licence as a fish
carrier, $2 per tonne of the fish-carrying capacity of the craft; licence as a support
craft, $1 per gross registered ton of the craft.

Auckland Home Guidance Advisory Bureau
(15/9/78)
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Housing: How many inquiries
for advice and assistance on housing matters has the Auckland home guidance
advisory bureau received to date in the current financial year, and how many-and
what proportion of all inquiries received-related to the refinancing of existing
mortgages?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: Returns are supplied
by the Auckland Home Guidance Bureau on a 4-weekly basis, and the nearest
starting point to 1 April 1978 has been taken as a base line. The figures are as follows:
for the period 17 March 1978 to 31 August 1978, a total of 4869 inquiries was received
by the Auckland Home Guidance Bureau, of which 1816 were by way of personal
interview and, of these, 1041, or 57 percent, concerned refinance. The balance of the
inquiries-3053-was by telephone. While some of these would have concerned
refinance, detailed statistics of telephone inquiries are not kept. However, the practice
followed is to invite telephone inquirers to call in person at the bureau to take
advantage of the benefits that this form of consultation can offer. Accordingly, it is
reasonable to assume that the majority of those with particular problems would have
followed this course.

Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua): I want to answer the Opposition's challenge, and to

regarding the prosecutions would be made by his department and the Crown Solicitor...."
A letter from the Solicitor-General's office dated 25 September, states: "It is a principle of
Government in this country that decisions relating to prosecutions, that is, whether they be
started or stopped, must be made by the prosecuting authorities without political or other
pressure". The letter further states: "Decisions in relation to prosecutions should be taken
by the departmental officers concerned with law enforcement of that department. The
permanent head of that department is finally responsible. A Minister is responsible for his
department to Parliament. It is accordingly appropriate for a Minister to indicate to his
departmental head general areas of enforcement action that the Government considers
desirable or necessary. Likewise, it is appropriate for a departmental head to indicate to his
Minister general enforcement action that he contemplates".
The Government brought in this type of legislation to deal with the freezing industry
because the public demanded it. Something had to be done to stop the disruption and unrest
in the industry. The voters of the country support the principle invoked by the Government
of making unions responsible for good industrial relations. I support that principle, which
the Government is upholding at present.

not proceeding that there has to be a reasonable, proper, and efficient performance within
the industry in the interests of productivity and the overall benefit of the nation. It is in this
direction only that prosecution penalties within any law should be exercised.
The head of the Department of Labour is competent within the law to make a decision.

enforcement officer. In yesterday's Southland Times the editor wrote: "Labour Party

of New Zealanders". I believe that is correct. The editor went on to state: "People would not
want the penalty provisions of the Industrial Relations Act repealed until there is clear

PERSONAL EXPLANATION
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): With the leave of the House I wish to make
a personal statement relating to the last comment of the member for Mt. Albert. I have been
asked a question about the events of last Thursday in the court in Invercargill. I shall be
giving the details from memory.
The court met at 10 a.m. to consider the joint application to be made by the two
counsel, including the QC representing the defendants. The first communication I received


## p. 3896 (#376) ###########################################

3896
27 September
Personal Explanation
from the court was a message in my secretary's handwriting. I understand it came from a
court official. Certainly it did not come from the Department of Labour's officer in
Invercargill. I know that to be a fact. It indicated that at about 10.40 a.m. the magistrate had
adjourned the case to consider the application for the adjournment.
The next message saying that the court had not resumed was received by me at 11.20
a.m. At 11.50 a.m. I received a message indicating that the court had resumed, and that the
magistrate had declined the application for an adjournment. All those messages were
conveyed to me by my secretary on pieces of paper. As I understand it, none came from
either Mr Jackson or from Mr Buchanan, the Department of Labour officer in Invercargill.
About 12.10 p.m. I received a message that the four cases had been dismissed for want of
evidence.
The first contact I had with the Secretary of Labour from Invercargill was between 1.15
and 1.20 p.m. when he told me personally what had happened that morning and of a decision
he had to make, together with Crown counsel, for the case to resume at 2 p.m.
I advised the parties who were waiting. Later, at the request of those in my office who
were to sign the agreement for the killing season—and specifically at the request of Sir Tom
Skinner, who refused to sign until I personally had phoned the court-I tried to make
contact with the court, both through Mr Buchanan of the Department of Labour office and
through the Registrar of the court. We could make no progress.
Finally, the magistrate adjourned the court during the afternoon proceedings to come to
the telephone to tell me that all the 192 cases had been dismissed. I went from the outside
office into my room, notified all the parties, and the signing took place.

LOCAL ELECTION AND POLLS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Local Election
and Polls Amendment Bill.
Mr Birch: This is tedious repetition.
Mr BEETHAM: It might seem so to the Senior Government Whip, but then, as his
capacity to understand what democracy is all about is limited, his comment hardly surprises
me. To be effective and truly democratic, the House should represent the views of all people
in New Zealand and not just the minority who voted for the governing National Party, a
mere 39 percent of the total eligible vote. I am not claiming the majority that members of the
National Party do. For this reason, in introducing the Bill, I hope that other members,
particularly those on the Government benches, will not continue to display the absolute
arrogance they have shown so far in their treatment and their superficial criticism of the
other Bills I have introduced. [Interruption.]
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I ask the member for Eden to remain quiet.
Mr BEETHAM: It is all right, Mr Acting Speaker. He is not worrying me at all. The Bill
should be given a fair hearing, and I hope that the Government does not use its power of
veto, based as it is on the franchise of a minority of electors. This Bill, like other Bills I have
introduced this year, is about people and their right to participate fully in democratic
decision making. It is concerned with decentralising power and involving more people than
at present in the decision-making process which goes with that power.
Let us hear no more nonsense from Government benches that the Bill smacks of
centralisation when, in point of fact, the purpose of the Bill is exactly the opposite. It
increases the number of people who can exercise the franchise and be involved, particularly
in local authority polls, with the rating qualification. The Bill gives more people say in
matters affecting their own future, particularly those relating to local government. Its
provisions will be of great benefit to women because the present law diseriminates against
women, particularly their capacity to be involved in decision making in an area that concerns
them.
What effect does the raising of local body loans have on rates? People should have a say
as to whether or not they will accept an increased rate burden. Women are affected to
perhaps a greater degree than men by the rate burden, because in most cases rates are paid
out of the family budget.


## p. 3897 (#377) ###########################################

27 September
3897
Local Election and Polls Amendment Bill
The specific purpose of the Bill is to amend the present Local Election and Polls Act so
that women will have a say in whether or not their family budget will be burdened with
increased rates due to the servicing of local government loans. I think this provision of
extending the principles of decentralisation, of decision making, and of participatory
democracy to include women is particularly appropriate in this year, which is Women's
Year. It will be most interesting to see how the member for Lyttelton and the member for
Raglan react to the Bill—that is if they turn up and speak on it. I should say that, if the
Government has any support for the concept of Women's Year and is not to be hypocritical
in its attitude, it should at least allow the introduction of the Bill so that it can be discussed,
so that the right of women to participate in the democratic process at least can be considered.
The Bill involves the fundamental principle of no taxation without representation,
because rates are a form of taxation to which women in the home contribute. In paying this
taxation it is vital, necessary, and just that they should have the opportunity of deciding, to a
degree, how their rates, a form of taxation, will be spent and whether or not they are
prepared to accept the injustices involved in the present rating system.
The Bill amends section 110 of the Local Elections and Polls Act of 1976. This is the
section which defines who is eligible to vote at any election or poll solely by virtue of rating
qualifications. The present section is restrictive. In point of fact it virtually says that on each
property only one person can exercise a vote. Where this matters particularly is in joint
family homes, because many homes in New Zealand now consist of two co-owners, in most
cases husband and wife. This idea of giving equality of opportunity to own property, to own
the family home, was initiated by the Joint Family Homes Act of 1964, which was a National
Party Act, as was its predecessor, the 1950 Act.
With husband and wife co-owners, the existing provisions of section 110 are so applied
in practice that the husband tends to become the one whose name is entered on the electoral
roll as having the rating qualification. This arises because the present Act says that it is the
first or leading name in the partnership of the tenancy that shall be deemed to be the person
so nominated to exercise a vote. The anomaly can be overcome by the usual bureaucratic
procedure of the parties making a declaration that a person other than the first named will
exercise the voting right. The purpose of the Bill, then, is to allow the second owner-who is
usually a woman-to have a vote by right and not in the form of a declaration if the husband
happens to be the first or leading name in the partnership.
The Bill does not amend provisions of the present Act to give voting rights where there
are more than two people. In fact, the Bill does not incorporate the principle-I can hear the
red herrings that will come from some Government members-of multiple voting. The Bill
does not provide for multiple voting as it applies to companies, trusts, societies, or
associations of persons. The Bill leaves the provisions in the present Act in this regard
undisturbed, and clearly establishes that the vote shall be related to the person as a property
owner and not to a body with a corporate status.
The Bill also provides for allowing a vote to people who are in flats or other premises
under the company system who, in effect, have their own home held jointly on a company
basis with other people in the form of a flat. At present they are denied a voting
qualification. The Bill puts the owners of premises under the company system on the same
basis as other owners of separate properties so as to give each a rating qualification for
voting; and where there are two owners of a separate unit, both will have a rating
qualification.
Mr Acting Speaker, I commend this Bill to the House. In moving its introduction I hope
that the Government will respect the fact that a very large number of concerned New
Zealanders agree with it. The Government will allow the introduction of the Bill if it is
consistent in its desire to see women and other people who are discriminated against under
the present legislation given an equal opportunity in the decision-making process,
particularly in the area of local authorities and local loan raising.

this is to allow both a husband and a wife to possess a rating qualification, it does, in fact,

upon an individual in three different circumstances: an individual who owns shares in a flat-

lease or licence of one unit with one other person; and a corporate body which owns shares
in the flat-or office-owning company and holds an interest in the lease or licence of one unit
either as a sole interest or with one other person or company.

Local Election and Polis Amendment Bill
general principle of the Bill, which turns the clock back to the pre-1974 position.
The freeholder qualification was abolished in 1974 for the following reasons. There
existed a wide range of interpretations of the qualification amongst local authorities, and
that resulted in some rolls containing a large proportion of freehold electors and others
containing none or very few. The freehold qualification was a very old one and existed
before either the rating or the residential qualification. Logically, it should have been
abolished when the residential qualification was introduced. There was no such qualification
in counties, and with the abolition of plural voting in counties the abolition of the property
qualification provided identical franchise for both counties and municipalities. Most people
who lost a freehold qualification by the abolition were owners who lived outside the district
and whose properties were let, the tenants paying the rates. The abolition of the freehold
qualification introduced the idea of only one rating qualification for each rateable
property-and I repeat that that is not sexist. I am sure the honourable member, if he were
of a mind to, could take a case to the Human Rights Commission, and he would be thrown
out of court, because there is nothing that implies that it has to be the male spouse who will
be entitled to have his name on the roll. It is at the nomination of the parties, as I indicated
earlier, and it does not follow that automatically the male spouse's name will be first.
Mr Prebble: There is a condition that the male name comes first on all legal documents.

## p. 3906 (#386) ###########################################

3906
27 September
Accident Compensation Amendment Bill
rearrangement of the finances of the ambulance service is something that the Minister of
Labour may well be proud of.
The Accident Compensation Act stated quite clearly that the Government would
continue to be responsible for the distribution of all medical expenses and medical services
that were at that time provided free under the Social Security Act. If the member had looked
properly at that Act, she would have found that the provision of ambulance services is not
included. Ambulance services in New Zealand are provided mainly by the St. John
ambulance service, but also by the Wellington free ambulance and by hospital boards. The
St. John Ambulance and the free ambulance services work under contract to hospital
boards. That has been the situation, although the Accident Compensation Commission has a
liability, which it recognised and agreed to, for paying the cost of ambulance services needed
for accident victims. That money has not, in general, been paid.
Several years ago, when the St. John Ambulance had a telethon and raised about
$500,000 it very wisely, and I think very shrewdly, used that money to rebuild a building in
Auckland, turning it into a very fine training centre for ambulance officers. When the
building was nearing completion, Sir Thomas Skinner, Chairman of the St. John Ambulance
in Auckland, came to me and said: "We have built a building. Who is going to pay for the
running costs? Who is going to pay for training?" I said that the Government would pay, and
it does. It costs the Government $330,000 a year, and it is money well spent. The training will
help to upgrade our ambulance services.
Money does not grow on trees, and it certainly does not come from the Labour Party
research section, where those scanty notes came from. The Government had to get some
hard cash from somewhere. When I looked at the financial arrangements of the ambulance
services, I found that the Accident Compensation Commission, not through its own fault but
through other circumstances, was not pulling its weight, because the general arrangement it
operates on is that, if an accident victim requires an ambulance, the ambulance service sends
that person a bill, he pays it, and then collects the money from the Accident Compensation
Commission. That is rather a poor way of doing business. St. John Ambulance, the
Wellington Free Ambulance, and similar organisations are not happy about the prospect of
asking an accident victim to pay the full bill. It could be a large bill for an ambulance service
that is standing by in an emergency, because it has to carry all the overheads, and all the
training costs, and it could be a big mileage in the middle of the night. It could involve more
than one accident, and many people have to be on stand-by, with telephone and other
services. That is the sort of superstructure and logistic arrangement behind it.
Money is needed to train ambulance officers, and we need to move into other areas. For
a start, double manning of ambulances is required in emergencies. Everybody will readily
appreciate the need to have not only a man driving the ambulance, but also, in some
circumstances, a man in the back of the ambulance, administering drugs, stopping bleeding,
holding things in place, supplying oxygen, and doing all that is necessary. I am sure that even
Opposition members would appreciate that two men are needed to carry a stretcher; it
would have to be a big, powerful, strong ambulance driver who could pick up both ends of a
stretcher and handle it, so double manning in an emergency is necessary.
With the full support of the Ambulance Advisory Council, St. John Ambulance, the
operators, and every hospital board in the country that has the responsibility, the
Government has introduced into this legislation an arrangement under which the Accident
Compensation Commission will pay the cost of the ambulances provided for accident victims
direct to the Government. The Treasury has arranged for a special account to be set up, from
which the money will be disbursed. Instead of the accident victim paying an individual bill to
the St. John Ambulance or to somebody else and later collecting it from the Accident
Compensation Commission, the Government will collect it. Last year the Accident
Compensation Committee paid the Government more than $200,000 in acknowledgment of
its responsibility, and, when the Auditor-General approved it, he said that ratifying
legislation would be needed; now we have it.
The ambulance services that the member for Avon was so concerned about will benefit
greatly from clause 10 in the Bill. As a result of the additional finance injected, the necessary
arrangements have already started. The training school was getting ready, and Mr
Mulholland, an experienced man, had been brought out from Scotland to run the first
courses; and another man is now under training. Something is being done for the ambulance
services, about which the Labour Government did nothing whatever when it was in power
for 3 years. I am pleased that the Minister of Labour, who is in charge of the Accident

Hon. T. F. Gill: Say, on the top of Mt. Cook.
