occurs at work, or when a professional driver is driving for his employer, or on the way to or
from work, then it becomes a charge on the earners' fund. That is as it should be, because it
has always been accepted that, for the purpose of this type of decision, work commences
when a person is actually going to work.
In the case of sporting accidents requiring the use of an ambulance, if the person to
whom the accident occurs is an earner then it becomes a charge against the earners' fund. If
the person is a non-earner, such as a schoolboy or housewife, then it is charged against the
supplementary fund. The fact is that all charges for ambulances do not go against the earners
fund. To that extent the employers in Auckland were mistaken. They have told us, and I am
sure they have told the member for Roskill-and indeed they have written it in a letter—that
the proposal to shift the cost of conveyance by ambulance entirely to the earners fund was

A clear definition of “New Zealand" is necessary for a number of reasons. Perhaps the
most important reason is that of cover. Section 4 of the principal Act gives cover to all
persons who suffer personal injury by accident in New Zealand. Section 5 removes the right
to sue for damages through the court in respect of accidents in New Zealand causing
personal injury. There are, of course, circumstances where cover is extended beyond New
Zealand. One of the circumstances is dealt with in section 105A of the principal Act, which is
consequentially amended by clause 9 of the Bill. It will be referred to by one of my
colleagues. Up to the present the Accident Compensation Act has relied on the definition of
"New Zealand" as set out in the Acts Interpretation Act 1924. When the Accident
Compensation Act was first passed in 1972-before the Labour Government was able to
extend it in 1973, as it should have been extended-section 2 stated that New Zealand
included the continental shelf as defined in the section 2 of the Continental Shelf Act 1964.

Mr ELLIOTT: I have had experience of claims taking some time to settle. I shall explain

permanent damage resulting from the accident. Such accidents cause concern to the people
affected.

provisions of sections 119 and 120. The Accident Compensation Commission has been
unable to complete this case until medical evidence shows that his condition has stabilised, or
until the amount of permanent damage can be established. Such cases are delayed for
medical reasons, not because of the commission's administration. As I said before, the
average case takes less than 12 days. Scheduled payments are made for loss of limbs and
other disabilities. Even though they may be part of a final payment for permanent disability,
those payments are made promptly.

This is a short Bill, containing 13 relatively minor amendments which have been put
together after careful thought by the commission and after discussion by the Government
caucus labour committee. The Opposition has been trying to make as much as possible out of
the Bill, and is trying to deny people the small but necessary improvements at this stage. I
support the proposed amendments. Section 2 of the principal Act is amended by improving
the definition of "New Zealand". This was considered necessary after passing the Territorial
Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1977 which extends New Zealand's territorial sea
from 3 miles to 12 miles. New Zealand fishermen in this area will now be covered, although
foreigners will not. Workers on oil drilling rigs off the coast will also be covered. I think that
is a worth-while improvement. The amendments clearly state the cover provided for people
other than New Zealand citizens. I hope that one of the major considerations in next year's
comprehensive review will be New Zealanders overseas, especially members of New
Zealand sports teams.
Clause 4 extends the rewards and penalty provisions, and gives wider options for
introducing systems for adjusting levies, for claiming penalties, and for granting bonuses in
recognition of an employer's accident record. This is not confined, as it is now, to amending
levy rates. The options will be based on actuarial records and will give employers greater
flexibility. The present Act will be improved.
Difficulties have arisen in determining precisely when a visitor does or does not have
cover while in New Zealand. The matter of completing disembarkation is unclear. It is not
clear whether a person has to be coming down a gangway, or has to fall and have an accident
on a gangway, or whether he has to have an accident on board a ship or on the wharf before
he is covered by accident compensation. The amendment in clause 7 confirms that cover will
be intermittent and will subsist only when the visitor is not on board the ship on which he
came to New Zealand or on which he proposes to leave New Zealand. The rights of persons
ordinarily resident in New Zealand will not be affected. An overseas visitor or a foreign
seaman injured while on board a ship or aircraft, will not qualify.

STATE SERVICES AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I indicated during the introductory debate, its main purpose is to introduce
the concept of absence for child-care purposes into the Public Service, and to provide a
preferential re-entry right for persons absent for those purposes. The concept has been the
subject of long and detailed negotiations between the State employing authorities and the
respective service organisations. A number of conflicting interests had to be weighed up
before determining how to give effect to this general concept. Not only was there the career
of the person taking the time off to care for a child, but there were also the matters of the
rights of all other public servants, of what was administratively possible within an
organisation the size of the Public Service, and, most importantly, of ensuring that the
concept of a career Public Service based on merit rather than on security was retained.
The Bill represents an agreement reached between the State Services Commission and
the Public Service Association. Opposition members speaking to its introduction touched on
a number of points that showed clearly the balancing of these respective interests. For
example, the concept of leave without pay rather than the officer having to resign from the
service was discussed. The practical effects of having persons on leave without pay for
indefinite periods of up to 5 years in an organisation such as the Public Service would have
created serious administrative problems. It would also have had adverse effects on staff
ceilings.
The concept of resignation and re-employment in the terms proposed in the Bill will
ensure that persons who resign for child-care purposes will not be disadvantaged when they
want to return to the service. The length of time of child-care absence was criticised as not
being sufficiently long. The period needed had to be realistic in terms of the child-care
purposes, yet it also had to recognise that, after a prolonged absence from the work
environment, the ability of officers to perform the duties required of them may well have
lessened over that time relative to the merits of those officers who continued to perform the
same duties. I believe that the current proposals strike a reasonable balance in this area.
The question of appeal rights against a person reappointed under the Bill's provisions is
closely related to the fixing of the maximum period of absence. Clause 2 provides that any
other officer of the Public Service will not have a right of appeal against the reappointment
of someone who has been on child-care leave, unless that person is appointed to a higher or a
different type of position. The person who takes child-care leave will be able to return to his
or her old position, or a similar position, without being subject to the normal appeal
provisions. This recognises the level of competence attained before child-care leave was
taken. No person who has taken such leave will be able to gain any advantage over any other
public servant in relation to service as a result of anything contained in this clause. Any
promotion in the Public Service must still be on the basis of merit, and will be open to
challenge before the Public Service Appeal Board.
The same clause also provides that a person who was an officer in the Public Service at
the time of resignation and has been substantially engaged in caring for pre-school children
shall be given preferential re-entry rights to the Public Service at any time up to 4 years after
resignation, or 5 years in the case of a woman entitled to maternity leave. In addition, a


## p. 3924 (#404) ###########################################

3924
27 September
State Services Amendment Bill
further 3 months is available on top of this period-a point that was raised during the
introductory debate. The period is the maximum available to any person and may be taken
at once or may be aggregated over a number of occasions. For a husband and wife caring for
the same child or children their absences are aggregated to a maximum of 4 or 5 years as the
case may be. The absence must be for child-care purposes and the person must not have
spent any substantial period in paid employment. The operation of this clause is not
mandatory, but is at the discretion of the employing authority.
There must be an appropriate vacancy for an appointment to be made. It is not a
situation that will allow staff numbers to be increased to cater for people returning from
child-care leave. The provisions of the same clause have been fully and fairly determined in
negotiations, having regard to the concept concerned and the competing interests that are
present. The Public Service Association has been kept fully informed throughout, and has
signified its agreement to the present clause in the Bill.
The remaining clauses have also been fully discussed with the Public Service
Association. Clauses 3 and 6 have been inserted at the specific and express request of the
association, to recognise the position that can arise when a retired employee of the PSA
would make an ideal member of a classification and grading committee or, indeed, of an
appeal board, because of experience gained during his time within a service organisation. As
the Act stands at present such a person, no matter how well suited to the task, simply cannot
be appointed.
Of the other clauses, only clause 10 makes any real change to the operation of the State
Services Act. It rewrites the third schedule to the State Services Act-the higher
appointments in departments that are exempt from appeal provisions. The schedule has
been repeated in full, because of the number of changes to it in other legislation over the past
few years. The only changes made are to the positions in the Inland Revenue, Scientific and
Industrial Research, and Trade and Industry departments. The PSA continues to object in
principle to the existence of positions exempt from appeal-a stand it has maintained since
1962. The association has noted, however, that in fact two of the three changes proposed
have actually removed positions from the schedule. Apart from the clauses mentioned, the
clauses in the Bill will not bring about any major changes in the Public Service. Again, the
association has been fully consulted on all of the proposals and has signified its agreement
with them.

person must not devote a substantial part of that period since resignation to care for pre-

has been defined as 5 years and 3 months. When the Minister introduced the Bill he said that
the period of paid employment must not exceed 15 hours a week. I think that is almost a total
inhibition. The time does coincide with the time children attend kindergarten, so it has
validity. Today a great number of women with young children who attend kindergarten are
forced to work in part-time jobs for more than 15 hours. That length of time is not a viable
time for most employers. The hours would fit some jobs, but most part-time positions for
women with young children would be for 20 or 25 hours a week. I think the period of 15
hours is unfair. Members should take a long, hard look at the provision, because they do not
want to make a cosmetic provision. We want to make the ideal provision.
Very often, too, these women, who may be very qualified and skilled and useful people
in the State services may, during that period away, do work that is unrelated to their
qualifications, simply because it fits in with their family circumstances. If it were not for the
family they would be back doing the job for which they were qualified. A total of 15 hours a
week will not cover work such as child care and cleaning that they accept for economic
reasons. Then, too, a woman may take part-time work in the private sector for longer than
15 hours a week, maintaining her skill and qualifications. If, by doing that, she will be better
trained and more useful in the State services, why should she be penalised? In my opinion
the limitation of 15 hours is too restrictive.
Another matter we shall have to consider seriously in the Committee stage is the period
for which the status in the State services is sustained. From my reading of the Bill it is 5 years
and 3 months, and that covers the pre-school period for one child only. The average family
numbers something over two, and it seems to me reasonable that the time might be extended
by another couple of years to take account of the average family and the circumstances of
people who might want to take advantage of that provision. That is worth considering. Then,
too, that period, added to the average age of mothers, means that they have reached an age
of maturity and experience that can make them of great value, particularly in some social
departments of State, in which people of maturity and understanding and feeling can often
be wonderful administrators, and wonderful people to deal with the general public that those
departments are set up to serve. Therefore, we should have a long and careful look at that
matter. I do not think the additional time would add very much to the cost, but it might add
to the number of women who retain their status. Since we have the courage at long last to

Mr MALCOLM: I, for one, had no doubts. As I was saying, it is important to protect
the rights of those who may be affected by women returning to the work force. The member

When a person leaves the Public Service but wants to re-enter and make use of the
provisions of the Bill, he or she has, in fact, resigned. Presumably the specific job is filled
and not kept vacant for 5 years. The purpose of the provision is to give the person who has
left the Public Service to care for a child the chance to come back at the same grading to a
similar type of job in the same department. It does not mean a person will return to the same
desk. If in the interim no job of a similar grading or type is available, that might be a
difficulty that cannot be overcome. In other words, the job is not entirely left open. What is


## p. 3927 (#407) ###########################################

27 September
3927
State Services Amendment Bill
made available is the opportunity to come back at the same level and in the same type of slot,
should there be one available, without too much loss of seniority or grading because of the 5-
year period of absence. It is important to understand that.
The other clause that I want to cover briefly is clause 5, which clears up some confusion
about the procedures that should be followed in the event of a State servant absenting
himself from work for 4 weeks. There has always been this difficulty. What happens when a
public servant—and I must hasten to point out that this is an event that very seldom occurs,
but there can be technically the odd occasion-is absent without leave from his job? Section
60 of the principal Act makes a provision whereby, when a person is absent without leave for
4 weeks, he is deemed to have forfeited office. Of course, that is not the only way a person
can lose his job in the Public Service, but that is one way. He is deemed to have forfeited
office if he is absent for 4 weeks without leave.
The confusion that has arisen is that, under the legislation which is now being amended,
there was a provision whereby you had to attempt to get in touch with that person and give
him notice that, because of his absence, he was about to be deemed to have lost his job under
section 60. Confusion arose about whether the letter that had to be sent giving a fortnight's
warning should be at the end of the 4-week period of absence, or during the 4-week period of
absence. The Bill clears that up and makes quite clear that the procedure to be followed is
that under section 60—if a person is absent from duty up to at least 14 days, and if a letter is
sent, and if the person has still not resumed work at the end of 4 weeks, then he is deemed to
have forfeited his job under section 60 of the principal Act.
I have heard some criticism voiced, saying that it is a shame that public servants should
be allowed to get away with staying away from their job for 4 weeks. I hasten to point out
that a provision has always been in the Act, and it should not be assumed that public servants
can absent themselves from their jobs with impunity, and not be on the receiving end of
some sort of discipline. If a public servant did so with any sort of regularity or any lack of
responsibility, I am sure he would be subject to discipline. Section 60 simply specifies one
way in which a person is deemed to have forfeited his job, and the Bill seeks to amend that in
a very small way so as to avoid any administrative misunderstanding. It will also bring the
practice of several different departments into line, because there has been some difference in
practice.
Clause 10 will doubtless not totally please the Public Service Association, because a new
schedule to the principal Act is added. The third schedule sets out officers and positions that
are exempt from appeal. The Public Service Association has always, on principle, indicated
that it would prefer to see no such positions exempt from appeal, or, in the event of there
being some, as few as possible. Successive Governments have always felt that it is important
for certain senior positions to be exempt from appeal. The changes in that area are not great,
and in some areas there is actually a very small reduction in the number of positions that are
exempt from appeal. So I am confident that, while the Public Service Association will no
doubt indicate its wish that on principle there be no such position, in fact it will not find the
provisions of the Bill unduly offensive, because, in the main, it is continuing what has been a
practice for some time.
The Bill is simple legislation, but it has come about after a long period of negotiation
between the State Services Commission and the representatives of State servants in the form
of the Public Service Association. It has the agreement of the parties—particularly the parts
that deal with the rights of women to re-enter the Public Service. I am sure that in the
fullness of time this piece of legislation will be seen as forward thinking and protective of the
rights of women who seek equal opportunities in employment.

WAR PENSIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister in Charge of War Pensions): I move, That this Bill
be now read a second time. The Bill gives legislative effect to several adjustments that have
been made to rates of war pensions since December 1977. These adjustments fall into two
main categories. First, adjustments to war disablement and war widows' pensions, and,
secondly, increases to war economic pensions, war service pensions, and war veterans'
allowances. The adjustments to war disablement and war widows' pensions are on the basis
of movements in the consumer price index.
Under an agreement between the Government and the New Zealand Returned Services
Association these pensions are reviewed annually at 1 April each year. From 1 April 1978
the rate of disablement pensions for total disablement was increased by $4.35 a week to
$33.80 a week. Pro rata increases were awarded to disabled pensioners with a lesser degree
of disablement. From the same date war widows received an increase of $3.20 to $24.95 a
week. The additional pension for the severely disabled, and clothing allowances, were also


## p. 3932 (#412) ###########################################

3932
27 September
War Pensions Amendment Bill
increased from 1 April. The increases in disablement and war widows' pensions are further
evidence of the Government's commitment to meet the needs of disabled ex-servicemen and
their dependants. Most of those pensioners disabled in wartime are, of course, now well over
the age of 50 and it may be that their disability has deteriorated with increasing age. I urge all
pensioners in this position, who are receiving a pension assessed at less than 100 percent
disablement, to approach their local social welfare office and apply for a review of their
disablement pension. Arrangements would then be made for them to be medically examined
and for the rate of their pension to be reviewed in the light of the medical report.
Other adjustments that are validated in the Bill are increases in war economic pensions,
war service pensions, and war veterans' allowances from 11 January 1978 and again from 26
July 1978. The increases in these pensions and allowances from 11 January 1978 were $4.96 a
week for married couples and $2.98 a week for unmarried persons. The allowances for
children of solo parent pensioners were increased by $1.98 a week from the same date. From
26 July 1978 the basic rates of these pensions were further increased by $3.48 a week to
$77.28 a week for married couples and by $2.09 to $46.37 a week for unmarried persons.
War orphans' pensions were increased to $24.10 a week and the allowances for children of
solo parent pensioners were also increased again.
There has been some misunderstanding about the rights of people receiving war
veterans' allowances or war service pensions to transfer to national superannuation. I want
to stress again that whether it is to their advantage to do so depends on their individual
circumstances, and any pensioner still in doubt about the best course of action would be well
advised to discuss his situation with a departmental officer. War veterans' allowances and
war service pensions should not be confused with war disablement pensions, which are paid,
regardless of financial circumstances, to compensate for a disability attributable to, or
aggravated by, service with the forces. Disablement pensions can be paid in addition to
national superannuation, which means that a disabled ex-serviceman who is over the age of
60 can receive full national superannuation as well as his disablement pension.
As I explained when I introduced the Bill, the new income test for beneficiaries
legislated for in the Social Security Amendment Bill is also extended to income-tested
pensioners in clause 9 of the Bill. These provisions will be of advantage to ex-servicemen and
their dependants receiving war veterans' allowances, war service pensions, or war economic
pensions. The new income test is to be introduced from 18 October 1978 and will increase
the allowable income from $17 to $25 a week. The rate of abatement of pensions for excess
income is also significantly relaxed, and I refer members to page 2 of the Bill's explanatory
notes for details.
Also validated in the Bill is the increase, from 26 July 1978, in the supplements payable
for dependent children of income-tested war pensioners. The additional amount payable for
the third and subsequent children of war widows is increased from $1.25 to $2 a week. The
additional amount payable for the second and subsequent dependent children of married
couple pensioners is also increased from $1.25 to $2 a week. As now worded, section 84A of
the War Pensions Act provides for war pensions to be paid by equal 4-weekly instalments.
Later this year it is proposed to change the frequency of payments to fortnightly. At the
same time, the facility for direct crediting to bank and savings accounts will be extended to
war pensioners. The present system of 4-weekly payments through the mail has proved to be
less than satisfactory for a number of pensioners. The new system will overcome many of the
present difficulties, and I know that war pensioners are looking forward to the change. The
necessary legislative machinery for the change in the payment system is provided in clauses 2
and 3 of the Bill.
Since the Bill was introduced the New Zealand Returned Services Association has
expressed to me certain reservations about the extent of these clauses, and during the
Committee stage I intend to move a number of amendments to clauses 2 and 3 by way of a
Supplementary Order Paper. The Supplementary Order Paper will omit, from clause 2,
subsection (3) of the new section 84A. This subsection was originally intended to replace the
proviso to the existing section 89 of the principal Act. Section 89 provides for war pensions to
be inalienable; that is to say, they cannot be assigned or passed to any person other than the
pensioner. However, the proviso to the section reads as follows: "Provided that nothing
herein shall be construed to prevent a war pensions board from authorising, with or without
the consent of the person to whom the pension or allowance was granted, the payment of the
whole or any portion thereof to any other person for the benefit of the person to whom it was
granted or for the benefit of his wife or of any dependent child or dependent children."


## p. 3933 (#413) ###########################################

War Pensions Amendment Bill

SECURITIES ADVERTISING BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. After being reported back from the Statutes Revision Committee on 25 August,
copies of the Bill, of the report, and of the speech of the chairman of the committee were
sent to the parties who had made submissions on the Bill. In the ensuing 4 weeks the
response to the Bill as reported back has been favourable, and reflects the hard work of the
Statutes Revision Committee and those who made submissions to it. One has only to glance
through the Bill as reported back to see the amount of work done and that the Bill has
undergone substantial rewriting.
The purpose of the Bill is to consolidate and amend the law relating to the raising of
investment money from the public, with a view to increasing the protection of investors. I say
protection advisedly, because the purpose of the Bill is not to insure investors against loss.
Risk is an inseparable part of an investment, and the Bill in no way purports to alter that.
But I do not regard as legitimate that part of the risk attributable to irresponsibility or
mismanagement. The Bill is aimed at redressing the balance in favour of the investor who, in
many of the financial collapses in recent years, has had little or no way of ensuring that his


## p. 3935 (#415) ###########################################

27 September
3935
Securities Advertising Bill
investment has been responsibly and properly managed.
The law regulating the raising of investment money from the public is at present to be
found in separate statutes that do not, of course, deal with all the ways in which investment
money can be raised. The Bill repeals those separate statutes or their relevant provisions that
deal with particular types of entities, and instead will constitute as comprehensive a source of
law as is practicable about the duties and responsibilities that arise when any entity raises
investment money from the public. Put another way, the Bill represents activity-based
legislation. Accordingly, the Bill is drawn in wide terms, and so the definition of what
constitutes a security is drawn widely and encompasses items that would not readily be
regarded commercially as securities. However, the wide definition of security must be read
subject to the fact that the Bill deals only with securities offered to the public, and subject to
the new clause 5(1), which contains a list of securities that are exempted because, although
coming within the terms of the definition, they are not the kind of securities that the Bill is
intended to cover, such as the offer for sale of chattels or land.
Clause 3, which defines what constitutes the public for the purposes of the Bill, has
undergone substantial rewriting to give more certainty, in view of the wide application of the
Bill, to precisely what is or is not an offer to the public. This is not to say that all the
vagueness of the concept of a public offer has been removed, but it does represent a
substantial clarification of this part of the law. The concept of a public offer has been
rewritten having regard to who requires the protection of disclosure, and thus clause 3(2)
now excludes from that concept offers, for example, to persons whose principal business is
the investment of money or who, in the course of and for the purposes of their business,
habitually invest money.
Clause 5(2) of the Bill contains a list of issuers of securities who are exempted from the
application of the Bill except for that part dealing with the regulation of media advertising.
The exemptions have been limited to cases in which existing statutory controls were
considered sufficient and not open to abuse. To have made further exemptions would have
impaired the activity-based approach of the Bill, and, more importantly, would have
provided the opportunity for less reputable issuers of securities to operate through a type of
entity that has exempt status. In individual cases exemption, wholly or partly, would clearly
be in order, and, accordingly, these should be left to be dealt with by the Securities
Commission.
As introduced, the Bill contained many detailed provisions such as those relating to the
contents of prospectuses and deeds, the keeping of proper accounting records, and the
constraints on the contents of advertisements. Apart from the vesting of wide discretionary
powers in the Registrar of Companies, these detailed provisions brought the most
constructive criticism from the commercial community. After long and careful study, it was
considered that such matters were of a technical nature and proper for regulations.
However, to meet any allegation of legislation by stealth inherent in that procedure, and
because those matters, though technical, are important, the procedure for making
regulations has been amended to include the involvement of the Securities Commission.
No regulations may be made under the Bill except upon the recommendation of the
Securities Commission, and only in accordance with its recommendation. Before making a
recommendation, the Securities Commission must do everything reasonably possible to
advise everyone likely to be affected by the contemplated regulations of the proposed terms
of its recommendation, and provide a reasonable opportunity for receiving submissions on
the proposal. The Securities Commission must also give not less than 14 days' notice in the
Gazette of its intention to make a recommendation, and make copies of the recommendation
available for inspection. This procedure, I believe, will represent the most highly written
consultative requirement in our legislation, and will ensure that the resulting regulations
have been fully considered before being made, and that persons affected by them have had
the fullest opportunity to make known their views. The involvement of the Securities
Commission in this way will complement its general law reform function, and will allow the
best use to be made of the commission's expertise and resources.
The single most important change in the Bill as reported back is, of course, the
provision for the establishment of the Securities Commission. The Securities Commission
will bring to this area of the law the flexibility to keep it up to date with commercial practices
and to deal with the application of the Bill to specific cases or classes of cases, either by its
power of exemption or power to recommend the making of regulations. In clause 6B of the
Bill two further functions for the Securities Commission have been specified. The first is to


## p. 3936 (#416) ###########################################

3936
27 September
Securities Advertising Bill
keep under review practices relating to securities, and to comment thereon to any
appropriate body. This recognises that the commission's review function is not to be limited
to legislative matters, but that it can make its contribution over a wider field. The second
additional function is to promote public understanding of the law and practices relating to
securities. This will enable the commission to take such action as it considers appropriate to
keep the public informed of changes in such law and practice and of its own role.
Clause 1 allows different provisions of the Bill to be brought into force on different
dates by Order in Council. I envisage that Part I of the Bill, which establishes the Securities
Commission, will be brought into force as soon as practicable. The remainder of the Bill
would then be brought into force once the Securities Commission had recommended the
necessary regulations and granted the appropriate exemptions. This may well take some
time, and the Bill may not be fully in force for some 12 months.
I commend the Bill to the House as an important development in our commercial
legislation. New Zealand, though a small country, has not infrequently led the world in
certain concepts of law reform. We have, however, allowed our commercial law to become a
little dated. I see no reason why, with the degree of help from the commercial community
that has been evident in submissions on this Bill, and with the benefit of the Securities
Commission, we cannot achieve as effective and rational laws in this field, appropriate to
New Zealand conditions, as there are anywhere in the world. We shall certainly, by the
concept expressed here, avoid the bureaucratic monstrosities that have developed in other
parts of the world. I commend the Bill to the House.

Milk Amendment Bill
MILK AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time.
Mr Minogue: In view of the obvious importance the Opposition attaches to this Bill, and
its desire to debate it at this hour of the night, I think it is very crucial that we proceed
responsibly. I suggest that the Minister's time be extended.
The ACTING SPEAKER (Mr Brill): It has been suggested that the Minister's time be
extended. Is there any objection to that course being followed? There appears to be none.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: I am very grateful to the House for its interest in this Bill. I can
only assume that the member for Hamilton West and members opposite are motivated by
their interest in fun milk, which I have been promoting of late. If some members had been
drinking more fun milk rather than something else in recent hours, I am sure the proceedings
would continue on a more stable basis.
This short four-clause Bill makes three substantive changes to the Milk Act 1967. Clause
2 amends section 25 of the principal Act. That section provides for the making of regulations
to fix the price of and conditions for the sale of milk. At present only the payments or non-
payments that can be made can be spelt out. In other words, a vendor can receive only the
full amount or no amount at all. Sometimes, because of poor service, some reduction in
payment is warranted, but under the principal Act this reduction cannot be made and the
Milk Board can only stop payment altogether. The Government believes that the penalty is
too severe, and the amendment in clause 2 will allow for greater flexibility. I am sure
members will welcome that.
Clause 4 inserts nine new provisions establishing a Milk Appeal Authority and defines
its scope and functions. The proposed new section 57A establishes the appeal authority,
determines its constitution, and regulates its proceedings. The only change from the section
in the Bill originally introduced is in the qualification of the chairman. The section is now
amended to require that the chairman shall be a person who has no financial interest in the
town milk industry other than as a ratepayer or as a member of the public. Throughout the
amended clause 4 the word "authority" has been replaced by the term “appeal authority" to
distinguish it from the Milk Prices Authority referred to in the principal Act.
Section 57c relates to rights of appeal. This section in the original Bill provided for a
right of appeal for any person aggrieved by a decision of a committee appointed by the board
under section 57 of the principal Act. Authority is limited to hearing appeals against
decisions of committees appointed by the board under section 57(1) to inquire into disputes
between persons or organisations relating to the production, supply, collection, treatment,
storage, distribution, delivery, or sale of milk, when such disputes have been referred to the
board. It also widens the scope of the authority to hear appeals against decisions of the board
pursuant to the following: section 17—to refuse to grant an approval to a vendor, or to
revoke, vary, suspend, or refuse to renew an approval, or to attach such terms or conditions
that unduly restrict the vendor's operations; section 18-to fix an amount required to be paid
to it by a vendor under section 18(2). This subsection provides that the board may charge
good will if the quantity of milk supplied on a round has increased because of zoning
changes. The amount is determined by the board after having regard to the market value of
similar classes of businesses-section 20-to grant a temporary approval for an area in which
a vendor has already been approved so as to maintain supplies of milk when the approved
vendor is unable or unwilling to do so; section 24-to refuse to grant, or to grant subject to
any condition, or to add or vary any condition to, or revoke, a consent to the establishment
of a milk station.
The provision in the original section 57c relating to the documents to be sent to the
appeal authority has been transferred to a new section 57c(a) and expanded to relate to the
different requirements according to whether the appeal is against a decision of a committee
of the board, or of the board itself. Section 57E deals with the powers of the appeal authority
on hearing an appeal. It makes it clear that the decisions of the appeal authority shall be final
and binding on all parties.
Section 57H deals with the status of decisions pending determination of an appeal, and is


## p. 3945 (#425) ###########################################

27 September
3945
Milk Amendment Bill
a new section introduced in response to representations from the vendors union and the Milk
Board. Unfortunately they could not agree on a common position. The union asked that a
board decision subject to appeal should not be implemented pending the outcome of the
appeal. The board, on the other hand, asked that it be made clear that the board's decision
should stand and take effect until such time as an appeal against it had been sustained. The
existing provision is silent on which of those two positions should be observed. The Milk
Board was particularly concerned that the power to revoke the approval of a vendor who
provided unsatisfactory service should stand, and considers that in the interests of consumers
an unsatisfactory vendor should be replaced immediately.
Because of the strength of competing arguments I had earlier sought comments from the
Public and Administrative Law Reform Committee. The committee noted in its letter on the
matter: "As to which of the two solutions should be favoured, we recommend that the
lodging of an appeal should not operate as a stay on the board's decision pending the
determination of the appeal." It noted that the board comprised representatives of several
diverse interests and that its principal general function was to ensure efficiency in the
production, supply, etc. of milk, and further, after canvassing some of the matters affected,
it stated: “In all the circumstances we consider that the board's decision should stand unless
and until it is reversed or altered." I am satisfied that that is the correct decision. The Milk
Board, as noted earlier, represents all groups interested in the town milk industry, and there
is no reason to doubt the impartiality or the care the board will exercise before taking the
final step of revoking a vendor's licence for unsatisfactorily carrying out the terms of his or
her contract with the board to deliver milk.
Subsection (5) of the proposed new section 57H provides that cases already before a
magistrate's court pursuant to section 26 shall be dealt with and disposed of. The new section
57c(a) sets out the documents and so on that shall be sent to the appeal authority. This is
simply to ensure that the appeal authority has access to all necessary and relevant
documents.
The Bill clarifies certain matters, introduces an appeal authority, and provides for
appeals where none existed before. The Milk Act is the legislative vehicle by which milk for
consumers in New Zealand is regulated. It is a complex system needed to reconcile the
interests of the farmer producers, milk treatment stations, vendors-of which there are two
groups at present-dairies, and of course the Milk Board, which has the responsibility of
carrying out the day-to-day organisation of milk distribution in the interests of all groups and
the consumers. The Milk Board has to administer the Act, and inevitably, from time to time,
disagreement occurs between various sectors. The Bill was before the Lands and Agriculture
Committee, when evidence from interested parties was heard. The Bill now before the
House includes the amendments recommended by the committee.
I believe the changes provided for in the Bill will ensure a better framework for the
administration of the town milk industry in New Zealand. Despite the courtesy of an
extension of time extended to me by the House, I do not believe it is necessary to spend
more time in putting forward arguments in favour of this very important Bill, which I am
quite certain will have the unanimous and wholehearted support of the Opposition.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): Mr Acting Speaker-
Mr Hunt: A point of order, Mr Acting Speaker. I suggest that the member's time be
extended.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I take it there will be no objection.
Hon. T. F. Gill: There is an objection. I object to time being wasted in this way.
Mr WETERE: I was a member of the select committee, and, with other members of the
Opposition, support the Bill. The Bill is important for the entire industry. As the Minister
pointed out, it deals with the fixing of prices and the conditions of sales of milk, and of
course establishes an appeal authority, something the industry has lacked. The Milk Board
has been looking for such an authority for some time; such matters were administered
previously by local authorities. The Bill gives vendors an opportunity to appeal and to be
heard on all counts and establishes the administrative and secretarial services for the hearing
of appeals. Cases may be stated in the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court. The
authority, of course, is to be the commission of inquiry. As the Minister pointed out, this is
an important Bill, and although it may be small in content it has wide repercussions. The Bill
has the full support of the Opposition.
Bill read a second time.

Animals Protection Amendment Bill
ANIMALS PROTECTION AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This is a short Bill of four clauses-three of which are of a machinery nature. It
has been to the Lands and Agriculture Committee and was reported back to the House
unanimously. The one exception will bring about a quite significant change in the law.
Clause 2 confers upon the court discretionary power to order the forfeiture to the
Crown of an animal that has been found by the court to be a victim of cruelty. For many
years the Royal Federation of New Zealand Societies for the Prevention of Cruelty to
Animals has advocated three changes in the law. It wanted the penalties increased,
disqualification made possible upon the first conviction, and for the animal concerned to be
taken away from the offender. Federated Farmers of New Zealand—although not entirely
opposed to the proposal-nevertheless considered it too harsh a penalty for a first offence,
especially for people whose livelihood was associated with animals. In view of this
divergence of thinking between the SPCA and Federated Farmers it is believed that the
forfeiture provision contained in clause 2 of the Bill is a satisfactory alternative.
I shall comment briefly on the Bill clause by clause. Clause 1 contains the title of the
Bill. Clause 2 has two subclauses—the first providing for the forfeiture to the Crown and the
disposal of the ill-treated animal, as the Minister thinks best, and the second providing for
the animal concerned to be held by an inspector until the court has dealt with the alleged
offence. Subclause (2) of clause 2 is simply a consequential amendment to section 10(4) as a
result of the amendment empowering a court to order forfeiture of an animal. Previously an
inspector could hold an animal only until a magistrate had dealt with a prosecution under the
Act by ordering the return of the animal concerned either to the owner or the person
charged with the offence. With the amendment relating to forfeiture, an inspector's power
will be extended to hold covering the forfeiture situation also.
Clause 3 provides for the increase of fines specified in the nine sections of the principal
Act. The monetary penalties have remained unchanged since the principal Act was passed in
1960, and with the effect of inflation over the years the fines are now considered an
inadequate deterrent. All things considered, it is believed that the revised penalties in the
Bill are in keeping with the present-day criteria in the context of punishment of offences
triable under the Summary Proceedings Act 1967, by which most offences under the Animals
Protection Act are dealt with.
Clause 4 amends section 18 of the principal Act by providing for a monetary fine for the
offence of obstructing an inspector. In the past, as the member for Dunedin Central would
know, inspectors have encountered serious trouble when trying to carry out their duties. At
present the only penalty for such an offence is imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3
months, but this penalty is never imposed. It is considered that this amendment, in providing
for a monetary fine, will give the courts some latitude to deal with, say, first offenders for
whom imprisonment is too harsh a punishment. It is a logical amendment bringing the
provision in line with that existing for the same offence in the Animals Act 1967.

MOUNT EGMONT VESTING BILL
Second Reading
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. For many people Taranaki is the mountain and the mountain is Taranaki. The
mountain is regarded by most Taranaki people with religious awe. That applies to both
Maori and pakeha. This was demonstrated in some of the submissions made to the select
committee. I shall quote two parts of the submission made by the Taranaki Maori Trust
Board. The following statement appears on page 2: "It is with great pleasure then that we❞—
that is, the trust board-"can say that in 1978 a measure of justice has been granted to our
people by this Government. We recognise the work of the Minister of Maori Affairs, the
Hon. Duncan MacIntyre, in gaining for the Taranaki people this long-awaited prize. Over
the 100 years since the confiscation and forced land sale, Government after Government has
been approached, and Ministers and Prime Ministers have made promises. Where others
have failed to live up to their promises, the Hon. Duncan MacIntyre fulfilled his promise to
the Taranaki people, and for this reason he will always have a special place amongst our
people." The member for Northern Maori may well laugh, but that is an extract from the
submission made by the Taranaki Maori Trust Board.
On this occasion the question of Taranaki land confiscation is not under discussion.
Historical facts, already made public, need to be recalled. The Taranaki Maori people were
deprived of their sacred mountain in a manner now generally acknowledged to be unjust. It
is my honour as Minister of Lands, but more particularly as member for Egmont, to guide
through the House legislation that will right a past wrong. The Mount Egmont Vesting Bill
provides for the symbolic transfer of the Mount Egmont National Park land to the Taranaki
Maori Trust Board, representing the Maori tribes of Taranaki, who then wish to formally gift
the mountain to the people of New Zealand—that is, the Crown. When this is done, the
Maori people of Taranaki in particular, and New Zealanders in general, will be able to say
that this great public treasure, the mountain, has been given to the nation by its original
owners, or, as a Maori might well say, by their traditional caretakers.
I must say at this time that these proposals were originally raised with my predecessor,
the member for Northern Maori, who, as Minister of Lands, proceeded some way with
them. The principles of the Bill have been discussed with representatives of the Taranaki
Maori people and members of their trust board. I can say without any question that the Bill
has their whole-hearted support. In the light of some recent events it is appropriate to add
that the Taranaki Maori Trust Board has always been most proper in its approach to the
Government on this matter. For its part the Government has accepted the importance the
Maori people attach to the mountain and has not acted under any duress or under any threat
of action. As I said during the introduction, every Government must from time to time with
fairness, sincerity, and determination, find a way through land issues that have been
inherited from the past. The issue today is the mountain of Taranaki. I am sure that the
House will appreciate the significance of this legislation, not only to the Taranaki Maori
people, but to the nation as a whole. It will remove a great shadow from the pride and mana
of the Maori people of Taranaki. I believe that future generations of New Zealanders will
look back with satisfaction on this dignified Act of Parliament.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): Although I support the second reading I am sorry
that the Minister found it necessary to refer me to that part of the submission by the trust
board acknowledging the contribution of the Minister of Maori Affairs. I have no wish to
detract from his credit in any way, but, in case anyone is misled, it is as well to record exactly
the events that led up to this Bill, and the part that the third Labour Government played. On


## p. 3951 (#431) ###########################################

27 September
3951
Mount Egmont Vesting Bill
9 September 1975 representatives of the trust board met the then Prime Minister, following
which a committee was established. It was chaired by the member for Eastern Maori, the
member for Wanganui and the member for Western Maori being members. Through their
encouragement and discussions with the board we were able to arrive at a point that is
reflected in the provisions of this Bill.
The principle in the Bill has the support of the Opposition, and that was conveyed to the
trust board on 22 October 1975. Perhaps the difference should be stated here. At that time
the Prime Minister wrote to the trust board and advised that the Government had agreed
that all of the land within the park be vested in the Taranaki Trust Board in fee simple, that
all the acts of authority were to continue, that all of the vested land be gifted to the people of
New Zealand, that the park be renamed Taranaki National Park, that all assets of every kind
owned by the then Egmont National Park be vested in the new board, that the land and the
park be exempt from mining, and that the appropriate provisions in the National Parks Act
be amended and repealed. The trust board was assured that those terms would be effective
as from 1 January 1976. However, the people of New Zealand decided otherwise. I thought
it as well to put this on record.
To gain a greater appreciation of the need for this Bill, it is necessary first to understand
the history of New Zealand. The New Zealand land wars began on 29 March 1860, when a
British warship, HMS Niger, stood off the coast of Taranaki about 25 miles south of New
Plymouth. I thought that the member for Waitemata, who seems to be making noises, would
be particularly interested to know that that vessel carried heavy armament, including the
kind of weaponry used by Nelson at the battle of Trafalgar. That ship pounded the small
mission at Warea for 2 days and nights. The point I am establishing is that this was prompted
by the refusal of the Taranaki people to sell Waitara in 1859.
This state of affairs spread from Taranaki to the Waikato and Tauranga, and led to
conflict that lasted for about 10 years. The Government then decided to act, and in 1863
introduced the New Zealand Settlements Bill. Judging from the callous indifference to the
feelings of others shown by Tory Governments, it would appear that Tory members have not
changed very much in 114 years. Many of them would like to forget, and perhaps we all
should, but the terms under which we should forget are important. We should be proud of
our history and the lessons we have learned, because we shall not rely on 600 policemen to
correct the claims of the Maori community, or rely on the actions that Tory Governments
have taken over the years.
Let us look at what happened in 1863, and perhaps we should ask ourselves what
changes, if any, have taken place since that time. In 1863 Mr Fox, in moving the first reading
of the New Zealand Settlements Bill, is recorded at page 782 of the 1861-1863 record of
parliamentary debates as saying: "The primary feature of its policy is the suppressing of the
existing rebellion. That is the first and principal thing we have to do. What is required is a
large population, practically outnumbering that of the Natives in those districts where
rebellion exists, or may exist, to be permanently settled, with ownership of the land, so that
they may not only have an interest, but the ability to defend their homes from future
aggression." Instead of using the military, which action had shown the Government to be
foolish in the extreme, Parliament adopted a constitutional measure to confiscate property
and raise loans on the lands that were confiscated. Mr Fox went on to say: "I am glad to say
that, on examining a carefully prepared approximate return of the acreage which is included
in those districts where rebellion exists-and in which alone, at present, the Government has
any intention of extended operations-there appear to be at least 4 000 000 acres of land
available for the purpose.' The Government thought it had 4 000 000 acres it could
confiscate.
It is interesting to note that only one voice was raised in the House in objection to that
obnoxious Bill. Mr Fitzgerald, at that time the member for Ellesmere, said: "I object, first,
upon the ground that it is contrary to the Treaty of Waitangi, which has distinctly guaranteed
and pledged the faith of the Crown that the lands of the Natives shall not be taken from them
except by the ordinary process of law-that is, taken within the meaning of the Treaty.
Again, I object because I conceive the provision to be in direct opposition to that section of
the Constitution Act which debars us from making any law which is repugnant to the law of
England."
The view held by that lone voice in 1863—although not listened to—is as relevant today
as it was then. We should ask ourselves what responsibility the present generation accepts
for the actions of its forebears. The present generation has inherited the benefits, the


## p. 3952 (#432) ###########################################

3952
27 September
Mount Egmont Vesting Bill
misgivings, and some of those difficulties. My purpose this evening is not merely to open up
those old wounds, but to draw the attention of the House to the fact that measures should
now be taken by the New Zealand Parliament, not to correct our history, but to enable a
greater appreciation so that we may learn from those incidents and avoid making the same
mistakes again. This matter has been the subject of a royal commission of inquiry and of
petitions to the House over many years. On page 11 of the report of the 1928 royal
commission we read this: "Both the Taranaki wars ought to be treated we think as having
arisen out of the Waitara purchase, and judged accordingly. The Government was wrong in
declaring war against the natives for the purpose of establishing the proposed rights of the
Crown under that purchase." It goes on to say: "We think that, in the circumstances, they
ought not to have been punished by the confiscation of their land."
We are talking abut a mountain. Half of the area was confiscated, and the other half was
the subject of forced purchase at 25c an acre. The royal commission pointed out that the
original area confiscated was 1 275 000 acres of which 557 000 acres were purchased from the
natives under forced sale and paid for by the Government; 256 000 acres were returned to
the natives, according to the royal commission report, leaving 462 000 acres as the total area
finally confiscated. The Bill refers to a portion of the 462 000 acres finally confiscated.
Payment was made by the Crown by way of contributions each year to a trust board.
One might ask why there has been no satisfaction and why people keep raising the issue,
when there was an attempt in 1928, and over the years since then, to try to correct it. Our
history books record any number of efforts to resolve what is essentially a grievance of 115
years' standing. The position was recognised by the third Labour Government, which
decided to move in a way that had never before been attempted. The Waikato people and
the Tauranga people were all affected by the same conflict, and no amount of simple cheque
book policy will restore the position or erase the memory. If in fact it was Parliament that
created the problem-technically a crime under the law-Parliament can take immediate
steps, 114 years later, to correct it. It is my earnest hope that the Government will
recommend to Her Majesty the Queen that the tribes of Taranaki, Waikato, and Tauranga
be pardoned for their actions in defending their homes and their lands and properties. What
is the grievance of the people concerned? Many of them spent years in jails in defence of
their homes and had their properties confiscated, because, under the law, they were
regarded as rebels. The people of Waikato, Taranaki, and Tauranga are proud people who
deserve better. Before we can move to compensate them for the economic development of
property they were deprived of, it is my firm view that the Government should recommend
to the Queen that the three tribes concerned be pardoned. Following that, the question of
damages arose.
Mr Wellington: How much?
Hon. M. RATA: In 1975 damages were assessed by the trust board at $10 million. That
was a conservative estimate. The Bill does go a long way towards meeting the damages.
Parliament can no longer avoid facing up to this matter. It cannot rely on time to erase the
memory of that long-forgotten period, because the dependants are becoming more active,
and properly so. Clause 6 envisages a gift to the Crown, but the first thing the Crown does is
to set down conditions by stating that it will consult. Among other things I shall examine the
individual clauses during the Committee stage. I want to stress that the matter is important,
not only to the Taranaki people, but as an indication of how best to deal with land and the
land claims of the Maori people. If Parliament does not see those claims for what they are,
New Zealand will suffer needlessly the type of action that took place in Auckland on 25 May
1978, when the Government had to rely on the constabulary and 600 policemen to restore
order in what was considered a disorderly situation. This need not happen again if the
Government combines the action it has taken in the Bill with monetary compensation and
the pardoning of the tribes concerned. They had not committed a crime, nor had they in my
view committed an offence. They would, in the view of most people today, be highly
honoured for defending their homes, their families, and their district. I shall conclude on a
lament, which, I believe, most appropriately expresses the strong feeling the Maori people
have about this matter.

New Zealand Settlement Act 1863. In earlier submissions to the committee the people spoke
of the mountain Taranaki as being the most sacred symbol of the Taranaki tribes. The
submission stated that the mountain's loss has been a continuing cause of grief. The people
feel that part of a great weight has been lifted from their shoulders and part of the cloud
removed from above their heads. Since the land was wrongfully confiscated in the 1860s,
generations of Maori people have fought and died, protested, and petitioned pakeha
Governments to gain justice. The 1928 royal commission on confiscated lands and other
grievances found that the Taranaki people should not have been punished by the
confiscation of any of their land. It stated further that when our people were driven from the
land, their houses destroyed, and their cultivations laid to waste, they were not rebels and
they had not committed any crime. Little has been done over the years to rectify the
injustice.
The submissions clearly point out the feelings of the Taranaki people, and the members
who served on the committee during the hearing of submissions will appreciate those
feelings. If the submissions made to the committee could be transferred to the House, their
full impact would be understood. I hope that what we are doing here tonight will throw some
light on the depth and feeling of our people throughout the years, and that the sacredness of
the mountain for every Maori in the country, particularly the people of Taranaki, will be
realised. The sacred waters from Dawson Falls are used by every Maori religious
organisation for spiritual water and healing. The member for Northern Maori dealt
adequately with the history of the mountain. The submissions go some way to restore the
mana of our people in Taranaki. The tribes represented in the submissions were from
Parinihinihi ki Waitotara. The measure has my full support.

## p. 3956 (#436) ###########################################

3956

Mount Egmont Vesting Bill
As far as the Government is concerned, the Bill is also symbolic inasmuch as it
encapsulates a patronising platitude to Maoridom. In clause 4 the Government vests the
mountain of Egmont in the Taranaki Maori Trust Board, yet clause 5 provides that the gift
shall be given back to the Crown. Consider for a moment those two consecutive clauses in a
mere 9-clause Bill. Clause 4 gives the mountain to the Maori people, and clause 5 takes it
away. There is no respect for the right of the Maori people to have the ceremony on their
own marae and determine when they give it back. There is no respect for the chiefs of this
magnificent tribe, who, in years of great sadness and dissension under nineteenth century
Tory capitalism, accepted parliamentary legislation that royal commissions subsequently
deemed to be unjustified. That is also symbolic. A twentieth century Tory Government is
now making this platitudinous gesture.
Thirdly, if the Minister had been genuine, he would have recognised in an earlier Bill
the right of the Taranaki people to be represented as of right on the Taranaki National Park
Board. It is recorded in Hansard that he did not. Only the protestations of Labour
Opposition members in the select committee caused that same Minister to recognise that
these people should be represented on the Mt. Egmont Trust Board as of right. That further
symbolises the lack of genuineness in this whole gesture, as does the fact that the Taranaki
people were not even invited to witness this debate. Some are resident here in Wellington.
There are representatives who support the Government-Maui Pomare, for instance. Dr
Love, who made his submissions with such vigour that they could not be denied, has not
been invited to observe this debate. One does not discuss matters of great moment without
the people concerned being present. I suppose it is sufficient that the breach is filled by the
four Maori members. The member for Western Maori, in particular, is the representative,
and the member for Northern Maori transacted this deal with Dr Love on behalf of his
people in a most satisfactory manner-more satisfactory than anything achieved in this Bill. I
have my own association with this mountain and these people, because my nieces and
nephews are there protecting what to me is a very precious piece of land in Waitara. As part
of this tribe, they are protecting the Kahurangi pounamu of my tribe and my family in the
lands at the foot of that mountain. May she rest is peace.
One cannot say of the Minister what was recently said by over 2000 Maori people when
they made perhaps cynical but sensitive observations on the attitudes towards them of
people who have not the same cultural heritage. They said to the Leader of the Opposition:
"Too few pakeha leaders have ever been able to express the rare magic in your words, rare
because your expressions had soul. They emanated from the font of wisdom from which our
elders partook. Like them, our leaders, you have made us proud to be Maori. We feel we are
someone, that there are some pakeha leaders who are fighting for us, protecting our rights,
prepared to cross cultural boundaries in an effort to understand us for what we are,
bicultural New Zealanders, sharing both worlds, and wanting to participate on equal terms,
not unequal in it—not as the subjects of patronage, seeing that we have something unique to
give to our country, but not often having other than the gift of our labour accepted. Yet we
have, as you have told us, so much more in our basket to offer our country."
They said to that leader: "We have been respected by you, not treated with patronage.
We have been lifted by you, not put down. We have been upheld by you because the gifts-
our precious jewels, our values that we offer to our country-are perceived by you as having
value, and not ignored. This moment, this tribute, will endure, and will be one of the
inspiring memories that our Maori youth will cherish. They will go forth from this occasion
prouder still to be Maori New Zealanders. You have earned a place of special veneration
among us. Your perception of the value of our elders, your philosophies thrill us. Your
vision inspires us." They asked that leader to accept the unique status of tangawhenua. They
called him, "Te Amorangi", meaning a "leader of vision". They said to him, "Your thoughts
have a soul. We are a people who have been taught to regard this highly. You have
succeeded in communicating events on a level that few pakeha leaders are able to. Your
address tonight had a spiritual dimension.”
That citation was expressed to the Leader of the Opposition before more than 2000
Maori people on 16 September. I was present, and I was very proud. Attitudes for which the
House cannot legislate are most significant, and are the supreme barometer for measuring
race relations anywhere in the world, but particularly in New Zealand. This was said of a
leader whom they regarded as Tama Rangi, a leader of vision. The point I am trying to make
is that while the Taranaki people under the noble leadership of their prophet Te Whiti-the
first apostle of passive resistance in the Western World before Ghandi-were striving to

CORNISH COMPANIES MANAGEMENT AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Cornish Companies
Management Amendment Bill be introduced. The purpose of the Bill is to extend the powers
of the statutory manager in relation to the realisation of the pooled property of the Cornish
group, and to complement the pooling of the property of that group by including the tax
losses of Mr Cornish.
The Cornish Companies Management Act was passed in 1974 in the face of the
impending collapse of the Cornish group of trading concerns. The Act made special
provision for the protection of depositors and creditors of the group by pooling its assets and
liabilities in one company, Cornish Investments Ltd., freezing that company's liabilities,
appointing a statutory manager, and by providing for the orderly disposition of its assets and
payment of its liabilities.
That orderly realisation and payment has progressed satisfactorily over the 4 years since
the passing of the Act. The statutory manager has sold as going concerns, or closed, about 12
of the group's trading concerns, and is operating the remaining concerns profitably. The
group's creditors have so far received an aggregate distribution of approximately $6,352,000.
Of the group's creditors, those who are unsecured, including investors, have received a


## p. 3961 (#441) ###########################################

28 September
3961
Cornish Companies Management Amendment Bill
dividend of 26c in the dollar, representing an aggregate distribution of $3,487,000.
The distribution to creditors will be substantially increased after the sale yesterday to
the Government Life Office of the World Trade Center in Wellington, the largest single
asset of the group. The statutory manager has indicated that, after payment of mortgages on
that asset, the sale should produce a further dividend of 38c in the dollar for unsecured
creditors. Settlement of the sale is expected to take place next month, and the statutory
manager expects, with other funds becoming available, to make a distribution of 40c in the
dollar about mid-November. That would bring the total dividend to 66c in the dollar to
unsecured creditors and an aggregate distribution to all classes of creditors to more than $12
million.
The advisory committee to the statutory manager has indicated to me that although it is
difficult to forecast when the realisation of the remainder of the pooled property will be
complete, there appears at this stage to be every prospect of creditors ultimately receiving a
dividend of 100c in the dollar. This, of course, would not have been possible had the Cornish
Companies Management Act not been passed. Although the remainder of the group is
operating profitably, the statutory manager indicates that given the present level of business
activity and the general lack of interest by potential purchasers, the present opportunities for
making further substantial realisations are negligible.
Under the Bill the statutory manager, with the consent of the advisory committee may
promote the formation and registration of a public company, and with the consent of
creditors and the sanction of the Supreme Court there may be transferred to such company
any part of the pooled property that the statutory manager considers cannot be
advantageously realised in any other way. In consideration of the transfer, the company is to
issue shares or other securities pro rata to creditors, and the value of those shares or other
securities is to be received by each creditor in satisfaction or part satisfaction, as the case may
be, of his debt or claim.
The Bill defines this method of disposing of any part of the pooled property as an
"arrangement"—and I wish to emphasise that a proposed arrangement can be put to
creditors only where the statutory manager considers that it cannot be advantageously
realised in any other way. To give more flexibility in disposing of any part of the pooled
property, the Bill also enables the statutory manager, with the consent of the advisory
committee, to promote the formation and registration of a company in order to sell to it any
part of the pooled property. This is an extension of the statutory manager's present power of
realisation, and will enable him to float a company publicly for the purpose of purchasing
pooled property. If the opportunities for making further substantial realisations do not
improve, these powers will provide the statutory manager with additional courses of action
to expedite the realisation of the pooled property.
The Cornish Companies Management Act pooled into one company not only the assets
and liabilities of other companies in the group, but also virtually all the assets and liabilities
of Mr Cornish. This was done because about 45 percent of the group's assets and liabilities
were those of Mr Cornish. The effect was to place Mr Cornish in a position analogous to that
of a bankrupt, without actually adjudicating him to be such.
At the end of the income year ended 31 March 1974, just 3 months before the Act was
passed, the Cornish group had accumulated substantial tax losses, of which about half were
attributable to Mr Cornish. However, the view was taken that tax legislation did not permit
Mr Cornish's tax losses to be set off against future assessable income of Cornish Investments
Ltd. This, in view of the pooling of assets and liabilities of the Cornish group. is anomalous,
and, accordingly, the Bill entitles Cornish Investments Ltd. to the benefit of the tax losses of
Mr Cornish as at the end of the present income year.
I wish to emphasise that this amendment is consistent with the original pooling of
property, and has been agreed to by Mr Cornish. The Bill arises from the representations of
the statutory manager and his advisory committee, and I take this opportunity of
acknowledging their progress and work in what is quite a complex job.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
HEAVY ENGINEERING RESEARCH LEVY BILL
Introduction
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): I move, That the Heavy


## p. 3962 (#442) ###########################################

3962
28 September
Heavy Engineering Research Levy Bill
Engineering Research Levy Bill be introduced. On 30 August this year the New Zealand
Heavy Engineering Research Association was incorporated. It is an autonomous body
whose function is to assist the development of the heavy engineering industry by carrying out
research into industry problems. With a board of control consisting of six industry
representatives and four Government nominees, it will be funded in part by an industry levy,
by membership subscriptions, and a Government subsidy through the Department of
Scientific and Industrial Research vote, and provision was made in the 1978-79 estimates for
$41,000 for this purpose.
The Bill empowers the Minister of Science and Technology to impose a levy, not
exceeding $5 per tonne, on specifiied types of iron and steel used as raw materials for heavy
engineering. Like the Government subsidy, the levy will be used to fund research in the field
of heavy engineering undertaken by the new research association. A viable heavy
engineering industry is essential and basic to our national industrial development. While the
existing industry has shown the potential for high-quality work, particularly in the
production of industrial plant and equipment that is forecast as a growth area, there is an
obvious need for a greater commitment industry-wide to research and development. This is
particularly true if the potential for export is to be realised, even though basic engineering
skills are well developed in New Zealand.
The proposal for a heavy engineering research association came from the heavy
engineering advisory committee, a committee serviced by the Department of Trade and
Industry. A report commissioned by the advisory committee indicated several areas where
industry performance could be improved, including the provision of basic statistics and
market intelligence and an increased level of technical research into production processes
and quality control. The formation of a heavy engineering research association has been
actively promoted by the New Zealand Manufacturing Engineers Federation, and has been
supported by the Ministers of Labour, Trade and Industry, and Science and Technology.
Major firms have taken an active part in the establishment of the association, and plans are
already under way for recruiting staff and establishing premises in the Auckland area.
As the Bill is not contentious and representatives of the heavy engineering industry
agree with the suggested levy to support research for their industry, I do not propose to refer
the Bill to a select committee.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

reply on behalf of the Minister of Internal Affairs. "No. The requirements of the Chatham
Islands air service call for a special style of aircraft, and the route involves long over-water
flying time and the use of a grass airstrip on the Chatham Islands. The operator must be able
to provide a regular schedule of flights over that difficult route with an aircraft capable of
carrying passengers, mail, and some freight on each flight. Those requirements have been
met very satisfactorily by the present operator over the past 10 years, and no other
prospective operator has demonstrated a similar capability. The contract with Safe Air Ltd.
is therefore being renewed."
Mr Kirk: Can the Under-Secretary confirm that no other operator has had the chance of
tendering for that service?

licence to operate to the Chatham Islands have failed because they could not meet the
desired specifications and would only reduce the efficiency of the Government's service by
competing for passengers and the main revenue-producing payload, and not providing
regular mail deliveries or any freight carriage. I understand that that decision has been
supported by the Air Services Licensing Authority. In considering the matter our concern
has been that, in addition to providing a service to the Chatham Islands-and I know we are
supported wholeheartedly by the member for Lyttelton-we ensure the safety of the crew
and passengers. That has been the paramount consideration.

fare increase thus avoided?

Telephone Exchange-Burwood
