ADJOURNMENT-FREEZING INDUSTRY
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received a request from
the member for Roskill to move the adjournment of the House in accordance with Standing
Order 89. The request, which was received this morning within the required time, reads as
follows: "I wish to give notice of my intention to move the adjournment of the House under
Standing Orders 89 and 90, because of immediate consequences on industrial relations in the
freezing industry by the release today of the report by Sir William Dunlop. The purpose of
the adjournment is to discuss the text and recommendations of the report to permit
Parliament to give a lead to the Government before any further unworkable legislation is
introduced, and to ensure that the legislation is such that it provides for industrial harmony.
Accordingly I submit: (1) it is a specific matter of recent occurrence; (2) the matter involves
a major export industry, proposed legislative changes, and is of such urgency that it demands
the immediate attention of the House and the Government; and (3) the matter clearly
involves the administrative responsibility of the Government."
The request is not framed in general terms-it deals with a particular case of recent
occurrence. For an adjournment motion to be allowed to proceed the matter must require
the immediate attention of the House or the Government. The report itself recommends
legislative changes, which it describes as being urgent. Because of the status of the inquiry
held by Sir William Dunlop into the penalty provisions of the Industrial Relations Act, I
think I must regard this report as being of more importance than the ordinary run of
recommendations for legislative action, which Governments continually receive from a
variety of sources. For this reason I believe the requirement that the matter demands the
immediate attention of the House or the Government to be met. Finally, the matter must
involve ministerial or administrative responsibility. The report deals with matters that clearly
fall into this category. For these reasons I am disposed to accept the application, and I ask
members who approve of the proposed discussion to rise in their places.
At least five members having risen in their places.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) said: A point of order, Mr Acting Speaker.

you are able to say that the report referred to urgent matters, obviously the embargo has
been breached. I also wonder whether this matter can be debated at this time, because few

seeks to advance the report of Sir William Dunlop in his defence. The fact is that the report

prosecutions at Ocean Beach. The fact is that those prosecutions arose as a result of political
influence; there is absolutely no argument against that, and it is substantiated by the report.
The report found that the Government had been considering the issue of industrial
relations at that time; and I read from page 4 to annex 1, paragraph 14: "The department
came under a good deal of pressure, some of it political, to initiate action against those who
stopped work at Ocean Beach. There is little doubt that the seriousness of the offence
measured in terms of loss was a major factor in determining political attitudes, and indeed, it
was this factor which distinguished the stoppage at Ocean Beach from others which had
taken place in the industry. It was on this basis also that a decision was made to initiate
action." The Minister can read what he likes from Sir William Dunlop's other remarks. The
fact is that the report states, first, that the decision to prosecute was a political decision, and
that the political decision arose because the situation was judged serious politically-and the
member for Invercargill and the member for Awarua can say “amen" to that. The fact is that
it was a political decision to institute proceedings against those workers.
The report notes that three conclusions can be drawn: the Government and the
department must be seen to be consistent in their policy of enforcement; there are inherent
difficulties in disentangling political considerations from any decision to initiate or withdraw
prosecutions against striking workers; and it illustrated the difficulties faced by the legal
system in processing a large number of informations simultaneously. That is quite clear.

relations. Secondly, in the view of the report and having looked at the Ocean Beach
situation, one cannot disentangle political considerations from initiating the decision to start

there is a ground for them. The problem is always to ensure that the terms of the Act are
operated and observed, so that there are no offences and therefore no penalties.
Let us look at the number of complaints made under the Industrial Relations Act during
the term of the former Labour Government, when the member for Roskill was the Minister
of Labour, and see what action was taken on those breaches. The 1976 annual report, which
quoted the figures for the 1975 year when the member for Roskill was Minister of Labour,
demonstrated that under the Industrial Relations Act 1973, 551 complaints were laid when
breaches were not disclosed; but there were 1534 complaints indicating breaches on which
the Labour Government, the Secretary of Labour, or his registrar took action. Then the
action to be taken was prosecution. Ten of 16 cases resulted in conviction, but 1201
complaints were found to be minor offences or excusable.
Now Opposition members are clamouring for prosecution for all offences, and taken
right through to the end so that the blood flows. That is crackers; it is crazy, unrealistic, and
stupid, and in fact history has proved that that does not happen. The Secretary of Labour
and his officers are obliged to exercise their discretion, and, in terms of the purposes of the
Industrial Relations Act, they almost always set out to improve harmony in industrial
relations. In the long title of the Industrial Relations Act are words to the effect that, "This is
an Act to make provision for improving industrial relations." For that reason the discretion
even to enter upon a prosecution is exercised very rarely, and there must be cases in which
the public interest demands that, once entered upon, they must not be taken through to the
end if the spirit of the Industrial Relations Act, which is enshrined in its long title, is to be
properly observed.
I believe that Sir William Dunlop's report is a very valuable document. The parties to
the conference unanimously recommended that his opinion should be sought, and I shall be
very interested indeed to learn their comments on Sir William's report to the Government.
The parties also unanimously agreed that, depending on the outcome, all stock on hand
would be killed before a stoppage, and the Secretary of Labour would prepare a
comprehensive report on the application of the legislation.
Sir William's comments and his conclusions are being made available to all the parties.
It was also agreed that, depending on the outcome, an approach would be made to the
Government by each party requesting that the prosecutions be annulled. Subject to the
Government acceding to the request of the parties, conciliation proceedings would begin
forthwith between the freezing companies and the freezing workers' unions, and the
consultative committee would resume.

The member for Roskill said that all informed advice to the Government was against
penalties in industrial law. He must have forgotten the advice the Employers Federation
gave the Labour Government in 1973 in submissions on the Industrial Relations Bill. The
federation said: "We know of no country in the world whose labour laws do not have the
capacity to ensure compliance with them. Legislation which conferred penalties and imposed
obligations but prescribed no penalties would be unenforceable and of little worth." and
later: "Those who ignore the procedures contained in the legislation would be subject to the
close scrutiny of the community, and consequently to the full rigours of legal disapproval."
The Labour Government heeded that advice and inserted sections 147 to 157 in the
Industrial Relations Act, which provide that either a party to an award or a collective
agreement, or the inspector of awards, may bring proceedings in the Arbitration Court for
breach of an award, and the Arbitration Court may, if it sees fit, impose a penalty of up to
$500 in specific circumstances. If that is not a penalty, I do not know what is!

I hope the House will continue in a normal manner without too much procrastination. I do

NEW ZEALAND FILM COMMISSION BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister for the Arts): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. Because of the lateness of the hour I shall be as brief as possible, but I believe that this
is a most important Bill, and therefore I feel that there are certain things I must say, even
though the hour is late.
When I introduced the New Zealand Film Commission Bill on 24 August I was
delighted by the enthusiastic response it received from both sides of the House. I believe the
whole House recognised that the Bill represents a major advance in the development of the
arts of this country. At that time I indicated that, in view of the extensive consultations that
the Interim Film Commission has held with interested parties, there was no need for the Bill
to be referred to a select committee. I did, however, express the intention that there should
be sufficient time to enable honourable members to examine its provisions more closely, and
that has been provided. I also indicated that if, after considering the Bill, any members had
thoughts they wanted to express to me, I should be only too happy to hear them. No one has
approached me, so I take it that, after looking closely at the Bill, Opposition members are
satisfied with it.
As I indicated in my introductory speech, the Bill provides for the establishment of a
fully independent statutory authority, which will play a major role in developing the New
Zealand film industry. The principal responsibility of the new Film Commission will be to
encourage, by financial and other means, the making, promotion, distribution, and


## p. 3992 (#472) ###########################################

3992
28 September
New Zealand Film Commission Bill
exhibition of New Zealand films.
At this stage it is appropriate to outline the basic objectives of the Government in
providing support for the film industry. Within the industry itself, different people have
differing views as to what our objectives should be. On the one hand, there are those who
regard films purely as an art form. To them the purpose of Government support should be to
enable the creativity of New Zealand cinema artists to be expressed. They would see the job
as being to create films that become part of New Zealand's heritage, and to help to identify
those features of our society that are peculiar to New Zealand, and which record for our
descendants what life in New Zealand today is like.
There are, though, others who look upon films as a commercial enterprise. Their
concern is to build an industry that will return a profit to investors. They emphasise that only
by orientating New Zealand production to the international market are film makers and
investors likely to achieve sufficient commercial success to enable them to continue. I believe
the dichotomy between those views to be more apparent than real. New Zealand film
makers have already been responsible for several high-quality feature films.
I had intended to deal tonight with what the Interim Film Commission has done, but,
because of the lateness of the hour, I shall not do so. However, if anyone is interested, I shall
be only too happy to discuss it with him. But if films like those already produced, and other
still better films in the future, are to be made regularly, to become a regular part of our lives
rather than occasional highlights, there must be an industrial base from which they can
spring. For that reason there is, to my mind, no contradiction between the commercial
aspect of film making on the one hand and artistic film production on the other. We need a
solidly based commercial film industry in New Zealand to sustain the employment of the
creative and technical skills of the industry.
However, a totally commercial cinema, concerned only with profits and orientated
mainly towards international audiences, is not sufficient. We must be concerned to have a
film industry that expresses New Zealand's character. The ultimate success of our policies
will be judged by whether we can develop beyond an industry of commercial profits to an
industry that makes a lasting contribution to New Zealand's cultural heritage. Having, I
trust, clarified the objectives of providing support for a film industry, I turn now to the
provisions of the Bill before us and assess them in terms of those objectives.
The commission's financial support for film production will fall into three broad
categories: first, preproduction costs, including script development; secondly, production
investment; and, thirdly, marketing. In selecting projects for assistance, the commission will
have two principal criteria in mind. On the one hand, it will have to satisfy itself that the film
is to have a significant New Zealand content, whether this is in terms of examination of
issues directly relevant to the New Zealand way of life, or in terms of substantial
participation of New Zealanders in any or all aspects of its production. The commission will
favour projects in which New Zealanders have determining roles in the production,
direction, writing, editing, photography, design, and acting. It will, therefore, be directly
concerned with financing essentially New Zealand films of cultural value which interpret the
New Zealand experience to New Zealanders.
The second criterion to which the commission will have to give attention will be the
financial viability of a particular project. In assessing any proposal it will be looking for
evidence of experience on the part of the personnel involved in the production. It will need
to satisfy itself that they have the ability and the experience to complete the project
efficiently, effectively, and to a high standard. In every case not only will the effectiveness of
the treatment on script as a piece of writing for the screen be assessed, but also its market
appeal, and the practicability of presenting it in visual form. The proposed budget will be
carefully scrutinised to assess whether it is realistic, and in accord with the nature and
content of the film. Assistance to the film industry through the commission must not be seen
simply as a handout to the arts. Although such assistance will benefit the development of the
arts, the commission's emphasis will be on businesslike investment, intended to encourage
further participation from other sources, and also to provide a satisfactory return on the
investment.
New Zealand's small domestic market creates a particular problem for our film makers.
The general rule of thumb overseas is that a film must return the box office four or five times
its production costs in order to break even. The small size of the potential audience in New
Zealand and its dispersal over long distances mean that box-office takings are limited and
distribution costs are high.


## p. 3993 (#473) ###########################################

28 September
3993
New Zealand Film Commission Bill
Our film makers face strong competition from high-cost, lavishly produced, and
strongly promoted films from overseas. Even a box office blockbuster on the scale of Jaws
would be unlikely to return enough in New Zealand to cover its costs. However, there are
two ways to alleviate what would seem, on the face of it, to be formidable obstacles to a
viable domestic operation. [Interruption.] If the member over there cannot understand that,
then I am sorry. Apparently, he is a wee bit thick. I am amazed that one we considered had
reasonable intelligence should be unable to understand that.
On the one hand, we must endeavour to keep costs as low as possible, right from the
script stage. On the other hand, we must look to other markets. That is why one of the major
fields of action of the Film Commission must, and will be, the promotion and the marketing
of films. It must begin to seek distribution deals at the script stage, or even earlier, when the
first treatment is received. It must not allow any producer the luxury of making a film
without ensuring that that film will have an audience. The Motion Picture Marketing
Association, which comprises representatives of the National Film Unit, TV1, and private
producers, has already achieved some successes in overseas marketing. This experience must
be built on.
The Film Commission will also be investigating the possibility of the co-production of
films in association with overseas film interests. Co-production has the dual advantage of
assuring overseas release while, at the time time, utilising at least a proportion of New
Zealand production facilities and personnel. Internationally, the track record for filra
making is reckoned to be about one successful undertaking to every nine failures. It must be
expected, therefore, that our fledgling industry will have its share of failures. However, I am
optimistic that it will have its share of successes, too. Given our isolation, our small home
market, and limited resources, the beginnings must be modest. With careful and judicious
assistance from the commission, which this Bill establishes, I have great faith in the ability of
New Zealanders to make films and to make them well. If this goal can be realised, the
benefits accruing to the country from such an enterprise will be considerable. Let me for a
moment consider those benefits under three headings. First, from the cultural point of view,
the development of a flourishing industry will benefit New Zealanders by providing them
with film expressions peculiar to this country. This will counter the largely unrelieved diet of
films from other cultures which till now, has been our lot. The New Zealand community
cannot but benefit from the renewed vigour of our film-makers as they find increased
opportunities to present, in lively and entertaining ways, their interpretation of our life style.
Moreover, the development of a lively film industry here will act as an incentive for skilled
performers, writers, directors, cameramen, designers, technicians, and a wide range of other
people to remain here rather than be forced to pursue their crafts outside the country. They
will enrich our cultural life across a wide spectrum.
Secondly, there will be social benefits. Film making will provide New Zealanders with
the opportunity to examine aspects of their own society through a medium of expression
which has a very broad appeal. I should like to think that motion pictures could become an
important means by which New Zealanders are helped to come to a better understanding of
themselves, and achieve a greater awareness of their role and responsibility as a significant
South Pacific nation. In addition, film will make it possible for the world at large to see New
Zealand and New Zealanders as they see ourselves.
Thirdly, we must not overlook the far-reaching economic benefits of this development.
Assisting film making is a highly productive form of financial patronage. The establishment
of a film industry in this country will provide employment opportunities for film workers,
actors, writers, musicians-in fact, all art-related employees. There will be a saving of
overseas funds on imports of foreign films for domestic screening, and there is also the
exciting prospect of the development of an export industry which could earn foreign
exchange, both directly through sales and indirectly through the publicity which we would
gain from overseas exhibition.
One of the commission's major functions will be to encourage and promote the efficient
use of available resources within the industry. Films assisted by the commission will be
expected to use existing resources in both the public and the private sectors, rather than to
require expenditure of overseas funds to purchase equipment and engage personnel
overseas. The largest single film-making resource in New Zealand is the National Film Unit's
new premises in the Hutt Valley. I believe that the unit's activities can be co-ordinated with
those of the new commission so that the National Film Unit will help to meet the demands of
an industry which requires various specialised skills.


## p. 3994 (#474) ###########################################

3994
28 September
New Zealand Film Commission Bill
I now turn to the question of the content of films assisted by the commission. There is
some concern within the community about the content of films to be financed by the
commission. I think that most people would not wish to see the commission becoming
involved in the making of films which exploit sex or violence, even if some such films are
potentially very profitable. Accordingly, clause 18(3) of the Bill specifies that, in carrying
out its functions, the commission shall have due regard to the observance of standards that
are generally acceptable in the community. In addition, of course, New Zealand films, like
others intended for exhibition, are subject to the normal censorship laws. The commission,
and other prudent investors who will be well aware of censorship requirements, will not be
keen to invest in a film which may not be able to be released, or alternatively which may be
approved for exhibition only to a highly restricted audience.
I turn now to outline, albeit briefly, some of the main provisions of the Bill. The new
Film Commission will comprise a chairman and between three and five persons, all
appointed by the Minister, and the Secretary for Internal Affairs. The present interim Film
Commission consists of the chairman and four members. The Bill, therefore, provides for
the appointment of one more person to the commission than the interim commission has. As
I indicated when I introduced the Bill, I am hopeful that all the present members of the
interim commission will agree to become members of the new commission. It has been
suggested that the additional member of the commission should be a woman, and possibly
one who will provide a family viewpoint. I certainly have it in mind to appoint a woman to
the commission, and I am sure that this will present no difficulty. The commission will be
able to employ staff and to establish committees. Its members may receive salaries or fees
under the Fees and Travelling Allowances Act 1951.
When the Bill was introduced, some members opposite asked about the funding of the
commission. As I indicated then, the New Zealand Lottery Board has provided funds to
support film-making projects by allocating $100,000 last year, and $500,000 this year and for
the next 2 years. While the Lottery Board has guaranteed funds for the first 3 years of the
commission's operations, there is no reason why, at some future date, funds should not be
appropriated by Parliament for this purpose. There is nothing in the Bill to prevent this. One
member opposite expressed some doubt about whether the commission could receive funds
from both lottery profits and the Consolidated Account. The Bill allows this to happen. In
fact, several statutory bodies, including the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council, the Council for
Recreation and Sport, and the Historic Places Trust now receive funds from both sources.
The key clauses of the Bill are clause 17, which sets out the functions of the commission,
clause 18, which sets out the provisions concerning the content of films that the commission
will have to consider, and clause 19, which details the commission's powers.
I commend this Bill to the House. I thank all those who have contributed towards its
formulation. I pay tribute to the members of the interim commission-in particular, to Mr
Bill Sheat, its Chairman, and Mr David Gascoigne, Deputy Chairman of the Arts Council.
Their knowledge, judgment, and vision have meant that, even before the commission is
established, it is away to a good start. Members of the industry have been generous in
providing advice and information to the interim commission and to officers of my
department. Thanks are due also to the members of a working party of the Queen Elizabeth
II Arts Council whose report 2 or 3 years ago provided the foundation on which most of the
subsequent development of the Film Commission will be based. For years the motion picture
production industry in this country has drifted without public policies or even internally
agreed guidelines. The Bill establishes a statutory commission, which will assist the industry
to realise its potential. Its aim will be to give practical help to solve practical problems. The
Bill does not aim to establish a mini-Hollywood in the South Pacific. However, it does aim to
encourage an industry that will benefit the country as well as talented New Zealand artists
and craftsmen. I have every confidence that the New Zealand Film Commission, to be set up
when this Bill is enacted, will achieve the objectives I have outlined.

film societies were. Let us have a look at it. Clause 18(1) reads: "In carrying out its
functions, the Commission shall not make financial assistance available to any person in
respect of the making, promotion, distribution, or exhibition of a film unless it is satisfied
that the film has or is to have a significant New Zealand content."
Like the member for New Lynn, I support that part of the clause, but I have some
reservations about the definition of "New Zealand content". Clause 18(2) reads: "For the
purpose of determining whether or not a film has or is to have a significant New Zealand
content, the Commission shall have regard to the following matters: (a) The subject of the
film..." That concerns me. If a group of New Zealanders wants to make a film on a subject
that appears to have nothing to do with this country, for example, a Western-and it seems
to me that just as the Italians can make Westerns so can New Zealand film makers—just
because the subject matter is a Western, that in itself should not preclude the possibility of a
grant. If we are to have a commercial base in the film industry, as the Minister mentioned, I
would have thought it would need reasonable flexibility in the topics that can be covered.
The Western is now an international type of film, and Westerns are made by countries all
over the world. The Western is a simple example, but I can imagine film makers wanting to
film subjects that might not necessarily appear to have a close connection with New Zealand.
I am a little concerned about that reservation.
I am also concerned about the question of the nationalities of the people who make the
films-authors, scriptwriters, composers, and so on. I can imagine a situation where there is
a desire to make a film from a book that may not be by a New Zealander, but which may
have a New Zealand subject. It seems to me that if someone wants to make a film in this
country we should not necessarily require him to produce his passport or birth certificate
before he can apply for a grant.
All these matters are not as serious as the final one—this is clause 18(3). That clause
reads: "In carrying out its functions, the Commission shall in relation to the content of any
film have due regard to the observance of standards that are generally acceptable in the
community." What does the Minister believe that clause means? Which part of the
community does it apply to? Is it the whole community, or is it just members of the National
Party? Will the Minister object to a film being made by a person with a New Zealand accent,
or will he want people to have a fruity accent, like members opposite? If they speak with a
New Zealand accent-[Interruption.]
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: A point of order, Mr Acting Speaker. Despite the lateness of the
hour, and although in other than parliamentary terms it is Friday morning, it seems to me
that the level of conversation—or whatever it is-is intolerable to those of us who are trying
to listen. I believe the level should be lowered, and I hope you will intervene.
Hon. T. F. Gill: While the member speaks as he does, and while he makes provocative

FARM OWNERSHIP SAVINGS AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The Bill will allow the wife of
a depositor to operate a farm ownership savings account and to be eligible for benefits on
savings, provided her husband is also a depositor and is able to satisfy the criteria of the
scheme. The Bill will also allow a depositor to withdraw savings and obtain benefits to enter
into an approved share-farming proposition. Such a person will not have to close his or her
account but will be able to continue to save for farm ownership.
Clause 1 gives the title, and states that this amendment is to be read as part of the
principal Act. Clause 2 enables an account to be opened by the spouse of a depositor. Clause
3 enables the spouse of an eligible depositor to qualify for benefits on savings, without
having had substantial practical farming experience as required by the principal Act,
provided all moneys payable to the depositor and to his or her spouse are used to acquire a
farm for their joint ownership and occupation.


## p. 4001 (#481) ###########################################

28 September
4001
Farm Ownership Savings Amendment Bill
Clause 4 will allow a depositor, who has received benefits for the purpose of share
farming, to continue to operate his or her account for the purpose of acquiring a further
grant or tax rebates to assist with the purchase of a farm. Any further benefits are subject to
two conditions: (a) the total benefits a depositor receives cannot exceed the maximum
allowable under the principal Act; and (b) the amount of savings taken into account in
calculating the initial benefits received cannot be taken into account when calculating future
benefits. Clause 5 allows a depositor, who received benefits to go share farming and who
subsequently purchases a farm, to retain those benefits. The Bill was referred to a select
committee, which recommended that it be referred back to the House without amendment.

Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
is merely a reiteration of what was said then. The only other two provisions to be drawn to
the attention of the House are first, the provision for 40 percent sales tax on record covers,
the same tax as that already applying to records themselves. This is to correct an anomaly
whereby record clubs enjoy a tax advantage over other record retailers. The second
provision is to strengthen the powers of customs officers to detain and search persons
suspected of carrying narcotic and other addictive drugs concealed inside their bodies, and to
seize any drugs found as a result of the search. The amendment is another way of more
effectively controlling what has become an enforcement problem. The Bill also makes it
clear that only a medical practitioner will be able to search a person's body cavities.
Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central): The Bill covers a number of matters to which I
want to refer. Clause 8 provides for changes to the provisions in the principal Act relating to
body searches by customs officers. The Minister will remember that I expressed some
reservations about the clause when the Bill was introduced. The Opposition will support to
the full any measures the Government wishes to take to stop drug trafficking, but I am a little
concerned about that clause, and express the same reservation about the powers given to
customs officers that I had when the Bill was introduced.
The clause states that such force as may be reasonably necessary may be used either by
the police or by a customs officer against that person to effect such detention or search.
When the Bill was being introduced I made the point that the police certainly had that right,
but I wonder whether we should be giving it to customs officers. Are the customs officers
prepared to accept that responsibility? Are they really trained to do that sort of thing? It is
desirable that body searches should be carried out by a medical practitioner, and that is
provided for in the Bill, but what worries me is that power will be given to customs officers to
use physical force if necessary to restrain people while they are being searched.
The other point I want to raise relates to clause 14, and the Minister briefly referred to
this. It is about the 40 percent sales tax on record covers. An article in the Evening Post dated
14 August quoted the Secretary of the Recording Industry Association, Mr Fred Smith, as
having said that he was not very happy with the move. He said the pending tax represented
another curb to the development of a true New Zealand artistic base. He said that, once
again, the Government seemed determined to penalise one of the single most popular art
forms in New Zealand-listening to music.
Mr Comber: The member was a Parliamentary Under-Secretary when the sales tax was
imposed.
Mr MacDONELL: I am quoting what was said by the secretary of the Recording
Industry Association. He and many other people are concerned about a 40 percent sales tax
on record covers. That point needs consideration by Parliament. After all, taxes are pretty
high at present. [Interruption.]
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: If we had fewer interjections we might make better progress. I
do not want a debate across the floor of the House.
Mr MacDONELL: I was making the point that I do not think this is a particularly good
idea. People are very heavily taxed with personal and sales tax. I do not think the extra
imposition is necessary. I ask the Minister to explain why the 40 percent sales tax will be
levied.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The Government has conceded that
clause 8 covers a sensitive area. I want to ensure that the powers are carefully prescribed and
will not be used without good cause. The customs officers need this power. While searching a
suspect they need to ensure that he does not walk away. They must have this policing power;
it is an integral part of the search procedure. I have ascertained that arrangements are being
made to ensure that the customs officers who will have the power will be suitably trained by
police training procedures. A degree of uniformity is desirable.
The purpose of the sales tax is to correct an anomaly. We can debate whether or not a
tax of 40 percent on record covers is too high. The fact remains that the tax on records is 40
percent. At this hour I shall not remind members which Government put the tax on records.
At the moment there is a glaring anomaly which allows record clubs to, in effect, dodge sales
tax on record covers when retailers must pay the tax. The Government thought that the
anomaly must be eliminated. That is the basis of clause 14.
Bill read a second time.

INDUSTRIAL TRAINING LEVIES BILL
Introduction
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Industrial Training Levies
Bill be introduced. It is a short empowering Bill, which implements a proposal contained in
this year's Budget. The purpose of the Bill is to enable industries that operate on a factory
basis to elect to put the financial arrangements of their industry training boards on a firmer
footing. The basis of financing industry training boards is that industry is required to meet a
minimum of 10 percent of the administrative expenses of each training board, with the
balance of approved administrative expenses being met by way of Government grant
through the Vocational Training Council.
In a number of industries contribution by individual firms to the industry's share is on a
voluntary basis. That has meant that in a number of cases the industry's contribution has
been met by only a small proportion of the total industry. It has also resulted in some
industry training boards facing financial difficulties. The levy facility proposed the Bill will
enable each factory-based industry with an industry training board to elect to have a more
equitable sharing of contributions among all firms in the industry. The important point is
that the Bill does not provide for a Government-imposed compulsory levy. It provides for
each industry to elect to have a compulsory levy inflicted on itself. The Bill provides for the
initiative in imposing a levy to lie with the industry involved. The procedure will be for the
industry training board to make written application for a levy to the Minister of Labour
through the Vocational Training Council. The Bill authorises the Minister to impose a levy
on each factory in that industry by notice in the Gazette, but he cannot publish such a notice
unless he is satisfied that the proposed levy has the support of the organisations most
representative of employers in that industry.
The maximum rate of levy that the Minister can impose will be set from time to time by
Order in Council. Any levy imposed will be collected with the annual factory registration
fee. The proposed levy facility has the support of the Employers Federation, the
Engineering Employers Federation, and the Vocational Training Council. I am confident
that it will assist the industry training boards concerned to carry out their important training


## p. 4008 (#488) ###########################################

29 September
Industrial Training Levies Bill
activities more effectively.

MAORI PURPOSES BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): I move, That the Maori Purposes Bill
be introduced. This is the annual washing-up Bill for Maori Affairs. It contains amendments
proposed to a number of statutes affecting Maoris and Maori land. After introduction it will
go to the Maori Affairs Committee. I do not consider that the proposed amendments are
controversial, but that committee will be able to sort them out.
The Bill contains 11 clauses. Clause 2 provides for payment of allowances in addition to
travelling allowances to judges and commissioners of the Maori Land Court. The
amendment is necessary to effect the recent determination of the Higher Salaries
Commission. Clause 3 proposes an increase in the value of assets in the estate of deceased
Maoris which can be dealt with by the Maori Trustee without the unwarranted expense of
obtaining a formal grant of administration through the Supreme Court. The amendment will
bring the Maori Trustee's authority in this area into line with that of the Public Trustee.
Clause 4 proposes an amendment of a purely machinery nature to give statutory authority to
the Maori Trustee's Account being overdrawn at the end of this financial year. Clause 5 gives
authority for payment of a capitalised sum to the Tainui Trust Board. That board wishes to
invest in a commercial building. It is intended that the annual grant payable to the board
during the next 20 years shall be capitalised for investment in that project. Clause 6 is
primarily a tidying-up exercise. The current law limits the appointment of countersigning
officers for Maori Trust Board account cheques to officers of the Public Service. That
restriction is considered to be no longer necessary.

Maori Purposes Bill
Clause 7 makes it clear that the Maori Land Court has authority to alter the objects of a
Maori incorporation constituted by Order in Council. Again, this is a tidying up measure.
Clause 8 proposes to increase to $3,000 the annual sum paid by the Maori Trustee to the
Queen Elizabeth II Postgraduate Fellowship of New Zealand. Clause 9 makes it clear that,

COMPANIES AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Companies
Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill makes five amendments to the Companies Act
1955. Of those five amendments three are minor, and are as follows. First, where the
registered holder of shares or debentures has died, the Bill increases the limit from $1,000 to
$2,000 in respect of a transfer of those shares and debentures that may be registered without
production of probate or letters of administration. This amendment will bring the limit in the
Companies Act in this respect into line with that specified in the Administration Act 1969.
Secondly, the Bill empowers the Supreme Court to substitute one Official Assignee for
another assignee for the purposes of winding up a company by the Supreme Court. This
amendment, which, in this respect, will bring the Companies Act into line with the
Insolvency Act 1967, will enable the transfer of a complex winding up to an assignee with
more staff and greater facilities, and will enable the transfer of a winding up to an assignee
located where the company actually carried on its operations.
The third minor amendment made by the Bill is to increase from $400 to $1,500 the
amount in respect of a claim for wages and salary accorded priority in the winding up of a
company. The amount of $400 has not been increased since the Companies Act was passed
in 1955. In 1973 the Macarthur committee set up to review the Companies Act
recommended an increase to $1,000. Having regard to increases in wages and salaries and
the drop in money values, the limit has been set at $1,500 with power to increase that limit by
Order in Council.
The two substantial amendments made by this Bill relate to the promotion of loan fund
schemes by companies and to the takeover of companies. The Bill inserts new provisions into
the Companies Act to prohibit companies from promoting loan fund schemes, or inviting
persons to contribute or subscribe to, or participate in loan fund schemes. This amendment
follows the Companies Special Investigations Order 1978, which applied the Companies
Special Investigations Act 1958 to a Christchurch group of loan fund companies on 18
September. That order was made on my advice, given on the recommendation of the


## p. 4011 (#491) ###########################################

29 September
4011
Companies Amendment Bill
Company Law Advisory Committee, which was moved to recommend further that the
promotion of loan fund schemes by companies should not be permitted.
I wish to emphasise that the Companies Special Investigations Order 1978 and this
amendment are not to be regarded as implied criticism of the management of the
Christchurch home loan fund schemes. If there is to be any criticism, that would emanate in
due course from the two receivers and managers appointed to investigate the companies and
to take appropriate action.
The Christchurch companies operated in a manner similar to that of building societies,
in that those who would later seek mortgages for homes paid regular monthly sums against a
future entitlement to a low-interest loan. For 4 to 6 years money was paid for an option to
take up shares, and the option was converted to shares after that time or as soon as a loan
was available, whichever came first. Because no interest or dividend was earned by the
subscriber for many years on payments, on shares, or on options, the low interest rate
tended to be illusory. The Company Law Advisory Committee advised me that it was
particularly concerned about the disparity in rights between, on the one hand, option holders
whose rights varied according to the prospectus upon which they subscribed and whether or
not they exercised their option to take shares, and on the other hand shareholders who may
or may not have got a mortgage.
The Government is particularly concerned about the risks involved for young people
saving for homes by the means of loan fund schemes. They should not be in the position of
being contingently liable for large sums of money. When options were to be converted into
shares, subscribers became liable for possible calls on those shares in the Christchurch
companies, or up to $30 per share, whether or not they had received a mortgage advance.
Because of the long-term repayments in the mortgages, the low interest rate, and the fact
that they were not usually restricted to trustee investment limits, such mortgages would have
a low asset value in any liquidation.
The loan fund scheme concept was imported from Australia, where similar problems
have occurred. In 1976 New South Wales enacted strict legislation which included a
requirement for $5 million net tangible assets in a company before it issued such options.
Despite this strict legislation, just over a week ago a Queen's counsel was appointed to
investigate the operations of the largest home loan fund company in New South Wales. I
understand that, under its consumer laws, South Australia has prohibited home loan fund
schemes, and other states are considering similar legislation. The amendment permits the
Governor-General by Order in Council to exempt a company from the prohibition on
operating loan fund schemes. This has been included not to derogate from the prohibition,
but to permit a dispensation for a company that comes within the letter but not the spirit of
the prohibition. The prohibition has been drafted widely. The power of dispensation has
been added as a precaution, in case the terms of the prohibition apply to schemes not
intended to be prohibited. The power of dispensation is also desirable because the Bill will
be enacted in the short time before the end of the session, and thus there will be little
opportunity to receive representations on the scope of the prohibition. I do not envisage any
circumstance in which the Government would agree to an Order in Council to permit a
company to promote a home loan scheme. The prohibition is considered an essential
measure, but not one that must be necessarily regarded as definitive. With the setting up of
the Securities Commission as soon as practicable after the passing of the Securities Bill, I
believe that the commission could well consider whether or not companies should be able to
promote loan fund schemes subject to strict statutory control, and recommend to the
Government accordingly. Meanwhile, the only other company known to be intending to
start a home loan fund has written to the Registrar of Companies withdrawing its proposed
prospectus from registration.
The other substantial amendment made is to amend the definition of "take-over
scheme" in the Companies Amendment Act 1963. That Act was designed, not to inhibit
company takeovers, but to ensure that a company proposed to be taken over has advance
warning of the takeover, and to ensure that shareholders receive adequate information from
both their company and the offeror company, to allow an informed decision to be made
whether to accept the offer. At present these disclosure provisions apply only to the making
of offers for shares which would entitle the offeror to exercise control over more than half of
the voting power at a general meeting of the company proposed to be taken over. The
amendment will apply the disclosure provisions to offers for shares that would entitle the
offeror to exercise control over more than one-fifth of the voting power. It is recognised that,


## p. 4012 (#492) ###########################################

4012
29 September
Companies Amendment Bill
particularly in relation to public companies with widespread shareholding, it is possible to
obtain control by holding less than half of the voting power at general meetings. It is this fact
which, in the past year, has led to some companies taking defensive action against
anticipated takeovers by means that the rest of the commercial community have regarded
critically, and which have the potential for abuse. This amendment should remove much, if
not all, of the need to resort to such measures.
In widespread consultation, including all listed companies, the Stock Exchange
Association of New Zealand has, over the past year, been formulating a takeover code in an
attempt to deal with those developments, especially "first come, first served" bids employed
to obtain substantial voting power without having to comply with the disclosure requirement
of the Companies Amendment Act 1963. The association has decided to withdraw its
facilities for dealing with such bids because of evidence of abuse, and has made
representations for this amendment to bring the disclosure provisions into operation at an
earlier stage of a takeover. The amendment will considerably reduce the number of "first
come, first served" bids, and will complement the association's takeover code, which it
proposes to bring into operation once the amendment is enacted.
I want to emphasise that the amendment will not apply to partial bids for up to one-fifth
of the voting power, and will not prevent a minority shareholder from acquiring additional
shares on the Stock Exchange in the usual way. I regard this amendment as only an interim
measure pending a thorough review of our takeover legislation in the light of the operation
of the takeover code. The amendment has been included in the Bill only after consultation
with the New Zealand Law Society, the New Zealand Society of Accountants, the Finance
Houses Association, the Merchant Bankers Association, the Institute of Directors, the New
Zealand Chambers of Commerce, and the Stock Exchange Association of New Zealand.
The New Zealand Law Society suggested that the 20 percent should be reduced to 10 percent
in cases involving amounts of $1 million or more.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I should like to ask the

clause 5 will have on a large and totally legitimate industry in New Zealand.

Electoral Rolls-Maori Voters
1. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the Minister of
Justice: Is he aware that staff at the Porirua Post Office have been telling electors that if they
have moved from another Maori electorate into Southern Maori they are able to choose
whether to go on to the Maori roll or the general roll; is this advice in accordance with
section 43B of the Electoral Act; and, if a voter did transfer from the Maori to the general
roll, would his vote be challenged?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I am not aware that any such advice is
being supplied by the Post Office staff at the Porirua Post Office, as the Porirua electorate
officer confirms that it is not. It is possible, however, that an elector moving to Porirua and
filling in a new application for registration as an elector could be enrolled on the general roll,
although previously on a Maori roll, if he did not supply the name of his electorate. Only the
previous address is asked for on the card. After all, as the honourable member would
know,somebody might give a Christchurch address that could well be in the Christchurch
Central electorate in which he has been enrolled, not the Southern Maori electorate, or vice
versa. The terms of section 43B of the Electoral Act, though difficult to police, are quite
clear, and such a person would not be entitled to be registered on a general roll, and would
therefore not be a qualified voter for that electorate.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: In the event of an elector who had opted for
Southern Maori finding his name registered on both that roll and the general roll, would his
vote be challenged? On what roll should he apply to cast a vote?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: One of the problems with such a question is that it is
hypothetical. If the member wants to put down a question with notice I can get a confirmed
answer. Section 43B of the Electoral Act states: “(1) A Maori who is registered as an elector
of a Maori electoral district"—and I think that is what the member had in mind-"shall not
be entitled to be registered as an elector of a general electoral district, except pursuant to an
application made by him under section 43A of this Act". On the face of it, that looks as
though a person who is registered in a Maori electorate by means of the Labour
Government's amendment in 1975 has to vote as an elector of that Maori electorate, and
cannot change that until the next census, which will be in 1981. That is the provision made by
the Labour Government. The elector would be caught and would have to continue to vote in
the Maori electorate.

Maternity Hospital Closures-Rural Districts
13. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister of Health: Will he advise whether he
will agree to a modification of regulations that threaten the closure of rural maternity units in
the Rangitikei and Waimarino districts so that vital services to these far-flung districts will
not be lost in a situation where the local authorities and local medical profession are adamant
about the social necessity of retaining these facilities?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I am not sure what modifications the member is
seeking, but perhaps he is referring to the requirement in the Obstetric Regulations 1975
that there shall be a midwife in charge at all times at a maternity hospital. I have some
sympathy with the local authorities and the local doctors on the need to retain these
facilities. However, the purpose of the Obstetric Regulations is to ensure a high standard of
safety for the mother and child. This must always be the paramount concern.
Mr Beetham: May I say to the Minister, before asking my supplementary question, that
he is correct in his assumption.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! The member must ask a question.
Mr Beetham: Well, I though he would like to know that. In view of the answer, can he
say whether the hospitals concerned are at immediate risk?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I want to give a concise answer, but I cannot answer concisely because
I think the member is entitled to be satisfied about this. In the annual inspection of nursing
services it was reported that the regulations were not being met at several hospitals. The
Department of Health wrote to the board and pointed this out, suggesting that the board
might deem it desirable to advise the general practitioners that the regulations were not
being fully met, and reminding the board of its legal obligations. This has been interpreted in
the press and some other quarters as some sort of direction that the hospitals should close.
This has never been so. In Taihape, for example, there are four or five midwives on call who
can work a roster. This is thought by some advisers in my department to be a reasonable
arrangement, but it is also reasonable that, if the hospitals are not meeting the regulations as
they should be, doctors who are referring patients should be advised so that they can exercise
their judgment on where they will refer their patients. I hear the news reports and I am told
by telephone calls what is in the headlines in the newspapers, but I really do not have any
concrete response from the area to the letter that was written to the board. I should be
pleased to give the member a copy of the letter if he would like it so that he can know exactly
what the Department of Health has done.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): A person who has been duly enrolled
for an electoral district ceases to be "ordinarily resident in New Zealand", and thus ceases to
be qualified as an elector, if he has been out of New Zealand continuously for more than 3
years, unless he or she is a public servant who is outside New Zealand on official duty, or the
spouse or child of such a public servant. This is the effect of sections 38 and 39 of the
Electoral Act.
Dr Shearer: Can he indicate whether he was chasing Sydney-siders downhill?

Radio Windy Talkback Programme-Complaint
20. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Prime Minister: Has he seen an article in the Evening
Post of 19 September in which it is stated that "Dr Erich Geiringer's late-night Monday
talkback programme on Radio Windy has been cancelled and a complaint about the
programme laid with the Broadcasting Tribunal", and, further, Dr Geiringer's statement
that Radio Windy had told him that the complaint was lodged by the Prime Minister's
Department, and, if so, did he or his department lodge such a complaint?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I reply on behalf of the Prime Minister.
"Yes, I have seen the article in question. Neither I nor any member of my department has
lodged any complaint about this or any other programme broadcast by Radio Windy, nor
about any programme with which Dr Geiringer has been associated. From time to time
members of the public write to me with complaints that should have been directed to an
appropriate constituted authority. It is my practice to forward such complaints, without
comment, to the appropriate authority. It might well be that, if some member of the public
wrote to me complaining about the programme that is the subject of this question, I would
have sent the letter on to the appropriate authority".

total grants paid out so far have been about $287,000. The cost per student works out at

produced an amending Bill.

Local Elections and Polls Amendment Bill
the member for Wellington Central was speaking and pointed out that, almost invariably,
the male name takes precedence on legal documents. If that is true, Government members,

The fact that the Labour Government abolished the freehold vote has been used by
Government members as another red herring. Henry May, probably the best Minister of
Internal Affairs the House has seen this century, moved to democratise the polls system, and
that was the first step in eliminating the property vote and recognising that everybody should
be entitled to vote. Phase 1 simply set out to ensure that everyone paying rates should be
entitled to vote. Most adults, and some who are not adults, pay rates in one form or another.
The idea that the democratic right to vote should belong solely to the property owner or the
landlord should be anathema to anyone who is a true democrat and desires the full
participation of all people in civic affairs. Henry May created major revolutions in local
government in the interests of efficiency, administration, and democracy. He could hardly
have been blamed if some administrative point escaped his attention. Perhaps the way in
which the first step was taken to remove the freehold qualification was, with hindsight, not
ideal. Notices were sent out to freeholders, and, if the notice did not come back, the name
was wiped from the roll. If the notice did come back, the qualification was changed from
"freehold" to "residential" on the roll. All that could have been done automatically, and it
just shows what is wrong with the administration of government in New Zealand. The
Government seems to be no more prepared than preceding Governments were to tackle the
malfunctioning of the Public Service system in New Zealand. My main point is that that
change was the first step in bringing rationality and democracy to the polls. The Labour
Government, in taking that step, was seeking to bring some common sense to our voting
procedures and underline our voting rights.
Three different Acts cover polling in New Zealand, and the methods for voting set out
in those three Acts are all different. In one the voter puts a cross next to his name, but in
another he scores out the name. How is it possible to have rationality and common sense in
the polling system when that sort of thing exists? The member for New Lynn said that the
time was well past when we needed to consolidate those three Acts to ensure that the rights
of individuals to vote took precedence over the rights of bureaucracy.
The Bill introduced by the member for Rangitikei is part of a first step that the Labour
Government would have taken had it retained office-an essential step if we are to
rationalise our voting processes and ensure democracy in New Zealand. The Wellington
Town Hall petition was cited as a good example. On that occasion many people had signed a
poll petition, but, because the woman's name came second, she was not entitled to exercise a
vote and her name was scratched off the petition. Why did the Wellington City Council not
recognise that a sufficient number of people believed there should have been a poll, and so
granted it?

VIOLENT OFFENDING COMMITTEE-INTERIM REPORT
Mr COUCH (Wairarapa): I am directed by the Violent Offending Committee to present
its interim report. The Violent Offending Committee was established by the House on 16
December 1977 to consider the incidence and causes of violent offending in New Zealand,
and the means of reducing such offending, including the adequacy of the law and penalties
relating thereto, and to make such recommendations as may be thought desirable. The
committee's hearings, which began in April this year, have generated a great deal of public
interest. In view of this, the committee considered that the House and the public might
benefit from an interim report on the progress being made towards the final determination of
the matters on which recommendations will be made.
Submissions were called for in February, and now total 142. A large proportion of these
have been submitted in response to the committee's direct efforts to seek evidence from
groups that it believed could make a valuable contribution, but which may not otherwise
have come forward. The submissions in hand represent a balanced range of interests and
experience. During 23 meetings, including meetings in Auckland, Christchurch, and
Dunedin, the committee has heard 62 submissions. In addition to hearing submissions, the
committee visited the television centre at Avalon to observe the process of television
censorship for violence, and also visited the Tapu te Ranga Marae in Wellington to discuss
with its members the value of urban work co-operatives. The committee also attended a
special screening of the feature film The Brute, which portrayed a situation of domestic
violence.
The main areas of concern that have emerged from submissions are violence on
television, domestic violence, the abuse of alcohol and drugs, the influence of the home
environment, the role of the education system, the relevance of capital and corporal
punishment, the adequacy of censorship and alternatives to the present censorship system,
and the protection of victims of violent offences. The evidence examined to date has
reinforced the committee's earlier expectation that the issue of violent offending, being one
of deep public concern, is characterised by a wide range of views as to its causes and possible
remedies. For this reason the committee accepts that all aspects of the question must be
given the most careful consideration possible before any conclusions are drawn and any
recommendations are formulated.
The committee has yet to complete its investigations. It is intended that the committee
shall visit institutions that deal with violent offenders at different levels, and the committee's
further investigations will include the consideration of three petitions referred to it during
the year. The committee understands that legislation on aspects of violent offending is likely
to be introduced to the House soon. Any such legislation should be scrutinised by the
committee in the light of the evidence obtained from its inquiries. It is also expected that the
committee will make recommendations that will require legislative change. During the
forthcoming recess the committee intends to complete its consideration of the matters
referred to it by the House. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
I have just read the official interim report of the Violent Offending Committee, of
which I have the honour to be chairman. It might help members if I now stand aside from
that role and, as an individual member of the House, make a few personal comments on
what I have observed during recent months on the problem of violent offending. I repeat
that these remarks are made as an individual and not as a committee chairman--they bind no
one but me. I have been much impressed by the wide range of submissions on the subject.
Most are thoughtful and concerned, many show learning and experience, and practical

Mr COUCH: I repeat that phrase—as responsibly as the majority want to be allowed to
do-because a growing number of people, especially those who are much alone, when
travelling or at home, now keep with them some form of weapon for their own protection.
One will not see this in written submissions, but many people will admit it privately, and they
do this not boastfully but in real fear for their safety, wishing there was no need to take such
a step, but knowing no other way to feel safe. That is a tragic situation that will not easily be
solved. In fact, it will not be solved at all until the various fragmented bodies that are
attempting to tackle the problem piece by piece join with each other and the ordinary law-
abiding citizen to solve it as a team. At present, the various sects sometimes seem to spend as
much time proving each other wrong as they do in tackling the basic problem. There are
hard-liners, do-gooders, law reformers, people reformers, and many other groups whose
continual disputes tend to leave the average citizen feeling, with some reason, that those
groups are more interested in the argument than in the subject. That does not help,
particularly when many of these experts make it clear that they consider that that same
average citizen has no opinions on the subject worth listening to. But the common sense of
the average non-expert citizen is what communities are based on, and I am sure that if we all
listened to him a bit more our laws would be a lot fewer and a great deal more effective.
At present there is wide divergence between three separate groups which ought not to
be separate at all. These are the law enforcement agencies, the academics and social
workers, and the public. They are the legs of a three-legged stool, and they are all needed;
but, for all our sakes, is it not time we joined them together at the top? As I see it from
reading, discussion, and experience, there are three aspects of any solution to crime. One is
that detection should be certain and punishment swift and just. The second is that society as
a whole must work to make sure that no person, young or old, is driven to offend because of
social background or deprivation. The third is that we must ensure that the law-abiding
majority of ordinary New Zealanders is helped to understand and support what is being done
in both these areas, because only through this understanding will we get public support and
help, and that is our strength. No one leg, nor any two, can support the stool without the
others, and only by working together will we have a chance of succeeding.
An understanding public can apply the lessons of the experts. It can reinforce them and
add a great deal more of its own. Only the public-as parents, family, and through churches,
schools, and social groups-can provide the leadership, guidance, and example that can
really help young people to grow up with worth-while goals. Only the public can provide the
24-hours a day example that will encourage young people to hold to the ideals they start out
with, and to reach for ever higher standards. That cannot be done through special groups,
laws, or bribes, but only by example.
It was fashionable a few years ago to label everything in ages—the atomic age, the jet
age, and so on. I would label this the age of greed-a time when possessions have become
more important than character, a time when we admire a man for his new house or car, and
not for his moral and practical standards. The hope for the future is that young people do not

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): As one of the
members of the committee who was present when every submission was made-in fact, I
missed only one meeting, which discussed the interim report to Parliament-I can say that
clear trends emerged. First, unemployment and idle time lead to crime. Economic pressures
that exacerbate tensions and cause excessive stress can be expected to heighten violence.
Since crime occurs in idle time, the current chronic unemployment must inevitably expand
the breeding ground for violence. Furthermore, in some cases the demoralising experience
turns the unemployed to alcohol or drugs. We were told that New Zealand has 50 000
alcoholics. It is said that more than 70 000 young people smoke marijuana, while a few of last
year's unplaced school leavers are already in psychiatric clinics, at a cost of $200 a week.
So much of the tragedy we hear about is alcohol related. Alcohol taken in excess is the
lubrication of violence. It releases people's normal socialised control over the tensions and
stress plaguing their lives, to the flashpoint of violence. One recently quoted male excuse for
excluding women from some hotel bars was that the sight of women could inflame men to
violence. Consider what this suggests about the behaviour of New Zealand men in bars. Dr
Moon, an Australian expert on drug addiction, has observed that New Zealand has 50 000
compulsive alcoholics. He has said also that this means that 7 out of every 100 New
Zealanders are directly affected by alcoholism, and that alcohol is responsible for enormous
losses in industrial production, for 1 in every 5 hospital beds used, for half the fatal road
accidents, for half the deaths by drowning, for half the short-term crime, for half the violent
crime, and for 1 in every 5 cases of battered children. Various submissions to the committee
from authoritative groups stated that alcohol was a factor in more than half the cases of wife
abuse. Why do we regard this as an acceptable level of casualty?
I consider that the supplementary comments to submissions questioning the role of
breweries were totally valid. We in New Zealand seem resigned to accepting uncivilised
boozing as the norm. We simply cannot continue to delude ourselves with the myth that this
is inevitable. It is not inevitable that excessive consumption of alcohol should continue to
destroy families as it moves like a tornado, reeling and colliding with human groups
throughout the community, and dividing and destroying families. I repeat that it is sheer
madness to accept as inevitable those casualties to which I have referred. To my mind,
civilised drinking in association with good food is one of the pleasures of life. However,
drinking to excess and then committing violence in anger, stress, or uncontrolled stupor is
both barbaric and uncivilised. We have encouraged this trend by constructing booze barns.
Submissions questioned the role of breweries in this regard, and, as I have already said, I
believe they are valid. Instead of building booze barns we should be promoting the smaller
English-type pub. We were told by the breweries that there are impediments in town and
country planning legislation to the construction of more of these precinct family pubs, and
that this was a major reason why more have not been constructed.
When considering the effects of alcohol our attention was directed to the concept of
manliness in New Zealand. What is manliness? It is neither amusing nor manly to drink to
excess. A person is predisposed to do so either through illness, excessive stress, because it is
a means of cowardly escape, or for some other reason. It seems to me that New Zealand
elevates this behaviour by accepting it as part of the New Zealand life style. On the other
hand, we condemn the Polynesian newcomer who learns a habit to which he would not have
been exposed had he emigrated to another country. We have found, too, that there is
ambivalence in official policy. During the 1960s it was official policy to relocate in our cities
Maori people and Polynesians from the Tokelau Islands who had hitherto lived in rustic and
remote simplicity. Yet today, a decade and a half later, this Government condemns the
result of that traumatic transplanting. So, too, does much of our community. It has also been
official policy to encourage emigration to this country from the Pacific Islands, but when a
few Pacific Islanders become engulfed in our boozing habits they are openly condemned as a
violent race. Can we really say, officially and with piety, that we aim to legislate for a non-


## p. 4030 (#510) ###########################################

Violent Offending Committee-Interim Report
violent society? In so many instances these dual standards bewilder the young, enticing them
as young recruits to crime. They are led to believe that drinking is manly, that aggressiveness
is manly, that physical violence indicates strength, and that noise and rowdiness also indicate
strength. Futhermore, they also see that our society appears to laud successful exploiters. It
is sufficient to be a millionaire to be notorious. The manner whereby this wealth is acquired,
whether or not it borders on bludging or exploitation, is rarely ever investigated. The
successful rip-off merchant becomes a folk hero.
We were told that New Zealand has proportionately one of the highest prison
populations in the world. However, prisons destroy. Look at their failure rate. They are a
breeding place for violence. In prison the worst offenders enjoy the highest status. The
tougher the man the greater hero status ascribed him. Toughness, as a quality, is elevated. It
is manly to be tough, to domineer, to dominate, to prove one's leadership and high status
with an occasional demonstration of public thuggery. Bullies are lauded. Some are even
elected as leaders. When toughness is equated with manliness and leadership, bullies
inevitably emerge. There are thugs in prisons as well as outside. They thrive when they are
admired.
There is a dire need for a reappraisal of New Zealand's mode and concept of manliness.
We were told that solutions are never simple. We realise this. Yet there was fundamental
simplicity in some of the best solutions suggested to us. Those solutions came from the Tapu
te Ranga Marae and Bruce Stewart. As he pointed out, people in prison should be taught
economic skills instead of learning criminal skills, as they do. We were told that there is a
need for homes in which outcasts can begin to feel secure, homes in which the qualities of
caring and concern are paramount. These people need and want work, not for payment
alone, but work that assures them skills-a basic requirement is for the supervisor to be
skilled and rehabilitation must surely be the keyword. After all, it is the keystone of the
welfare State, and an integral component of the social security system. As another from this
background put it, there is a need for more vocational choices at secondary schools, and the
preparation of pupils for more skills. Bruce Stewart told the committee of the success his
solutions had had.
We were told also about domestic violence. While violence in the street is treated as a
serious crime and grievous bodily harm and mugging are universally deplored, the same acts
if committed behind the doors of a private house, are largely ignored. With utter disregard
and even piety the unspoken attitude is; it is not the policy of society to interfere with the
sanctity of marriage. Yet violence in the home and within the family is not new. Although we
were told a great deal about it, little is being done. It is said that violent crime is often a
function of the lower social and economic strata and that physical violence is a poor
substitute for verbal retaliation. All the more reason why we should seize on the falling
birth rate and the decline in school rolls to improve child health services, remedial teaching,
and verbal skills. There is also clear need in our society for the establishment of more
informally run women's refuges. Dedicated women have established a few, but they are
forced to manage on a shoestring. Caring local and central government should be assisting
those self-help groups.

The committee looked at the question of corporal and capital punishment, and the

learned, I believe, from looking at some of these programmes. We are going to have to be
more vigilant in what we show and what we allow children, in some cases, to see.
