how good a teacher is.
I have served on the committee for only some of the time as its meetings conflicted with
those of another committee. Although the report is called an interim one, I strongly suspect
that it will really be the final report. That is because after hearing 140 or so submissions, the
committee has concluded that violence is a problem that the Government should do all it can
to solve and that the legislation we have at present is quite adequate. What is needed is not
tougher penalties but a much better direction by the State and, particularly, by the
community and the family.
I congratulate the member for Southern Maori for her emphasis on alcohol. I have been
the Labour Party's spokesman on health over the past 2 years, and I have noticed that
alcohol is increasingly a problem that cannot be swept under the carpet. One of the most
disturbing experiences I have ever been through was at the accident and casualty centre at
Auckland Hospital one Saturday evening from 9 p.m. to 1 a.m. where I went to see at first
hand the victims of accidents. The night I was there, nearly every person—and indeed every
accident-was somehow involved with excessive alcohol. I felt sorry for those who came in
maimed or dead. Most of all, however, one feels sorry for the innocent—those who obey the
law, who do not drink, but who suddenly find themselves involved in an accident with a
maniac.
If we list alcohol as one of the most important factors contributing to violence, we must
look at it two ways. First, we must try to deprive the person who drinks excessively of the
opportunity to drink. That is why I firmly believe that a good punishment for those who use
alcohol excessively is weekend preventive detention over a period of months. From 4 p.m.
on Friday until 7 a.m. on Monday offenders are unable to drink. When they are also given
hard but constructive work to do, I am sure that is much more effective than some of the
methods now used. I know that this system is used to some extent already, but I think it
should be extended.
I was a member of a committee about 8 years ago, when the first breath analysers were
introduced, and we found that five-eighths of fatal motor accidents occurred within half a
mile of the victim's own home. Although many of those accidents involved alcohol, just
about as many involved stress. How many times have we ourselves had an argument with
someone, got into a car, and taken out our annoyance on the car-which also meant on all
the unlucky people who happened to be in our way? Stress is as much of a problem as
alcohol, and of course the two go together.
That brings me back to the point I started with. We must improve the environment. The
environment starts with the family and continues into the community. We must encourage
schools to provide suitable programmes when the family is inadequate. I am one of those
who has felt a certain amount of concern at the way in which the schools seem to have
become the repository for every thing the family cannot do. However, I am not one of those
who say that the schools should not do anything, because if they do nothing nobody will, and
we shall have chaos. In many cases the schools are the only bulwark against a state of
anarchy. The stress teachers are under at present-quite apart from any argument about
salaries should indicate that improvements must be made to lessen their load and to
improve facilities.
When the committee looked for possible legislative changes, all it could come up with
was the idea of plastic jugs in bars, and similar suggestions. Really, that is just fiddling with
the problem. The member for Southern Maori, the member for Whangarei, and the member
for Raglan-and I am disappointed that she cannot contribute to the debate today—realised
that our present laws are quite adequate. The problem is the way in which they are enforced.
There is no need to increase this or that sentence by so many years or months.
We should get to the basis of the problem, and I offer three suggestions from the interim
report. First, if there is misuse of alcohol by young people, preventive detention spanning a
weekend and continuing for 3 months should be imposed after the first conviction instead of
waiting for the second or third conviction. That would mean a loss of weekend freedom for 3
months, a loss of the opportunity to booze it up and then drive or behave stupidly. Secondly,
there must be a great deal more research into the causes of stress and anxiety. Obviously, if
people turn to alcohol because they have nothing else to occupy their minds they have not
been given assistance by their parents.
My third and final suggestion is that there must be more emphasis in the education
system on education for parenthood and adulthood. If parents and grandparents continue to
communicate with their children less well than they did in the past, we will have increasing

NELSON CITY FORESTRY EMPOWERING BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Nelson City Forestry Empowering Bill. The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table.
The purpose of the proposal was to empower the Nelson City Council to engage in
forestry on certain defined lands, and also to empower the council to acquire land in the
future for afforestation. This is not in any way questioned because general powers along
those lines will be introduced in legislation towards the end of the session. There are also
general empowering provisions commonly associated with such legislation. Controversy
arose over clause 3(k) affecting an area known as Waahi Taakaro. The proposed amendment
incorporated in the Bill being reported back simply validates and clarifies the use and status
of that land.
The Bill as introduced and referred to the Local Bills Committee permitted the
afforestation of the land known as Waahi Taakaro although such use could be disputed on
the grounds that it is a pleasure ground in part, and was purchased partly with reserve fund
moneys. It is worth noting that the land in question has an underlying use in afforestation.
Concern was expressed by a group known as the Friends of the Maitai, the Nelson branch of
the Native Forest Action Council and the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society who


## p. 4038 (#518) ###########################################

4038
29 September
Nelson City Forestry Empowering Bill
wanted assurances that the river flats would remain a reserve and that the hills would revert
to natural bush for long term conservation orientated planting. Their main concern was that
the scenic backdrops of the city would be spoilt by a dark green belt of Pinus Radiata. One
member even went so far as to express total opposition to any commercial operations.
In the event, the committee has recommended amendments to clause 3(k) and in doing
so has added two schedules to the Bill. It might help to clarify the position if I quoted the
amended clause: "Exercise all or any of the powers contained in this Act on part of the land
known as Waahi Taakaro including the land described in the first schedule to this Act, but
not the land described in the second schedule to this Act, notwithstanding any restriction or
reservation expressed or implied to the contrary". In other words, the hills can be forested
and the flats will become a recreational reserve.
This acknowledges in law the use of reserve fund contribution moneys to purchase part
or the whole of the Waahi Taakaro area. We are supported in this by an indication of actions
taken already by the Nelson City Council to ensure that the amendment is honoured. I
believe the recommendation of the committee is a happy solution which has the total support
of the members of the Local Bills Committee.
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson): As the member who introduced the Bill, I thank the
chairman and members of the Local Bills Committee for the time and consideration they
have given to the Bill, which is important to the people of Nelson. I am sure the wording
changes and suggested amendments will go some way towards satisfying the differing points
of view.
From what the chairman of the committee said, it appears that the main amendment will
have the effect of more clearly defining and giving protection to a specific part of Waahi
Taakaro as a recreational reserve or pleasure ground, subject to the Reserves Act 1977. This
will be quite satisfactory. Indeed, I shall go further and say that I am confident the changes
will be acceptable. With the passage of the Bill the Nelson City Council will be able to
continue its land management plans for the remaining sections of Waahi Taakaro.
The Nelson City Council has one of the largest, if not the largest, areas of recreational
reserves of any local authority-as measured against the number of ratepayers. The
maintenance of these reserves places a considerable and increasing burden on ratepayers.
With the passage of the Bill Nelson people will be able to look forward to some financial
return from forestry projects to assist with the maintenance and development of various
recreational reserves in their district.
In conclusion, I take the opportunity of commending the Friends of the Maitai, who
want more indigenous forestry in Nelson, in particular in Waahi Taakaro. I support that
objective, and think it should be encouraged. However, maintenance and further planting of
indigenous forest will need considerable funds. The compromise suggested by the committee
is one way to obtain the financial assistance needed. In the long term all points of view will
be satisfied.
Motion agreed to.
LOCAL LEGISLATION BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to

In view of the observations of the member for Porirua on the introduction of the Bill, it
is as well to point out that members of the committee have received from the Department of
Internal Affairs this advice relating to the proposed grant: "It is made for the specific
purpose of ensuring that the gymnasium would be a community asset." In other words, the
reserve contribution fund money is going into something that will be used by the community
at large in future. "The town clerk of the Kapiti borough states that the gymnasium will be
available for community use outside school hours for at least 30 hours each week. There will
be a management committee for the gymnasium comprised of eight members of whom two
shall represent the board, two shall represent the borough council, two shall represent
community user groups, and two shall represent the school staff. It is conceded that no
formal agreement has yet been signed." I am in no doubt that that will be done in the future.


## p. 4039 (#519) ###########################################

4039
Local Legislation Bill
In fact, it is one of the requirements under which other moneys have been given from the
recreation and sport ministry. The committee was further advised that the gymnasium would
be available to the community between the hours of 6 p.m. and 7 a.m. on 3 weekdays during
school terms, every weekend, and at any other time when the school is closed. I think that is

Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): Clause 5, authorising the Kapiti Borough Council to make a
grant of $70,000 to the Porirua College for a gymnasium, was discussed at some length in the
committee. The member for Porirua and I were concerned that this was a heavy grant from a
reserve fund built up by contributions for reserve purposes from subdivisions within the
borough council district. It was the size of the sum that we noticed, and we felt that the
Department of Education was looking more and more to local body contributions and
utilising a fund that was not specifically set up for the creation of educational institutions. We
seriously questioned the provisions in the clause. We commend the building of a gymnasium
at the college and there could be a good argument, as has been suggested by the member for
Wellington Central, for some local body contributions, if we could be sure of public use of
the gymnasium. There has been a tendency over the last 4 or 5 years for more of our school
facilities to be made available for public use, but I am concerned that there is as yet no
formal agreement.
Under the law, in the absence of any formal agreement, there could come a time when
the owners of the land on which the building stands—that is, the college itself-could say
they did not wish to honour the agreement any further, because of the property needs of the
school, or because of some other attitude towards the public. Then the participation of those
representing community-user groups and the borough council would come to an end.
If the clause is to proceed through the Committee, the agreement should be signed
forthwith, and the terms of the agreement should be written into the clause. If we do that, I
believe we shall have honoured the rights of the community which is making a substantial
contribution to the gymnasium. We want to ensure that the rights of the two representatives
of the borough council and the two representatives of the community-user groups are given
legal recognition. As I said before, if that were done formally, the agreement should be
incorporated into the clause.
The Local Bills Committee was told of one other instance in which such a grant was
made. It also heard what happened to the grant of $20,000 made by the Waimairi County
Council in Christchurch to Burnside High School for a gymnasium. The clause that validated
that transaction in 1975 shows that the $20,000 was provided from the council's land
subdivision schemes. As some of the subdivision bordered on Burnside High School, part of
the profits were given back as a grant towards a gymnasium to be available for use by
neighbours, including those who had subscribed to the subdivision. There is a difference
between that situation and one in which the contribution comes from the reserve
contribution account.
The Opposition will continue to object unless there is formal agreement by the time the
Bill reaches the Committee stage. If there is no agreement, and even though this is a
washing-up Bill in which there should be no contentious issues, I am afraid the clause will
have to be deleted.
Motion agreed to.

I do not recall the comments of the Acting Leader of the House when he moved
urgency. It is the custom to refer to the reason, although it has long ago been decided that
extensive reasons do not have to be given. Indeed, in the absence of any reason being given,
the House is acquiescent to urgency being taken. The absence of a reason would not
invalidate the decision of the House. Standing Order 47 simply provides the opportunity for

the House normally rises. It is clear that you should rule that the decision to take urgency

Mr BRILL: I shall summarise very briefly the changes to the Bill proposed by the select
committee. First, we recommend an amendment to clause 1(3)(c), and a consequential
addition of a new subclause-(1A) to clause 24—to make it clear that the jurisdiction of the
Act extends to any New Zealand citizen who is charged with any offence under the Act,
although it shall be a defence to the charge if the defendant proves that the act or omission
constituting the offence took place beyond the outer limits of New Zealand fisheries waters
and did not contravene any international agreement to which effect had been given by
regulations made either under the Marine Mammals Protection Act or any other New
Zealand legislation. I want to make it clear that the Act relates to the full 200-mile economic
zone, because some doubt was expressed by conservation interests about whether it
extended only to the 3-mile or to the 12-mile limits.


## p. 4043 (#523) ###########################################

29 September
4043
Marine Mammals Protection Bill
Secondly, the select committee recognised that problems could arise if there was an
absolute prohibition on the movement, in and out of New Zealand, of items of personal
adornment or apparel that were made from a marine mammal product, and therefore
recommends a new clause 4(5)(c) exempting from the legislation the taking from, or bringing
into, New Zealand any marine mammal product being an ornament or an item for personal
use or adornment, made wholly or principally from any part or parts of a marine mammal, if
that product accompanies the person from or into New Zealand, or comprises part of that
person's belongings, and was in existence at the time the Act came into force.
Thirdly, a number of submissions, particularly the submission from Project Jonah (New
Zealand), argued that any application for a permit under clause 5 of the Bill to take or
import a marine mammal or marine mammal product should be made to an independent
commission and should be subject to rights of objection from the general public. The select
committee takes the view that the establishment of such a commission is unnecessary to give
effect to the purpose of the legislation and that, instead, when the Minister of Fisheries is
contemplating granting a permit to take or import marine mammals—and particularly when
he might be contemplating granting an application to hunt or kill such mammals--he should
be required first to give notice of the application in the Gazette, and allow 28 days for
objections to be lodged with him before the matter is finally considered. This provision will
not apply when the Minister is satisfied that it was expedient for the notice not to be
published, when the application relates to an emergency situation or is solely for the purpose
of research.
Fourthly, we recommend a new clause 7A, requiring the Director-General of
Agriculture and Fisheries to maintain a register of permits granted by the Minister, such
register to be open to public inspection. Clause 12 of the Bill gave a very wide power of entry
and search without warrant. It was the opinion of the committee that such a wide power was
both unnecessary and undesirable, and we therefore recommend that the provision be
amended so that it is exercised only in what amounts to cases of emergency or when the
delay involved in obtaining a warrant could result in the evidence being disposed of in some
way. In all other circumstances an officer would be required to obtain a warrant.
The Fishing Industry Board, while supporting the Bill, drew our attention to the fact
that clause 21(2)(b), which placed an absolute prohibition on the use of a purse-seine net in
any area in which marine mammals are present, without having in the net an escape panel or
aperture known as a medina panel, from which any dolphin or porpoise could readily escape,
would have an unnecessarily detrimental effect on New Zealand fishing trawlers using purse-
seine nets, without in any way giving further protection to porpoises and dolphins. The
board pointed out that New Zealand trawlers were involved in fishing only for pelagic
species of fish that did not run with marine mammals, and that the protection was necessary
only in the case of larger purse-seine nets used in fishing for yellowfin tuna. In those
particular circumstances it is necessary to make provision not only to protect marine
mammals but also to ensure that tuna caught in New Zealand waters can be imported into
the United States. Accordingly, the committee proposes a new clause 15A, which prohibits
the use of a purse-seine net for the purpose of fishing unless the net has an escape panel and
also unless the vessel follows a fishing practice acceptable to the Director-General of
Agriculture and Fisheries, but it gives the director-general power to exempt any person,
other than someone using a purse-seine net to fish for yellowfin tuna, from these particular
provisions.
Other changes proposed are relatively minor in effect. The committee is grateful to the
officials of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries and to Dr Baker of the National
Museum, as well as to the various organisations that made submissions to the committee, for
their assistance in making improvements to this important piece of environmental
legislation.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): I shall not speak very long on the report, but I was on
the select committee, and I take a personal interest in the matter not only because it is so
important but also because I have interests relating to recreation. Probably a message came
out of the committee's hearings. The environmental people making submissions to the
committee seemed to me to have almost a lack of confidence in the capacity of the Executive
and the Minister to serve and give effect to the legislation to the level they would wish. They
asked for a separate marine mammals commission. I argued with them, as I think other
members of the committee did, on the point that this ministerial association with
administration of such a matter is, by and large, not as respected as it deserves to be.

Jean K. Sunderland
I do not know whether we convinced these people that an organisation set up and
responsible to Parliament through a Minister would serve better than perhaps an
environmental commission designed for the American scene, with its many parliaments all
over the country. We have one central body whose proceedings are broadcast to the nation,
and the elector, if he so wishes, can find out Parliament's attitude on the protection of such
important animals as marine mammals. The message I got, and it has been given to me
before, because of a certain cynicism about it, is that we in the House do not do enough to
educate people to understand that our type of system means that, not only is the Minister
held responsible to his own party and Government, but his own actions and decisions are
also under far more surveillance than are those of semi-private organisations having such
power. We should jealously guard the elected representatives who have this kind of power,
rather than legislate away our authority. We must give the people an account of our
stewardship from time to time, but statutory bodies, although cosmetically they may appear
to be independent, are not accountable day by day for their responsibilities in quite the same
way.
I am very much in favour of being accountable to the people. Members on the select
committee will recall that I argued fairly strongly, and probably to my political disadvantage
temporarily, for that principle. It would be very easy to make political capital out of the
present environmental mood, and yet not to do the right thing by Parliament and the people
for the objective of protecting our marine mammals. I do not make that point in a hectoring
kind of way, but I know that, as parliamentarians, we do not always stand up for that concept
as often as we should. Instead, we allow people to say that something is under ministerial
control, as if that was some kind of crime-it is not. Obviously, certain areas must be
removed, but the system evolved for administering such important matters as the
environment, although coming in for a good deal of criticism over the years, sometimes for
political party advantage, has in my opinion proved itself. I have always said that I would far
rather deal publicly with a Minister on matters of importance than be obliged to go to a body
not immediately accountable to Parliament, and therefore to the nation.
I do not have an amended copy of the Bill, but various details can be discussed in the
Committee stage. I know that a number of amendments have been designed to get rid of
some matters that could be difficult to administer. The Bill enjoys the support of the
Opposition. Speaking for myself and having the courage to face up to this just before an
election, I think the committee made a wise decision in incorporating the policy of
ministerial control rather than control by a separate commission. It is to be commended for
doing that.
Motion agreed to.

URGENCY-SPEAKER'S RULING
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I want to report on a point of order on which I ruled shortly
after 1 p.m. today, when the member for New Lynn raised the question of whether urgency
had been broken because the reason for the urgency had not been given. I have studied this
matter at length and these are my findings. Standing Order 47(1) requires the mover of the
urgency motion to inform the House of the reasons why urgency is claimed. Standing Order
47(3) provides for the supervening offence that may interrupt and break that urgency.
There is a basic distinction between matters falling within paragraphs (1) and (3) of the
Standing Order. Failure to comply with Standing Order 47(1) does not break urgency, as at
that stage urgency has not been accorded. Urgency is accorded only when the question has
been put from the Chair and determined with or without a division by the House. When
urgency has been accorded it can be broken only by a subsequent interruption of the
proceedings. The alleged failure of the Minister to give reasons when moving the motion is
obviously not a subsequent interruption of the urgency, and, therefore, talk of urgency
having been broken is misplaced.
It is significant that, on the last occasion on which a point about the failure to give
reasons was successful—1976 Hansard, Volume 405, at page 2019-the point was taken
before the question had been determined. Mr Speaker Jack ruled that the motion had not
been properly moved and the proceedings up to that point were nugatory. The motion was
then moved again and carried. However, once the resolution has been agreed to by the
House, it is too late to raise the question that the motion should not have been accepted by
the Chair. That is a point which should be taken by the Chair when the motion is moved; or,
if the Chair overlooks it, it may be raised as a point of order before the question is decided. If
it is valid, as in 1976, the motion will be ruled out of order as not in compliance with Standing
Order 47(1), but once urgency has been accorded there can be no occasion to reopen the
events that occurred before the determination of the question by the House. Although my
previous ruling was not as long, there is no doubt that it was correct.
The House adjourned at 4.35 p.m.

Christchurch-Lyttelton road tunnel would be abolished. The Bill provides that from 1 April
of next year the toll charges are abolished, the Christchurch-Lyttelton Road Tunnel
Authority dissolved, and the assets and liabilities of the authority vested in the Crown. The
intention is that the capital assets and liabilities become a Government responsibility, and
the expenses of operating and maintaining the tunnel a charge against the National Roads
Fund. In effect, the tunnel becomes part of the national highway system with the Ministry of
Transport taking over traffic law enforcement.
Negotiations are under way with the Lyttelton Harbour Board for the board to take
over maintenance of the electrical, mechanical, and ventilation systems installed in the
tunnel. The Bill authorises the board to provide these services after agreement has been
reached with the National Roads Board as to the apportionment of costs.
The remaining clauses are of a formal nature, and deal with the continuance of
proceedings relating to matters happening before 1 April next, and the saving of existing
bylaws and bylaw-making powers. Finally, the Bill repeals the Christchurch-Lyttelton Road
Tunnel Act 1956.

INDUSTRIAL LAW REFORM BILL
Introduction
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Industrial Law Reform Bill
be introduced. The Bill is being introduced to meet urgent requests for legislation, principally
following an adjournment debate in the House last Thursday and Sir William Dunlop's
report. The Bill amends the Industrial Relations Act, the State Services Conditions of
Employment Act, and the Aircrew Industrial Tribunal Act, and is designed to give effect to
four principal objectives.
First, it gives effect to two major recommendations contained in Sir William Dunlop's
report on the application of penal provisions in the Industrial Relations Act, namely, the
change in the liability under sections 81, 125, and 125A of the Industrial Relations Act from
criminal to civil, and the withdrawing of all existing prosecutions under these sections. The
second objective of the Bill is to tighten the existing balloting provisions under sections 101A
to 101E of the Industrial Relations Act. The Minister of Labour will have the power, at his
discretion, to advise the Governor-General to remove the unqualified preference provision
from a particular award in the event of failure by a union to supply to the Registrar of
Industrial Unions a list within 2 months of being requested to do so. This power will be used
sparingly only in the event of the most blatant disregard by a union of the requirement to
provide such a list.
The third objective is to introduce a new procedure relating to the insertion of the
unqualified preference provision, the essence of which is to require every union to hold a
special meeting of its members at 3-yearly intervals to discuss and vote on the question of the
unqualified preference provision. This proposal was developed and put in the legislation in
the light of recommendations by the working party of the Employers Federation and the
union representatives on the Industrial Relations Council.
The fourth objective provides a means by which 10 percent or 50 financial members of a
union can apply to the Arbitration Court for an inquiry in relation to ballots conducted
under sections 100 or 101A, and under the new procedure. The final aim of the Bill is to
facilitate the amalgamation of unions by streamlining existing procedures in the Industrial


## p. 4062 (#542) ###########################################

4062
3 October
Industrial Law Reform Bill
Relations Act, and meets a recent request from the Federation of Labour.
Clause 3 removes the restrictions on the activities of the judge who customarily acts as
chairman of the public sector tribunal. This will enable him to perform the full range of
duties of a judge and act as the chief judge or as deputy for the chief judge should he be
absent. Clause 4 provides for a new section 39, which relates to the salary and allowances of
judges of the Arbitration Court, and provides for payment of a wider range of allowances.
Clause 5 implements the report of Sir William Dunlop by changing the liability under
sections 81, 125, and 125A, but individual liability is maintained, as is union responsibility in
section 125A. Subclause (6) withdraws existing prosecutions. Clause 6 amends section 101B
(3) of the Industrial Relations Act, and requires the Registrar of Industrial Unions to specify
a date by which the union must supply a list for the purposes of a ballot. That date must be
not more than 2 months after the date of request. Clause 7 repeals section 101C of the Act.
The substituted procedure provides that, should a union fail to supply the list within 2
months of the date of request, the Registrar of Industrial Unions must inform the Minister,
who may-if it is permissive-recommend to the Governor-General the removal of the
unqualified preference provision.
Clause 8 enables an application to the Arbitration Court by 10 percent or 50 financial
members for an inquiry into alleged irregularities in any ballot held under sections 100 or
101A of the Act. An inquiry may also be initiated in the event of a failure by a union to
comply with the procedures set out in clause 10 of the Bill or if the procedures are
inadequate in a particular case. Clause 9 confers on the magistrate's court jurisdiction to deal
with actions under sections 81, 125, and 125A to the exclusion of the Arbitration Court. It is
consistent with the findings of Sir William Dunlop. Clause 10 provides for the insertion of a
new rule into the rules of every union, the objective being to ensure all members have prior
notice of and can attend a special meeting to discuss and vote on the insertion of the
unqualified preference provision in the relevant awards. The special meeting must be
conducted every 3 years.
Clause 11 prescribes a procedure whereby a union can require its members to pay a levy
for the purposes of meeting a fine or penalty imposed on a union. Clause 12 is designed to
facilitate the amalgamation of unions. The registrar may agree to an amalgamation if he is
satisfied that the unions concerned have notified all members of the proposed
amalgamation, and the majority is in favour of it. Members are assumed to favour the
amalgamation unless the registrar receives objections from 10 percent or 50 financial
members of the union concerned within one month of application for amalgamation. As
Opposition members will be aware, we have one such application at present. In the event of
objections to that order being received, a ballot of members on the question of
amalgamation will then be required.
Clauses 13 and 14 relate to the State Services Conditions of Employment Act 1977, and
provide that the provisions contained in clauses 5 and 9 of the Bill shall apply to that Act, if
that Act is brought into force. Clause 17 makes minor amendments to the Aircrew Industrial
Tribunal Act 1971, consequent upon the replacement last year of a one-man tribunal with
the present three-man tribunal. Clause 18 amends section 47 of the Aircrew Industrial
Tribunal Act relating to personal grievances, and changes the words "wrongful dismissal” to
“unjustifiable dismissal", as spelt out in the Industrial Relations Act.

The introduction of this Bill is a confession that over the past 3 years the National

industrial scene.

that is why we have such disastrous industrial relations. That is why, on the eve of an
election, the Government has been forced to bring this legislation before the House. Will the
Bill do for the Government what the Government implies that it wants done? Or is the Bill
really designed to resolve the present situation? Does the Government believe the Bill will
do the job that it alleges needs to be done? The proposal to take industrial relations disputes
out of criminal law is a good one, but in the Bill the Government only takes the disputes out
of the criminal law and puts them into civil law.
The Government is merely transferring disputes from criminal courts to civil courts in
spite of past experience, in this country and overseas, that industrial relations matters cannot
be dealt with effectively in civil courts. If courts are to be used in industrial relations matters,
industrial courts should be used. New Zealand has one of the best records in the world for
using industrial courts to promote industrial peace. If anything is needed at the present time,
it is industrial peace. One basic argument that business interests, legal commentators, and
unions have raised against penalties in legislation of this kind is that in industrial matters the
penalties are largely unenforceable, because of the large number of people involved. The
ability to sue in civil courts—and we had that experience recently with people not involved

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The events of the past few weeks, particularly the adjournment debate last Thursday,
have clearly demonstrated the urgency which members on both sides of the House-

## p. 4076 (#556) ###########################################

4076
3 October
Industrial Law Reform Bill
weekend the Government has drafted legislation that, except for one small possible
amendment, is an adoption of the broad text of Sir William Dunlop's recommendations. The
Government's 1975 election manifesto policy included an undertaking to introduce
provisions for various offences resulting from strikes and lockouts which, with one notable
exception, had been deleted by the Labour Government from the 1972 Bill. These
provisions were subsequently enacted in 1976 and created a series of criminal offences. The
recently released report by Sir William Dunlop illustrated-and I accept it quite
categorically-the inappropriateness of criminal offences in industrial law, and
recommended a change from criminal to civil liability. I am already on record as saying
publicly when the legislation was passed, and, indeed when it was first espoused in 1972, that
we did not have a thing called the Wanganui Computer Centre where criminal convictions
would be placed and recorded. That is a minor change in the law, but, nevertheless, it is
significant and involves a human aspect. The criminal process provides the prosecuting
authority with little flexibility in the administration of the law. We have seen that in the last
week or two, and indeed the Secretary of Labour has had to sweat that out. Yet by its nature
the law-particularly criminal prosecutions-in the industrial relations field must be
administered with discretion.
Mr Wetere: You must be joking! It must be embarrassing for him.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It was not embarrassing for the Secretary of Labour. If the
member is suggesting that the Minister is not accepting responsibility, I must disabuse him of
that straight away. I endorse everything that the Secretary of Labour has done. Indeed, the
Deputy Prime Minister and I have commended him for doing what he did. There was no
dereliction of duty. I admire him for his courage, and as Minister I am totally responsible for
his administration. The industrial relations law must be administered with discretion. I have
yet to hear one Labour member in either the adjournment debate-and I am only making
fleeting reference to a past debate-or on the introduction of the Bill, suggest that the
discretion should not be there.
The Bill we have before us incorporates Sir William Dunlop's recommendations on the
transformation of liability, and further recommends the withdrawal of the existing
prosecutions under the relevant sections-in other words, the informations that have been
laid, plus some that could have been laid had the decision been that the prosecutions should
remain. The decision to withdraw the prosecutions-to which the member for Invercargill
objects--follows logically from the decision to change the nature of the liability.
I should like to take this opportunity to correct a slight misinterpretation by a leading
newspaper this morning on the use of the word "unconstitutional". I put the word
"unconstitutional" first when it was put last in the report. I said it was unconstitutional to
dismiss one information and then charge a man for a past offence under a new law. It would
clearly be inequitable to proceed with the prosecutions in view of the legislative changes that
will take place when we pass this Bill. I should make it quite clear that Sir William Dunlop
did not recommend the removal of the penalty provisions from industrial law. This is where
the Labour Opposition and the National Government part company. Since the report
became available that point has been ignored by the media and by the Labour Opposition
this afternoon. The Government remains committed to the principle of protecting the public
interest from the effects of strikes or lockout activity, a principle which is evidently not
accepted by the Opposition.
It is naive for Opposition members to argue that the industrial law should not be
enforceable. I invite members opposite, if they propose to vote against the penal provisions,
to tell us how they will make the legislation work without the sanction of penalties. It is
interesting to note that I do not know of any country-and neither do my officers and New
Zealand advisers, and they have travelled widely-that does not include sanctions against
strikes and lockouts in statutes or in collective agreements. In New Zealand we have
differentiated in regard to essential industries. Under section 125A we have the freezing
industry. We have a sanction against striking when people are in conciliation. That is section
81. The Government, in the absence of parties agreeing on appropriate methods of enforcing
collective agreements and appropriate codes of practice, has a responsibility to establish or
to encourage them.
As I already indicated earlier to the member for Avon we will be accepting Sir William
Dunlop's recommendation that we must encourage what he specified as codes of practice.
We shall persevere with diligence under the chairmanship of Mr George Whatnall, as
recommended. Indeed, I should point out that the Opposition's policy for the removal of all

moved along a little faster. No major problems have been experienced in holding the ballots.

chance to exercise a democratic vote has been frustrated by the procedures being used-for
reasons best known to the unions involved. This frustration has resulted from delays by
union officials in providing lists of persons eligible to vote. I accept that continuing
difficulties are faced by some unions.
I met one union subject to a warrant, and I gave an assurance that I would not interfere
with the warrant that had been issued. I met the union because it was unable to supply a
membership roll to comply with the provisions of the Act. In that case there were mitigating
circumstances. I accept that some unions may have difficulty in supplying rolls within a
reasonable time. However, in other cases delaying tactics have been used. For this reason
the Bill provides for a time limit for the compilation of lists, and if this is not done I have the
discretion-not a mandatory or obligatory power-to recommend that the Governor-
General should remove the unqualified preference provision from the award in question.
That need not necessarily be done by passing an Order in Council; it could be done at the
expiry of the award-a point raised by the member for Heretaunga. I should again
emphasise, as I did earlier, that I shall exercise this discretion only in extreme circumstances.
However, it is the Government's view that the principle is sound; namely, that if ballots
initiated by the Minister are frustrated he should have remedies available. After all, what is
wrong with a democratic vote within a union? Of what are unions frightened? The new
provision will apply to requests already made by the registrar.
The Bill also incorporates an entirely new procedure regarding the inclusion of an
unqualified preference provision in awards. This procedure is in addition to, not in
substitution for, present procedures. I should like to correct a news item on TV1 tonight,
which implied that this was an easing of the Government's policy on ballots. The legislation
on ballots has not changed-it is added to, and the options are open for the Minister and the
unions to move. In practice, sections 100 and 101A stand as they have been for the past year.
The second option has been developed in the light of proposals submitted to the
Government by the working party of employer and union representatives on the Industrial
Relations Council. I should add that the report was unanimous, but I must be fair and make
the point that the Government has not accepted all the points made in the report.
The principle behind the new procedures is that before negotiating assessors should
have positive instructions from the union regarding the inclusion of the unqualified
preference provision, arrived at in a democratic way. This would be achieved by requiring
each union to hold a special meeting of members, or by notifying their members every 3
years, and at these meetings a secret vote would be taken under the supervision of the
Registrar of Industrial Unions. This procedure reinforces, and is consistent with, the late
Tom Shand's amendments, which were incorporated in the 1961 Act. I am sure he envisaged
that his amendments would operate in this way, and that a vote would have been taken and
the rights of union members would have been clearly spelt out to the assessors before they
went into conciliation. That they did not is the fundamental reason this became an election
issue in 1975. It is the reason it is in earlier legislation, and it is the reason we are amending it
tonight.
Also included in the Bill is a provision whereby 10 percent of the financial members of a
union, or 50-whichever is the fewer-may apply to the Arbitration Court for an inquiry
into the conduct of ballots under sections 100 and 101A of the Act, and into actions taken
under the new balloting procedure referred to above. The Federation of Labour expressly
requested that the balloting procedures under section 101A should be subject to appeal to
the Arbitration Court. This is provided for. I accept this principle without qualification, but
would point out to the House that it cannot be used to delay the conclusion of a ballot. The
application under this section, and under section 100, can be lodged only within 1 month of
the result being certified.
Finally, I draw the attention of the House to the new provision designed to facilitate the
amalgamation of unions. The provision has been included to meet a direct request by the
Federation of Labour to further streamline procedures, and it is entirely consistent with the
Government's policy to encourage union amalgamation. I think that on this clause at least
there should be a degree of unanimity. I believe this is a significant amendment from the
point of view of the future size and structure of trade unions. The new provision removes the
necessity for ballots to be conducted by all unions in all circumstances, but still protects the
rights of those who object to amalgamation. We now have a case where a relatively small

management maintain an equitable attitude to each other fair treatment by both sides.

the trade unions, otherwise it meant excommunication or deregistration. All other penalties

I want to read from Sir William's report, because it is essential to an understanding of
the Bill. The report begins by referring to the relevant sections of the Industrial Relations
Act dealing with the breach of sections during conciliation, and going on strike—and there
are special ones in the major industries, particularly the freezing industry-sections 81, 125,
and 125A. Among other reasons for his conviction that criminal processes are inappropriate
in enforcement legislation of this kind he says at 3(iii): “The decision to strike is usually
taken by the majority. The present legislation places those who oppose the strike, but are
none the less bound by the majority decision, in an untenable position. Either they must
leave the industry or carry the risk of a criminal conviction, with all the consequences that
this entails." I believe that this is plain and simple and easily comprehended by everyone as a
good reason for moving to the civil type of action.
The report goes on to state: "The Ocean Beach experience provides an excellent
illustration of the point. As the senior adviser to the Government on industrial relations the
Secretary of Labour was, in my opinion, duty bound to consult with the Government on the
consequences of initiating and subsequently proceeding with the prosecutions. His decision
to apply for an adjournment of the Ocean Beach prosecutions, and, failing this, not to offer
any evidence was, in my opinion, the correct one having regard to the delicate state of
industrial relations in the industry. He was fully aware that such a course of action would
provoke allegations of political direction in criminal proceedings. I am satisfied that such
allegations are unfounded and consider that the secretary acted correctly in informing the
Minister of his proposed action in the event of the court declining the application for
adjournment." I do not propose to go into his fuller explanation in the annexes to his report,
but I agree with him and I have not the slightest doubt that the Secretary of Labour acted
independently as he must, and arbitrarily as his own character and nature would dictate.
Sir William then went on to recommend his immediate course of action: “As a matter of
urgency, I consider that legislation should be promoted transforming liability under sections
81, 125, and 125A of the Industrial Relations Act from one that is criminal in nature to one
that is civil in nature. This legislation should also include a provision withdrawing all existing
prosecutions under these sections." Again, I agree that, where there is an agreement in the
nature of a contract, although the ordinary law of contract does not apply to it, that men will
get certain pay and conditions of work available to them for certain work and certain
performance, it should be possible not only for the worker to recover his full wages, the full

There are a number of minor matters too, but the other major matter in the Bill is the
provision of a more democratic way of deciding whether a union should have compulsory
coverage of all those who work in a given field. They might be clothing workers, freezing
workers, waterside workers, or clerical workers. Many people want to be members of their
union, and because they want to be members the unions are better unions. But since 1936,
when the first Labour Government came into power, for a long time we had completely
compulsory unionism, apart from the inclusion in each award or agreement of a provision
known as the unqualified preference provision whereby everybody in the industry covered
by the award had to be a member of the union.
This Bill provides for periodic checks to determine whether or not workers in an
industry or occupation want their unions to be compulsory, or whether they want it to be
completely voluntary as are the Public Service Association and Federated Farmers. The Bill
gives proper expression to the democratic principle that the majority shall not unreasonably
use its power over the minority. Under the Bill, if 10 percent of the members of a union, or
50, whichever is the smaller, want to take action to force a ballot, the power is there for this

Mr McLAY: I agree, it would not be fair. I say this personally with a heavy heart,

Like the Minister of Justice I agree with those who say that you cannot direct people to
work. However, I want to put the record straight because the Opposition has not done so in
the course of the debate. The legislation does not force people to work. Rather, it imposes
penalties for breaches of disputes procedures, such breaches of disputes procedures as we
had in Birkenhead recently, when the Birkenhead Transport drivers refused to follow the
disputes procedures laid down in the Industrial Relations Act, and instead went on strike for
more than 3 weeks at great inconvenience to local citizens. Ultimately, their stand was not
upheld by an independent industrial mediator. Second, tonight we are debating penalties for
breaches of the terms of awards and agreements. We are debating a law that imposes a civil
liability, enforceable in much the same way as a civil debt.
It is appropriate that we should look for a moment at the legal background to the change
from criminal to civil action—a change recommended by Sir William Dunlop. I should have
thought that most members of the House, and most people generally, understood the
difference between criminal and civil actions. However, it is clear from what Opposition
members have said during the introductory debate and during this debate so far that they do
not understand. A criminal offence is an act or an omission for which a person can be
punished under an Act of Parliament, either by the imposition of a fine or by some other
penalty. Essentially, civil liability arises between two or more individuals—in this case the
individuals being the general public interest-either in a contract, which is similar to an
award or agreement, or under some tort or civil rule. In 1973 the law provided no penalties
at all for the breach of industrial laws, and in 1976 penalties were introduced by the National
Government.
Hon. M. Rata: You were wrong.
Mr McLAY: The member who interjects forgets that if a procedure is laid down and
penalties are not provided for non-observance of that procedure the law has no teeth and
no effect, and can command no respect. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition said the
industrial law required an effective disputes procedure. How can a procedure be effective if
the law does not provide a sanction or penalty for those who would break it?
It is appropriate that we should look for a moment at the law amended by the Labour
Government in 1975. Sections 147 to 157 provide for the Arbitration Court to impose a
penalty for a breach of the terms of an award or agreement. The member for Roskill said
tonight that he and his Labour Party colleagues did not agree with penalties, yet in 1973 he
put a penalty into sections 147 to 157 of the Industrial Relations Act. He also put one into
section 81 of the same Act.
I wonder if a Labour Government would remove those provisions from the law now that
the member for Roskill has told the House that he no longer wants to see even civil penalties

Policy commitments were made to introduce the remainder of the penalties into the
Industrial Relations Act, but they were only part of a total package of changes to this
legislation. In its early stages the present Government changed the definition of “strike",
and introduced legislation to control rolling strikes. Do members opposite oppose that
change? Apparently they do not. Do they oppose changes in the Commerce Act that allow
action to be taken against political strikes, and allow proceedings to be instituted when there
is a failure to resume work and the public interest is affected? I raise that specifically because
it was under those provisions that employers in the freezing industry went to court, and both
employees and employers were prepared to be bound by the adjudication of the court, which
finally resolved the matter in dispute by referring it to conciliation.
The former Labour Government also inserted penalty provisions in the Act relating to
pilots, which is one of the issues dealt with in the amending Bill before us tonight. The
proposed new section 101C, as set out in clause 7, changed the existing law to enable the
Minister to take proceedings by Order in Council to declare a union voluntary by
withdrawing the unqualified preference clause if he is frustrated in the implementation of the
voluntary ballot warrant that he has issued. That is an important change.
The changes made in the civil penalty provisions are also substantial, but in fact they are
consistent with National Party policy, which was placed before the people in 1975 and
strongly endorsed by a large proportion of the electorate. Tonight we are introducing
changes that will make the law work better. We admit that some of the provisions we
introduced may have been too tough, and that some may have been unfair, particularly when

improved industrial relations.

Motion agreed to.
Rt. Hon. W. R. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): A point of order, Mr Speaker.
I suggest tp you that the action that has just been taken by the Government, and the
consequent division, have broken urgency in terms of Standing Order 47(3), which states:
"Where urgency has been accorded any such Bill, matter, or other proceeding, such urgency
shall be deemed to have lapsed if, when such proceedings have been entered upon, they are
interrupted for any purpose other than the following: (a) By matter of privilege suddenly
arising: (b) By words of heat between members: (b) By question of order: (d) By an answer
to an Address: (e) By a member appearing to be sworn: (f) By a motion that strangers be
ordered to withdraw: (g) By notice being taken and the House being counted: (h) By the
making, by leave, of a Ministerial statement: (i) By the reading of a Message from the
Governor-General relating to the matter under discussion: (j) By the suspension of the
sitting between 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. on a Friday." The action taken by the Government, and
the consequential division, do not fall within any of the categories listed in that Standing
Order. Therefore, urgency has lapsed.
Mr SPEAKER: I do not need any further advice. I have been having a good look at the
matter, because I have been rather interested in the question of urgency. We had a similar
case either last year or in 1976. Standing Order 47(2) provides that the “Bill, matter, or other
proceeding" for which urgency has been accorded "may be proceeded with". The Standing
Order does not say that it has to be proceeded with.
Standing Order 47(3) provides that urgency shall be deemed to have lapsed if, when
such proceedings have been entered upon, they are interrupted for any purpose other than
the following matters, and then follow the matters that have been listed by the Leader of the
Opposition. Speaker's ruling 107/5 provides that it is quite in order for business on the Order
Paper to be postponed, and that a motion so to postpone Orders of the Day may be moved
by any member without notice.
The motion to postpone cannot be an interruption for the purpose of Standing Order
47(3), because it is within the power of any member to move it, and it would be
inconceivable that any member could have the power to break urgency by such a simple
expedient. Most of those motions are, of course, in the hands of a Minister only, but under
the Speaker's ruling it can be moved by any member. Obviously that was not envisaged by
the definitions of the word "proceeding". Such a motion is clearly a part of the proceedings
that are included in the urgency motion. For example, Orders of the Day 1 to 23 were
postponed until after Orders of the Day for local Bills, all under urgency, on 9 December
1976.
Therefore, it is not a matter of saying we shall not deal with those matters, but is a
matter of saying we will take certain matters ahead of certain other matters within the
bracket of topics agreed to for discussion by the House in terms of the urgency motion. In
terms of my interpretation of the Standing Orders, of the Speakers' rulings, and of the
precedent that was set in December 1976, it seems to me that it is quite in order for the
House to postpone consideration of one matter until after consideration of another. I must
therefore rule that urgency has not been broken by that procedural motion.
Dr WALL (Porirua): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I am not disputing your ruling that
a simple motion by any member to postpone the Orders of the Day would not break
urgency. However, I draw your attention to the fact that Standing Order 47 is exclusive. It
states that anything other than the points listed will break urgency. I submit it is not the
moving of the motion that would break urgency, but the fact that the House has been
interrupted by a division on that motion, which is a different procedure from a motion being
moved by a member, which could be defeated immediately. The proceedings of the House
were interrupted when the division was called for. That would not have been of any
significance if the Standing Order had been written differently and had listed certain things
that would break urgency. However, all it states is that there are certain things that do not
break urgency. All other matters do break urgency. I submit that it is not the moving of the
motion but the division of the House that has interrupted proceedings and broken urgency.
Mr SPEAKER: I am gratified that the honourable member did not disagree with my
ruling that the lodging of a procedural motion cannot break urgency. However, the divison
that followed from the lodging of that motion is clearly part of the motion, and if the motion
itself did not break urgency then obviously a division of the House in consequence of that
motion cannot break urgency either.

MOUNT EGMONT VESTING BILL
Third Reading
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That this Bill be now read a third time.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): On this third reading it is worth reminding ourselves
that the principal objectives of this important Bill remained unaltered when it emerged from
the Committee of the Whole House. That principle is to vest the land now known as the
Mount Egmont National Park, consisting of more than 86 752 acres, in its former owners. I
do not intend to traverse the history of this matter, because that has already been covered.
This land was confiscated as a result of the provisions of the New Zealand Land Settlement
Act 1863, and 50 percent of the land concerned was bought by forced purchase. The Minister
may shake his head if he wants to, but that is a fact. This move by the Government is new in
principle and could be regarded as extremely generous.
The submissions made by the Taranaki Maori Trust Board, which would have meant
only a minor amendment to the title, were not considered by the Government, even
although the Opposition moved in the Committee to have the word “Taranaki" added so
that the short title would have read, "The Mount Egmont (Taranaki) Vesting Act 1978”.
That amendment was defeated. It was the only request made by the people representing the
former owners and their descendants. However, the Government considered it could not
support that move.
I believe formal steps should be taken to recommend to Her Majesty the Queen that the
eight tribes of the Taranaki people, who have been adversely affected since the outbreak of
the land wars, should be granted a pardon. Then the use of the land would have been vested
in perpetuity in the people of New Zealand. The Opposition's views were not acceded to and
the name of the Act remained unaltered. It is to be earnestly hoped that the Government
will seriously consider extending a formal pardon to those people whose land has been
affected and who have been gravely wronged, as is shown in our records. I shall not say any
more other than that this is an important move for our country and may heal some of the
grievances that have been felt over the past 115 years.

CORNISH COMPANIES MANAGEMENT AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill extends the power of the statutory manager in relation to the
realisation of the pooled property of the Cornish group, and complements the pooling of the
property of that group by including the tax losses of Mr Cornish.
Clause 2 entitles Cornish Investments Ltd. to the business losses of Mr Cornish as at the
end of the present income year for tax purposes. The Cornish Companies Management Act
pooled into Cornish Investments Ltd. the assets and liabilities of not only the companies in
the group, but also of those of Mr Cornish, which amounted to 45 percent of the group's
assets and liabilities. This amendment is consistent with and complements the original
pooling of assets and liabilities, and has been agreed to by Mr Cornish. Clause 3 empowers
the statutory manager, with the consent of the advisory committee, to promote the
formation and registration of a company so as to transfer to it, pursuant to the new section
inserted by clause 4, or sell to it parts of the pooled property. This will enable the statutory
manager to float a company for the purpose of purchasing pooled property.
Clause 4 provides that Cornish Investments Ltd. may transfer to a public company any
part of the pooled property that cannot be advantageously realised in any other way, in
consideration of the issue of shares or other securities by that company to the creditors of
Cornish Investments Ltd. The value of any shares or securities so issued to a creditor shall be
deemed to have been paid by Cornish Investments Ltd. to the creditor in satisfaction or part
satisfaction, as the case may be, of his debts or claims against it.
The public company to which pooled property may be transferred pursuant to this
amendment can be a company independent of the Cornish group or a company promoted by
the statutory manager pursuant to the amendment in clause 3. This method of disposing of
pooled property is termed an "arrangement" that can be effected only with the consent of
the advisory committee, the sanction of the Supreme Court, and the consent of a majority in
number and three-quarters in value of creditors at a meeting, notice of which is to be sent to
each creditor, setting out relevant information upon which to base an informed decision. The
amendments in clauses 3 and 4 will provide the statutory manager with additional courses of
action to expedite the realisation of the group's pooled property if the opportunities, at
present negligible, for making further substantial realisations do not improve.

MINING AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time.
The Bill was introduced towards the end of last session, and, as required by the Standing
Orders, it was referred to the Lands and Agriculture Committee. The principal purpose of
the Bill is to encourage exploration and prospecting for minerals in our national parks.
When the Mining Act 1971 was enacted, it introduced for the first time in the country's
mining legislation a provision giving the holder of a prospecting licence a right to exchange a
portion of that licence for a mining licence. This new provision was seen at the time as an
incentive to the mining industry to undertake the high-risk expenditure necessary in
prospecting for and proving an economic mineral deposit.
The right to mine any proven deposit is conditioned by existing provisions in the mining
legislation. Under these provisions, conditions are attached to the mining licence specifically
to protect flora, fauna, and unique natural features, and to prevent when practicable
unnecessary damage to the land surface and to provide for its restoration when mining is
complete. However, although provision is made for these safeguards to be written into any
mining licence granted in exchange for a prospecting licence, the various national park
boards have been most reluctant to allow mineral prospecting to proceed in their parks. The
park authorities consider that an application for a prospecting licence is tantamount to one
for a mining licence. In fact, since the commencement of the new mining legislation in 1973,
no licences for prospecting for minerals have been granted over national parks.
National parks cover about 10 percent of our country, and include many areas which,
because of their geology, are most likely to contain significant mineralisation. It is not in the
national interest, therefore, that the present situation of prospecting being stopped
altogether should continue. In an effort to rekindle prospecting of our mineral resources in
national parks, the Bill provides for the replacement of the right of the holder of a
prospecting licence to exchange a portion of that licence for a mining licence, with a right of
priority to apply for such a mining licence. This amendment to the rights of the holder of a
prospecting licence will be applicable only inasmuch as the licence relates to a national park.
While the mining industry was reluctant to see any change to the existing provisions of
the legislation, it has accepted that a change is necessary if prospecting in the parks is to take
place. This is a major concession by the industry. If the Bill is passed, a mining company
would be invited to prospect in a national park without any assurance that it would be able to
recover its exploration costs in the event of an economic mineral deposit being discovered.
I am hopeful that the industry will be able to accept this change, which is designed to
ensure on the one hand that the extent of our mineral resources is known in as much detail as
possible, and, on the other, that the unique values of our national parks are adequately
recognised and safeguarded. Armed with this knowledge we shall then be in a much better
position than we are today to make decisions in the best interests of the country as a whole
on the best use of its land resources.
By leave of the House, a further clause has been added to the Bill since it was referred
to the Lands and Agriculture Committee. The additional clause, which is unrelated to the


## p. 4118 (#598) ###########################################

4118
3 October
Mining Amendment Bill
27
principal purpose of the Bill-namely, to get mineral exploration revived in national parks—
amends the existing provisions of the legislation pertaining to the review of the rate of
royalties payable under a mining licence. Currently, the Minister of Energy may review only
at 10-yearly intervals the rate of royalty payable under a mining licence. It is proposed that
for all mining licences granted after the Bill is passed the Minister of Energy may review the
rate of royalty at 5-yearly intervals instead. A shortening of the period at which the
opportunity for review may be taken is desirable in the light of more rapidly changing
economic factors. A new provision is also added, allowing the Minister of Energy to reduce
at any time the rate of royalty payable under a mining licence.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): As the Minister pointed out, the Bill opens up very
important and sensitive matters involving national parks and reserves. Prospecting in those
regions is a very emotive matter indeed, and I think the Minister would be the first to agree
that the trustees of national parks hold that responsibility with some authority and do not
lightly give way to any suggestion that there should be prospecting or mining in their parks.
After all, they are the trustees on behalf of the Government and the people of New Zealand,
and that responsibility is not lightly held by them. Possibly the Minister would agree with me
that quite often the trustees-the national park boards-have gone to the other extreme. In
fact, since 1971 there has been no prospecting whatever in national parks.
The Minister has just said that no less than 10 percent of the country is locked up in
national parks and reserves. That is a very big slice of New Zealand. As he has said, we need
to know the extent of mineral deposits and the wealth that those deposits might yield to New
Zealand, and the Bill has been introduced to break the present impasse. It is 7 years since
there has been any prospecting in national parks. The 1971 legislation did not become
operative until 1973. It has not met with any success. It has not enabled prospectors to get
into national parks to see what is in those areas.
The trend in New Zealand is for the establishment of more parks and reserves, national

not give any automatic right to mine in a national park. The Minister has conceded that, to

The exchange of a prospecting licence for a mining licence will have to be negotiated.
The only right a prospector will have under the Bill is that of priority over others. That
means that, should he be successful in an application to mine in a national park, he will be at
the head of the queue. Almost impossible conditions may be imposed by the department or
the National Parks Board that would make it prohibitive for him to be granted a mining
licence in a national park. How long will that last?

LIQUID FUELS TRUST BILL
Second Reading
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time.
The Bill promotes the establishment of the basis of a liquid fuels policy for New Zealand. It
provides the resources for investigating and developing alternatives to imported fuel used for
transport purposes in New Zealand. The establishment of the Liquid Fuels Trust Board,
responsible for considering all aspects of transport fuels-including efficient production,
processing, distribution, and final use-is a major step in the construction of a
comprehensive liquid fuels policy. This policy will complement those policies already
implemented by the Government to achieve the objectives of a reduced dependence upon
imported oil, to encourage a more efficient use of energy resources, and to accelerate the
development of New Zealand's indigenous resources, particularly renewable forms of
energy.
Since the Government resumed office in 1975, it has vigorously pursued energy policies
that recognise the immense value of New Zealand's indigenous resources, and that aim at
reducing our dependence on imported fuels. Undoubtedly, the highlight has been the
Government's resolution to make New Zealand as self-sufficient as possible in transport
fuels, as an act of policy. The major alternatives available for achieving this objective are:
blends of methanol and gasoline, blends of methanol and diesel, and synthetic gasoline.
These three options, and other alternatives suggested as a result of subsequent work, will be
investigated by the Liquid Fuels Trust Board.
As a first step the Government is proceeding with design work for an optimum-sized
methanol plant that would be capable of at least meeting a 15 percent methanol - 85 percent
gasoline blend requirement as well as our total requirement for chemical methanol. It is
almost certain that a 15 percent methanol - 85 percent gasoline blend could be used
successfully in cars. To verify this as rapidly as possible, the Government announced in this
year's Budget its intention to conduct extensive market feasibility studies and large-scale
trials. Preliminary studies by Government departments to consider potential uses for
available quantities of Maui gas concentrated on blends in which gasoline was the principal
component. However, the lower requirements of gas for electricity generation have released
substantial quantities for other purposes. More recently, transport fuels substitutes requiring
much larger amounts of gas have been proposed for study by the Liquid Fuels Trust Board,
as provided for under clause 4 (2) (a) of the Bill.
Possibilities to be considered by the board now include blends of methanol and gasoline
in which methanol is the base blending component, blends of methanol and diesel containing
up to 90 percent methanol, and synthetic gasoline. Synthetic gasoline is not a novelty, but
development work on it received low priority while petroleum was so cheap in the 1950s and
1960s.
The proposed levy of 0.1c a litre on motor spirits and automotive diesel used in New
Zealand will raise about $3.25 million annually. Clause 4 (2) (b) provides that the board can
promote, in various ways, practices that are efficient and economic for the handling and the
provision of liquid fuels. The sort of circumstance that is contemplated here is when some
aspect of a development such as the provision of an LPG storage facility is in the national
interest but not commercially attractive. However, with financial assistance under clause
10-for example by way of grants, loans, leases, or ownership-development can be
expedited. We have strong policies with respect to energy generally, but the transport
sector, because of its huge reliance upon imported liquid fuels, requires special
consideration. The Bill formalises that consideration and will facilitate the work of not only
the Liquid Fuels Trust Board, but also the DSIR and other research groups investigating


## p. 4121 (#601) ###########################################

Liquid Fuels Trust Bill
alternatives to imported fuels for transport purposes in New Zealand.
