TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 3)
Second Reading
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. I know that the House, having adopted the report of the select committee that
sat for 2 years on this matter, will forgive me if I am brief, because I am certain every
member of the House knows what is in the Bill. Two complementary areas are covered by
the new legislation. The existing blood-alcohol provisions of the Transport Act are
substantially amended, and the criteria relating to the granting of limited licences is
tightened. The opportunity has also been taken to correct one or two anomalies in the
existing transport legislation. I shall refer to these when I explain the content of the Bill, but


## p. 4124 (#604) ###########################################

4124
3 October
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 3)
I would remind members that I have already done so on the first reading.
There is no need for me to go into detail about the blot on our society of people who
drive when they have drunk too much. I do not intend at this hour of the morning to go into a
lot of detail by going over that ground again, but the measures in the Bill will, I believe, help
us to fight and combat this menace.
The present system of testing for blood-alcohol levels in suspects has two main
disadvantages. First, it is time consuming. By the time a doctor has become available and
blood samples taken, up to 2 hours may have elapsed since the suspect was first
apprehended. Secondly, if a blood sample is taken and analysed, the offender does not know
for about a week if he is guilty or not. The overall impact of these factors is to impose
undesirable limits on the efficiency of enforcement. The select committee, under the
chairmanship of the member for Hamilton West, has recognised that this is an intolerable
situation, and accordingly has recommended the introduction of evidential breath testing.
It is the view of both the Government and the select committee that breath testing
should substantially replace blood testing. As I said in introducing the Bill, the introduction
of evidential breath testing will mean that the courts must accept as evidence of an offence
the result of an evidential breath test showing a breath-alcohol proportion of more than 500
micrograms per litre of air, as long as this test is preceded by one positive alcotest R80 or
similar screening test. This is one of the major changes in the legislation. The Government
has also decided to reduce the blood-alcohol level of 100 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood to
80 of alcohol per 100 ml of blood.
The system will serve two purposes. First, it describes a safe level up to which drivers
may drink without infringing the law, and, secondly, taken with the intrinsic error of the
testing device used, it defines a higher prosecution level. The Government is satisfied that
the existing legal level of 100 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood is not sufficiently effective. In
deciding upon the level of 80 mg we are adopting the policy of a number of other countries. I
mention the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia with the exception of Victoria; most
Scandinavian countries have even lower levels, while in the United States the levels range
from 80 to 150. This is also, of course, to provide a more effective deterrent.
A number of fines for offences involving alcohol are to be increased by well over 100
percent, and this is another major change in the legislation. The new maximum fines are
those recommended by the select committee.
I mentioned earlier that there are two main aspects of the Bill. I have discussed the first
amendments to the blood alcohol provisions of the Transport Act. The second is an
adjunct-the criteria used to issue limited licences are to be tightened. The present law
provides a limited licence may be issued if it is considered that disqualification has resulted
or will result in undue hardship to any person. However, no person convicted for the second
time of a specified type of offence within 3 years of the first such offence can be issued with a
limited licence except on the grounds of extreme hardship to some other person.
The Bill seeks to change that. The court will still be able to issue a limited licence if it is
satisfied that disqualification has resulted or will result in extreme hardship to the applicant,
or undue hardship to any person other than the applicant. However, no person who is
convicted for a specified type of offence for the second time and within 5 years of the first
shall be issued with a limited licence. Further, no order granting a limited licence can take
effect until 1 month after it is made. Finally, no licence shall be issued until every person who
signs an affidavit supporting the issue of a limited licence has made an appearance in court
for examination of the contents of that affidavit.
When I introduced the Bill I quoted from a survey conducted by the Ministry of
Transport, which found that 36 percent of the community favoured more severe penalties to
deter drinking and driving. Only 7 percent favoured a more lenient approach. In the Bill the
Government is taking direct and effective action to deter the drinking driver. I shall now go
through the Bill briefly, clause by clause.
Clause 1 relates to the short title and the date of commencement. Clause 2 amends
section 29 of the Transport Act 1962. This section empowers the making of regulations
relating to motor drivers' licences. This will have a twofold effect. First, it will empower the
making of regulations providing that all certificates of approval issued to driving instructors
shall continue in force for a limited time only. This shall apply to all licences regardless of
their date of issue. Secondly, it provides that passenger service vehicle licences shall be
issued only to those applicants who are considered by the issuing authority to be suitable to
hold such licences. The clause also validates certain existing regulations relating to passenger


## p. 4125 (#605) ###########################################

3 October
4125
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 3)
service vehicle licences, and provides that such licences may be revoked in certain
circumstances.
Clause 3 amends section 30 of the principal Act and concerns penalties relating to
driving offences involving alcohol, and to offences against the Transport Licensing
Regulations. The maximum fine for causing injury or death through drunken driving or
driving under the influence has been increased from $2,000 to $4,000. The maximum fine for
causing injury or death through dangerous driving has been increased from $1,000 to $3,000.
The maximum fine that may be imposed in respect of a blood-alcohol offence is increased
from $400 to $1,500, and the maximum fine for an offence relating to careless or
inconsiderate use of a motor vehicle has been increased from $200 to $1,000.
The opportunity has also been taken to increase the maximum fine for an offence
against the transport licensing provisions of the Transport Act 1962. The maximum fine is
increased from $200 to $2,000. This applies mainly to people who offend against the 150 km
limit. These offences are economic offences, and the only practical and effective method of
deterrent is a substantial fine. Unlike the position with transport offences relating to road
safety, it is not possible for the courts to take licences from individuals or transport operators
who commit transport licensing offences. The increase in the maximum level of fines for such
offences therefore reflects the economic importance of these offences and is seen to be
timely in view of the change to the distance limit on road and rail competition.
Clause 4 amends section 32 of the Transport Act, as amended by section 2 of the
Transport Amendment Act 1970. Section 32 refers to the disqualification of persons from
holding drivers' licences following application from certain persons. The new amendment
effectively gives the Commissioner of Police the same rights of delegation as are at present
held by the Secretary for Transport to make an order disqualifying any person from holding
a driver's licence. The Police and the Secretary for Transport are now brought into line.
Clause 5 refers to the issue of limited licences to disqualified persons. Section 38(2) of
the Transport Act is amended in three ways: first, to provide that the court may order the
issue of a limited licence if it is satisfied that disqualification has resulted, or will result, in
extreme hardship to the applicant or undue hardship to a person other than the applicant;
secondly, to provide that no person may be granted a limited licence following a second
driving disqualification of a specified type within 5 years of the first; thirdly, a proviso is
added to the effect that a limited licence shall not be issued until the expiration of 1 month
from the date of commencement of the disqualification order.
This fifth clause also adds a new subsection—(2A)—to section 38(2) of the principal
Act, providing that, unless the court decides, otherwise no limited licence may be issued
until every person who has filed an affidavit in support of the application has appeared in
court for examination on the contents of his affidavit. Section 38(3) is amended by subclause
(2), the effect of which is to empower the court to specify in any order authorising the issue
of a limited licence such matters as the court thinks fit. This subclause is deemed to have
come into force on 1 February 1971, in order to validate the condition found in nearly all
limited licences-namely, that the limited licence be carried while driving.
Clause 6 makes a drafting change to section 41 of the Act, which relates to appeals
against disqualification. Clause 7 repeals sections 58 to 58D of the Transport Act and
substitutes the proposed new sections 57A to 58F. The Government has adopted the
recommendations of the select committee concerning blood alcohol offences, and the new
sections in clause 7 put these into effect. The principal differences between the existing
sections and the proposed new sections are outlined.
Section 58 prescribes a new offence--driving a motor vehicle while the proportion of
alcohol in a person's breath exceeds 500 micrograms per litre of breath. The evidential
breath test is undergone after an initial breath-screening test and in place of the second
breath test provided for at present. The result of an evidential breath test may not be
admitted in evidence if the suspect has requested a blood test. Section 58 provides also for
the lowering of the allowable limit of alcohol in the blood from 100 milligrams of alcohol per
100 millilitres of blood to 80 milligrams of alcohol.
The new section 58A further widens the grounds upon which an enforcement officer
may request a suspect to undergo a breath test. These are as follows: good cause to suspect
that the person has been drinking before or while driving; that the person was the driver of a
motor vehicle involved in an accident or, if it is not clear who the driver was, that the person
was in the motor vehicle at the time of the accident; good cause to suspect that the person
has recently committed an offence against the road safety provisions of the principal Act or

regulations pursuant to it that involve the use of a motor vehicle.

covers the Bill for the purpose of the second reading. No doubt members might want to

CONTRACTUAL REMEDIES BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Contractual Remedies
Bill be introduced. It is proposed to refer the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee for
recess study. The Bill implements the 1967 report of the Contracts and Commercial Law
Reform Committee on misrepresentation and breach of contract. It follows the draft Bill
that was incorporated in a supplementary report and reprint of the original report published
this year.
Comment on the reprinted report was sought from a variety of interests, including the
Consumers Institute, lawyers, and Government departments. None of these interests has
expressed opposition to the implementation of the report. The defects in the existing law on
remedies for misrepresentation and breach of contract are discussed in detail in the
committee's report. The problems arise from the complexity of the law, which makes it
difficult for an innocent party to decide on his remedy, and from the inadequacy of the law,
which means that the appropriate remedy is not always available.
Under the law at present the remedies available to a party aggrieved by a
misrepresentation inducing a contract or a breach of contract depend on the classification of
the statement on which he relies. A statement may fall into one or more of some 13 classes.
It may, for example, be classified as an innocent misrepresentation, the remedy for which is
recision, or it may be classed as a warranty, the remedy for the breach of which is an award
of damages. The practical difficulties are graphically portrayed in the committee's report of
an actual case in which the court considers five possible classifications for one statement, as
set out on page 63, paragraph 7.2 of that report. The Bill modifies and simplifies these rules
by giving a single set of remedies for misrepresentation inducing the making of a contract
and for the repudiation or breach of a contract. The existing categories of statements will
remain, but they will lose much, if not all, of their practical importance.
Damages may at present be claimed for a fraudulent misrepresentation, but not for an
innocent one. The Bill allows damages to be claimed for an innocent misrepresentation.
Misrepresentation, repudiation, and breach presently give rise to recision or similar
remedies. The Bill replaces these "recision-type" remedies by a single new remedy to be
called "cancellation". Cancellation is to be available for repudiation, or for a


## p. 4132 (#612) ###########################################

4132
4 October
Contractual Remedies Bill
misrepresentation or a breach of sufficient seriousness to warrant this remedy. Its effects are
stated in the Bill, as is the power of the court to grant relief. Damages may be claimed
instead of, or in addition to, cancellation.
The position of assignees in respect of the new remedies is set out, and parties are
empowered to exclude the new remedies in their contract. Some written contracts contain an
exception clause, which precludes the court from determining whether a statement was made
during the negotiations for a contract, and whether it was a representation inducing a
contract or became a term of the contract. The Bill gives the courts discretionary power to
ignore such a clause and to ascertain the real position. The Bill is another instalment in the
continuing review of the law of contract, and is a worthy measure to stand alongside recent
Acts on contractual mistakes, illegal contracts, and minors' contracts.

TOXIC SUBSTANCES BILL
Introduction
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the Toxic Substances Bill be now
introduced. The Bill has been prepared to replace partially the present Poisons Act 1960 and
its amendments, and to provide for an improved system to regulate the sale, availability, use,
storage, transport, packing, labelling, importation, notification, sampling, and analysis of
toxic substances other than medicines. The present Poisons Act deals with both medicines
and non-medicines. The Restricted Drugs Bill-a companion to this Bill-dealing solely
with medicines, will be introduced shortly.
The separation of the Poisons Act 1960 into different legislation to deal with medicines
and non-medicines was a consequence of the report of the advisory committee on
commercial, household, and agricultural poisons. The committee received a considerable
number of written and oral submissions, and its recommendations form the basis of the Bill.
The present Act is widely considered unsatisfactory, not only because of the inadequate
breadth of its provisions, but also because it is very difficult to understand and its
terminology is confusing. For example, the terms "poisonous substance", "poison” and
"restricted poison" are used to define three classes of substance of widely varying toxicity.
To the lay observer these three terms appear to mean roughly the same thing. In the new
Bill, the more descriptive terms, "deadly poison", "dangerous poison", "poison", and
"harmful substance" will be used for different categories of poisons according to their degree
of hazard.
Under present New Zealand legislation there is no straightforward way in which
substances having an effect on the natural environment may be regulated. The definition of
"toxic substance", which represents the broad category of substances covered by the
legislation, refers only to substances that may have a toxic effect on the human body. Thus,
substances such as fluorocarbons, which are suspected to have an effect on the ozone layer,
cannot be regulated, because their effect is not one of toxicity. They may, however,
indirectly cause an increase in the incidence of skin cancer. The definition of "toxic
substance" in the Bill includes any substance that may directly or indirectly adversely affect
the environment. Thus, a means to control environmentally harmful chemicals is afforded, if
needed, and separate legislation for this purpose is avoided.
Clauses 11 to 18 provide for the establishment of a Toxic Substances Board to advise me
and the Director-General of Health on various matters relating to the regulation of toxic
substances. The board consists of nominees of the Ministers in charge of the Government
departments involved with chemicals, as well as nominees of the Consumer Council, the
Medical Association, the Manufacturers Federation, the Federation of Labour, and the Fire
Service Commission. It is hoped that the establishment of the board will alleviate suspicion
that the regulation of toxic substances is a bureaucratic affair that fails to take into account
the broader considerations of the community at large.
Clauses 19 to 31 deal with the sale, packing, and custody of poisons and, other than in


## p. 4134 (#614) ###########################################

4134
4 October
Toxic Substances Bill
"
matters of detail, are substantially the same as the provisions in the Poisons Act except for
clause 29 dealing with storage. This clause clearly spells out the storage requirements for
poisons and harmful substances and is in response to wide criticism that the equivalent
provisions of the Poisons Act are vague and subject to wide variation in interpretation.
Clause 32 gives the director of the division of public health power to require certain
information from importers, manufacturers, packers, and preparers of toxic substances. The
Department of Health proposes to use the information obtained to form a registry, which it
is hoped will contain details of all the toxic substances used in New Zealand. Although there
is a similar provision in the Poisons Act, it has been shown to be full of legal loopholes and
manifestly inadequate for the purposes of compiling such a comprehensive registry. This
registry should prove invaluable in providing information for emergency use and for
ascertaining whether substances falling under suspicion overseas are used here. Clauses 35 to
40 cover the licensing of sellers and packers of poisons, and, while representing an
improvement over present legislation, are substantially similar.
Clauses 41 to 46 provide for an improved control over the importation of toxic
substances. The legislation in this area has been quite inadequate in the past; witness the
Parnell fiasco of some years ago. Clause 44 requires the master of a vessel with a leaking
toxic substance aboard to notify the medical officer of health as soon as practicable. The
leaking containers may not be landed without the permission of the medical officer of health,
and then only subject to such conditions as he may impose. Had these provisions obtained in
1973 the Parnell incident might not have occurred. Clause 43 is also new and provides that
every person intending to import certain toxic substances must, before importation, give
notice to the local medical officer of health in whose district the toxic substance is to be
landed. The toxic substances to be covered will be specified by regulation.
Clause 46 provides for a heavy fine for any person who attempts to import a toxic
substance under a false description. In the past this fine has been less than the extra cost for
the transport of dangerous goods. Clauses 53 to 57 provide new provisions governing the
taking of samples of toxic substances, the analysis of such samples, and the presentation of
evidence of analysis. Clause 57 provides power for the Collector of Customs to detain
imported consignments of suspected toxic substances until an analysis of samples is
complete. Clauses 58 to 78, although containing numerous modifications, are similar in
substance to the provisions of the Poisons Act 1960, although clauses 68 to 71 relating to
appeals are quite new.
The regulation-making power of the Bill is broader than that of the Poisons Act. In
particular, there is more power to make regulations governing the transport of toxic
substances an area where the present law is quite inadequate. A further power is given to
make regulations governing the testing of tobacco products and prescribing the maximum
amount of specified toxic substances that may be present in tobacco products. Tobacco
products are included in the definition of “toxic substances", and, therefore, it follows that,
as with other toxic substances, the Bill provides power to make regulations governing their
labelling and advertising, should such be considered necessary at any time. It is proposed
that the Bill, together with the Restricted Drugs Bill and the Pesticides Bill, be referred to a
select committee.

RESTRICTED DRUGS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the Restricted Drugs Amendment
Bill be introduced. This is a companion measure to the Toxic Substances Bill, which makes
provision for the control over the distribution, labelling, and advertising of non-medical
poisons and, accordingly, removes those poisons from the ambit of the Poisons Act. The
residue of the Poisons Act will then apply only to medicinal substances. With the enactment
of the Toxic Substances Bill the provisions of the Poisons Act 1960 will continue to apply,
but only with regard to medicinal substances. To avoid confusion, the amendment renames
the Poisons Act as the Restricted Drugs Act, and consequential amendments are made
through the Bill to apply such of its provisions as are still required to medicinal substances
previously covered by the Poisons Act. These substances are renamed restricted drugs; that
term to include prescription drugs. The Poisons Committee is also consequentially renamed


## p. 4137 (#617) ###########################################

4 October
4137
Restricted Drugs Amendment Bill
the Restricted Drugs Committee.
The general provisions of the present legislation remain unaltered. Clause 2 changes the
title of the principal Act from the Poisons Act 1960 to the Restricted Drugs Act 1960, with
consequential amendment to amending Acts. Appropriate definitions in section 2 of the
principal Act are amended by clause 3 of the Bill. The term "poison" is replaced by the
terms "restricted drug" and "prescription drug". The designation of the Registrar of Poisons
is changed from the Director, Division of Public Health, to the Director, Division of Clinical
Services, as the latter division is the one responsible for the administration of the laws
relating to medicinal substances.
Clause 4 is a re-enactment of section 4 of the Poisons Act and enables the Governor-
General, by Order in Council, to declare any substance to be a restricted drug or a
prescription drug, as he did formerly for poisons and prescription poisons. Clause 5, in
effect, substitutes the name "Restricted Drugs Committee" for "Poisons Committee”. The
membership of the committee and its terms of reference remain unchanged. The final clause,
6, provides for consequential amendments throughout the Bill, thereby removing all
references to toxic substances, poisons, etc., and substituting the terms "restricted drug❞ and
"prescription drug" where appropriate. As the Bill is complementary to the Toxic
Substances Bill it is proposed that it will also be referred to the Social Services Committee
for consideration.

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The principal Act to be amended is the Poisons

where every consequential amendment will lie. I just cannot do that.

PESTICIDES BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Pesticides Bill be
introduced. The first piece of legislation passed in the country to govern the sale of chemicals
for use against plant diseases and pests, and of chemicals for use as weed killers, was the
Fungicides and Insecticides Act 1927. About 32 years later, in 1959, the Act was repealed
and replaced by the Agricultural Chemicals Act so as to bring the law up to date to cater for
the changes that had taken place in the intervening years. Now, almost two decades later, it
is again necessary to revise and consolidate the law by repealing the Agricultural Chemicals
Act and replacing it with a measure to be called the Pesticides Act.
The proposed new Act, as the title of the Bill indicates, will make better provisions for
the regulation and control of the manufacture, sale, and use of pesticides. Under the new
Act the control will extend to include public health and domestic pesticides and any bacteria
declared from time to time as subject to control. The new measure will also require
pesticides sold for industrial and public health use to be registered, and will establish a new
class of pesticides to be known as "controlled chemicals". Pesticides of this class can be used
only by qualified persons. This is at present provided by the Agricultural Chemicals
(Vertebrate Pest Control) Regulations.
Some of the other changes in the Bill are, first, that the membership of the new
Pesticides Board will be the same as that of the present Agricultural Chemicals Board, but
will be strengthened by the addition of a nominee of the Minister for the Environment.
Although the Agricultural Chemicals Board has paid due attention to the environmental
effects of the use of chemicals, the use of pesticides requirement is now specifically stated in
the Bill.
20-Vol 421


## p. 4138 (#618) ###########################################

4138
4 October
Pesticides Bill
Secondly, the registration for restricted use is a new concept to enable pesticides that
may be highly toxic, have severe environmental effects, or have other peculiarities, to be
registered and subject to special terms and conditions, including the type of application.
Thirdly, the introduction of experimental use permits is a form of registration that will have
limitations similar to provisional registration under the present law. Fourthly, with regard to
the review of registration, the board will be empowered to require the proprietor to appear
before it. Fifthly, label directions for agricultural chemicals are, with a few exceptions, not
mandatory. However, the board will now have the mandatory power to direct the use or
application of pesticides. Sixthly, the Act will provide that a person using a controlled
pesticide must have a licence, and will prescribe the requirements to govern licensing and to
regulate procedures. At present, controlled chemicals, including 1080, cyanide, and arsenic,
are controlled by the Agricultural Chemicals (Vertebrate Pest Control) Regulations 1977.
The Bill also has provisions to cover the procurement and analysis of samples, and sets
out procedures relating to evidence of analysis. It also provides for hearing of appeals by the
Administration Division of the Supreme Court on points of law, or on whether the board
acted unreasonably on reaching a decision. The Bill provides for an increased penalty of
$2,000, quadrupling the present maximum fine of $500. The maximum term of imprisonment
is to remain unchanged at 3 months. The rationale behind the increased monetary penalty is
that, when the motivation for the commission of an offence is economic, a heavier fine could
be imposed rather than a long term of imprisonment.
Finally, I point out that the proposed provisions of this new measure have been arrived
at after consultation with the principal users and manufacturers of pesticides, who generally
agree with the proposals. I intend to move that the Bill be referred to the Social Services
Committee for recess study in conjunction with the Toxic Substances Bill.

Primary Products Marketing Regulations Confirmation Bill
PRIMARY PRODUCTS MARKETING REGULATIONS CONFIRMATION BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Primary Products
Marketing Regulations Confirmation Bill be introduced. This is an annual washing-up Bill to
validate and confirm regulations made this year under the Primary Products Marketing Act
1953. Sections 3 and 4 of that Act provide that all its regulations shall be laid before
Parliament and shall expire on the last day of the session in which they were laid except so far
as they are expressly validated or confirmed by Act of Parliament passed during that session.
The regulations specified in the schedule are confirmed by the Bill, as are the amendments to
the Honey Marketing Authority Regulations affected by section 14 of the Hive Levy Bill,
which has recently been passed. In addition, the opportunity is being taken in clause 3 to
repeal the previous year's confirmation Acts. This repeal, however, does not affect the
validity of any regulation validated or confirmed by them. It is now the practice to repeal the
previous year's confirmation Acts when the annual confirmation Act is passed.
The Egg Marketing Production Entitlement Regulations 1970, Amendment No. 3, are
included, and allow entitlement licences previously issued as non-transferable for small
flocks of 101 to 1000 laying birds to be transferred if the farm to which the licence relates is
also sold or leased as a going concern. Regulation 5 authorises the Egg Marketing Authority
to be the sole buyer of entitlement licences sold off-farm for a period of 2 years from 28 July
1978.
The Honey Marketing Authority Regulations 1975, Amendment No. 1, which were
promulgated on 3 July, made minor amendments to the rules for the election of Honey
Marketing Authority members and extend from 7 to 9 days the time within which voting
papers must be posted after nominations close. They also extend the closing date of the
poll-technical amendments to suit the convenience of the returning officer.
Under the Egg Marketing Authority Regulations 1953, Amendment No. 15, the
authority's balance date is on 30 June each year. To simplify accounting the amendment
extends by 1 month from 31 May to 30 June the terms of office of all authority members. In
addition, the month for annual election of the authority chairman is altered from June to
July. This brings the election month into line with that of the Poultry Board, and will simplify
election procedures, as one person nominally holds both chairmanships.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Opposition finds no difficulty in supporting the
Bill, because, as the Minister said, it is primarily a validating and confirmation Bill of
regulations set under the Primary Products Marketing Act 1953. Accordingly, the
Opposition supports the Bill.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

savings stock is an important part of the measures to finance the fiscal deficit, but it is by no

5. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Local Government: Has he seen the
article in the Hawke's Bay Herald-Tribune of 26 May 1978 in which the Mayor of Hastings,

Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): It is incorrect and misleading to

been prepared in accordance with the law. This does not mean that the present commission
may not vary the weightings attached to each factor when bringing down the final scheme.

Motor Fuel Production from Lignite Coal
16. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Does he support the
statement of Mr A. D. Smith, fuel technologist, that “it would take between four million and
five million tonnes of lignite coal to produce New Zealand's annual gasoline needs if this
resource was to be converted to motor fuel", and, if so, what is the economic feasibility of
such a project for New Zealand?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): Annual gasoline requirements in New Zealand
amount to 1700 000 tonnes. Based on information available, this would require
approximately 9 500 000 tonnes of lignite to produce. Current costs and operating efficiency
mean that such a project is not economically feasible in New Zealand at the present time.
Work is currently being done overseas to improve the efficiency of the process, and I expect
that in New Zealand the Liquid Fuels Trust Board will investigate the viability of producing
synthetic gasoline from coal as part of its programme.
Hon. F. Colman: Has the Southland lignite coal been subjected to any special research,
either in New Zealand or overseas, to test its suitability for the manufacture of liquid fuel?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I understand not, but my recollection from reading the liquid fuels
report produced earlier this year by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research is
that the department considered it was a type of coal that was not particularly suitable; but, of
course, technology improves, and it could well be that technology will resolve this problem.

Electoral Roll Registration Cards
23. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Justice: Are the application cards
for electoral registration, which apparently constitute the electoral roll, all centralised in
Wellington, and, if so, what method will be used to check special votes against the roll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The application cards for all electorates
are held in Lower Hutt. At this stage it is intended that special votes will be checked against
the roll in the following manner. First, special votes cast outside a voter's electoral district
will be sent to the appropriate returning officer, who will check the name of each special
voter against his main and supplementary rolls, and, if that name is found, the vote will be
allowed by the returning officer. Secondly, when a special voter is not found on the main or
supplementary rolls, the returning officer will send the declaration accompanying the special
vote to the electorate officer, who will be holding the application cards of those entitled to
apply for registration after writ day. When the voter's card is held, the electorate officer will
return the declaration to the returning officer endorsed with the word “qualified". The
returning officer will then allow such a vote. Thirdly, if neither of these procedures enables
the vote to be treated as valid, he will forward the declaration to the Chief Electoral Officer,
who will check to see whether an application has been received from the special voter. In
addition, he will check the 1975 roll to see whether the special voter was on that roll.

Voting Eligibility-Expatriate New Zealanders
26. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to


## p. 4146 (#626) ###########################################

the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the headline “Rowling chases Sydney-siders' election
votes" in the Dominion of 22 September, and can he indicate what procedures will be
adopted to check the voting eligibility of these expatriate New Zealanders?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have seen the headline referred to.
The same procedures will be adopted this election as in the past. The law provides, in effect,
that a New Zealand elector who has been absent from the country for more than 3 years is
not qualified to vote. The special voting declaration issued to those voting overseas requires
such voters, other than servicemen or public servants, to declare that they have not been
absent from New Zealand for more than 3 years. These declarations will be forwarded to the
Chief Electoral Officer, who is obliged to ascertain whether a person named in such a
declaration is a registered elector or otherwise qualified to vote under section 99 of the
Electoral Act.

general legislation can be made. That is why the amendments to the Bill have come to the

they are relatively minor. The main change repeals section 102 of the principal Act, which
prescribes the maximum charges. That provision has now become obsolete because of
inflation. The board is now getting near the point at which it would go over the maximum it
is allowed to charge. The opportunity has been taken at the same time to review the whole
Act, and to bring in several other machinery clauses. When the time comes to review the
general legislation it may well be that the Local Bills Committee might look seriously at
including the Auckland Electric Power Board in it.

STATUTES AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Statutes Amendment Bill. The committee has carefully
considered the Bill, with the exception of clauses 77 to 79 and 88 to 90 inclusive, and
recommends that it proceed without amendment. I move, That the report do lie upon the
table. Opposition members have expressed reservation about two matters, even though the
proposed clauses had previously been cleared by Ministers after consultation with the
Opposition spokesmen.
Mr Malcolm: Who were those Opposition members?
Mr McLAY: The member for Auckland Central and the member for New Lynn. In
addition, three further amendments for inclusion on the Supplementary Order Paper have
been considered and approved by the select committee. The committee also has a series of
amendments, all of a similar nature, to recommend in respect of the Bill.
I shall deal first with those matters about which Opposition members have expressed
reservations. Clause 20 substitutes for the existing section 27 of the Electric Power Boards
Act 1925 a new section enabling payment to the deputy chairman of an electric power board
of an annual allowance not exceeding 10 percent of that of the chairman. Opposition
members claimed that similar remuneration is not paid to the deputy chairmen of hospital,
harbour, or catchment boards. The matter has therefore been referred to the Minister of
Energy for discussion with the Opposition spokesmen on these matters.
Clauses 83 to 112 amend the private and trustee savings banks Acts. In each case the
principlal Act provides that every savings bank shall at all times hold certain proportions of
their deposits in liquid form, such deposits to be available for payment to depositors. The
amendments would enable the savings banks to use those funds for payment to depositors by
permitting them to hold less than the specified proportions for such a period and subject to
such terms and conditions as may be specified by the Minister of Finance. Although Reserve
Bank officials were present and assured committee members that the amendments were in
accordance with sound trustee savings bank and private savings bank practice, some
Opposition members took the view that a policy change such as this should not be included
in the Statutes Amendment Bill. Even though the matter had previously been agreed to by
the Opposition spokesmen, the Minister of Finance has been asked to clarify the matter
further with the Labour Opposition.
In addition to the provisions contained in the Bill the committee considered three
further statutory amendments, which will be included in a Supplementary Order Paper. The
first is an amendment to the Immigration Act 1964, which empowers the Governor-General
to prescribe various forms under the Act by Order in Council. A problem has arisen with the
form of the entry permit used by successive Governments since 1962. That form is now being
challenged in the courts. The amendment will not affect those court proceedings. All
members of the committee accepted the need for this change, and commend it to the House
for consideration during the Committee stage.
The second proposed amendment inserts a new section 640A in the Local Government
Act 1974, which would repeal section 62(6) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1977.
This amendment has been widely requested by various district law societies and town
planners, and will rectify a serious problem that has arisen in the Town and Country
Planning Act. The third additional amendment to the Tourist Hotel Corporation Act 1974
empowers that corporation to establish and conduct hotels in Western Samoa. At present
the corporation's activities are limited to New Zealand and the Cook Islands.
The Bill contains several proposed amendments to the Bush Workers, Construction,
Factories, Machinery, and Shops and Offices Acts to extend the power of inspectors to make
inspections, examinations, and to conduct tests. While the committee saw the need for these
provisions, all of which are related to worker conditions and safety, it was concerned that the
right to inspect appeared to be an absolute one, and that the reasonableness of the
inspector's decision could not subsequently be questioned in a court of law. The committee
therefore proposed a minor amendment to all the provisions, the effect of which is to
introduce an objective rather than a subjective test of the necessity to conduct these
investigations. These changes have been agreed to by the Department of Labour, and will be
incorporated into a Supplementary Order Paper to be considered during the Committee
stage.

Statutes Amendment Bill
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I wish to comment on a few of the matters
contained in the Bill, which is noncontroversial, but which has technicalities that need the
approval of the whole House. I know there will be a great deal of interest in the amendment
being considered. As a result of a present court case it is possible that the regulation by
which entry permits into New Zealand are issued is ultra vires. In other words, all permits
granted are not legally valid. The Opposition is reluctant to pass retrospective measures such
as this.
Mr McLay: It is not retrospective.
Mr PREBBLE: Inasmuch as it will validate all permits it must be retrospective. The
Opposition has agreed to the measure because it would be undesirable for thousands of
people in this country who believe they have proper residential permits to suddenly discover
overnight, as it were, that because of a court case their permits were not valid. I wonder
whether the Statutes Amendment Bill is the right one for this provision, or whether there
should be a special Bill. However, the Opposition has agreed to the legislation because of its
urgency.
The committee members are holding further discussion on a couple of matters
mentioned by the chairman. The first is the suggestion that trustee savings banks should no
longer have to hold a fixed amount of liquid assets at 3 percent. I believe that the banking
laws should not be changed in a Bill such as this. Parliament, having set up the banks and
having given them special legislation, should ensure that public confidence in the banking
system remains. We should not undermine that confidence in any way, and we should not do
it on the eve of an election, when there might be a suggestion that the Government was
trying to artifically hold the bank ratios so that it could pump in a little extra cash on the eve
of an election at the expense of good banking practices. I want some further assurance that
that is not the reason for the Bill.
The question of an allowance for deputy chairmen of power boards was also raised. It
seems interesting to me that this is another case of a power board wanting legislation. In this
case, power boards are asking for something that other boards do not have. In the committee
we asked whether other local ad hoc bodies have the same right to give their deputy
chairmen a payment. It appears that quite a number of them do not. It seems to me that if we
are going to make a change, and it may well be desirable that deputy chairmen get an
allowance, there is a case for deputy chairmen to get a special payment. But, from my own
experience on a local authority, I believe it applies to all local authorities--catchment
boards, hospital boards, and so on. It seems wrong that we should make a policy change in
the Bill for power boards only. I feel that we should make it for all local authorities, and that
is one reason for the reservations held by the Opposition, which I still think are valid.
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): I want to refer to the way in which the chairman presented his
report to the House. He tried to chastise certain members of the Opposition for opposing
certain clauses in the Bill. I want to draw to the attention of the House the fact that this Bill
of 133 clauses was introduced yesterday afternoon. There were a few copies printed at the
time, but if members look in their Bill book they will find that they do not have a copy. That
shows the stress and the strain the committee was under because of the unnecessary haste
from the Government and from the chairman. I protest at that. Members will be aware that
the Bill is considered generally to be a washing-up Bill; and members of the committee
agreed with most of the clauses in the Bill. In past years, when I was on the Statutes Revision
Committee, 2 weeks at least were allowed for consideration of a Bill. First, there is the
preliminary canter through the Bill to find the clauses with which the members agree. It is
then established whether there are any further questions, and time is provided to get
information. The Opposition is not convinced that the Government has given answers as to
why the matters relating to the private savings bank and the trustee savings bank should go
forward in a washing-up Bill. They should not go forward in a washing-up Bill. These are
matters of policy that the Opposition believes should have more general legislation. The
committee is thoroughly entitled to do what it has done, and so are the members of the
committee in protesting about those clauses. I therefore speak in support of those members
of the committee, and ask the chairman, if he is to continue in that job at any other time, to
give consideration to the fact that members have a responsibility to see that the clauses that
go through in a Bill are mainly machinery ones. To ensure that members rights are pro-
tected, reports should be furnished on any matters with which they disagree. The Bill has
been processed too hastily, and the chairman has tried to chastise members of the
Opposition for their lack of co-operation. I have been forced to speak in this way because I
believe that Opposition members have given a lot of co-operation to the committee.

amendments.

## p. 4170 (#650) ###########################################

4170

Trustee Companies Management Amendment Bill
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill amends the Trustee Companies Management Act of 1975. When
replying during the second reading of that Act, my predecessor in office, the member for
Henderson, said that it was a holding and emergency piece of legislation, and that further
provisions might be needed. The amendments proposed for passage tonight arise directly
from the 1975 legislation, passed with the full co-operation of both parties to preserve the
Perpetual Trustees, Estate and Agency Co. of New Zealand Ltd. from the financial
difficulties into which it, as a trustee company, had fallen. The preservation of the company,
and more importantly of its business as a trustee, agent, and attorney, will prove impossible
without the amendments now proposed.
The amendments are required so that the company, despite the court proceedings
already commenced or for any other reason, can survive over the next few months. With the
dissolution of Parliament shortly and the probability that the new Parliament will not sit for
some months, there is a considerable risk that Perpetual Trustees will require help during
that time. To reassure all persons dealing with Perpetual Trustees, and all of its staff, let me
say from the outset that the trustee and other businesses of Perpetual Trustees must continue
to operate, and this Bill will see that this aim is realised. The prospect that a trustee company
could not continue in business is untenable. That prospect was temporarily averted by the
1975 Act. Lengthy discussions were held with the Chairman of the statutory board, Mr S. J.
R. Chatten, and the board's professional advisers before the Government decided that these
amendments should be introduced.
During the 3 years of the statutory board's operations it has extensively cured much of
the liquidity and cash flow problems of Perpetual Trustees. I can thus repeat what the
member for Henderson said in 1975, and assure everyone that funds held by the company, as
distinct from its own funds, are safe and, since the statutory board gained full control of all
Perpetual Trustees' businesses, that the funds are as well administered as any trustee funds
in any other trustee company. Pursuant to its responsibilities, the statutory board has
conducted an investigation into alleged breaches of trust that led to the 1975 Act, and as a
result commenced breach of trust proceedings. If the court holds that there were breaches of
trust, the liability of the company will most likely be more than the net worth of the company
together with the reserve liability of $10 a share.
The 1975 Act does not provide adequately for the consequences of the possible
insolvency of the company. The proceedings may be heard during the next few months, and
could cause unjustifiable concern about the administration of the company but justifiable
concern about the company's future. The Bill therefore provides for the continuation of the
trustee business without in any way prejudging those proceedings or interfering with the
rights of the parties to those proceedings. The Bill provides for the transfer of the liabilities
of the present company, including the existing proceedings, to a new company and for the
transfer of existing shareholdings of Perpetual Trustees' shareholders to the new company,
which will become the sole shareholder in Perpetual Trustees. Only when necessary to do so
can the new company sell to a new owner the shares that it holds in the old company. The
proceeds of the sale will then be applied by the new company for the benefit of the old
shareholders and those entitled as former creditors of the old company.
The Bill amends section 18 of the Act to empower the court to limit the amount
recoverable under breach of trust proceedings to the net worth of the company, including an
amount equivalent to the reserve liability on its shares. In view of the great good will there is
for this company, this amendment will enable the company to be taken over with its liability
quantified should it be held to have been in breach of trust. The application of the 1971
amendment to Perpetual Trustees' own Act, restricting the voting rights of any person
holding more than 2 percent of its shares, is modified in relation to any takeover made
pursuant to the Companies Amendment Act 1963 where the offeror has the consent of the
statutory board to make its bid. Therefore it will be possible for a substantial New Zealand -
based concern to make a takeover for Perpetual Trustees, and as a result settle the court
proceedings with no further loss to its existing shareholders in the reasonable expectation
that its own costs and expenses would be limited to the amount of the settlement approved
by the court.
In conjunction with the 1975 Act the Government, because of the probable invalidity of
the security then held by the National Bank of New Zealand, made arrangements for an
advance by the Bank of New Zealand. I am satisifed that it was the Government's intention


## p. 4171 (#651) ###########################################

4 October
4171
Trustee Companies Management Amendment Bill
that this should be an advance equivalent to that made to a liquidator during a liquidation,
and that it should have the priority usually accorded such an advance. However, in the event
of a liquidation of the company, the Bank of New Zealand would rank as an unsecured
creditor. If the courts should hold that a large sum of money is owing for breaches of trust,
then under the terms of distribution specified in section 18 of the principal Act much of the
bank's money could end up in the hands of a charity, and the bank would call upon the
Government to meet its guarantee. As the moneys were advanced to support both the
company and its beneficiaries, it is quite illogical and unjust that that support action should
produce this result. A sum in excess of $5 million could be involved.
None the less, the Government was concerned not to be seen to be assuring its own
position at the expense of any persons, and for that reason an opinion was sought from the
President of the New Zealand Law Society, Mr L. H. Southwick, Q. C. A copy of Mr
Southwick's opinion was made available today to the Leader of the Opposition, and for the
record I quote part of it: "In my view it would be 'right' for the Government to alter the
position of the Bank of New Zealand loan vis-à-vis any beneficiary or charities whose
entitlement arises out of any breach of trust where that entitlement had not been established
in terms of section 18 of the Trustee Companies Management Act 1975 at the date of the
Bank of New Zealand advance."
After the statutory board took office and reorganised the company's affairs, it was able
to investigate the Nuhaka farm forestry scheme, which it had been informed, quite correctly,
was a viable and sensible farm forestry development. It was discovered that the minimum
subscription provided for in clause 5 of the deed controlling the scheme had not been met by
the date set out. Little excuse for this breach of trust can be mustered. The scheme itself is so
economically sound that the units have continued to trade at a reasonable price on the stock
exchange, even though the statutory board has publicly announced the difficulties involved
with continuing the scheme. To bring such an action for breach of trust seems a most
unprofitable way of solving the problem. As the main breach of trust action could strip the
company of all of its assets and any reserves, any further action for breach of trust will likely
be an expense not recoverable by the beneficiaries involved.
The statutory board has asked, and the Government has agreed, that the Act shall
provide that the failure to reach the minimum sum set out in the trust deed shall not void or
invalidate the scheme. The Government does not believe that this will create a precedent for
any such future case, because the situation I have presented for such an interference is
peculiar to Perpetual Trustees and the Act under which it was placed in 1975. As a result of
the Trustee Amendment Act 1976 the trustees have been able to sell less profitable parts of
the scheme and produce a fund that should enable the scheme to develop the full potential
possible on the lower initial capital structure. I commend the Bill to the House.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I want to make it clear at the
outset that the Opposition does not contest the facts or the developments as outlined by the
Minister of Justice. There could well be some divergence of opinion on what caused the
initial trouble and the way in which some elements of the problem have been handled since,
but the Opposition wants this legislation to go through the House in reasonable time after
adequate discussion so that the people concerned will know what is involved. I think this is
an occasion on which justice needs to be seen to be done, because there are quite a few
innuendoes that, if wrongly developed, could lead to a very mistaken impression of the
Government's or the previous Government's reasons for action.
In 1975 the Labour Government felt that it was necessary to support the continued
existence of the trustee company. As the Minister of Justice has indicated, that is also the
opinion of the present Government. Therefore, it becomes a matter of deciding how best to
achieve that objective. Owing to a court decision, one of the decisions taken in 1975 now
needs some support. I think that is the best way of describing it, because I do not think there
was any doubt that in the earlier Bill both sides of the House were concerned to make sure
that the company was able to continue, and that the Government stood behind the company
to the extent that the support was needed, but not that a winding up should benefit people
entirely outside the company-and, as the Minister has indicated, that could happen. In this

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): As the member said, it is a fact that the
Bill arises from the 1975 legislation, and, had all the ramifications been foreseen, the clauses
in this Bill might have been included in the 1975 Bill. Some time ago the Minister of Justice
brought this to my notice, in my capacity as Minister of Finance. Essentially, three things
need to be done. First the company must be put in order so that, as a company, it can be
transferred to other administration and ownership. There is no reason why that should not
be done, because the alternative is that these various estates that are being administered
would not be able to be administered on a continuing basis and a great deal of fruitless and
costly litigation would arise, which would benefit no one. There is no difficulty about that.
The Nuhaka forestry matter was another matter where there was a neglect to take certain
steps. However, the problem can be rectified very easily and a viable venture enabled to
continue.
The third issue is whether or not the defect in the security of the Bank of New Zealand
advance should be remedied. When the position was put to me I found that, whereas I could
agree with the suggestion that we remedy the first two problems, I agonised over the
principle that we should remedy a defect in the security for an advance from the Bank of
New Zealand, which is completely owned by the State. I asked myself, "Who will suffer if we
take this action, if we give an effective security and save the bank and the taxpayer a loss?”
It was pointed out to me that essentially, at some considerable remove, it would be certain
undisclosed beneficiaries, who might in fact turn out to be various unidentifiable parties,
who would get it as a windfall. I was still not entirely happy about it, and my indecision
persisted for some considerable time while my mind turned back and forth.
Finally it was suggested that we should ask the president of the New Zealand Law
Society to look at the problem as an independent observer to see whether he felt that it
would be proper to introduce remedial legislation. We did so, and the president wrote and,
in essence, said that in his view it would be proper. As far as I was concerned, that was it. I
had obtained an independent view on a solution that clearly made sense but which, from the
Government's point of view, had to be considered very carefully in that the entity that would
benefit was the Bank of New Zealand and, in a second remove, the taxpayer; we had to be
very careful before we promoted and passed law to do that. However, with the support and
the analysis of the president of the Law Society, we have brought the legislation forward,
and I think we have done that correctly.
The only other point I want to make is that it is necessary to introduce similar Bills from
time to time, but before we introduce them we have to scrutinise them very carefully indeed,
because they cut across the normal application of the law. Whenever we consider the
introduction of a measure of this type we have to see not only who benefits but also who may
be penalised and perhaps denied their proper legal rights. We should not lightly interfere to
save individuals from the consequences of the application of the law if, at the same time, we
infringe upon the rights of some other parties to the matter. Fortunately in this case no such
problem arises. Therefore, we have been able to bring forward the Bill without undue
concern. However, that question does arise in some matters involving the collapse of
complex financial institutions and organisations, and we have to be careful before promoting
special legislation to deal with the matter. That is all I want to say. I am satisfied that the Bill
is a proper one, and I support it.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I rise to support the second reading of the Trustee
Companies Management Amendment Bill. In doing so I comment that I do not often find
myself in agreement not only with what the Prime Minister has said but also with the
sentiments he has expressed. I believe the sentiments he expressed about the Bill were
accurate, as were those of the two earlier Government speakers, the Deputy Prime Minister
and the Minister of Justice. I should like to begin where the Prime Minister left off.
When Bills of this type come before the House Parliament as a whole must scrutinise
them very carefully, because they cut across the established law of the country. We must


## p. 4174 (#654) ###########################################

4174
4 October
Trustee Companies Management Amendment Bill
ensure that the Bill will not mean that some individuals or some groups of people will lose a
right they would otherwise enjoy. I thank the Minister for the opportunity he gave me and
the Leader of the Opposition to be briefed about the contents of the Bill, and for the reasons
he gave for its introduction. With the assurances we have received I am confident that no one
will be adversely affected by any of the provisions in the Bill, and that many groups will in
fact receive substantial benefits as a result of its passing. However, I cannot subscribe to the
statement made by the Minister that it is inconceivable to allow a trust company to become
insolvent. Although that is not an agreeable occurrence, and it is one no one likes to see
happen, I should not like the trustee companies to think that, because we are salvaging
Perpetual Trustees, we as a Parliament are establishing a principle and are acting as
guarantors for trust companies. We are not; they have a strict responsibility placed upon
them, and we are undertaking a salvage job in this particular case because we are able to do
so without penalising any other party. I intend to go through the provisions in the Bill to
explain why we are prepared to support it.
The concept being put forward is that, if the company finds itself insolvent,
automatically a substitute company will come into existence, with a share transfer in effect
creating two entities. Existing trusts and estates would then find themselves in a company
free from liabilities, while the liabilities that could occur through breaches of trust or because
of findings in a court case would be the responsibility of a separate company. Shareholders in
that substitute company would be liable for the reserve amount, equivalent to $10 a share.
Anyone having a claim under a breach of trust would still be able to claim against the
shareholders for that reserve amount, just as though the two companies had not been
created. Therefore, no one who might have a possible claim against Perpetual Trustees
would lose anything. The important point is that if the split in the company occurred, the
trust company that continued would have a very valuable asset. As the Prime Minister hinted
in his speech, many companies would be interested in making an offer for such a company,
because it would be free of the debts of the old company while the existing assets would still
represent a considerable amount. This is an imaginative approach to a very difficult
problem, and I see no reason why such a scheme should not succeed.
A new power is to be given to the court in the new subsection (5A) to be added to
section 18 as altered by clause 11 in Part II. This provision states: "When the court is
satisfied that the amount that could be recovered under a judgment given against a company
under this section would be more than the net worth of the company, the court may at any
time (whether at the time the judgment is given or thereafter) make an order determining
that the maximum amount that can be recovered under the judgment is the amount that the
court considers is the net worth of the company as a going concern (including any unpaid
capital and any other amount liable to be contributed by the shareholders to the company in
the event of the winding up thereof)." This is a novel provision. Instead of the court making
an award for the total liability of the old company, the award may be equal to the amount the
company is actually worth.
Normally, in making an award against a company, the court takes into consideration the
total amount of the damages, and not whether a person can pay them. In civil cases, the
court does not take into consideration the fact that its award will make you bankrupt, but
only the true amount you owe. The fact that you cannot pay it is your own problem. I have
some doubts about passing such provisions, because I should not like it to be considered that
Parliament was trying to influence or direct the court. I am making it quite clear that
Parliament is not saying that a court must do that, but only that it may do so. We should give
the court this power because, on analysis, no one would be adversely affected if the court
decided to make such a ruling. Those claiming would not be able to collect more than the net
worth of the company anyway. Under that court case they could not claim anywhere else,
and we are not taking away any other rights they might have had against, say, the auditors of
the company, or some such party. If a court decided to take advantage of this power it would
not adversely affect any other party. That is the only reason the Opposition is prepared to
accept that clause. I am satisfied that no one would be adversely affected if such an order
were made. I am also satisfied that while this may be taken by the court to be a large hint as
to what it may do, it is not a direction from Parliament. Should some other factors arise of
which we are not aware the court does not have to do what we suggest. We cannot be said to
be interfering in the court case. I hope that the court will regard this provision as an attempt
by Parliament to assist the court to reach a satisfactory conclusion.
I should now like to turn to the provision dealing with the loan by the Bank of New

Hon. W. L. YOUNG: The Christchurch-Lyttelton road tunnel was authorised to be
constructed by a special Act called the Christchurch-Lyttelton Road Tunnel Act passed in
1956. The Act established an authority to construct and maintain the tunnel, and also


## p. 4179 (#659) ###########################################

4 October
Christchurch-Lyttelton Road Tunnel Authority Dissolution Bill
4179
provided for the raising of loans for construction purposes, and the levying of tolls on
vehicles and goods passing through the tunnel to recoup costs. The tunnel was constructed
and first opened to traffic in 1964. In spite of raising tolls, as at 1 April this year the revenue
received by the authority is estimated to be sufficient to meet only operating costs, with a
small margin to spare. The scope for significantly increasing traffic and increasing tolls
appears limited, and it is expected that within a year or two the authority will find it difficult
to meet operating costs without more assistance from the taxpayer. In the meantime, loans
that were financed at about 5 percent are becoming due, and their refinancing could be at
double that rate, thus adding to the authority's difficulties in meeting its outgoings.
From 1 April 1967, the National Roads Board has paid the tunnel authority $200,000
per annum. This was to have been for a period of 4 years to enable tolls on goods traffic to be
reduced, thus promoting the use of improved port access facilities. Contributions have
continued each year since 1967 to help the authority. In 1969, the National Roads Board
declared the road from Christchurch to Lyttelton to be a State highway, and has met full
costs of construction and maintenance, apart from the tunnel. This was part of the board's
policy to accept increased responsibility for access to our major ports. Salaries and wages
represent about two-thirds of the operating costs of the authority, and the abolition of tolls
will enable a substantial reduction in operating costs to be made. The principal costs of
operating the tunnel would then be confined to maintenance and periodic cleaning, with a
consequent large reduction in costs. The National Roads Board has agreed to meet these
costs on the tunnel becoming toll free.
Capital liabilities of the tunnel authority amount to $4.77 million, and, of this, $967,000
is due for repayment in the 1980-81 financial year. The Government has agreed to take over
these liabilities. If the Government did not do so, the authority would be faced with annual
loan repayments and interest of the order of $300,000 to $350,000 until the year 2010-2011.
The Bill represents substantial assistance from the Government and the National Roads
Board to the people of Christchurch and surrounding districts.
Discussions are taking place for redundant workers to be absorbed into the staffs of
adjacent local authorities, for electrical, mechanical, and ventilating services to be provided
on agreed terms with the Lyttelton Harbour Board, and breakdown services to be provided
by the Automobile Association. Progress is being made and I am hopeful of satisfactory
agreements being reached.

who spoke in the same vein for about the same time, exactly why we are able to abolish the

The amount of $4 million to $5 million is very small compared with total Government
indebtedness. That meant that instead of increasing the toll charges, which would have been

said it was prepared to do a bit more, the harbour board said it was prepared to assume
responsibility, and one or two other people said they were prepared to assist. It all arose
from a meeting organised some months ago by the member for Lyttelton to enable me to
meet representatives of local authorities in Christchurch.
Members have asked why the suggestion was turned down earlier. It was turned down
for the same reason the present Deputy Leader of the Opposition turned it down in 1975
when he was Minister of Finance—a Government departmental report stated that it would
not be appropriate and would cost a certain amount. He accepted that report when he was
Minister of Finance, as I have accepted a similar report. I was asked by the member for
Lyttelton to meet the local bodies, which one by one said they could not commit their
boards, although they would advise them to take on some additional responsibility and to
pay some money, which changed the position considerably. When I asked them formally,
some boards were not prepared to go as far as some of their representatives had been
prepared to go.
However, in the meantime I had a chat with some National Roads Board
representatives, who were more helpful. They said yes, it would be a good idea. They knew
the arithmetic of the tunnel, and they knew that if nothing was done tolls would inevitably go
up. They said yes, we could chip in with a bit more. So they had a meeting and decided that
they could. At that point all I had to do was to say that the Government would take on the
indebtedness and transfer it to the Government. It was done as simply as that, and there is
no mystery about it.
The member for Christchurch Central spent all his time asking all kinds of questions to

Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): We would not be debating the Bill if there had not been an

the Christchurch-Lyttelton Road Tunnel Authority should be dissolved when it is prepared
to take over all the liabilities of that authority? Provision has been made for toll rates for the
road tunnel to be approved by the Minister of Finance. He can either lift those toll rates as
high as he wishes or abolish them. Ample provision is made in the principal Act for the road
tunnel authority to continue in existence.
The Crown, in taking over responsibility for the road tunnel, is looking to another local
body to carry out substantial maintenance work on the tunnel-a crazy situation. Under the
principal Act the authority had responsibility to control and maintain the tunnel, for which
purpose it built up an organisation of qualified staff. Section 71 states: "Subject to the
provisions of this Act the authority is authorised and empowered to construct, maintain,
manage, and control the tunnel through the Port Hills between Christchurch and Lyttelton.'
Why is it necessary for the authority to be abolished? After all, the Minister can abolish tolls
if he wants to without abolishing the authority. We have local bodies whose liabilities and
expenses are met by the Government, and hospital boards come to mind particularly. The
tunnel authority could remain in existence. Under clause 4 we find that the Crown is taking
over the liabilities, and clause 7 authorises the Lyttelton Harbour Board to provide in
respect of the tunnel, the electrical, mechanical, and ventilation maintenance services.
An Hon. Member: It is maintenance only.
Mr T. J. YOUNG: Yes, it is maintenance only, but the tunnel authority was set up for
the purpose of carrying out that maintenance. What will happen to the staff of the authority?

unsuitable and are in no way related. If this is to be carried out we should amend the
functions of the Lyttelton Harbour Board at the same time.
I believe that the Government is looking for another body to carry the can in regard to
the liability, because clause 7 says that the Lyttelton Harbour Board may recover such
apportionment of cost and expenses as may be agreed upon between the Lyttelton Harbour
Board and the National Roads Board, but there is no assurance that in carrying out this
maintenance the Lyttelton Harbour Board will fully recover its costs. In other words, the
revenue of the harbour board could be called upon by the Government for the maintenance
of the tunnel. That is stupid, and it is stupid that we should be asked to pass such legislation.

receive a satisfactory answer I am not in favour of the Bill as it is drafted. The principle
