MISUSE OF DRUGS AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time.
A few weeks ago I introduced this legislation designed to strengthen existing law that
controls the misuse of drugs. The Bill has since been examined by the Statutes Revision
Committee, and recommendations made by the committee will, I feel sure, improve the Bill
in several aspects. I thank those organisations that made submissions to the committee, and
also the members of the committee for their contribution.
The Bill, as introduced, was divided into six parts. The House will recall that only Parts
I to V were reported back from the Statutes Revision Committee, which decided that Part
VI required further consideration. Part I will be administered by the Department of Health,
and the remainder by the Department of Justice.
Provision is made in clause 2 for the Minister of Health to provide and publish reports,.
information, and advice about the misuse of drugs and the rehabilitation and treatment of
persons suffering from the misuse of drugs. It is intended to appoint a committee under
section 5 of the Health Act to advise on these matters. The increased penalties of


## p. 4208 (#688) ###########################################

4208
4 October
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
imprisonment in Part I of the Bill recognise the argument that commercial involvement in
drug dealing is premeditated and thus appropriate for deterrent penalties, while the
increased fining ability on the part of a magistrate's court threatens the profitability of drug
dealing, and may thus act as a deterrent. The offence of conspiring to deal in controlled
drugs is removed by clause 4 from the general provisions of the Crimes Act 1961 and
included in the Misuse of Drugs Act as a specific offence carrying an increased maximum
penalty of 14 years' imprisonment for class A drugs and 10 years for offences involving class
B drugs. The maximum penalty for conspiracy provided by the Crimes Act is 7 years'
imprisonment. It is further proposed, in clause 5, that courts are to be required to consider
imposing a fine as well as a prison sentence for dealing offences involving class A or class B
controlled drugs.
Clause 9 provides for the protection of police officers from being charged with an
offence in respect of acts done in the performance of their official duty. A prosecution may
not be initiated in these circumstances without the leave of the Attorney-General. Clause 12
provides the means whereby controlled drugs detected at the point of importation by
Customs officers can be allowed to proceed to delivery for the purpose of establishing a case
against the drug importer.
Provision is made, in clause 13, for Police and Customs officers to place a tracking
device-a small transmitter or responder-in vehicles or other movable objects believed to
contain drugs. The use of this power must be followed by a report to a magistrate, who may
make recommendations to the Commissioner of Police or the Comptroller of Customs if the
circumstances warrant. On the committee's recommendation, subclause (5) of clause 13
makes clear provisions for the custody of records. The broad scheme is that the Police may
apply to a judge of the Supreme Court for a warrant if they want to intercept private
communications by means of a listening device.
The Bill seeks to impose effective safeguards for the protection of the privacy of the
individual. The Bill details, in clauses 15 and 16, the mode of application for an interception
warrant, the matters on which the judge must be satisfied, and the matters to be set out in
the warrant. On the recommendation of the committee, these have been established in set
form and attached as a schedule to the Bill. An emergency permit may be sought in cases of
urgency when there is not time to obtain a warrant. Provision is made in clause 24 for the
exclusion of evidence obtained from unlawfully intercepted communications subject to a
discretion in the court. This type of provision is regarded overseas as a necessary sanction
against the misuse of eavesdropping powers. Accordingly, if there are to be effective
safeguards against unlawful eavesdropping the legislation should not permit the use of
evidence obtained with no warrant at all or pursuant to a substantially defective warrant.
Clause 25 deals with the problem that unlawful interception may yield all kinds of
incriminating information about a suspect and his associates, quite unrelated to drug-dealing
offences. The use in court of a privileged communication intercepted by means of a listening
device is barred by clause 26. The communication is inadmissible unless privilege is waived.
Clauses 29 to 36 deal with the question of bail applications by defendants charged with a
drug-dealing offence. Clause 29 provides that no person charged with a drug-dealing offence
may be admitted to bail other than by order of a judge. Clause 30 provides that, on granting
bail, a judge may impose conditions for reporting, and he is also given new and wide powers
to impose other conditions to ensure that the defendant reports as ordered. Clause 31 allows
a member of the Police to arrest without warrant any defendant who he believes to be
absconding or who is about to abscond.
I turn now to the special provisions relating to fines. On the recommendation of the
committee a new clause 36A has been introduced. It provides that, if a court is satisfied that
any money or assets owned by the defendant at the date of his trial have been acquired by
him directly or indirectly, from the offence for which he is charged, then it may impose a
greater fine than it would have otherwise imposed. Clause 37 empowers a court, in certain
circumstances, to impose on a person convicted of a drug-dealing offence a higher fine than
it would otherwise impose having regard to the money or assets of the convicted person
which have been derived from earlier drug-dealing offences. The court may have regard to
earlier drug-dealing offences whether or not the offender has been charged with or convicted
of those offences, but may not have regard to any offences of which the offender has been
acquitted. In seeking the imposition of such a fine the Crown must give the defence 5 days'
notice of its intention to do so, and must satisfy the court that the assets in question were


## p. 4209 (#689) ###########################################

4 October
4209
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
derived from earlier drug dealing. The offender's inability to satisfactorily explain the source
of any money or assets owned by him may be accepted as evidence that the money or assets
were derived from such offending.
Clause 37(1) has been completely rewritten in an attempt to meet criticisms made in the
submissions. The major change is that the Crown must now satisfy the court beyond a
reasonable doubt—that is, to the criminal standard of proof-that the offender has
committed drug-dealing offences other than the offences for which he is before the court. It
is only in establishing that assets were derived from earlier offences that proof of the balance
of probabilities will suffice.
By clause 45 a judge sentencing a drug dealer to 10 years' imprisonment or more will be
able to order that the offender shall not be eligible to have his case considered by the Parole
Board for period not exceeding 7 years. The current law provides that any offender
sentenced to imprisonment for 5 years or more is eligible to have his case considered by the
board after he has served one-half of his sentence, or 34 years, whichever occurs first.
Consequent upon the provision of life imprisonment for certain drug offences, clause 48
provides that such offenders shall have their cases considered by the Prisons Parole Board
after they have served 7 years. This places them on the same footing as those undergoing
preventive detention or imprisonment for life following a conviction for murder. The clause
also makes it clear that the existing power of individual Parole Board members to take
individual cases before the board and to make recommendations to the Minister is retained,
notwithstanding a court order. This power is a safeguard for use in exceptional
circumstances.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): Drug trafficking is a scourge on society, and
in the modern world is a major cause of social, and, in some cases, political corruption.
Drugs lead to great social distress and to economic loss to individuals and their families and
dependants, and can affect economic performance and undermine law and order. Drugs are
a major threat to society, and need the urgent and continuing attention of the Government.
The Labour Government inherited a fast deteriorating drug scene. Reported drug
offences increased from 10 in 1963 to more than 1500 in 1974-a one hundred and fifty-fold
increase. By 1975 the number of reported cases had reached 2000, and is higher now. As
Minister of Police and Customs I took immediate action to increase the resources committed
to the war against drugs by significantly increasing manpower in both the Police and the
preventive service of the Customs Department. Dogs trained to detect drugs by smell were
introduced, and steps were taken to improve equipment and technology used in the fight
against drug traffickers. I directed the Comptroller of Customs to examine anti-drug
techniques abroad and to report back to the Government.
So serious a view did the Labour Government take of the escalation in drug trafficking
that, in 1975, it introduced the Listening Devices Bill, which included provision for the
Police, under proper safeguards, to use listening devices in the war against drugs. Because
this was a far-reaching initiative, the Bill was referred to a select committee for recess study
and for the taking of evidence from the public. Before the legislation could become effective,
the present Government came into office, and, unfortunately, it failed to act immediately
and decisively on this aspect of the drug problem.
Had the present Government proceeded with the Labour Government's Bill it would
have had the support of the Opposition, and the legislation could have been passed in 1976;
and the Police could have had the advantage of that legislation and of acting under its terms
in the war against drugs. Instead, the Government allowed the Bill to lapse-at a time when
drug offences were increasing—and thus denied the Police the benefit of the technology for
which the Labour Government had provided. Further, in allowing that Bill to lapse, the
Government put nothing immediately in its place and, as a consequence, only now, in the
dying stages of this Parliament, has it introduced legislation of its own.
Labour's legislation struck a balance between the measures necessary to tackle drug
trafficking effectively and the rights of people in a free society, with a measure that
represented a significant advance in technique for the Police and was acceptable to them, but
which stopped short of telephone tapping. Many people are concerned about the proposal in
the Bill to tap telephones. It recalls to them the great public controversy over the Security
Intelligence Service Bill. Many people see telephone tapping as the ultimate infringement of
personal liberty. They assert that the Government should use the tapping of telephones only
as an ultimate and extreme measure if no other satisfactory alternatives are available. Some,
indeed, will say that the Government has moved arbitrarily to legislate for telephone tapping


## p. 4210 (#690) ###########################################

4210
4 October
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
when there are interim steps open to it that have the potential to enable the drug problem to
be tackled effectively.
When fundamental human liberties are involved it is wise to proceed with caution, with
ultimate measures always being available as a last resort should circumstances demand.
There are great public sensitivity and concern about proposals to tap telephones and use
listening devices, and many consider that Parliament should not authorise extreme measures
beyond those shown to be necessary to enable the Police and Customs to act effectively. The
Labour Government acknowledged the need in this area. It was considered in 1975 that the
Listening Devices Bill could be adequate to equip the Police to handle the drug situation in
an effective way. Having regard to the fact that personal liberty is involved, we should in fact
move with caution.
There are grounds for asserting that the Government could have served the interests of
New Zealand better when it was elected if it had immediately adopted the Labour
Government's measure. Why has the Government delayed so long in bringing this measure
before the House? As everyone knows, the drug problem has continued to worsen. The
Government had the opportunity to use preventive measures at an early stage, and with less
intrusion into personal liberty if it had then moved to adopt and bring into effect Labour's
legislation. Even now it is not too late for the Government to reconsider whether the step it
is taking is greater than may be necessary to deal with the problem.
I shall say no more, except that a Labour Government is committed to wiping out the
drug traffic in the country. A Labour Government would have moved, as Opposition
members have indicated, with the Listening Devices Bill. Other ultimate weapons were
available to the Government. Until it could have been demonstrated that what was
contemplated was not effective, the ultimate measures should, in my view, not have been
taken.
Concern has been expressed that, under the measures in the Bill, doctors' rooms,
solicitors' rooms, clergymen's rooms, and even confessionals could be bugged. I know that
Government spokesmen have denied that, but when one studies the provisions in the Bill
one finds they are qualified provisions. If the Government intends that premises of that
nature are not to be bugged it should amend the Bill now and place that matter beyond
doubt. The provisions in the Bill are qualified provisions. If the Government does not intend
to bug rooms, then it should state that in the Bill. Between now and the Committee stage the
Government should study that aspect of the Bill.
The Bill is directed against hard drug traffic. I see no real difference between hard and
soft drugs. Those who start on soft drugs ultimately tend to graduate to hard drugs.
Experience has shown that. On many occasions when traffickers and users are apprehended
for drugs they are found to be in possession of both soft and hard drugs. The drug
environment in New Zealand is such that there tends to be a multiple drug-use problem,
because soft and hard drug-users tend to come together. Some people who start on soft drugs
are tempted to experiment, and do experiment and get hooked on hard drugs. If we are to
tackle the drug problem-that is the narcotic drugs and prescription poisons--both soft and
hard drugs must be attacked.
The illicit use of drugs is very real. The decision to take drugs is being made today by
young people. The age of taking drugs is dropping, and there is reported use of drugs even in
primary schools. The psychological and other effects of drugs on people are uncertain, but
modern research is fast removing that uncertainty. I refer those who still argue that
marijuana is a soft and harmless drug to a quotation from the American Congressional
record of a few years back. This document, which reported on the impact of drugs, stated:
"The epidemic effect of marijuana was also encouraged by a widespread belief that it was a
harmless as well as a pleasant drug . . . . The collective testimony of eminent scientists who
appeared before the subcommittee points to massive damage or potential damage to the
entire cellular process, to the reproductive system, and to the respiratory system. The
evidence also pointed to the serious possibility of irreversible brain damage and genetic
change."
The Opposition is as firmly committed as the Government to the elimination of drug
trafficking in the country. In the few years in which it was in office the Labour Government
took major initiatives through manpower and other resources to deal with the problem, and
introduced legislation that would place more superior technology in the hands of the Police
than they had under the existing law. If that legislation had been brought into force
immediately the National Government came into office-the Bill had been placed before a


## p. 4211 (#691) ###########################################

4 October
4211
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
select committee for recess study-then the Government could have had the advantage of
enabling the Police to use the technology from 1976 onward to assess its impact on the drug
scene before contemplating the use of some other measure.
A Labour Government will be elected in November, and is committed to eliminate drug
trafficking in New Zealand. The only way to stop drug trafficking is to cut off the supply of
available drugs-of drugs entering the country, or being cultivated here. All efforts should
be directed to that end.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I do not wish to say very much to the
member for Wigram other than that no amount of shopworn political rhetoric can hide the
fact that this Government has left the previous Labour Government for dead in its efforts to
combat drug abuse. I again find the Government being criticised by the Opposition for going
much further than did the previous Labour Government when dealing with a major social
problem.
I think I can say without any fear of contradiction that in no other area of law and order
has the Government had a more impressive record than in combating drug abuse. It has
greatly tightened the surveillance net facing illegal drug imports, has provided the Customs
Department with extra staff, sophisticated new equipment, new launches, extra drug dogs,
and has strengthened personal search powers. It has also strengthened police powers, their
manpower, training, and facilities. Publicity and education have also been strengthened, and
now the Government is tightening the legislation.
I believe that the moves taken should satisfy most people who want a hard-line
approach on drugs. I think they should also satisfy all reasonable defenders of civil liberties.
I should like to acknowledge the work of my parliamentary colleagues, particularly the
Minister of Health, who has been consistent both in Government and in Opposition in his
single-minded opposition to the growth of drug abuse; and I also acknowledge the support
he has given to his ministerial colleagues, myself, and the Minister of Police in the
acquisition of more staff and equipment. For that, I sincerely thank him.
I must also pay tribute to the work done by you, Mr Speaker, in your capacity as
member for Hawke's Bay when you were chairman of the Government caucus committee on
drugs; also, the member for Kapiti, who, in my view, brought not just a first-rate mind, but
also weeks of intensive work to bear on the legislation. The country owes the Government
caucus committee a debt for the massive amount of meticulous care that its members put into
this major piece of legislation.
I also take this opportunity to thank very sincerely my counterpart, the Hon. Wal. Fyfe,
Australian Federal Minister of Business and Consumer Affairs, whose jurisdiction includes
the Australian Customs Department, for his co-operation and help during the period when
we had personal discussions in Canberra, as well as before and afterwards. We have a mutual
interest in a joint trans-Tasman approach to this legislation, and what has resulted is the
near-simultaneous appearance of two pieces of legislation, not identical, but substantially
the same in most major respects.
The aim of the legislation, briefly, is to strengthen the hand of the law enforcement
authorities in a number of practical ways; to increase the risks both to personal property and
to personal freedom of participating in hard drugs dealing; and to ensure that the
international drug dealer will not in future regard New Zealand as an easy target compared
with other countries. The legislation is seen as an important part, but a part only, of a
comprehensive approach by the Government to the drug problem. It also, of course,
embraces such matters as treatment, rehabilitation, education, and international co-
operation. So it would be far from the truth for anyone to say that New Zealand's approach
has been largely or exclusively penal. The statistics cannot fully indicate the anguish for
those involved in, what I think the member for Wigram rightly calls, this "scourge to
society".
Much has been said and many statistics have been quoted, but I do not want to
elaborate here. The point I do wish to make, however, is this-and I make it advisedly as the
Attorney-General: it has been considered necessary, in the course of the legislation and in
the course of administering the attack on the drug problem, to impinge on a number of
individual freedoms in the areas of personal searches, telephone tapping, listening devices,
tougher imprisonment penalties, and restrictions on bail.
In other contexts there is no question that interference in such areas would provoke a
nationwide roar of opposition. In fact, the legislation has been widely acclaimed, and has
met with only fragmentary and mild opposition. That, in my opinion, is clear proof that the


## p. 4212 (#692) ###########################################

4212
4 October
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
country recognises that a price has to be paid if we are effectively to get on top of this most
pernicious problem.
I want, in the short time I propose to take, to comment on one or two individual matters
by way of supplement to the comments already made by the Minister of Health. First, when I
went to Canberra I was privileged to see a draft of the Australian legislation, which I brought
back to this country. There are substantial areas of coincidence between the Australian and
the New Zealand legislation it is proposed to pass into law. Both provide for a maximum
term of life imprisonment, both introduce a specific offence of conspiracy in drug dealing,
both provide for the use of listening devices and telephone interception, and both have
tightened bail provisions.
In only one major respect do they differ, and that is in the treatment of assets acquired
from drug dealing. The Australian legislation is considerably more Draconian than ours. It
provides that the Comptroller of Customs may take civil action in the federal court for the
recovery of a pecuniary penalty where it can be established, on a balance of probabilities,
that a person has been engaged in narcotics dealings. The court can order the payment of a
pecuniary penalty whether or not the person has been convicted of any offence and whether
or not moneys or other goods have been seized under the provisions of the Customs Act.
When our caucus committee examined this provision it was felt that we could not wear it,
and I fully support the provision we finally embodied in the Bill.
I wish to say something briefly, also about the telephone-tapping powers provided in the
Bill. We could have introduced power to tap telephones to track down drug dealers through
the Post Office Act. In the opinion of the Crown Law Office, this could have been done
merely by using the existing section 158, which makes it an offence to interfere with or
connect any apparatus or any part of a telephone without the Postmaster-General's consent.
I was firmly opposed to this extension of the use of section 158, believing that no one should
be given any grounds for fearing that the use of telephone-tapping powers would be
extended beyond the detection of drug dealers to other activities. For this reason, I
advocated the inclusion of this power within the Misuse of Drugs Act rather than the Post
Office Act to clarify beyond doubt that its use should be restricted to fighting the hard-drug
trade, and the Government caucus was in full agreement. I honestly do not believe we could
have gone further with safeguards in this respect.
A number of people have asked me, "Why is it necessary to give the Police the power to
tap telephones?" Naturally this was the first question we ourselves asked the Police. The
reply was that, on the basis of information gained from undercover agents and informants,
the Police do need this power, and specific examples were cited. For example, the dealer
must communicate with his customers in some way. Some communications are by telephone.
The dealer will not always be able to shut off people who want to deal with him. Sometimes
they will want to talk in code or jargon, but we are informed that it is not hard to gauge the
meaning in most cases.
Then there are conversations that appear completely innocuous in themselves, but when
set in a wider surveillance context, look very different. Another important example is the
overseas telephone call. A dealer may need to make contact with his source of supply
overseas—that is, if he is not fool enough to try to communicate by cable or undergo the
expensive, time-consuming, and risky course of meeting his overseas contact in person each
time. The evidence left no doubt in our minds that telephone tapping could not be excluded
from the package of new powers to fight the drug war.
There is also a provision in the Bill to make it clear that public servants may deliver a
controlled drug by reintroducing it into the postal delivery system with a view to tracing the
recipient. This would arise following the interception of international mail by the Customs
Department pursuant to the present law. As with telephone tapping, this will be effected
through the Misuse of Drugs Act and not through the Post Office Act.
Clause 12 and clause 13 have particular relevance to the Customs Department and are
self-explanatory. However, I feel it is worth mentioning that the customs operation cannot
be divorced from other enforcement activities, and the total Bill must have an effect on the
proper execution of customs tasks. Thus all the other sanctions, the increased penalties, the
use of listening devices, and the like, present the intending offender with additional
problems and with consequences that it is hoped will place importation beyond an acceptable
risk. We have proof that drug importers can be deterred if the risks are real enough, even to
the extent of their sending drugs to New Zealand and then refraining from landing them.
I have a particular interest in the new reworded clause 9, which, in its original form,


## p. 4213 (#693) ###########################################

4 October
4213
Misuse of Drugs Amendment Bill
provided a defence for a police officer who committed a drug offence "in the performance of
his duty." Civil liberties and other groups, whilst recognising the problems encountered by
undercover policemen, criticised the clause. After careful consideration, the committee
decided that the best approach would be to provide that no undercover officer or any officer
assisting him could be prosecuted under the Act except with the leave of the Attorney-
General. From the point of view of the Police, and for that matter other Government
departments involved, we feel this is a better solution to the problem, and at the same time it
should be more acceptable to those who opposed the original provision. I stress the point
that the power embodied in clause 9 is similar to that conferred on the Attorney-General in
certain existing sections of the Crimes Act and the Official Secrets Act; so there is no new
power here.
I see that time is running against me; I undertook to be as brief as I could. I conclude by
giving my enthusiastic support to the Bill, which represents, in my view, the culmination of 3
years of outstanding work by this Administration in fighting drug abuse. In every single
respect this Administration has advanced and tightened the power of the law to fight this
menace; and there has been an advance in the other directions already referred to. I
congratulate the Minister of Health and the caucus committee, as well as all others who had
a part in the introduction of the legislation.

and if the member checks Hansard he will find that the Bill did not mention drugs. The
Labour Government had an airy-fairy approach to listening devices, and eventually got cold
feet and shelved the idea.
I am pleased that the member for Wigram recognises the results that have been
achieved, and accepts them. I wish he had been gracious enough to congratulate the
Government instead of appearing to be envious of the National Government, which had
made the progress that the Labour Government could not. I thank the Ministers involved,
the members for Kapiti and Birkenhead, and the officials in the various departments for the
work they have done. During its committee stage the Bill will be broken down into the
Misuse of Drugs Bill, the Criminal Justice Amendment Bill, the Penal Institutions
Amendment Bill, and the Summary Proceedings Amendment Bill. Everyone knows that
drugs are the scourge of our society. The Government has worked hard, and members have
travelled the country and put in a great deal of time on this matter. I hope the end result
proves successful.
Bill read a second time.
FIRE SERVICE AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Afairs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill contains a miscellany of amendments to the principal Act, found to be
necessary or desirable as a result of 2 years' experience of Fire Service Commission control
of a nationalised fire service. They do not involve any major alterations to the structure of
the commission, neither do they denote any policy changes. Some are little more than fine
tuning, but an organisation such as the Fire Service needs this sort of adjustment from time
to time, especially so far as its authority and powers are concerned. After all, we are dealing
with a major public service which, last year, spent almost $33 million-a service that
employes 2400 permanent personnel, and is responsible for 6200 volunteers. During the
calendar year 1977, brigades answered almost 43 000 calls. It is, perhaps, a reflection of the
times that almost 2300 of those calls were malicious false alarms.
Turning to the details of the Bill, one of its principal objects is to formally recognise the
involvement of defence fire brigades in providing fire-fighting services in areas adjacent to
major military establishments. The Bill provides for the operational integration of those
brigades with the Fire Service in co-ordinated fire protection schemes. It sets out in clause 13


## p. 4218 (#698) ###########################################

4218
4 October
Fire Service Amendment Bill
the functions and powers of defence fire brigades and their firemasters when operating
outside defence areas, and in those circumstances extends to them the same degree of
protection from liability for damage as is available to the Fire Service generally. One
consequential effect of this statutory recognition of these brigades will be that their members
will qualify for membership of the United Fire Brigades Association, an organisation
principally for volunteer firemen, which has a meritorious record of service to the
community over many, many years, and to which firemen are proud to belong.
During the committee stage I will introduce amendments which will have the effect of
excluding the Woodbourne and Ohakea brigades from these provisions, as they are in a
slightly different category. They were established under the authority of the Forest and
Rural Fires Act 1977. Other clauses have the effect of making the Fire Service Commission a
local authority for the purposes of the Reserves Act, a legal requirement necessitated by the
fact that some stations are on reserves land. This does not mean that the commission intends
to seek authority to use any further reserves lands for Fire Service purposes. The intent of
the relative clause-clause 3—is simply to enable the commission to continue to occupy a
few fire stations that have been built on reserves. Also on the question of occupancy of land,
the Bill clarifies that, where negotiations on a transfer of ownership of land occupied for Fire
Service purposes before the commission came into being have not yet been completed, the
commission will continue to have authority to occupy that land pending the completion of
negotiations. Only a few cases are involved-about six or eight-and in most of them there
have been doubts about whether or not the land really belonged to the former urban fire
authority.
The Supplementary Order Paper on this Bill will also contain an amendment to clause
10 to remove any implication that this clause may be used to compel the installation of fire
alarms in private premises. I will move to have this clause clarified and also to correct one or
two minor changes of a drafting nature. I do not think there are any other clauses calling for
special mention at this stage. I can say that, since the Bill was introduced, discussions on it
have been held between the Fire Services Commission and union representatives, and, as far
as the Bill goes, it appears to have their general agreement. It is fair to say that the Northern
Union has asked for some further amendments to the principal Act, but these will call for
further negotiation and there is no point in holding up this legislation because of that
request. I can say, however, that there is nothing in this Bill that will inhibit further
discussion on the points at issue.
Bill read a second time.
HOWARD ESTATE BILL
Second Reading
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Acting Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office): I move,
That this Bill be now read a second time. The Bill consolidates and amends the Howard
Estate Act 1919 and its amendments. The original Act carried out the wishes of the late
Josiah Howard, who left his estate to the Crown as a farm training foundation. His estate
comprised 700 acres of freehold land, 20 miles from Waipawa, and it carried 14 500 sheep
and 270 cattle. The property was badly neglected and it was uncertain that Mr Howard's
wishes could be met, despite the farm's potential. In the absence of an appointed executor
the Public Trustee was asked to administer the estate. Later in 1919 the Howard Estate Act
was passed, providing a framework within which an attempt could be made to set up the
training facility. By 1927 the farm had been improved to the point where this was
practicable. An advisory board to help the Public Trustee with training facilities was
established, comprising five members-mainly local farmers.
Today the training farm, known as the Smedley Boys' Training Farm, has 25 000 sheep
and 2000 cattle. It runs a comprehensive 2-year training programme for 16 cadets, 8
first-year and 8 second-year boys. The Bill has carefully preserved the basic purpose of the
existing legislation, but 60 years of experience have shown that a number of changes in the
detailed administration will allow the intentions of Mr Howard to be more effectively carried
out in today's conditions.
The Bill proposes three main changes. The first will give both males and females the
opportunity to undertake tuition at the Smedley Farm while continuing the existing very
successful scheme of both practical and theoretical farm training. For consistency the name


## p. 4219 (#699) ###########################################

4 October
4219
Howard Estate Bill
of the farm has been changed to the Smedley Cadet Training Farm. These changes are
incorporated in clauses 12 to 16 inclusive. These clauses permit females to train at the farm,
provide a framework for the training of cadets, and allow for extra financial assistance in the
form of subsidies or scholarships for further study to be made to those showing exceptional
promise and ability.
The second principal change transfers the overall responsibility for the estate to the
Public Trust Office. At the moment responsibility for the estate rests with the Minister of
Agriculture and Fisheries, although the assets are vested in the Public Trustee, and the daily
administration of the property and the conduct of the training scheme are carried out by the
Public Trust Office. The Public Trustee is assisted in this by the guidance and advice of the
advisory board. Retention of overall control by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries was
a logical step in 1919 when the farm had yet to be established, and during its formative years.
However, this divided control is no longer considered necessary for two reasons: first, the
greatly improved financial position of the estate, and, secondly, the high calibre and wide
experience of those on the advisory board. The change in overall responsibility will not affect
the training given to the cadets, and officers of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries will
continue to provide help and guidance in this area.
The functions of the board are more clearly outlined in the Bill and its members will
have an increasingly important part to play in the administration of the property. These
matters are defined in clauses 17 to 27 inclusive, which set out the functions of the board.
These are: first, to define its membership, their length of service, travel allowances and
expenses, and meeting requirements; secondly, to provide for the appointment of a
chairman and secretary; and thirdly, to provide for the Local Authorities (Member's
Interests) Act 1968 to apply to contracts made between the Public Trustee and members of
the board.
The last main change defines and widens the powers of the Public Trustee. The present
administrative provisions, while appropriate in the 1920s, are out of step with today's more
modern conditions and practices. Some of these alterations, therefore, are needed to bring
those powers more into line with the modern standards and practices of trustees. However,
the Bill retains the requirement for ministerial approval for matters of principle, and, in the
particular case of acquisitions or sale of land, the joint approval of the Minister of
Agriculture and Fisheries and the Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office will be
required. It also requires the Public Trustee to submit annual reports and accounts to the
Minister in Charge of the Public Trust Office, the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries, the
Auditor-General, and the Secretary to the Treasury.
The other changes in this area reflect the increased responsibility the Public Trustee will
have under the Bill and the wide role the advisory board will have in the future. These
matters are all incorporated in clauses 3 to 11, which deal specifically with the administration
of the estate, and in clauses 28 to 34, which clear up the other miscellaneous machinery
provisions required. The detailed provisions have been discussed fully with members of the
advisory board, the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries, and his departmental officers,
who concur with them. I give notice of my intention to move amendments to clause 19 during
the Committee stage.
Bill read a second time.

Mr COURTNEY (Nelson): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. This local

legislation, all of which allowed the three regions to involve themselves in afforestation.
The Nelson City Council is pleased with the Bill as it has come back from the Local Bills
Committee. Word changes have been made that have improved the Bill. A new clause has
been inserted-clause 10-because of the concern of the Local Bills Committee that the
legislation might override other Acts. In its wisdom the committee has included that new
clause, which alleviates the concern expressed and brings the Bill in line with other Acts,
such as the Forestry and Rural Fires Act, the Water and Soil Conservation Act, the Reserves
Act, and the Town and Country Planning Act. That is right and proper.
I notice, too, that the committee has deleted clause 8. It felt that the borrowing powers
there were not necessary, because there were already powers under the Local Authorities
Loans Act. The committe took out of clause 3(k), and put into a first and second schedule,
reference to specific areas. The Nelson City Council, I understand, has indicated that it is
prepared to make 62 ha-the river flats area of the Waahi Taakaro, a recreational and
pleasure ground area-a reserve under the Reserves Act 1954, and then the remaining area
of about 640 ha will be available for the land management plan it wants to proceed with. We

AUCKLAND ELECTRIC POWER BOARD BILL
Second Reading
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. As
is my duty as the member for the area, I should explain that the Auckland Electric Power
Board is unique in New Zealand in that it has its own power board Act. The Electric Power
Boards Act 1925 is pre-dated by the Auckland Electric Power Board Act 1924. The board
has expanded under that Act to become one of the largest power boards in New Zealand. It
now needs a new Act to cover its activities. One of the reasons is that it appears likely, from
the projections being made, that some classes of commercial users will strike the maximum
tariff legally chargeable under the old Act, and will go over the maximum next year. For that
reason the board believes a new law is an urgent matter.
The second reason given for the new law is that the old law provides for a roll of
electors. The power board has not followed that provision and has used the electoral rolls.
There has been some question about whether that is correct. The board has assured the
committee it believes it has been legally correct in its actions and that it did the practical
thing by using the electoral rolls. I believe the power board has established a need to review
the Act. The obvious question is whether the Auckland Electric Power Board should
continue with the anomaly between it and other power boards.
When considering the Bill, members should realise the differences between the
Auckland Electric Power Board Act and the Electric Power Boards Act 1952. The Acts have
a number of differences. I have listed them. On the whole the differences appear to be
minor. The Auckland Electric Power Board admits one glaring difference: that is, that under
the Electric Power Boards Act the other power boards are divided into wards. The Bill
provides only one ward. The members of the board will be elected on an at-large system. I
believe the House should be aware of the uniqueness of electing representatives. The
Auckland Electric Power Board has 316 775 voters, or about a third of a million. They will
elect a small 8-man or 12-man board.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Eight-man? Does the member not know?
Mr PREBBLE: Eleven men and one woman. Happy?
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: That's more like it.
Mr PREBBLE: The area has about 316 000 eligible voters, of whom 120 000 cast votes
at the last election. The House should consider whether this system should be agreed to.
While I want to do the best for my board, and I do accept that it needs a new Act and a
regularisation of its position, I do not accept this as being a fair method of election. I do not
believe that the Bill should proceed with the provision. For that reason, and after having
listened to the evidence and then considered the question, Parliament should tell the
Auckland Electric Power Board it has not established a case for any at-large system of
election. If the proper way of electing people is the one being legislated for the Auckland
Electric Power Board, then every other local body is electing representatives by a defective
system. One cannot have a system under which the Auckland Electric Power Board is in step
and the other boards are out of step. I cannot accept that, and I am sure it is wrong. I am sure
the provision for an at-large system of election is wrong. It is contrary to democracy, and
Parliament has a duty to ensure that the people can vote properly for power boards and
other organisations, and also that an individual should have a reasonable chance of standing
for a local body or a power board.
It has not been possible for an independent person to gain election to the Auckland
Electric Power Board in the last 20 years. It can be seen not to be possible when one
considers that the area has 500 000 people. A person trying to campaign an area with more
than 300 000 voters would have a mind-boggling job to canvass everyone. Campaigning must
present difficulties to political parties, but it must be an impossible hurdle for an
independent candidate. Parliament is abrogating the right of a person to stand realistically
for the Auckland Electric Power Board. I am unhappy about that, because I believe it is
wrong. I do not think members should accept from people who have been successfully
elected, an assurance that the system is satisfactory. That is like asking someone who has
won a race whether the race was properly run. Every person who ran the race must be asked,

5 October
Auckland Electric Power Board Bill
not just the person who managed to get over the hurdles. It may be that the race had a
particular handicap. I suggest that the handicap is against the ordinary person who might
want to vote for any person who might want to stand. The provision is not democratic.
The electricity division of the Ministry of Energy has stated that all the legal
requirements of the Auckland Electric Power Board could be met by incorporating the Act

the Department of Internal Affairs suggested to the Local Bills Committee that the

Citizens and Ratepayers Association or the Labour Party-the only two organisations that

government of the people, by the people, for the people. That method of election in the
Auckland Electric Power Board area is not being proposed in the Bill. It would be more
democratic if the power board were covered by the 1925 Act.
I find it incredible that, in the great rush of legislation going through at the end of the

its maximum levy. That should have been done. I suspect that power board members have

over other groups. That association has a close affiliation with the National Party. It is totally
wrong for a political party to interfere with the election process. I am surprised that
Government back-benchers have allowed this to happen, as I know some are trying to
uphold fairness in local body matters.
It has been suggested that it is a good system because many people vote. Last election,
37.9 percent of the people voted, which is more than the percentage in some other local body
areas. However, 37.9 percent is an appalling figure. There is no doubt that, out of the

on the power board because it has the largest area. For some reason the area has managed to
have several representatives on the power board, although some boroughs have not had
even one. A ward system would ensure that did not happen. We have accepted, in other
local body laws, that the local people-not people from other areas-should be represented.
The Auckland Electric Power Board is not a bad board. That is not the issue. I am not
saying it has not made a case for new legislation. However, it has not made a case for this
particular method of election. As one of the local members-and other local members might
also disagree with it-I think the Bill is wrong, and should not be given a second reading.

HUTT VALLEY DRAINAGE AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. This is a


## p. 4229 (#709) ###########################################

5 October
4229
Hutt Valley Drainage Amendment Bill
short Bill, the main provision of which is to alter the calculation of assessment between
various local bodies that contribute to the operation of the Hutt Valley drainage scheme.
The local bodies are the Lower Hutt City Corporation, the Petone Borough Council, the
Upper Hutt City Corporation, the Hutt County Council, and the Eastbourne Borough
Council. The Bill also makes a few amendments needed by the board, including an alteration
to the definition of the main sewer so as to allow the board itself to determine which parts of
the sewer line in the Hutt Valley will not be deemed to be part of the main sewer.
However, the main intent of the Bill is to create new methods of assessing the
calculations for the commitments of the contributing local bodies year by year. The
commitment is defined in the Bill as being allocated as follows: one-third of the amount
involved will be according to the water usage of the local bodies, one-third will be calculated
on the properties, and one-third on the design capacity of the sewer.
The Hutt Valley Drainage Board came into existence in 1948, and this is the third
amendment to the method of assessment of the liability of the various authorities towards
the expenses of the board. Originally the board's activities were shared on the basis of
population and the distance that the sewer line had to be carried. In 1967 there was a further
slight amendment, because it was found that there were certain parts of the board's area
that, because of growth, needed a high capital commitment. The alteration provided for loan
charges to be allocated on the basis of design capacity to the various areas of the constituent
authorities. In its wake this has brought problems, because in those developing areas the
ratepayers had to carry the loan commitment for the area.
The board has undertaken a complete reassessment of their position, and it has come
out with this new formula that will, in effect, give some relief to those local bodies whose
areas are furthest from the outfall, particularly Upper Hutt and that part of the Hutt County
surrounding the Pinehaven area. The board drains a very wide area-the whole area of the
Hutt Valley-in sewage and trade wastes disposal.
During the committee hearings on the Bill I was concerned to hear the submissions of
the Department of Health and the Ministry of Works and Development on the Hutt Valley
drainage scheme. Recently this matter was brought to the attention of the loans board on an
application by the Hutt Valley Drainage Board for further improvements to the sewer line.
Parts of the sewer line have been there since 1908. The average age of the sewer is more than
35 years, and, of course, deterioration occurs over such a period. Lines that were laid 30 or
40 years ago are much more likely to attract seepage in an area like the Hutt Valley, where
much water seeps through in some places. This is the result of the development of a river
delta.
Valiant efforts have been made by the constituent authorities and by the board to get
the storm water out of the sewer. There was a time when it was thought that the sewer should
take the storm water. When large State housing areas were built in the Hutt Valley the storm
water was connected to the Hutt Valley sewer. Over the last 10 or 12 years much attention
has been given to correcting that.
Mr Minogue: Not enough.
Mr T. J. YOUNG: I am interested to hear the cry of the member for Hamilton West-
"Not enough." All I can say to him is that, on a population basis and design capacity, the
Hutt Valley sewer is much more effective than the Hamilton city sewer. The design capacity
of the sewer, and the allowance for the extra capacity in wet weather, appear to be well
within the limits of the design manual of the Ministry of Works and Development. I am
happy that the committee agreed to the amendments that were brought forward by the Hutt
Valley Drainage Amendment Bill. Many appeals to members of the Local Bills Committee
have resulted in the Bill's proceeding to the point it is now at. I thank the members of the
Local Bills Committee for their generous consideration of the Bill.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): I was one who, in 1967, expressed concern at the
levies that were to be imposed on the local authorities in the Hutt Valley Drainage Board's
area. We have come some way along the line of bringing a little more equality into the
method of rating the local authorities served by the board. However, I still hope for a
uniform rate throughout the area. I see no reason for a differential rate. I feel the community
as a whole would be served much better if we had a uniform rate.
I am pleased that the Local Bills Committee allowed the Bill to proceed virtually
unaltered. The rating of areas like Pinehaven, Silverstream, and Upper Hutt would have
been intolerable if the rates had not been reassessed. However, although the rating system is
now better than it was, I am still not entirely happy with it. We could still go a lot further,

Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Clause 16 hits at Beth Furmage and the hundreds like her. The clause was introduced by
the Minister in a fit of pique. This sorry amendment came about because of one woman,
Beth Furmage, who had been badly treated for years. She has suffered great anguish and
concern for her children, and has been subjected to unnecessary officiousness by the
Department of Social Welfare. She was found by the Supreme Court to have been unjustly
treated. Because of the amendment many women will be affected in the same way.
During the Committee stage I referred to the various women's groups throughout New
Zealand. The phrase "in the nature of marriage" is regarded as being totally unclear. It is
too subjective and open to individual interpretation. We are subjecting thousands of New
Zealand women to this vague and woolly interpretation. The phrase has not been
interpreted by the courts, so the interpretation is entirely in the hands of the Minister and his
department. He has tried to introduce a legal technicality whereby a person's motive and
intent are totally disregarded, and are no longer the main criteria of judgment, which is
replaced by limitless power in the hands of a Government department. Unless someone can
go to the expense and suffering in bringing a case before the Supreme Court, all power
remains in the hands of the Minister and his department. I shudder to think of the effect this
will have on many others like Beth Furmage. Together with women's groups I shall monitor
the situation.
Will the Minister use the clause to complete the punitive act he directed against Beth
Furmage, but from which she was able to escape by arbitration? If a person does take a case
to the Supreme Court, not only the individual, but also the children of that individual must
suffer. Therefore, in practice, any chance of a constitutional voice has been almost
annihilated. Many people cannot afford it and will not take the action because of the possible
effect on their children. We have seen the effect on Beth Furmage, who has had to be
admitted to a psychiatric clinic. We have also seen the effect on her children.
The alteration was made because the Minister was dissatisfied with the result of her
case, so one must presume that the criterion by which all beneficiaries will be judged will be
a sexual one, which is not acceptable to reasonable people in the community, and certainly
not to me. When a Government and a Minister equate marriage with sexual relationships
there is no awareness of everything else concerned.
Hon. H. J. Walker: Rubbish.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN: The Minister might say "rubbish", but
this has been the motivation behind the clause. Catching a couple who might be seeking to
establish some sort of a relationship, each after some years of anguish and unhappy
marriage, is not the role of the Government. I have said that in the House before. What
happens in the bedrooms of the nation is not the concern of the Government, nor of
legislation. Ministers who will not agree to such a scrutiny of their own lives--and I include
the Prime Minister-should not subject others to this.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The honourable member has strayed beyond the bounds of what

Before the law was altered, in order to achieve what the original legislation was

labour, just as a firm can withdraw its commodity while waiting for a price increase, and later
sell it at a higher price. The Government has not solved that problem. It is part of the
difficulty of running a democracy.
I should like to refer to another matter which shows the degree of ambivalence of the
Government's attitude to industrial relations. In 1976 the Government wrote a provision in
the Industrial Relations Act that provided for the Arbitration Court to have the right to deny
an unqualified preference provision to a union and an employer if they failed to provide rolls
for a ballot to be conducted on the matter. This Bill takes that out of the hands of the
Arbitration Court. It cancels the Governn.ent's provision passed in 1976 and replaces it with
a clause that now gives that power, after 2 months, to the Executive to be applied insecret by
the Minister. That will allow for the removal of the unqualified preference provision from
collective agreements or awards, something which may well be agreed to by both the
employer and the union.
Now the Government is to intervene and deny an employer the benefits of unqualified
preference—and many see the benefits-just because a union has failed to do something
within 2 months. The court will not decide the matter; Cabinet will. This provision has been
deliberately inserted in the Bill to take the power away from the court and give it back to
Cabinet so that it can be decided by Order in Council. By that means the Minister can take
away the unqualified preference provision, even though both parties may willingly want to
have it in their agreement. I do not see how anyone can believe that he can build a cohesive
industrial society with such rushed thinking, with such a lack of expertise, and with such total
ineptitude.
We told the Government, as we have told it throughout the last 2 or 3 years, that it
should set aside its prejudice; that it should build a cohesive society; that it should listen to its
Planning Council; that it should listen to the Industrial Relations Council; that it should
listen to the Employers Federation, to the Federation of Labour, and to the Combined State
Service Organisations. Then it could legislate with the good will of the people, and with
common sense. That would save the Government from the embarrassment we have had in
the past 2 or 3 weeks because of its bad law. We will write a better law. We will build a better
society. We will encourage greater productivity and help the country out of the shattered
mess it finds itself in economically and industrially.

NEW ZEALAND NATIONAL AIRWAYS CORPORATION DISSOLUTION BILL
Third Reading
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): On behalf of the Minister in Charge
of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services, I move That this Bill be now read a third time.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): At last we have come to the third reading of the
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill introduced earlier this session,
the second reading of which took place 14 weeks ago. During the Committee stage, which
continued over a protracted period of some 2 months, the Opposition raised the objections it
had raised during the second reading. Various amendments were promoted and debated, but
were ruled out of order on the ground that they involved an appropriation. The Opposition
has said all along that the Bill is an NAC destruction Bill. We have now reached the final
stage tonight when the National Airways Corporation, "the Wings of the Nation", goes out
of existence officially and legally.
Six months ago, on 1 April, Air New Zealand took over NAC, and since then-and
until the passage of this legislation tonight-has been acting illegally. That is clearly borne
out in clause 3, the validating clause, which was debated at some length during the
Committee stage. The Opposition has continually asked the Government to realise the
report on which the decision to amalgamate, or take over NAC by Air New Zealand, was
made. However, the Government has stubbornly refused to give any information to justify
and support the takeover. If the weight of evidence in the report is as compelling as the
Government would have us believe, it should come clean and tell the people. Every flimsy
excuse advanced by members opposite, from the Prime Minister down, has been inadequate
and unacceptable. If the case were as sound as Government members would have us believe,
they would come forth with the evidence. However, as I said before, they have stubbornly
refused to give that information.
The Government also breached solemn undertakings given to the staff of NAC and Air
New Zealand that there would be full and frank discussions. Although this was argued
during the debate on the short title, the breach of agreement had occurred 12 months ago
when the Minister in charge of the Bill gave the employees of NAC and Air New Zealand an
assurance that they would be consulted if a takeover was to proceed. In December that
Government announced that the takeover would take effect on 1 April. The report has not
been made public, and discussions held with the employees of the two corporations have
been very scanty. The Government has kept the committee recommendations, and
information that any advantages totally outweigh the disadvantages, a closed secret. We
were told by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport that the merger would result
in a profit of $10 million a year.
In the Committee stage I moved the following amendment to clause 3: "In determining
applications made by Air New Zealand Ltd. for increases in fares for the carriage of
passengers and increased charges for the carriage of goods, the Air Services Licensing
Authority shall take into account that savings in costs of $10 million per year have been
effected by the merger of Air New Zealand and the corporation." As the application had
been made, and subsequently granted, I, and members from this side of the House, felt it
would be reasonable, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, and because Government
members have said time after time that a saving of $10 million a year would be made, that
the authority should take this into account before granting any fare increase on domestic
services. The amendment was defeated in the Committee stage, although it was debated at
some length. Other amendments were moved, and clause 4 of the Bill was also discussed. At
that point, too, I attempted to move that all future audits of Air New Zealand Ltd. should be

There was also debate arising from the Minister's report following the announcement of

the level of service on domestic airlines would not be affected. The report is undated, but it is
an official report explaining the Government's decision of 19 December. A section of the
final paragraph on page 13 states: "On the basis of the evidence put to the Government, no
diminution of levels of service for the domestic or the international traveller, or of standards
of service to any particular centre within or beyond New Zealand, is foreseen as a result of
the merger." Since then the Minister's statements have not been so clear. They have
contained qualifications, and they were debated on the short title and on clause 4. The
Opposition sought an assurance from the Minister that domestic services would not be
adversely affected. The Minister refused to give such an assurance, but in his earlier report
there is a firm statement to the effect that there will be no reduction in the level of service.
Job assurances for the staff of Air New Zealand and NAC were referred to, because
contradictory statements have been made by the Minister, the Prime Minister, and others.
On 3 August the Prime Minister assured the staff that the merger would not result in job
losses because of wholesale transfers. Since then the pilots have been told that the
Wellington base will be reduced to a minimum, and given the choice of transfer to
Christchurch or Auckland.
In the Committee stage we sought an assurance that pilots who elected to stay in
Wellington would not suffer loss of promotion or be penalised in any other way. No
assurance was forthcoming from the Minister in charge of the Bill or from any other
Government speaker. The Government failed to answer matters raised by the Opposition
during the Committee stage. However, the main objection from this side of the House was

NEW ZEALAND COUNCIL FOR POSTGRADUATE MEDICAL EDUCATION BILL
Second Reading
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time.
The Bill will have wide-ranging effects on the postgraduate medical education scene, and
hence on the health services of this country. Until between 10 and 15 years ago most New
Zealand medical graduates looked overseas, particularly to the United Kingdom, for their
specialist education. Improved knowledge, skill, and teaching facilities in New Zealand
mean that most New Zealand medical graduates can now gain postgraduate education in this
country. Responsibility for most postgraduate education, particularly the necessary
standards of such education, will continue to be the responsibility of the various professional
colleges. The Bill in no way impinges on their traditional areas of responsibilities or
functions.
Essentially, the Bill gives statutory responsibility to a council which hitherto has
operated without any legislative backing and with the absolute minimum of financial
support. For some time representatives of the various medical organisations, including the
Medical Council, the medical schools and the colleges, which have a concern for the


## p. 4258 (#738) ###########################################

4258
New Zealand Council for Postgraduate Medical Education Bill 5 October
standards of postgraduate medical education, have met under the aegis of the council. They
have recognised, however, that the lack of statutory recognition and the paucity of available
funds have impeded their effectiveness. The Government has recognised that the efforts of
the council must be supported in a practical and effective manner. The Bill seeks to provide
that support.
Earlier I mentioned family medicine, and I should like to expand on that. General
practice is now recognised as a speciality in its own right. Until recently, however, it was the
only substantial branch of medicine that had no specific training for doctors wishing to
provide primary medical care. Responding to this need, the profession itself commenced a
small pilot scheme in Southland in the late 1960s. Building on that experience the previous
National Government undertook the funding of a G.P. registrar scheme. It was designed to
enable young doctors wanting to enter general practice to obtain practical and supervised
experience. Over the years variations and improvements have been made to the programme
culminating in 1977 in a complete overhaul and redesignation of the scheme. It is now called
the family medicine training programme. With the passage of the Bill the council will, among
other things, accept responsibility for this most important postgraduate medical activity.
I have heard it said by some sceptics that from any given group of five doctors one can
get six different opinions. Suffice it to say that there is no dissent from the medical profession
on either the need for this council or the objectives incorporated in the Bill. As to the detail
of the legislative provisions incorporated into the Bill, its text-as a departmental draft—was
considered at a series of meetings of the council. I can say with confidence that the provisions
of the Bill meet with the approval of the council and the various medical bodies represented
on it.
Clause 3 establishes the council as a body corporate consisting of 17 members. I draw
attention to the wide representation of the various medical bodies allowed for. Clauses 4 to
10 are the usual provisions stipulating how the council shall regulate its activities. Clauses 11
to 13 are essentially organisational matters enabling the council to create a regional
organisation for both the collection of information and the ease of administration of its
educational programme.
Clauses 14 to 18 relate to the position of the council as a local authority for certain
purposes, and all that stems from this. Clause 19 requires the appointment of a secretariat
for the council, and clause 20 establishes that members of the council and of its committees
and the council's staff are not public servants. Clauses 21 to 23 set out the functions and
powers of the council. In this respect I draw your attention to the fact that the council is
required to advise the Minister of Health on matters of postgraduate medical education. This
will meet a long-felt need. However, the council will also be responsible for initiating and
administering programmes of medical education. I have already drawn attention to the fact
that the council will take over responsibility for the family medicine training programme.
The council already has in mind certain other areas for additional programmes. Clauses 24 to
33 deal with financial aspects.
Clause 34 provides for the council to supply the Minister of Health with an annual
report, which must be laid before Parliament. This will provide an opportunity for the House
to gauge the success of this most important adjunct to our health services. The first and
second schedules are self-explanatory. I should comment that the regions proposed in the
first schedule have been debated and discussed extensively and a consensus has been reached
by the various organisations consulted.
I am convinced that the enactment of the Bill will be a significant step in the history of
our medical education. If I may be permitted a medical allusion, its conception has been a
labour of love by many informed and concerned people; its development has been tended
and nurtured with the utmost care and attention; and the Government, by providing the
legislation, will see its birth into a medical world keen to make it thrive. I am sure the
Government will also ensure that the finance it requires will be forthcoming, so that over the
next few years the council will be able to initiate and support the postgraduate medical
education programmes our health services require.
The council is just one more building block in the Government's endeavours to improve
our health services in a rational and phased manner, with the advice and support of the
medical profession. I am extremely disappointed that the member for Southern Maori, who
is trying to interject, has no interest in this most progressive and forward step in the care of
the family and mothers in the community that the country has provided for many years. It is
quite apparent that the depth of her interest in these matters can be measured by whether
the red light is on or not.

It so happens that the Opposition members of the committee who protested have had
long experience with local bodies. We know the commitments of local bodies for the
provision of reserves and reserve facilities, and the difficulties local bodies face when raising
loan moneys for reserve development. When subdivisions are developed reserves must be
provided, and the legislation has long provided for a contribution from a subdivider
according to the value of the subdivision, whether it be in land or money.
There are two provisions in the original Bill. One is that the 150 m² per allotment was
reduced by the National Government to 130 m² without any request from or knowledge of
local bodies until now. The monetary contribution also has been reduced-where they
accept money instead of land—from 10 percent to 7.5 percent.
In the clause that was struck out a similar provision was placed before the committee by
the National members of that committee. We were told that there could be no variation-it
was a decision of their caucus. The provisions affect the ability of the territorial local bodies
properly to finance capital needs for reserve development where residential settlements in
their area expand. The Opposition protests about this, because the result of the reduction is
not being handed on to the public. An extra liability will be thrown on to the ratepayers to
meet a shortfall that otherwise would not have occurred. That is quite unnecessary and
undesirable. There would be a greater profit and greater payout than would otherwise occur
to the subdivider of the land. The Opposition registers a strong protest, and its members will
have something more to say as the Bill progresses.
It is a rather technical and important Bill, and I am certain that the committee has given
many months to studying its contents. There are fresh procedures for certain schemes
relating to subdivisions. For example, legislative provision is made for concept plans to
proceed ahead of scheme plans. Under some conditions it is necessary for a concept plan to
be provided in optional conditions.
of
A scheme plan must be signed by a registered surveyor and submitted to the council
before any work involving disturbance of the land surface or excavation is done, or any other
work except clearing vegetation or other investigative work needed for surveying. The
provision does not necessarily apply if no more than two parts are created by the subdivision.
The concept plan is required where a subdivision involves more than 50 allotments, any
which are to be used solely or principally for commercial, industrial, or residential purposes,
or for any two or more such purposes. A concept plan is also required where there are
special or unusual features. The concept plan must be referred to other local authorities,
which have 35 days in which to consider it. The local authorities may then set out conditions
relating to subdivision.
The new section 279(2)(g) became necessary after an unusual rake-off by a subdivider of
the Himitangi Sands. I am happy to see the provision, though its importance may have
escaped the gaze of some Government members. It states: “(g) Provision be made to the
satisfaction of the council for the protection of the land or any part thereof, or of any land
not forming part of the subdivision, against subsidence, slippage, erosion, or inundation
from any source (being, in the case of land not forming part of the subdivision, subsidence,
slippage, erosion, or inundation arising or likely to arise as a result of the subdividing of the
land on the scheme plan):". Unfortunately some subdividers are pirates, and the Himitangi
Sands subdivision certainly met with the public's disapproval. It also met with the
disapproval of the Opposition.

that the matter, in fact, is sub judice. Can the honourable member help me?
Mr T. J. Young: No, I cannot help you further, Mr Speaker.
Mr SPEAKER: Thank you.
Mr Lange: As far as I know, proceedings have been issued. These have been served on
the defendant, and publicity has attended issuing and service. It is not known whether any
formal application has been made to the registrar to set down the matter, but I would be
content to accept the assurance of the member for Kapiti when he told the House that
application had been made.
That is not the issue. The issue is not simply and so barrenly one of whether or not the
matter is sub judice, but whether or not the material mentioned in the House is of such a
nature as to prejudice the outcome of judicial determination of the issues. This House is not
aware of the issues which have been litigated pursuant to that writ or statement of claim. The
rule about sub judice is an unusual one. It ought never to be a muzzle on free debate within
Parliament so long as that free debate is not such as to preclude a judge from engaging in a
proper, balanced determination of the issues before him. We do not know what the issues
are. We do not have any statement of claim. I am sure nothing said here tonight will in any
way influence a judge yet to be appointed to determine the issues.
Mr SPEAKER: I thank the member for Mangere for drawing my attention to that point.
The purpose of the sub judice rule is to protect the courts of justice, but it is also included in
the Standing Orders in such a way that, if it is necessary for Parliament to legislate, it may
always do that, despite the fact that a case is before a court. However, when there is a
reference to a case before a court by way of illustration of a point in a Bill, that does not
mean that Parliament is legislating on that particular case. Moreover, when the case involves
a member of the House we must be bound by other Standing Orders. References to a
member's private affairs can be made only if those references are not in any way offensive.
Exception has been taken to the reference, particularly on the ground that the case is
sub judice. The member for Kapiti has informed the House that the case has been referred to
the court, that the case is being pursued, and an application for a hearing is being made.
Standing Order 183, which deals with matters awaiting judicial decision, states that the
Standing Order shall have effect in relation to cases other than criminal, from the time when
proceedings have been initiated by the filing of the appropriate document in the registry or
office of the court. From what the member for Kapiti has told us, I understand that that has
happened. Therefore, the matter is strictly sub judice and should not be referred to. It would
have been better had the point been raised, as a point of order should be raised, when the
matter was first referred to, and not when the Deputy Leader of the Opposition informed
the House that he would be getting off the topic in any case. I rule that there shall be no
further reference to it by the honourable member.

CO-OPERATIVE FORESTRY COMPANIES BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Clause 2 contains definitions. Clause 3 provides for the adoption by a company
of model articles of association especially tailored for co-operative forestry companies.
Clause 4 provides for the memorandum of a registered co-operative forestry company to be
read subject to any model articles of association adopted by the company. Clause 5 makes
the registration of a co-operative forestry company conditional on the approval of the
Minister of Justice, which can be given subject to certain conditions. Clause 6 provides for
the registration by the Registrar of Companies of co-operative forestry companies. Clause 7
requires a registered co-operative forestry company to limit its area of operation to such
geographical area as the Minister may determine in respect of the company.
Clause 8 relating to the numbering of shares and clause 9 relating to the use of the word
"co-operative", are the usual provisions contained in co-operative companies' legislation.
Clause 10 allows only qualifying shareholders to vote at meetings of a registered co-operative
forestry company. Clause 19 provides for payment of levies and subscriptions by members to
their registered co-operative forestry company to enable the company to supplement its
revenue, such levies and subscriptions to be subject to limits prescribed by notice in the
Gazette. Clause 20 empowers registered co-operative forestry companies to form or join an
association representing the interests of the timber and forestry industries or associated
industries. Clause 21 makes special provision for the application to registered co-operative
forestry companies of certain provisions of the Companies Act 1955. Clause 22 enables
