EDUCATION AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill repeals the Whangarei High Schools Act 1878 and contains seven
clauses making miscellaneous changes to the Education Act 1964. The Bill has been referred
to a select committee. A number of representations were received from interested
organisations and individuals, and as a result of the select committee's deliberations two

provided only for the rates of bursary to be extended. Apart from the two amendments the
Bill remains exactly the same as when introduced, and at that time it was thoroughly
explained to the House.

MARINE MAMMALS BILL
Second Reading
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Bill, which was introduced last August, is a most important conservation measure,
and I can assure the House that it is a forerunner to similar legislation to be enacted
overseas. As the House was informed when the chairman of the select committee reported
back, five groups presented evidence, after which suitable amendments were made to the
Bill. One submission suggested that the responsibility for granting permits for the taking of
mammals should be transferred from the Minister to a commission. However, this was
declined because of the importance of the protection of marine mammals. It was decided
therefore that it should come under the direct control and jurisdiction of a Minister. It was
also considered necessary that the Government should be totally involved, because of the
need to be able to control the taking of marine mammals in accord with international
conventions.
The Bill is designed to preserve not only whales but also all species of marine mammals.
I believe it will achieve this objective. One of the problems for New Zealand and other
nations seeking to conserve marine mammals is the lack of sufficient data. The Bill makes
provision for programmes to monitor sightings and for the tagging of marine mammals so

5 October

that data can be provided to ensure their future conservation. In the distant past New
Zealand was one of the nations involved in the exploitation of marine mammals. However,
the Bill takes us a long way in the other direction and gives us one of the most stringent
conservation measures in the world. This Bill will be a hallmark in the conservation
legislation passed by the House.

INDUSTRIAL TRAINING LEVIES BILL
Second Reading
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. As I indicated when the Bill was introduced, it is purely and simply an empowering
Bill. Its aim is to help industries to help themselves. The agreed basis on which the
administrative expenses of industry training boards are funded is that the Government
provides up to 90 percent of the approved administrative expenses of each board with
industry providing a minimum of 10 percent. The total Government contribution towards
the administrative expenses of the 26 industry training boards is to be $1,117,000 in addition
to the $438,000 made available to meet the operating costs of the Vocational Training
Council itself.
These boards face constant financial difficulty. It is not an equitable basis for raising the
industry contribution. The chairmen and executive training officers of these boards have to
spend far too much of their time on fund raising instead of promoting training. If an industry
elects and I emphasise that—to have a levy imposed, the result will be a more equitable
sharing of industry contributions with its training board, as well as a training board that is
better equipped financially to pursue its statutory goals.
I reiterate the point made during the first reading that the Bill does not provide a
Government-imposed compulsory levy. It provides for each industry to elect to have a
compulsory levy inflicted upon itself. The Minister then has to satisfy himself, and notice is
subsequently posted in the Gazette. The remaining clauses of the Bill are of a relatively
machinery nature. The Bill itself is aimed at encouraging additional training and boosting
industry within New Zealand.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): the Opposition has examined the Bill and given it
careful consideration. It sees no reason why it should not proceed. Since this Bill is the last
on which the Minister of Labour will make a second reading, I take this opportunity to
convey to him and to Mrs Gordon the Opposition's good wishes for his retirement.
Opposition members are not unaware of the difficulties he has faced as Minister, and
appreciate some of the circumstances surrounding those difficulties. We hope, however, that
in retirement he will recognise that others will have taken up the same difficulties, and we
know, of course, that his sympathy will be with whoever has that particular warrant.

Orakei Block (Vesting and Use) Bill

Maori Trust Boards Act 1955. The clause further provides that the beneficiaries of the board
shall be the descendants of Tuperiri, ancestor of the Orakei Hapu of Ngati Whatua.

than 100 years ago. The elders of the Ngati Whatua have acknowledged that this is a
generous settlement on the Crown's part, and have readily accepted it.

designated for the purposes specified in the thirteenth schedule. Such zonings and
designations may not be altered during a period from the passing of the Bill to a term of 5
years from the date the present proposed reviewed scheme of the Auckland City Council
becomes operative.

Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): One thing is certain-after 3
years the Minister of Finance has reduced Parliament to the same state of chaos he and his
Government have produced in the economy. The House and the country will be glad to see
the back of his style of government. The Government has made a continuing and increasing
mockery of the whole democratic process.
I must recall the circumstances that led up to tonight. For the first time in the country's
history the Prime Minister has announced that Parliament would complete its work the
following day. Normally a week's notice is given. It is worth recalling that when such notice
was given in October 1975, with far fewer Bills on the Order Paper than there were at the
beginning of this week, the then Leader of the Opposition wanted another fortnight in what
he called the interests of orderly government and orderly management of the House.
On Tuesday the Order Paper had 36 Bills, not including the local Bills. Since then 13
Bills have been reported back from select committees. Three Bills of some importance have
been introduced this week, and one Bill of very considerable importance has been passed
through all its stages. It is clear that the Prime Minister and those who let him go his way do
not give a hoot for this place. In fact, they hold this institution in absolute contempt. This
action is underlined again and again. It reflects the sheer hypocrisy of the slogan "New
Zealand the way you want it" used in the election campaign by the National Party. The
country has been fed a diet of political bilge about the National Party's strong leadership.
What has that strong leadership meant in the past 3 years?
Mr Friedlander: This is boring rubbish.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: The member for New Plymouth can yawn, but he will go
back to his electorate and defend the so-called strong leadership of the National Party, which
has produced a hitherto unprecedented level of industrial chaos in this country; which has
increased unemployment to a level exceeded only in the days of the depression of the


## p. 4275 (#755) ###########################################

5 October
4275
Appropriation Bill (No. 2)
1930s; which has brought about the greatest exodus of New Zealanders in the history of the
country; which has achieved, in the name of strong leadership and what the people were told
was good economic management, the greatest Budget deficit the country has ever had;
which is responsible for the greatest borrowing in a comparable time ever seen in the history
of New Zealand; and which has politically abused both the law and the people to a degree
never before witnessed.
At no time in the history of this country have our people been so divided and sour as
they are under the present Administration. Because of the administration of the National
Government and the present Prime Minister, no one in the community is looking forward to
the future with any confidence. What the country needs, and what the incoming Labour
Government will give, is the kind of leadership that will bring our people together, using
their talents for their families, their communities, and themselves, again making them proud
to be New Zealanders. I was interested, as have been many others in the past few weeks, to
hear the Prime Minister say that the election would be fought on the grounds of credibility.
We welcome that, because the Prime Minister has the lousiest track record possible in the
matter of credibility. He is Mr Facing Both Ways. No wonder he claims to have two of
everything. No wonder the National Party produced two manifestos.
Let us look at some of the issues in more detail, starting with overseas borrowing,
because this was an issue that the then Leader of the Opposition pursued up and down the
country in 1975. The phrases flowed: "the profligate Government", "the country in hock",
"in pawn to the moneylenders”. Many people were undoubtedly influenced by the kind of
talk they heard from the then Leader of the Opposition. Although there was a change of
Government there was also a change in the country's export income, predicted with great
accuracy from this side of the House. What happened with borrowing? Was there any
change in borrowing? No; onward and upward went the borrowing. No matter where one
looked, overseas borrowing under the National Government was greater in 2 years than in 3
years under the Labour Government. [Interruption.] Members opposite yelp now, but these
are the facts, and the facts and National Party members have not rested very easily together.
The total net official borrowing in the 3 years of the Labour Government was $665 million
compared with $709 million in 2 years under the National Government. Under the Labour
Government the external debt increased in 3 years to $899 million compared with $984
million in 2 years under a National Government. The gross official borrowing for 2 years
under a Labour Government was a round $924 million compared with $1,450 million in 2
years under a National Government. And the Minister of Finance, who is also the Prime
Minister, wants to fight the election on the grounds of credibility!
We have heard something about industrial relations in another context tonight from the
Government that was going to get tough. The unions were going to get it where the chicken
got the chopper. How they pandered to the backwoodsmen in the National Party ranks. But
what happened? In a little over 2 years a million working days were lost, with all the
consequences to the work force, the country, families, and industry. Did the Government
get tough? Yes, on one occasion the Government did get tough. It got tough with the
taxpayers and took $3 million of the taxpayers' money and gave it to the freezing companies
to pay the wages bill. The Government got tough in the industrial relations field only once,
and that was with the taxpayers and no one else. Finally, of course, there was the fiasco in
Invercargill, which completely annihilated any credibility that the Government might
possibly have retained in industrial relations. Ministers scuttled around all over the place,
sheltering behind civil servants, Federated Farmers, you name it-anyone would do. Did
Government members stand up and assume their ministerial responsibility-admit an error
and clean it up? No, not on any occasion at all. Someone else always had to carry the can
when ministerial responsibility was at stake. So much for credibility in that area.
Let us consider credibility in the field of unemployment, because this is worsening. It is
reaching out now to touch many New Zealand families. More than half of the people
affected are young people under the age of 21, and many in that age group have not been
near the unemployment office to register. I remember well the words of the National Party
in 1975. I quote: "People without jobs represent waste of productive effort. We support full
employment." They were words no one could quarrel with. What have been the
consequences of the National Government's actions? Almost immediately it assumed office
it began to destroy job opportunities-more than 100 000 jobs were destroyed. More than
90 000 New Zealanders have left the country because of the lack of future in New Zealand-
the lack of opportunity here because of the Government. Never before have we been so
desperately bled of our human resources than we have in the last 3 years.

Appropriation Bill (No. 2)
But let us come closer to something that is dear to the heart of the Minister of Finance:
the Budget deficit. The Minister of Finance, who was the Leader of the Opposition in 1975,
was loud in his condemnation of the Budget deficit at that time. But what happened then was
a tiddler compared with what he produced this year. The Minister of Finance knows, and
many of the people know, that what we have seen is far from the finish of the story. The
monstrous supplementary estimates--$603 million against the $250 million that he
predicted—are a pretty fair indication of what is to follow. I do not know whether the
Minister of Finance intends to participate in the debate tonight, but if he does it would be a
good idea if he indicated to the country the measure of the deficit over the last 6 months,
because that would give a clear indication of the trends that are growing in this very critical
area. I remember, as other members will remember, that when I predicted in March a
Budget deficit of $1,000 million, the Minister of Finance went into print pouring scorn on it.
It was the Minister of Finance who also had to admit he did not have a figure himself. When
the Budget was produced the deficit was $1,050 million. Also, the Prime Minister protested
that his supplementary estimates would be sufficient, when he was told by the Deputy
Leader of the Opposition and myself that they would not. Time has proved who could make
a reasonably accurate assessment in this area.
The Prime Minister and Minister of Finance wants to fight the election on the grounds
of credibility. Remember the general wage order? There were threats that any employer
who paid the general wage order across the board would be prosecuted, although the
Government was exhorted again and again that this was the fair and proper thing to do in
order to restore confidence. The Government said no-not just once, but four times-on 11,
13, 17, and 21 July. There was to be no across-the-board payment of the general wage order.
When the member for Roskill introduced a private member's Bill to validate the court
declaration, up came the front benchers on the Government side shouting that it would open
the floodgates of inflation. The Minister of Justice, the fellow who played around with the
rolls, led the push. It is a pity he did not lead the push and clean up the rolls. Eleven days
after the eloquent condemnation of the member for Roskill's proposal, the Government
decided that the payment would be across-the-board. And the Prime Minister wants to fight
the election on the grounds of credibility!
What about the National Party's 1975 advertisements on freedom? The Minister of
Agriculture will be interested, because he was the one who sat there staring soulfully into the
television camera, making promises that all the people would be free. There would be free
speech, free thinking, and protection and support for the rule of law and the rights of the
individual. We do not hear much from the Minister of Agriculture now-certainly not
tonight! He has retired from the television business and from the freedom business, together
with his National colleagues. The glossy manifesto contained something about freedom:
"We will deal with the spate of recently introduced regulations that have complicated
everybody's lives." So what did the National Government do? Each year there has been a
record number of regulations. Within 2 years 100 new statutory bodies and commissions
have been formed to regulate the lives of New Zealanders-to tell them that they shall do
what "big brother" says, not that they shall do what they think best. In 1973 the member for
Mt. Albert was responsible for introducing the Export-Import Corporation Bill, which was
bitterly opposed by the then National Opposition.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: As creeping socialism.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: Yes, that phrase came up again and again, and the Minister

happened. They waited in 1977 to see the big dismantling process, and still nothing
happened. But, lo and behold, in 1978 out came the Budget, but it did not dismantle the
Export-Import Corporation-it extended it into new spheres of activity.

LIQUOR LICENCES SELECT COMMITTEE
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That a select committee be
appointed consisting of seven members to inquire into the operation of general ancillary licences
and caterers' licences under the Sale of Liquor Act 1962 and into certain other provisions of that
Act, and that the terms of reference of the select committee should be to consider: (1) the law
relating to general ancillary licences and caterers' licences and its operation, and whether it
adequately gives effect to the intention of Parliament in creating those licences in the Sale of
Liquor Amendment Act 1976; (2) the circumstances in which sports clubs should be authorised
to sell liquor, and in particular: (a) whether the sale of liquor should be ancillary to a particular
sporting activity; (b) whether and in what circumstances sporting organisations should be able
to sell liquor to their members and guests at social gatherings irrespective of whether those
persons have actively participated in a sporting activity, or whether those gatherings are
preceded by sporting activities; (c) the hours of sale available to sports clubs under general
ancillary licences, including Sunday sales; (d) the implications for other licensees and
chartered clubs, and for the public, of any extension of the law permitting the sale of liquor by
sports clubs; (3) whether the legitimate needs of sports clubs can most appropriately or
conveniently be met under the general ancillary licence or whether a separate form of licence or
charter should be created for sports clubs and, if so, what its scope and incidents should be; (4)
whether the standards being imposed on the holders of general ancillary licences by health and
fire authorities and local bodies are excessive or unreasonable and if so what remedial action is
required; (5) whether the current annual licence fee of $150 for a general ancillary licence is
appropriate, and in particular whether it is desirable and practicable to provide for a graduated
fee related to the size of the organisation concerned; (6) the circumstances in which
organisations other than sports clubs should be able to obtain a general ancillary licence, and
whether the present law is adequately meeting the needs of such organisations of various kinds
in accordance with the intention of Parliament; (7) whether any changes are desirable in the
law relating to caterers' licences to meet the needs of the holders of such licences and of persons
and organisations who may wish to obtain liquor from such licensees; (8) whether the
community cafe licence proposed by the 1974 Royal Commission on Liquor should be
introduced and, if so, in what form; (9) the form in which the wine cafe licence recommended
by the 1974 Royal Commission on Liquor should be implemented, if at all; (10) the current
operation of extended hours and special permits, whether current practice accords with the
original intent of Parliament and whether there is a need to revise these permits and if so in what
manner; and (11) such other matters as appear relevant to or arise out of the above issues, the
select committee to have power to adjourn from time to time and from place to place, and to
consist of Mr Quigley, Mr Friedlander, Mr Bell, Marilyn Waring, Hon. R. J. Tizard, Mr
Isbey, and Mr MacDonell.
Motion agreed to.

Family Proceedings Bill
FAMILY PROCEEDINGS BILL
Introduction
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Family Proceedings
Bill be introduced. This Bill gives effect to the Government's commitment to make
irreconcilable breakdown of marriage the sole ground for divorce and to revise the law
relating to maintenance. The Bill replaces the Matrimonial Proceedings Act 1963 and the
Domestic Proceedings Act 1968, but the Supreme Court and magistrates' courts retain, in
substance, the jurisdiction they have under those Acts. For example, the Bill provides for
the Supreme Court alone to be able to grant dissolutions of marriage. I want to make it clear
at the outset that this in no sense represents a rejection of the proposal of the Royal
Commission on the Courts for a family court. The reason why existing jurisdictional
arrangements are preserved is that it is not practicable to do otherwise until a restructuring
of the courts has taken place. I am hopeful that this can be done before the Bill is enacted. In
fact, it may even turn out that the present Bill will be withrawn after the taking of evidence
and a fresh Bill introduced which takes account of the submissions received and of progress
made in establishing a family court, assuming that the Government endorses the proposal.
Inevitably, a Bill of this kind re-enacts much that has proved serviceable in the present law. I
propose to pass over these aspects and to concentrate on the areas of significant change.
First, counselling and conciliation. Clause 12 provides that a husband or wife may
request the registrar of a magistrate's court for counselling in respect of the marriage. If
counselling fails the registrar will refer the matter to a recorder appointed under clause 6.
Recorders will be lawyers and will work on a part-time basis. A recorder will have power to
convene a conciliation conference attended by the husband and wife, their solicitors if they
so wish, the marriage counsellor who counselled them, and a representative of the
Department of Social Welfare if a domestic purposes benefit is being paid. The object of the
conference will be to isolate matters at issue between the spouses and to see whether they
can be brought to agreement on those issues. By consent of the parties the recorder will have
jurisdiction to make binding orders on maintenance, custody, access, and possession of the
home and chattels. If consent orders can be made on the matters at issue this will avoid the
need for recourse to formal court proceedings.
Secondly, divorce. Existing law on divorce and the dissolution of voidable marriages
will be replaced by a single, non-fault ground for the dissolution of marriage-namely, that
the marriage has broken down irreconcilably. This ground may be held to be established in
two circumstances only. The first is when either the husband or wife has filed an application
for marriage counselling not less than 2 years and not more than 4 years before the
application for dissolution, and they have been living apart for at least 6 months immediately
preceding the application. The idea behind this is that parties should not have to live apart
for 2 years to qualify for a divorce. When a marriage is in difficulties it is in the public interest
for an attempt at reconciliation to be encouraged, not discouraged. Hence, the parties who
attempt to reconcile will not be penalised by having to wait longer for a dissolution if
reconciliation fails.
The second circumstance founding a grant of dissolution is that the parties should have
lived apart for a period of at least 2 years imediately preceding the application. This caters
for such situations as desertion, or where the parties have simply drifted apart by mutual
consent. In all cases, a simple application for dissolution, not a petition, will suffice and
provision is made for joint applications. The court will make an order instead of a decree,
and the decree nisi/decree absolute procedure is abolished. There will be no right of appeal
against a dissolution order in undefended cases.
Thirdly, the Bill abolishes separation orders, which lose much of their point with the
alteration in the grounds for dissolution. Also, separation orders made on the ground of
serious disharmony would cut across the new ground for dissolution-irreconcilable
breakdown-while separation orders on fault grounds would plainly be inconsistent with the
non-fault approach of the Bill.
Fourthly, the Bill thoroughly overhauls the law on maintenance, and maintenance as
between husband and wife is put on an equal footing. Maintenance will not be paid except in
accordance with the principles in Part V of the Bill, or such other law as is not inconsistent
with those principles. During marriage there will be a right to maintenance if the effects of
the marriage result in an incapacity to meet reasonable needs, and in certain other limited
circumstances. After dissolution there will be a temporary right to maintenance if the effects
of the marriage result in an incapacity to meet reasonable needs. The right to maintenance


## p. 4283 (#763) ###########################################

6 October
4283
Family Proceedings Bill
may be extended if, having regard to the ages of the parties and the duration of the marriage,
it is unreasonable for the dependent party to maintain himself or herself. Misconduct will be
irrelevant to the question of maintenance unless the misconduct has been gross and palpable.
No person shall be required to pay maintenance to a spouse of such an amount as to deprive
him, or dependent members of his household, of a reasonable standard of living. With
regard to the variation of maintenance orders clause 93 of the Bill substitutes more flexible
criteria, which direct the court's attention to the principles of maintenance set out in Part V.
Fifthly, the Bill makes special provision for the Department of Social Welfare to apply
ex parte—that is, without notice to the respondent-to a registrar of a court for a family
maintenance order in cases where a domestic purposes benefit or emergency maintenance
allowance is being paid. The application will specify the amount claimed, and the registrar
must make the order if he is satisfied that the respondent is the husband, wife; or parent of
the beneficiary. A dissatisfied respondent may file an appeal or application for rehearing
and, pending a hearing, may apply ex parte to the registrar for variation or suspension of the
order. The registrar may grant relief if good cause is shown. A family maintenance order will
expire after 6 months unless sooner discharged.
Sixthly, the offence of wilful disobedience of a maintenance order is abolished. Clauses
115 to 117 substitute an inquiry before a registrar as to the reaons for default followed by
further steps to obtain enforcement of the maintenance order. The attachment of wages will
be facilitated by a provision that where a person defaults on payment of maintenance for
more than 14 days he shall be liable to automatic attachment of his wages.
Seventhly, Part VII contains new provisions that will enable the Government to become
party to the United Nations Convention for the Recovery of Maintenance Abroad, if it so
decides. This would assist New Zealand residents to obtain maintenance from persons
residing outside the country.
Eighthly, the first schedule to the Bill makes three main changes to the Guardianship
Act 1978. There is to be a clear statement that neither parent is to be preferred as the
custodial parent by reason only of the sex of the parent. There is to be a new offence of
deliberate and of unreasonable obstruction of access to a child. Finally, section 16 is
expanded to allow grandparents, uncles and aunts, and brothers and sisters of a child to be
granted access to that child if a parent is not making use of the right of access.
These eight points touch on the major areas where the Bill differs from existing law.
There are, of course, many other differences of detail which do not require comment at this
stage. I believe the Bill represents a major step forward in the important area of family law,
and I now want to throw the Bill open to the widest possible public discussion and comment.
Therefore, I shall be moving at the appropriate time that the Bill be referred to the Statutes
Revision Committee for recess study.

VALEDICTORY
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That this House do now adjourn.
As is usual in an election year, there have been some lively exchanges in this session of
Parliament, but this is, after all, a debating chamber. Members must be expected to express
their minds, if, of course, they have minds to express. All round, however, I think it has been
a fairly smooth session, that is, up until the last few weeks, when the Opposition's reaction to
the introduction of the supplementary estimates was such that the debate was extended over
2 days and spread over nearly 24 hours in total. This was unprecedented. I suggest it is a
matter to which the Standing Orders Committee might give attention, because in the past the
House considered the supplementary estimates and, indeed, estimates, as items of
expenditure that had to be justified rather than an occasion for general debate on the topics
covered by the particular estimates.
It is my considered view, and I say this in an entirely non-partisan manner, that we are
departing from the constitutional parliamentary process of voting money to the Crown when
we use the occasion of the estimates and the supplementary estimates for a general all-round
debate on policy and the affairs of a particular department of State. I believe that the select
committee, which will consider the Standing Orders next year, should consider returning to
what was the case previously, that on estimates we discuss in detail the reasons why the
Crown requires the money provided in those estimates. In recent years we have certainly not
given proper scrutiny to those reasons, and instead have embarked on lengthy and
occasionally acrimonious policy-type debate. [Interruption.] It is customary on valedictories
for members to behave in a slightly different manner from the way in which they have
behaved during the remainder of the session. It appears that this is another custom that will
be broken this morning by the Junior Opposition Whip, who has broken so many of the well-
tried customs of the House during this session.
I was about to say that this has been a smooth session, but I am bound to say, in the light
of the interruption we have just had, that when the Leader of the Opposition, at the
beginning of the session, called for a better standard of behaviour in the House I readily
responded, but I expressed doubts considering the man he had appointed as the Junior


## p. 4286 (#766) ###########################################

4286
6 October
Valedictory
Opposition Whip. Those doubts were well founded. This session will go down as one in
which one of the most junior members of the House did the most damage to parliamentary
traditions, and indeed to the undertaking given by his leader. I do not know whether he is
proud of that, but he certainly has no cause to be.
The session began with a new Speaker, whom we have all found to be firm and fair. He
is well established in the respect of all members, as he was when Acting Speaker in 1977. The
new Chairman of Committees and Deputy Speaker had a fairly noisy passage in the early
stages, due to his good nature. His good nature was not ruffled, and he moved gradually and
quietly to assert himself. While the Acting Speaker, during the fortnight's absence of Mr
Speaker, he was by the second week well in command.
During the fourth session of the thirty-eighth Parliament the House has sat on 87 days
extending over 5 months. The third session last year lasted nearly 7 months and covered 118
days. Select committees of the House began sitting on 31 January, and by the time the
session began in May they had met 45 times. Since then they have met 223 times. As
members of the House know, committee hearings during the session occupy the mornings of
most members, which turns their day into a working morning, noon, and night. No one can
deny that this is a strain, yet there are those who would deny members of Parliament a fair
reward. From time to time one hears criticism about the calibre of members. The
responsibility for that--and I do not concede it to be a criticism-that can be too widely
levelled-rests with those who selected them as candidates and in turn those who voted them
into Parliament. There may be some who visualise the ideal Parliament as a place full of
highly qualified academics and theorists. It will be a sad day for the country if the House ever
lacks a leavening of good practical men with their feet on the ground, with an acquaintance
with the facts of an unsheltered, uncloseted life, and with a record of success in a competitive
world, whether it be professional, industrial, farming, trade, or other occupation.
This year the Government was in the happy position of having already put most of its
election promises on the statute book. As a result, few controversial Bills have been
introduced. During the session the Government introduced 75 public Bills and the Statutes
Amendment Bill, which was later divided into 50 small Bills, to correct minor items in
existing legislation. Last year the grand total of public Bills was 118, with an additional 50
arising from the Statutes Amendment Bill. I do wish the news media would not lump them
all together and give a grand total of Bills passed through Parliament, including the many
amendments in the Statutes Amendment Bill. It gives a totally false picture of the amount of
legislation passed. Properly these two items should be kept separate-the Statutes
Amendment Bill being merely the tidying up of totally non-controversial matters that have
been revealed in the various statutes.
Ten local Bills were passed this session, and 16 were passed last year. This year 17 private
members' Bills were introduced, more than three times last year's total. I am bound to say
some of the pressure, in terms of time, that came on the session towards the end resulted
from two things-private members' Bills and motions to adjourn the House. Thirty Bills
were referred to select committees, the hearings on 24 being open to the news media.
The House sat for 471 hours before midnight, 76 hours after 10.30 p.m., and 62 hours
after midnight. I believe I am correct in saying that when the House remained on the air until
midnight last night it was the first time for 6 years that it had occurred, other than for purely
formal purposes. It did not occur during the term of the Labour Government, and this was
the first time during the term of the present Government. Last year's hours of sitting before
midnight totalled 679, and the House sat for 67 hours after 10.30 p.m. It sat for 60 hours after
midnight. The sitting hours for this session have been about 200 fewer than last year. It is
traditional to include such figures in valedictory speeches, but because of changing
circumstances and different political realities during the passing years statistics can give a
distorted and unrealistic picture of Parliament.
This morning on the radio I heard one of those left-wing academics to which Radio New
Zealand gives so much time. He mentioned how members should run the business of
Parliament and pass legislation. These people are given time to discuss matters of which they
have no knowledge. I wonder whether we are wasting money paying salaries to those people
in their ivory towers. This morning we were told that things were much better when the
country had a second Chamber. I pulled out at random a volume of Hansard and found that
in 1903, when we had a second Chamber, the House sat for no fewer than 191 hours after
midnight, and that was not the record. In those days the hours of sitting after midnight were
no better. I venture to suggest that, in terms of rushed legislation, most of this session's


## p. 4287 (#767) ###########################################

6 October
4287
Valedictory
legislation has been of an amending nature. What the academic apparently failed to
appreciate is that most of the topics dealt with in the last week or two had already been dealt
with at great length by other procedures. Many people think that what is done in the
Chamber is the whole legislative process. It is not, as members well know. Bills such as the
Transport Amendment Bill (No. 3)—that is, the Bill on road safety-and the Misuse of
Drugs Bill had been for many months, indeed years, in the hands of members. The Road
Safety Bill has been in the hands of both sides of the House and the Misuse of Drugs Bill has
been in the hands of members on this side of the House, getting very close and detailed
scrutiny before they came into the House.
The same applies to other legislation. The vexed Bill on industrial law reform was
debated in the Chamber several times before it was introduced. The subject was debated at
great length, and members were thoroughly familiar with it before it came into the Chamber.
That is a factor that many of those self-appointed amateur reformers of the parliamentary
process totally fail to understand—that work on legislation continues outside the Chamber.
It is quite wrong to think that the legislating is done totally in this Chamber.
I want to make particular reference to one or two items of legislation. The Misuse of
Drugs Amendment Act provides, among other things, for more severe penalties for those
engaged in the pernicious drug trade. Similarly, the Transport Amendment Act (No. 3)
includes higher penalties for drunken drivers. The Marine Mammals Act will safeguard
whales, seals, and other mammals in New Zealand waters. A further step in the amendment
and consolidation of local authorities was taken with the passing of the Local Government
Amendment Act. That is another case when work was done in a select committee rather
than in this Chamber. This line of action will be continued next year. Regulations affecting
Maori affairs have been codified by a Bill passed this session. A New Zealand Film
Commission was set up by legislation this session, marking a forward step in the domestic
film industry. All the Acts I have mentioned have been put through with a minimum of
contention.
Although the strain has been heavy in the last week or so, the session overall has been
light. While I have personally attracted a good deal of attention and personal attack, in so far
as it is possible to contain it within the rules of the House there is nothing overcritical to say
about behaviour in general, apart from the one comment I made earlier in my speech. In this
respect I am grateful to the Leader of the Opposition for his quiet unassuming role, which is
so much in contrast to that of one or two of his less mature colleagues.
It is a time-honoured custom to make some comment about the men and women who
help this House to run smoothly and efficiently. At the head is the Clerk of the House, and it
follows that if the leadership at that level is courteous to all, regardless of their position, then
others take their cue from that example. I have noticed the considerable use being made of
the executive wing foyer and reception hall in the Beehive. An estimated 10 000 people of all
ages have been entertained there this year as guests of members of Parliament-who, I
might say, meet the expenses incurred-and of the Government. We have had parties of
constituents, many from outside Wellington. I pay particular tribute to the member for
Palmerston North in that respect. He must have created an all-time record, and one that will
be very hard to beat. Book-launching ceremonies, school parties, farewells to bands,
welcomes to visiting footballers, and State luncheons: in all these the Manager of Bellamy's,
Mr Frank Sumner, and his staff have acquitted themselves really well. Visitors have had the
opportunity of acquainting themselves with what can be prepared by or under the
supervision of a chef like Mr Joe Pereira. Heads of Governments and school children alike
are well catered for according to the nature of the occasion.
The Hansard staff have had a particularly trying time recently. I pay a tribute to them
for the way in which they have carried on during the very long sittings. Members can come
and go, and go to their rooms to sleep—indeed, it appears some, in quite considerable
numbers, can go home-but the Hansard staff have to stay on the job. They have to be here
when they are required. We put a great burden on them. I pay a very sincere tribute to them
for the manner in which they have carried out their duties, particularly during the past 3
weeks. The messengers continue to do their bit. Many of them have seen many members and
Governments come and go. The General Assembly Library is there to assist members, and
its staff do just that cheerfully and competently. The outside staff do such a fine job with the
grounds that on warm days, at least, hundreds of people get great pleasure from relaxing on
the lawns. I wish more would come inside and see Parliament at work. Our Post Office, a

I leave until last the Minister of Labour, who came in with me in 1960 and who has been
a close personal friend ever since. Among those who have served in Parliament in our time,
there is indeed no man who is held in higher regard by the public, quite apart from his
parliamentary colleagues. He also is retiring prematurely for health reasons, and he also will
have other tasks to do for his country. As the Minister of Labour in recent years, and before
that as Minister of Transport, he was the man who succeeded in everything he turned his
hand to, simply because of his transparent integrity and honesty. I know that in the trade
union movement particularly that attribute has enabled him to do things that another
Minister would have found impossible.

Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): Looked at over a 3-year period
this Parliament has been a sad, and in some cases rather sick, institution. Too often in that
period have issues given way to personalities, something that is reflected in the considerable
public disillusionment with Parliament--and any member of the House, irrespective of
political opinion, who does not recognise that deludes himself.
The problem has undoubtedly been compounded by the actions of the Government,
particularly the kind of action that has been evidenced this week. In his comments the Prime
Minister talked about the customs of the House and the breaching of them. It is a fact that
customs have been breached on too many occasions, and certainly by those who ought to
have given more concern to the status of the institution.
Perhaps the most recent incident in that respect is the announcement that the
parliamentary session would be concluded within 24 hours, when, in fact, it has always been
the practice to give at least a week's notice. So Parliament has found itself concluding its
formalities for the parliamentary term at the end of a week that saw on Tuesday no less than
36 Bills on the Order Paper, 17 Bills subsequently being referred back from select
committees, all having to be put through all stages. Three more Bills have been introduced
and passed through all stages in the course of the 3 sitting days, and it is little wonder that
under these circumstances there is a lessening of public respect for both the institution and
the laws that are passed.
We all recognise that it is not possible to pass adequate laws under such circumstances. I
make a point that has been made on many occasions: that a great deal could have and should
have been avoided by a much more sensible spread of the parliamentary session. But that is
something that the Government, or he who purports to represent the Government, has
decided against. The Prime Minister made a comment about the extension of radio hours. I
would not like to let that pass unremarked, because the comment happens to be wrong. He
said that radio hours had not been extended, as far as he knew, for a 6-year period-
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Other than formal business.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING:-for other than formal business. In fact, radio hours were
extended on 10 October 1975 for a period of 9 hours and 27 minutes beyond the normal
broadcasting hours of the House. That, of course, was the last opportunity the previous
Administration had for extending the broadcasting hours. I refer the Government to
Hai sard, Volume 402, at page 5399. The public will expect and deserve something rather
better from the next Parliament.

from the inside, and the Police had left some of those on the outside. That is something that
the public will reflect on. The Parliamentary Counsel often go unremarked on, but they have
an incredibly difficult and exacting role during the parliamentary session. During the session
Hansard reporters showed both a personal and a public reaction to the long sitting hours of
the House. In their own way they not only endeavoured to properly protect their own health

Catholics. After consulting the local police sergeant and, since I am a Presbyterian, the
Presbyterian minister of the area-which was not close to me—and a distinguished member
of Federated Farmers, I fought tooth and nail, and succeeded in getting the adoption
through just before Christmas. Then I had to get the baby flown down in the cockpit behind
"Mudguts" Pirie in an NAC DC3, to get it there in time for Christmas. I watched with
satisfaction as that child grew to a worthy New Zealander in a caring home.
Of all the decision making in ministerial portfolios, I believe the toughest test on myself
was the decision to extend Rongotai Airport in 1970. Here I acted against the advice of most
departmental officers, civil aviation experts so-called, and, initially, most of my colleagues. I
was told that it was not possible to get an instrument-landing system at Rongotai, and I was
certainly told it was not possible to get a four-engined jet in.
After some somewhat turbulent flying at Kaitak, which is in Hong Kong, with a four-
engined Convair 999, the decision was made to extend Rongotai. Rongotai now has an
instrument-landing system on runway 18 to the south, and I believe my personal decision has
been justified by the fact that the regularity of the DC8s is just on 2 percent above that
projected when I made the estimates and took the decision. The frequency is close on double
that which Air New Zealand told me would make it economic to come in, and I have a letter
in my safe telling me DC8s could operate till 1982 on the basis of the forecasts made in 1969.
It may surprise a few to learn that one man stood with me in that intense area of decision
making—and I presume I can break this rule-my then leader -now the Governor-General.
I must add as a parting and personal thought that Rongotai should be extended again—and I
expect to get a pin in the left side of me fairly shortly. After all, no matter what figures are
used-and my cobber, Harry Lapwood, at the back has got a real boomer-it would cost less
than the price of one single aeroplane; yet we talk about orphan aeroplanes. But that would
be an interesting comparison to make after my relatively accurate assessment on one of the
major decisions I made that came out correctly. I believe it should be extended—when and
how, I leave to my successors. I also leave the contentious 737 versus BAC 1-11 decision to
historians. That might also record a certain degree of difference between my Prime Minister
and myself!
Thrust unwillingly into the tremendous change of the Labour portfolio, I look back
much more morosely. The challenges are there, challenges that should inspire, challenges
that should be completed, and challenges I reluctantly leave to my unenvied successor. The
one satisfaction I have had has been the establishment of the Industrial Relations
Foundation, and the privilege of announcing the first Prince Philip overseas scholarships in
human relations, largely overlooked-regrettably-by the press, by the people, and by the
unions; one that must grow, and one that has got to grow if people are to understand
industrial relations in their broadest aspects.
I sincerely hope that my short and enforced abbreviated tenure of office has allowed
some more understanding between humans in the field of industrial or human relations. In
this role I have preached—and it is not my normal manner to do so-innumerable sermons
on communication, mutual trust, and respect. Regrettably, their extent has been
immeasurable, and I do not take the statistics of the last 2 days as being any indicator;
indeed, the economy has had a great role to play in the number of man-days lost.
Whether history will show that there has been a hardening of attitudes surrounding the
Labour portfolio-even tougher than they were before-is a moot point. I merely suggest
that New Zealanders should exercise their democratic rights in a responsible way, especially
on the industrial scene. That applies as much to managers as it does to union officials and the
workers who make decisions at stopwork meetings or on strike ballots. Unless they do so, we
will have a continuation of the crisis-to-crisis saga of the past 3 years—and I believe it has
gone on even longer. If New Zealanders can exercise that responsibility on 25 November and
support everybody standing for the House, apart from retiring members, surely they can do
so at their monthly meetings-whether they are union meetings or meetings of boards of
directors.
A rather saddening matter, which my colleague the Minister of Social Welfare has seen

My name is Paddy Blanchfield, I represent West Coast;
I know it is an honour, of which I'm proud to boast.
I've mixed with men of stature and some-all froth and foam;
Now far off mountains beckon and Westland calls me home.

We wonder how you feel about retiring as M.P.,
My answer is I've made my mark, with eloquence and "Poem”,

We'll bow to Mr Speaker and sadly turn the page;
I shan't forget these members, as south my footsteps roam,

When nerves are frayed and tempers displayed,
Sure it's just like living in hell;
Yet I'll miss all my fiery colleagues who fight like gladiators of Rome;
'Cos the tree ferns shade and the peaceful glade
Whisper, "Paddy, it's time to come home"
Yes, for 18 years I've laboured, and built my reputation
For helping needy Coasters; now here's my invitation
To all my sterling colleagues who buzz in Beehive's dome,
Come visit me in Scenicland when West Coast calls me home.

Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): First, I should like to thank all my
colleagues for their kind remarks today, and to express appreciation to the colleagues I have
served with and who are going out with me today: the Minister of Labour, Peter Gordon; the
Minister of Tourism, Harry Lapwood; and my old fiend, Paddy, from the West Coast. We all
came here the same day, and are all going out the same day. I must say how delighted we are
to see Paddy back in the Chamber, if only to say farewell. I should like also to express my
appreciation to other members who are retiring: the member for Henderson, the member
for St. Albans, the member for Marlborough, and the member for Taupo. The member for
Henderson and I spent a few days overseas recently, and I shall be referring to that a little
later. The member for St. Albans, the Opposition spokesman on defence—what a grand
man he is. I could confide in him about anything, knowing that he would always hold the
required security. The member for Marlborough, as chairman of the Defence Committee,
has been of great help to me. With his great capabilities, it is very sad to see him go.
During the 18 years I have been in the House I have made many friends. Although
differing in our political views, we can sometimes co-exist peacefully. The member for
Henderson and I spent a very peaceful 10 days in Germany last month, and my wife and I
appreciated very much the company of Martyn and Peg. I do not think we talked politics at
all there, but I do thank him for the assistance he gave me at that conference. When I first
entered this Chamber I shared a bench in the overflow over there with my friend, Duncan
MacIntyre, now Minister of Agriculture, and later I had the pleasure for some years of
sharing a bench with our Governor-General. It is a great pity I was not at Kinloch to hold
that ladder for him, because then he might not have had that sojurn in Taupo Hospital.
During my period here I have served under three leaders of the National Party, all with
different personalities: Sir Keith Holyoake, Sir John Marshall, and now the Rt. Hon. Rob
Muldoon-all great men, all born leaders. It has been my privilege to serve them loyally
throughout my term of office. I have always given my full loyalty to whoever has been the
leader. I have seen many changes in names of electorates. As a case in point, although I have
lived in the same house, I have been in three differently named electorates in the past 6
years. No wonder the Prime Minister had some difficulty in remembering what electorate I
represented, because sometimes I have had to think myself what it was.
As many members know, I followed my late father-in-law into this House. He served
the people for 14 years, and I have served them for 18 years. That means the family has
served the district for 32 years; it is a long time. It is interesting also to note that during my
period in the House I have seen 93 members come and go; 32 have retired, 27 have been
defeated, and 34 have passed away. It has been a pleasure for me to represent the district
that has returned me on the last six occasions. This will be the first election campaign in 24
years in which I shall not be competing and asking for support, but I shall be asking for
support for some of my colleagues. No member of Parliament can be a success without the
assistance of his wife. My wife has always given me her help and her time unstintingly, and, I
am proud to say, on many occasions her advice. My retirement will give her a richly deserved
break.
Many thanks go to many people in this building. I thank my private secretaries, who
have given me loyal service. I want to mention Bryce Gapes, Maurice Corkery, Joan
Farrance, Paul Sinclair, Campbell Pope, Martin Proffitt, and Jim D'Ath. I would not like
people to think I have a team of private secretaries as large as that. Those are the people who
served me in the different portfolios I have held since I have been in Cabinet. I thank my
typists, Barbara Duthie, Eileen Brennan, and Rona Billens. Rona comes in every morning
to tell me what the weather is like at Trentham. I doubt what she says sometimes, because I

say thank you.

I should like to mention one incident in my life. Many years ago I lived in a very small

when the postmaster made me so angry I said to one of the boys outside, "When I become
Postmaster-General the first so-and-so I sack will be old Wilson." Forty years later when I
became Postmaster-General the first telegram I received was, "Congratulations. You may
now sack the boss. Don Wilson." We talk about tough bosses; he was the toughest boss I
ever had. When I look back over the years I think he did me more good than anybody I
know. A little discipline does everybody the world of good, and I think therein lies much of
the problem we face today. People are not receiving discipline, and when someone tries to
administer it to them they do not like it.
I am leaving this House with the greatest of satisfaction. I want to say, in regard to my

family support I have enjoyed. There is little need to elaborate on what has been said, other
than to say that I have been fortunate enough to have had this in full measure. I do really
appreciate and publicly acknowledge that.
Custom dictates that on this occasion those who are departing voluntarily, as
distinguished from those who are doing so with great reluctance and resentment—and whose
lamentations go unheard and representations unheeded-should mark their severance with
some kind of oratorical flourish. I must say that I do not greatly relish the opportunity of
doing so, and would have gladly faded quietly and gently into the background. However,
convention looms large in our activities, and one must bow to it. I relish still less the habit of
embroidering the remarks made with poetic embellishment. I propose none the less to
conform in all respects, although I have absolutely no desire to emulate my distinguished
colleague who sits in front of me-the member for West Coast. What one says on this
occasion is supposed to be weighty and to convey a message. That is a difficult task to
perform without being pompous or pretentious, or both.
I propose to seek refuge in the inspired versification of another. My approach to the
principles and practice of politics, or political life at any rate, has been to be wary of labels,
slogans, capsules, or "isms"-as the Americans call them. I believe they mislead much more
than they inform. For guidance and as a philosophy, if that is not too grand a word, I have
turned repeatedly, not to textbooks or dogma but to Thomas Grey's deeply moving and
profoundly understanding "Elegy". To sit, as I have done, in Stoke Poges graveyard and
read it aloud has brought tears to my eyes and a greater comprehension of what government
is all about than any academic or professional pundit has ever been able to convey. Such
lines as these are sobering, deflating, and salutary:
The boast of heraldry, the pomp of power,
And all that beauty, all that wealth e'er gave,
Await alike th' inevitable hour,
The paths of glory lead but to the grave.
Some village Hampden, that with dauntless breast
The little tyrant of his fields withstood;
Some mute, inglorious Milton here may rest,
Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood.
Let not ambition mock their useful toil,
Their homely joys and destiny obscure;
Nor grandeur hear with a disdainful smile,
The short and simple annals of the poor.
I believe that last line to be one of the most moving lines in all poetry, and I am not
surprised that General Wolfe, who was instrumental in saving Canada for what was then the
British Empire against the onslaughts of the French, claimed that he would rather have
composed those lines than have conquered Quebec. It is by these sentiments, tempered with
the pragmatic reasoning of such as James K. Galbraith-now fashionable through TV, but
long a mentor of mine--that I have tried, not always successfully, to practise the profession
of politics.
One other nugget of wisdom that I offer to those colleagues whom I shall be leaving
comes from a man I was honoured to regard as a friend, as well as a teacher-Professor
Harold Laski, who is portrayed by many, and to many, as a wild revolutionary, but who was
in fact a firm and dogged constitutionalist. He said, "Men"-and I suppose in these sexless
days it should be "People"-"who live differently think differently." Without embracing the
whole geographic and ethnic spectrum that Kipling claimed to embrace-one is tempted to
say, when considering the inability or, at any rate, the unwillingness of the rich nations to
relieve the increasing poverty of the poor developing world, that North is North and South is
South, and never the twain shall meet.
Leaving that kind of thing aside, I should like to give an illustration of the kind of
misunderstanding that can arise from different ways of life by citing this quotation that came
to my notice recently: "For the middle class, the Police protect property, give directions, and
help old ladies. For the urban poor, the Police are those who arrest you." I say that because
we have to remind ourselves time and time again that the language we use in the House,
whether by exchange of words here or by putting them into Acts of Parliament, does not
always mean to others what it means to us. Indeed, we do not always succeed in saying or
conveying in words exactly what we do intend them to mean. The aphorism that those who
live differently think differently, expresses, I believe, a profound truth.
One final word of warning-one that I believe is timely as the electors brace themselves


## p. 4299 (#779) ###########################################

6 October
4299
Valedictory
for their triennial participation in the democratic process-and that is this: that any politician
or any aspiring politician who claims to know all the answers, is deluding himself and the
public. It is enough, at any rate for a start, to know the right questions to ask. The only claim
I make with certainty and honesty after 18 years' practice of the art or craft of politics is that I
believe that I am better equipped to ask the questions which, hopefully, may lead to the right
answers to the truths one is seeking.
So much then for theory. I turn now for a moment to practice. From time to time, there
has been criticism of the Standing Orders, and I note that a committee has again been set up
to review them. That is a useful exercise, but for my part I think that the committee should
comprise not only members of Parliament but also an outsider. I think the fresh untainted
vision that he would bring to the deliberations would be useful. But, in the absence of that, I
am disappointed to find that the committee is made up entirely of senior members-those
who have become indoctrinated and inured to the practices of the House. I think it would be
a worth-while innovation if at least one first-termer were included on the committee. There
is, however, less need to reform our Standing Orders than to reform ourselves. The fatuity
and the futility that are so manifest in respect of many of our proceedings need no comment,
but I believe, as the Minister of Labour indicated, that they are no worse than those of most
Legislatures I have witnessed, and better than some. The truth is, it is the. nature of
politicians to bend the rules, and, however firm we make them, there will always be attempts
to bend them; and, indeed, there are some who believe they exist simply to be broken.
One other aspect of the Standing Orders and parliamentary practice generally that does
trouble me is the ease and speed with which we can and do legislate. Without subscribing
entirely to Mentesquieu's doctrine as to the division of powers and the checks and balances
upon which the American system is based, I am more and more convinced of the need for a
mandatory built-in braking mechanism. We have these features, which are not common
elsewhere. First, we have a single chamber; secondly, we have little, if any, constitutional
restraint; thirdly, an unfettered right is conferred on the Government to settle the Order
Paper and to determine the order of business; fourthly, the Government is empowered to
take urgency and ram Bills through the House from go to whoa-indeed, from go to woe!—
all in a single sitting; and, finally, we have the mechanism of the closure, generally unknown
elsewhere at any rate, in the way in which we have it. No would-be dictator could ask for
more, and Hitler overthrew the Weimar Republic with much less.
The power all this gives to a Government to extend its term or even perpetuate itself is
frightening. Our accepted convention is that the British political system, like the common
law, is perfection itself, but we have much to learn from others and from the variants of
parliamentary democracy to be found in the United States and Western Europe. In
particular, I believe we could as a whole, compensate for some of our much criticised antics
in the open House by giving more standing, dignity, and, indeed, more power, to
parliamentary committees. The committees of the United States Congress, both of the
Senate and the House, enjoy an esteem that is denied to ours, and this I think is largely due
to their more extensive jurisdictions. This could well extend in New Zealand to much of the
work we now entrust to commissions of inquiry. If members of Parliament lack the expertise
of those appointed to such commissions, they go far to make up for it by the sound common
sense they usually display when acting collectively.
There is, however, a mounting misconception that could undermine this potentiality. I
have been disturbed in the last 3 years to hear criticism levelled at Opposition members for
speaking and acting in the Chamber in a manner different from their conduct in a committee.
I believe this criticism reveals a failure to grasp the nature of the Opposition's role. Its job in
the House is to resist or delay, by all means at its command, the passage of legislation its
members think harmful to the country. In a committee, however, Opposition members
should reconcile themselves to the inevitable and accept the fact that the Government's
majority must ultimately prevail and its proposals carry the day. Opposition there ceases to
be fruitful, and destructive criticism should give way to constructive suggestions, making the
best of a bad job. Similarly, there is a responsibility on Government members in a committee
to regard the rights of minorities and consider reasonable concessions.
One other factor that militates against an optimum use of committees and their
maximum public acceptance is our constant changing of their membership. It is little use
asking a committee to investigate and report on a matter, whether it is a Bill, the activities of
a Government department, or whatever, if its personnel varies from day to day and members
who have heard today's submissions will not be available to compare or contrast them with


## p. 4300 (#780) ###########################################

4300
6 October
Valedictory
the views to be aired tomorrow.
It pleases me greatly that in a committee one can to a very considerable extent put aside
party affiliation, and all members can work co-operatively. That is not to imply that I
disapprove of the party system-I do not. It works clumsily, sometimes tediously, and often
offensively, but it works-with better and much greater human satisfaction than any
conceivable substitute. If it trivialises issues, the news media are equally to blame, because it
is the triviality, the heated words, the insults, that catch the headlines, and not the serious
work that Parliament does sometimes dedicate itself to. In determining its priorities, in
emphasising some of our activities, but downplaying or overlooking others, no doubt the
news media are giving the public what it wants, and so we turn the full circle. The truth is
that Parliament is a microcosm, a reflecting mirror of society-and so it should be. If we, the
people, do not like what we see in it, it is time to turn away from the mirror and take a close
critical look at ourselves.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): First, I thank all those members who
have said nice kind things about me and ask those people who, over the past 18 years, have
claimed they would win the Rotorua seat to reflect on their claims and now consider the
worth of what they might have been thinking. I thank my family for all they have done in
supporting me as a member of Parliament. Our youngest daughter was 1 year old when I
came into the House. I did not know what politics was all about-and I still wonder what it is
all about. However, I thought I could fix the affairs of the country in a fortnight, but found it
would take a little longer.
I remember one occasion when my wife met me at the Rotorua Travel Centre after a
long all-night journey on the train. It was about 10.30 in the morning. She told me she had
been asked for directions to Whakatane by a stranger. After giving him directions he asked
who was the fellow who had recently been defeated in Rotorua. My wife gave the name. The
man said there had been much progress in the area under his guidance and said he did not
know the new bloke, but no doubt he was there to feather his own nest. I asked my wife what
she said in reply. In those days she did not have the temerity to make a retort, but she is a
little better trained now.
I recall my first two interviews as a new member. Strangely, they were over similar
issues. I told the first person I would take the matter up with the local department, and if I
was not satisfied I would take it up with my colleagues in Wellington. That was all right on
the first occasion. On the second occasion my young daughter, who had been listening, said,
"That was what you told the last man, Daddy." So daddy had to become a little more astute.
I joined a very good team of people under very fine leadership. I was told at a political
meeting by a very astute person that the definition of a politician was a chap who shook your
hand before an election and your confidence after it. All I can say is that the people in
Rotorua are mighty slow thinkers. I have seen some great improvements in parliamentary
procedure in the past 18 years. In earlier days the government took urgency for estimates on
Fridays. Members knew that the last train left at 7.30 p.m. The House then had all the
ingredients to give parliamentarians ulcers. One of the greatest improvements is the earlier
closing of Parliament on Friday--and I hope I shall be finished by 1 p.m.
I have met many characters in the past 18 years. I have mentioned train travel. Members
always had a sleeper. I was invariably put in a sleeper with an old colleague who could fix thẹ
affairs of the country if only he was given the speaking time. I would sleep in the bottom
bunk and he would sit on it and give me the answers. If I slept on the top bunk he would
stand and give me the answers. As a Whip I remember calling upon him to fill in in an
emergency, when the famous claim was made- "Let me give you the facts, and settle this
once and for all." I also recall a very heated debate when one of the then front-bench
Opposition members was going flat tap about what he thought was a very serious cause. An
interjection from one of the characters on this side of the House made the member stop. In
answer to the query from this side, "What has happened?" he said, "Something passed
through my mind." A voice from this side was heard to say, "There's nothing to stop it."
What a critical bunch!
I am told that the old system of selecting speakers in political campaigns was to draw
straws. The chap who got the long straw spoke first, and so it went until everyone had
spoken. On an occasion in Eħgland it was said that, of two characters standing for the one
seat, one was a renowned orator and the other was a complete raw rookie. The orator spoke

half right." So I lost again.
I praise the great friend of the nation, Rob Muldoon. It is a funny thing, you know, but

The highlight of my political career, I feel, is a pretty humble one. Years ago I was an
ordinary policeman on the beat, and one of the group that trained with me later got to the

time, I suppose! My great claim to fame was the fact that I have had the privilege of being

For those retiring, I am reminded of the story of the three old politicians reminiscing on

age, Joe, something has to go." He said, "It happened only last night. It was pension day,
and I went to the club and I had a few more drinks than I should have had. I went home, and

advice was, to say the least, overwhelming and indeed unanimous-that being that I must
relinquish many of my responsibilities, including that of being a member of Parliament. I
believe that this is an appropriate moment to apologise to my colleagues for the extra duties I
have placed on them because of my illnesses.

transcends the floor of the House.

not-is of the havoc the press can create through often irresponsible reporting. It can destroy
families. It can create tragedy, well beyond the imagination of people who read these
reports, let alone the authors of such documents. For a moment I should like to address
myself to all journalists, wherever they might be, working in whatever sections of the media
that handle news. Forgive me if the quotation I am about to give may not be exactly word
perfect, but it is that of one of the greatest politicians and leaders of men the world has ever
known-Sir Winston Churchill. Referring to the responsibilities of journalists as he saw
them, he said: "It is essential for the survival of democracy that the freedom of the press be
preserved, but it is that very freedom which, if abused, will create and contribute to the
destruction of democracy and, in turn, the free world."

Speaker: there is a subtle difference between "House" and "home". In the House at least I
usually have the last word; at home I have to share that privilege with several who are
younger than I.
I thank the Chairman of Committees, my deputy, for standing in so frequently for me,

advice to me. He said that during one of the State assemblies there had been a report of a
bomb scare. The Clerk approached the Speaker and said, "Mr Speaker, it has been reported

I thank the retiring members who have contributed to the debate. The contribution each

characters. I count all of them among my friends, and I deem it a great privilege and pleasure
to have been associated with them. It is sad to me, as I am sure it is to all honourable
members, that so many of them are retiring directly because of health, or indirectly for the

themselves but also on their wives and families. I feel privileged to have known the wives and
families of those members who are retiring, and I thank them for their contribution to the
work of their husbands. Anyone who doubts the toll that service in Parliament takes of a
member should walk along what is commonly called the "Speaker's corridor", look at the
photographs of members, and compare that of such-and-such a member in the last
Parliament with the photograph taken when that member came in 12, 15, or 18 years ago. I
believe that the visible ageing is far greater than it would have been had that member not
come here as a member of Parliament. New Zealand is all the richer for the services of those
members who are retiring. Parliament will be the poorer and the less colourful for their
going.
I thank all members for having elected me to represent them as their Speaker. It has
indeed been a great honour, and I thank those members who referred to it during the
debate. I thank the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, and their deputies.
Obviously, there have been occasions when we have had differences of opinion, but I think
they always deferred to the office of Speaker, if not to me, and I thank them for it. That is
the only way this Parliament, or indeed any Parliament,can perform satisfactorily. My wife
and I have been conscious of the fact that there have been deep differences in many cases
between members, and between Parliament and institutions and people outside Parliament.
For that reason my wife and I have attempted to bring together in our quarters here
members from all parties, and members together with people from outside Parliament, so
that there could be a beginning to a breaking down of the prejudices and the ignorance that
some people have about other people and other institutions. I have a feeling that we have
achieved something in that regard.
If we believe the editors-and, of course, most of us do-we recognise that the New
Zealand Parliament is not much different from that of any other Commonwealth country.
We are told that we are held in fairly low regard by the public. Certainly, that was one of the
messages that came through loud and clear to me at the Commonwealth Parliamentary
Association Conference in Kingston, Jamaica. Throughout the Commonwealth there is
criticism of the institution of Parliament and of its members. We are to have a Standing
Orders Committee; but changing the rules will not necessarily of itself improve the standard


## p. 4305 (#785) ###########################################

6 October
4305
Valedictory
of Parliament. I often think that the rugby union people who change the rules do not always
make a better game of football. So much depends on the players. Their attitude and their
understanding of the game are important. So I believe it is with Parliament.
Parliament's functions, as I see them, are, first, to provide the Executive. We are the
Legislature; we also provide the Executive. The second function is to scrutinise Government
policy; Government expenditure. The third function is to legislate, and that includes the
passing of legislation levying taxes. And the fourth function is to provide a forum for the
public discussion of important issues. I have a feeling that there has been a tendency for
Parliament to concentrate too much on the first-that is, the provision of the Executive-
and the last-that is, the provision of a forum for the public discussion of important issues. In
recent years-I am not particularly referring to this Parliament-there has been, in my
opinion, a tendency for Parliament not to be as effective as it should be on the scrutiny of
Government expenditure and policy and on the preparation of legislation.
My concern is for Parliament as an institution-the institution of the people in a
democracy, promoting their interests-and my concern is for the members of Parliament. If
Parliament is controversial, if its members are in that category at times, I believe that reflects
the community that sends the members here and the attitudes of that community. I invite
honourable members to read occasionally the letters to the editor columns, from which they
will see that often the writers of those letters concentrate not only on issues but also on
personalities. Perhaps it is not surprising, then, that that sometimes happens in this place.
Perhaps I could call on the Almighty to bless those departing and to make those
returning more faithful than before. Would I be considered biased if I were to wish all
members the success at the polls that they deserve and that they anticipate. Finally, I wish all
honourable members and their wives and families, and the staff that worked so devotedly for
Parliament, a merry Christmas and a happy New Year.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I would not want the debate to conclude

so that the valedictory speeches, which concluded at 10.27 p.m. on that Friday, could be
broadcast. I thank the National Party research staff for again giving me correct information.
Motion agreed to.
