4.
Development Capital Expenditure-Broadcasting Portfolio (21/9/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Broadcasting: What
is the total amount of development-related expenditure on building, construction,
and capital equipment in each of the geographical regions relevant to his port-
folio in the years ending 31 March 1976, 1977, 1978, and 1979?


## p. 4309 (#789) ###########################################

6 October
4309
Questions and Replies
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: I am advised
by the BCNZ that it would have very great difficulties in providing meaningful
and reliable figures on the expenditure the honourable member is seeking. Records
of expenditure on the items sought are not compiled in terms of geographical
areas, and to obtain even approximations would involve a considerable number
of man-hours of research, even if a clear indication of what constitutes the
geographical boundaries could be supplied. The corporation has also indicated
that such expenditure in broadcasting terms can overlap geographical areas, such
as television transmission systems, the benefit of the development of which can
extend to more than one geographical area. The question is in a similar category
to that asked by the honourable member for Roskill earlier this month when he
sought expenditure figures for Auckland. On that occasion I was advised by the
BCNZ that it was unable to isolate in its accountancy system the true expenditure
for this area alone. To illustrate the problem, it was pointed out that a television
service operation is on a network basis for the whole country, and the BCNZ
did not have a complete breakdown of specific area costs.

9.
Alcohol and Cigarette Tax-Allocation to Education (21/9/78)
Department
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Education: What
amount has been allocated to his department from the alcohol and cigarette tax
this financial year, and what is the nature of the projects on which the funds
will be expended?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: An amount of $90,000
was approved for inclusion in the 1978-79 estimates. That amount is to be spent
on: (a) The provision of additional specialised teaching equipment for handi-
capped children who need special education. This will either be supplied direct
to special schools and classes, e.g., specially designed calculators for blind children,
or held in district pools for use as may be needed, e.g. electric typewriters for
physically handicapped pupils in ordinary classes. (b) The development of proto-
type modular school furniture for use by seriously physically handicapped
children.

(21/9/78)

Railway Seats, Wellington
(21/9/78)
5. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Railways: How
many seats are at present provided on Wellington carriage trains actually in
service, and how many will be provided by the new units when they enter service?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railwavs) replied: At present a
total of 3485 seats are provided in the carriages allocated to Wellington, although
the number can vary from day to day depending on carriage availability. The
new multiple units will have seating for 6336 passengers. The increase in capacity
will be utilised to permit a reorganisation and overall improvement of the Welling-
ton suburban train services.

15.
TV2 Reception-Lyttelton Electorate
(21/9/78)
Mr KIRK (Sydenham) to the Minister of Broadcasting: Will he publish
the sections of the works programme of South Pacific Television that establish
that the member for Lyttelton was successful in obtaining TV2 reception for
almost 5000 of her constituents 2 years ahead of time, as stated in a full-page
advertisement by the Lyttelton National Party in the Observer, a Christchurch
bi-monthly newspaper?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: No, I cannot
publish the sections of the works programme of South Pacific Television. As I
indicated in the debate on the Broadcasting estimates, the works programme of
the BCNZ does not itemise the works for individual translators which it installs
for the expansion of television services. Such works, for both TV1 and TV2, are
covered by a bulk amount which for 1976-77 was $92,000 and for 1977-78 was
$150,000. As for the Lyttelton advertisement, I can say that the original plan-
ning date of 1976 for the Redcliffs - Sumner area was seriously delayed on several
occasions, first because of town planning objections involving a shift in site,
replanning, and different equipment requirements, and then by further environ-
mental difficulties. The energetic representations, throughout the period, by the
member for Lyttelton, helped ensure the completion of the project earlier than
would otherwise have been the case.
16.
Primary Schools-Special Educational Needs
(21/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: How are
special educational needs defined for the purpose of allocation of additional
staff to primary schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The allocation of
additional staff to primary schools for special educational needs is based on the
following criteria: (a) Schools with special needs resulting from English being
the second language for a significant proportion of the pupils. (b) Schools with
special needs resulting from the socio-economic status of the pupils and the local
community. (c) Schools with special needs resulting from particular staffing
problems. (d) Any other special needs which affect the function of the school.
17.
Primary Schools-Special Education Staff Cuts
(21/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: In the years
1976, 1977, and 1978, which primary schools had cuts in the number of additional
staff to which they were entitled for special educational needs, to what degree
has the staffing at each of these schools been cut back, and what were the rolls
of those schools in the years concerned?

4313
Questions and Replies
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: In the time available
for answering this question it would not be possible to make the far-reaching study
to provide the roll details for each of these schools. Staffing may change for a
variety of reasons, including changes in the roll either up or down and by changes
in the teacher-pupil ratio, such as occurred at the beginning of 1977. Another
complicating factor was the introduction of notional roll staffing in a selected
group of schools with exceptional special needs, also at the beginning of 1977.

28.
Kindergarten Construction, Camborne, Plimmerton
(22/9/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Education: What is the present
position regarding the new kindergarten to be erected in Camborne, Plimmerton,
and what delay is expected before the local association will be able to call
tenders for construction?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: It was not possible to
include the proposed kindergarten at Camborne, Plimmerton, in the 1978-79 pre-
school building programme because of other projects receiving higher priority.
The Paremata Free Kindergarten Association has received authority to prepare
plans for the new kindergarten, and planning is almost complete. This project
will be considered for inclusion in the 1979-80 pre-school building programme,
following discussions on priorities and needs with the New Zealand Free Kinder-
garten Union within the amount of finance allocated for pre-school purposes. If
the need and priority for the Camborne kindergarten is established and finance
is available within the amount allocated I would expect tenders to be called early
in the 1979-80 financial year.

Primary Teachers-Retraining Courses
(22/9/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: How many
of those primary teachers who have completed retraining courses since February
1977 are now in (a) permanent appointments, (b) relieving positions, (c) part-
time positions, and how many have not found employment?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The number of primary
teachers who have completed retraining courses since February 1977 is 587. Of
these, 106 are in permanent appointments, 310 are in relieving positions, and 90 are
in part-time positions. It is not known how many have not found employment. It
is known that 81 of the retrained teachers are not employed in State schools.

42.
Native Trees Logging-Whirinaki State Forest
(27/9/78
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Forests: In the light
of the fact that no management plan is available for Whirinaki State Forest nor any
completed surveys of wild life requirements or any opportunity for public com-
ment or submissions, on what basis was he able to make his decision to allow
logging of native trees to continue in the Whirinaki State Forest with only a
gradual reduction over the next 12 years?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The decision to allow logging
of native forest in Whirinaki State Forest to continue was based on the known
extent of the wood resource, the knowledge that adequate ecological and wildlife
reserves could be set aside, and the fact that sufficient information and experience
existed to suggest that areas zoned for production can be carefully selectively
logged to permit the subsequent regeneration and perpetuation of the forest. The
decision of the Government was not so much an option to continue logging, but
rather the announcement of a progressive reduction in indigenous logging to a
level only 17 percent of the present rate of cut over the next 12 years. A progressive
substitution with maturing exotic resources over that period will ensure a continua-
tion of employment and economic support for the workers and communities in the
area. This regional policy is entirely consistent with the Government's overall
indigenous forest management policy, and it was of necessity formulated in a
central North Island context rather than on a forest-by-forest basis. The public
will have an opportunity to have a say on the proposed management of the forest
when the board policy is expressed in a draft management plan and put out for
public comment.

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied:
I am aware that retailers have received advice of the price increases in question.
The extent of the price increases on this occasion and on the previous occasion
are shown below, as are the dates of the clearance by my department of the
present price increases. In many cases the clearance of the department was not
required, either because the manufacturers had a turnover less than $1,500,000
a year (these items are indicated thus*) or because the items are imported and
are priced by importers on the basis of the landed into-store cost plus the estab-
lished lawful profit margin (these items are indicated thus **). A treble asterisk
indicates the date on which increases were implemented, although these were
not notified to my department, and N.A. signifies that my department was unable
to acquire the information in the time available.

60.
Erosion Protection and Flood Control
(28/9/78)
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister for the Environment:
Has he seen the statement in the Evening Post of 22 August 1978 quoting him
and claiming that an enormous amount of money is devoted by the Government
to environmental protection through Government Departments-for example,
$8,321,000 for river control and land drainage and $5,136,000 for catchment
works; and, if so, how much of the $8,321,000 for river control and drainage and
$5,136,000 for catchment works was for erosion protection and flood control, two
problems associated directly with environmentally unsound land use and river
headwaters?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment) replied: The figures
quoted by the Minister for the Environment appear in vote: Ministry of
Works and Development for 1978-79 under Programme VIII, National Water
and Soil Conservation. Three items are recorded under the heading of "Catchment
Works":
Catchment works
River control and drainage works
Soil conservation works
$(000)
5,136
8,321
2,773
$16,230
Because such works are planned on a multipurpose basis it is, in fact, difficult
to separate out "erosion protection" and "flood control" aspects. However, in
broad terms, the first item "Catchment Works" covers large catchment schemes
generally in the upper areas of catchments. They have erosion control as a
principal objective. The item "Rivers Control and Drainage Works" covers
schemes in the lower parts of catchments. They generally have a very
large flood protection component. The item "Soil Conservation Works" covers
grants for implementing individual land management plans for farms in hill-
country areas. These have the principal objective of fostering sound land
use in such environmentally sensitive areas. It is misleading to suggest that the
need for erosion protection and flood control works in New Zealand stems
principally from unsound land use practices. Firm action has been taken in
recent years by the Government to control burning, overgrazing, and noxious
animals.
An equally important factor in our needs for erosion protection and flood control
is the pattern of farming and settlement that has evolved in New Zealand. For
example, the development of pasture in upland areas has increased run-off, thus
requiring the widening and straightening of rivers. Similarly, sustained production
from poorly drained land and from fertile river flats has often required extensive
drainage and flood protection schemes. Building our towns alongside rivers-a
convenient means of access in early times-has committed us to providing high
standards of flood protection to safeguard lives and property.

Disabled Persons-New Benefits
(28/9/78)
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Social Welfare: What new policies
within his portfolio have been introduced for the benefit of disabled persons
since December 1975?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: The following
new policies within the Social Welfare portfolio have been introduced for the
benefit of disabled persons since December 1975:
(1) Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act-The Government has pro-
gressively introduced the provisions of the Disabled Persons Community Welfare
Act, which provides for financial and other assistance to be made available to
26-Vol 421


## p. 4330 (#810) ###########################################

4330
6 October
Questions and Replies
disabled persons. Apart from one or two minor provisions, the Act is now fully
operative. Provisions include: (i) the setting up of the Advisory Council for the
Community Welfare of Disabled Persons, to examine the needs of the disabled
and advise the Minister (Part I-November 1976); (ii) payment of expenses and
other costs if a disabled person is required to undertake treatment, examination,
or assessment (s. 13-1 October 1977); (iii) provision for walking frames or
similar prosthetic appliances to be available free of charge (s. 15-1 October
1977); (iv) requirement in the future construction of streets and premises open
to the public to make provision for access, conveniences, etc., for disabled persons
(s. 24-25-November 1976); (v) suspensory loans for motorcars to enable a
disabled person to obtain or retain employment or undertake vocational training
(s. 26 (3) (i)-introduced 1 October 1977-loan maximum upgraded from
$3,000 to $3,500 from 1 October 1978); (vi) suspensory loans for alterations
to private homes to cater for a disabled person's particular disability (s. 14—
September 1978).
(2) Assistance to Organisations-Subsidy assistance to organisations catering
for disabled people has been upgraded as follows: (i) capital subsidy assistance
for residential facilities, sheltered workshops, and day-care centres for the dis-
abled has been increased from 664 percent of actual and reasonable building
costs to 80 percent of such costs; (ii) the capitation subsidy for the residential
care of intellectually handicapped children has been increased from $3.50 to
$5.40 a day, and also extended to cover organisations providing residential care
of physically handicapped children; (iii) an annual grant towards the cost of
the New Zealand Society for the Intellectually Handicapped's field services was
introduced at $50,000 and increased to $100,000 from 1 April 1978; (iv) an
annual grant of $20,000 has been introduced towards the NZSIH's national
administration costs.
(3) Ir.come Maintenance Provisions-(i) Rates of income-tested benefits have
been increased 6-monthly in line with movements in the consumer price index;
(ii) Additional amounts of benefit for second and subsequent children were
increased from $1.25 to $2.00 weekly from 26 July 1978; (iii) a revised income
test is to be introduced from 18 October 1978; allowable income will increase
from $17 a week to $25 a week, and the rate of abatement for excess income is
to be relaxed.
(4) Handicapped Children's Allowance-From 18 October 1978 a non-incoine
tested aliowance of $8 a week will be paid to parents of seriously physically or
mentally handicapped children other than those already being cared for in full-
time residential institutions, in recognition of the heavy additional costs of caring
for these children. Criteria for the allowance are set out in the Social Security
Amendment Bill (No. 2) at present before the House.

64.
Medical Schools-"Drop-out" Rate
(28/9/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: What was the "drop-
out" rate of medical students at (a) Otago University Medical School, and (b)
Auckland University Medical School, for first-year and second-year students for
each of the past 3 years?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: There are two aspects
of "drop-out" by students: those whose courses are temporarily delayed by failure
in one or more of the examinations but who are permitted to repeat and resunie
their courses, and those who abandon the course permanently. The University
of Auckland admits 130 students a year direct from school to the first year of a
first degree in human biology. The numbers who have failed and then repeated
have been in the first year-1 in 1975, 1 in 1976, and nil in 1977; in the second
year-1 in 1975, nil in 1976, and 11 in 1977. The numbers who have abandoned
their course have been: in the first year-2 in 1975, 3 in 1976, and 1 in 1977;
in the second year-1 in 1975, nil in 1976, and 1 in 1977. The University of
Otago admits 200 students a year after an intermediate examination, and, in the
first 2 years in the school, students take the second and third examinations. The
numbers who have failed and then repeated have been: in the second examina-
tion-9 in 1975, 10 in 1976, and 10 in 1977; in the third examination-3 in 1975,
7 in 1976, and 14 in 1977. The numbers who have abandoned their course have
been: in the second examination-7 in 1975, 6 in 1976, and 5 in 1977; in the
third examination-nil in 1975, 2 in 1976, and nil in 1977.

Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Health: What new policies within

since December 1975?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: Since 1975 the following new
policies within the Health portfolio have been introduced for the benefit of disabled
persons:
1976—(1) May: Care of the Aged-Subsidies of $2.5 million dollars were
approved to six organisations in the voluntary sector, towards the cost of homes
and hospitals for the elderly.
(2) July: Prostheses for Mastectomy Patients-A subsidy of up to $30 for the
initial prosthesis only.
(3) December: Care of the Aged-Subsidies of $2.02 million approved for nine
projects by religious and welfare organisations-homes and hospitals for the aged.
Meals-on-Wheels-Additional funds provided for expansion of this service. Cost
of meal increased to 50 cents.
1977—(1) June: Care of the Disabled-A subsidy of $275,000 was approved to
the Laura Fergusson Trust (Christchurch) to provide a residential home for the
disabled.
(2) July: Artificial Eyes—A subsidy of up to $50 for the initial adult prosthesis
and for all prostheses for those under 16 years of age was approved.
Care of the Aged-Subsidies totalling $1.194 million were approved for two
old people's homes and hospitals.
(3) September: Development of Community Care Programme-Funds from the
additional duty on alcohol and tobacco to be used to extend existing services or
the establishment of new ones within the scope of care in the community. Approval
was given to a wide range of community health care projects, e.g., extension to
district health nursing, meals-on-wheels, home help, geriatric and psychiatric
services, etc.
Expansion of Home Renal Dialysis Treatment-The expansion of home renal
dialysis treatment was to enable more people to be treated at home on machines
provided by hospital boards.
(4) November: Old People's Hospitals and Homes-Subsidies for five old people's
homes and hospitals totalling $2,275,000 were approved.
(5) December: Old People's Hospitals and Homes-Approval was given to three
projects for old people's homes and hospitals. Subsidies totalled $2,840,000.
1978 (1) January: Syringes and Needles for Diabetics-It was approved that,
as from 1 April 1978, non-disposable syringes and needles would be supplied free
of charge from retail pharmacists on a doctor's order.
(2) April: Medical Hairpieces (Wigs)-A supplementary benefit of up to $100
for the initial provision of a wig or hairpiece for those suffering hair loss as the
result of a specified medical condition or as a result of treatment. In the case of
children the benefit is also available for replacement wigs.

Phosphorous-Use in Pest Control
(4/10/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Agriculture: Is he aware that
local pest control authorities are using phosphorous in jam baits in Auckland's
west coast regions, and, if so, is this action one that is officially supported by
his department?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Phosphorous is used
quite extensively in the North Island for pest control purposes. It is recognised
as being a very useful means of rabbit and opossum control, and over the years
has played a big part in reducing the rabbit population. Its use is supported by
my ministry and the Agricultural Pests Destruction Council, not by choice, but
more as a matter of necessity because no suitable alternative is available. 1080 is
currently the most effective and humane poison that pest destruction boards and
the Forest Service have at their disposal. It does, however, have disadvantages in
some situations, and other methods or poisons must then be considered. Phos-
phorised jam is preferred in two situations: where land can be cleared of stock

for limited periods only, or where there is a considerable risk of secondary
poisoning of domestic animals if other poisons are used.

(4/10/78)

Tidal Road Development, Papatoetoe
(4/10/78)
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Works and Development:
Will he state the exact nature of the developments for the Puhinui Road tidal
road link in Papatoetoe?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: The present
main route between Mangere and Wiri is State Highway 20, which passes through
the Papatoetoe City centre and extensive adjoining residential areas. At times
considerable delays are experienced by traffic using this route and environmental
problems occur in the areas it traverses. A recommendation was made in the
Auckland comprehensive transportation study review for provision of a four-lane
limited access road between Massey Road and Puhinui Road as an alternative
route. As a first stage it is possible to construct a two-lane facility between Portage
Road and Puhinui Road at a cost of approximately $1 million. This work has
been approved by the National Roads Board and funds are provisionally pro-
grammed to allow a start to be made in 1979-80. In general terms, the new road
is a continuation of Tidal Road, starting near the bend joining Tidal and Portage
Roads, and swinging on to the corridor reserved for the south-western motorway.
Before reaching Puhinui Road the new link swings off the motorway line in an
easterly direction to provide an easy movement on to Puhinui Road. Access to
existing facilities will be maintained by tee intersections at Portage Road, the
Papatoetoe Cemetery, and Puhinui Road west.
98.
Souvenir Coin Issue-Overseas Dealers
(4/10/78)
Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Finance: How many overseas
dealers are on Treasury's souvenir coin issue list and what was the average
purchase of each overseas dealer of (a) proof dollars and (b) proof sets of the 1978
New Zealand souvenir coin issue?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: This question and
question No. 4 should be answered together, as both are governed by the same
conditions. Because the coins will not be in the country until late October and
orders are still being received and processed, it is not possible to provide figures
relative to a completed 1978 issue. The questions can be answered, however, in
the following way. There are approximately 50 overseas dealers and 40 New
Zealand dealers on Treasury's souvenir coin issue mailing list. From each issue
a maximum number of proof items is put aside for distribution to dealers, includ-
ing those in New Zealand and overseas. From the 1978 issue, 1000 proof dollars
and 1000 proof sets have been tentatively put aside for this purpose. From the
above quantities an initial offer has been made to dealers, some of whom have
accepted all or part. Some have not responded as yet and others have requested
an increase. This is a normal response, but further proof items are offered only
if it becomes obvious from the demand of collectors that there will be a surplus.
For some years it has been Government policy to limit the number of souvenir
coins minted, with special emphasis on the proof items, and this policy has been
favourably received by coin collectors generally. Treasury's prime concern is to
ensure that as many individual collectors as possible have the opportunity to
obtain each new issue from them. Order forms are sent to each name on the
mailing list and if collectors complete and return the order forms within a
reasonable time they can be quite confident of having their orders filled. Because
individual collectors are invited to purchase their coins direct by joining the
mailing list, it follows that dealers are not free to order and receive the quantity
of New Zealand proof items that they desire.

Farms Financed by Rural Bank-Average Deposit
(4/10/78)

Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation: What is the average
deposit for (a) Rural Bank financed farms, (b) farms financed from other sources,
for both sheep and dairy farms?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation) replied: The Rural Bank does not keep statistics of the average
deposit on farms financed by it, but this may be as little as 15 percent of the
total ingoing price under its special settlement scheme, while for normal settle-
ment loans it would be expected that the applicant would have a contribution
of approximately 20 to 30 percent. The Rural Bank has no figures of deposits on
farms financed from other sources, but understands that lending institutions, such
as life assurance offices, normally require that applicants have an equity of 40 to
60 percent.

Farm Settlement-Crown Land
(5/10/78)
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Lands:
How much land has been purchased for farm settlement in 1976-77, 1977–78, and
1978-79, and in which regions are these prospective farms?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The areas of land acquired
by the Crown for farm settlement over the past 3 years have been: 1976-77,
2514 ha: 1977-78, 54 ha; 1978-79, 158 ha to date. These areas will provide farms
for settlement in south Auckland, Gisborne, and Westland. In addition to the above
acquisitions, the Government has provided $1 million for expenditure in 1978-79
on purchase of land suitable for quick settlement, and these funds will be spent
by 31 March 1979.

107.
Prescriptions Pricing Policy
(5/10/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: (a) Is it departmental
policy to employ former departmental officers to work at home on the pricing of
prescriptions before payment to chemists, and, if so, (b) how many people are
employed and in which departmental areas does this practice occur?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: It is no longer departmental
policy to employ former departmental officers to work at home on the pricing of
prescriptions before payment to chemists. From 1974 the department gradually
increased the number of full-time staff to enable home pricers to be phased out.
The sole home pricer now working for the Department of Health is at the
Wanganui office, but her services will shortly be dispensed with.

Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Postmaster-General: (1) What are the
locations of all public call boxes accessible on foot from the new Beach Road arc.
subdivisions at the south end of Amberley, and how many are there; and (2) how

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied. A public telephone call
box is situated on the main street of Amberley, some 600 metres from the new Beach
Road area subdivision and another is some 450 metres further away outside the Post
Office. Five applicants were awaiting service from the Amberley exchange, but they
were given service on 4 October when the exchange was converted to automatic
working.

metres from the Collingwood Street subdivision, and another in High Street is about
1400 metres away from the subdivision. About 60 applicants are awaiting service
from the Rangiora telephone exchange, but none of these is in the Collingwood Street
area.

(6/10/78)
Drug Charges
Dr WALL (Porirua) to the Minister of Health: Which of the following
drugs--Drixene, Neo-synephrine, and Otrivine-are on the free list, and which
has a part charge for the patient; what is the amount of the part charge in
each case, and is the drug that is free to the patient identical in action and as
free of side effects as the drugs for which a part charge is made; and, when the
drug is available in bulk, what is the total dispensing charge for dispensing in
a dropper bottle or spray bottle similar to the original pack of the proprietary
product?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: All three products are listed in
the drug tariff. The medicine Otrivine, however, carries a part charge to the patient
as it was recommended by my expert advisory committee that the amount paid for
this preparation should not exceed that paid for Drixine. Both preparations are
considered to be equivalent, both in action and freedom from side effects. In addition,
there is a charge on the small original packs of Drixine as these cost more than the
equivalent quantity being dispensed by a pharmacist from the bulk dispensing pack.
The following part-charges to the patient apply: Drixine 0.05% nasal spray or
drops-$0.45 per 15 ml; Drixine 0.025% nasal drops-$0.58 per 15 ml; Ötrivine
0.1% nasal spray or drops--$0.48 per 14 ml; Otrivine 0.05% nasal drops-$0.55 per
10 ml. All forms of Neo-Synephrine are available free of charge to the patient.
The dispensing charge for dispensing in a dropper bottle or spray bottle from a
bulk pack would be $0.67, plus the cost of the container and the ingredient cost, plus
20 percent. Therefore, the total cost to public funds for dispensing those products
carrying a part-charge is: Drixine 0.05% nasal spray and drops-$1.38 per 15 ml;
Drixine 0.025% nasal drops-$1.38 per 15 ml; Otrivine 0.1% nasal spray and
drops-$1.40 per 14 ml; Otrivine 0.05% nasal drops-$1.27 per 10 ml.

(6/10/78)
Secondary School Pupils-Unemployment Situation
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Education: Could he
advise whether any surveys have been carried out to determine the number of
reluctant pupils returning to secondary schools as a result of the unemployment
situation, and, if so, what are the results, and has he plans to make extra money
available for schools to provide counselling and guidance for these young people
and their parents and to help with courses designed to train young people in the
skills required to apply for work?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: A survey of secondary
school leavers has been made on 30 September each year since 1975. It is a survey of
the intentions of pupils in secondary schools at that date. No reliable estimates of
pupils returning reluctantly to school could be made from the survey. The survey is
an assessment only of intentions. These can be expected to change quite significantly
depending on circumstances such as publicity about the availability of employment,
examination results, and the courses schools will be offering in 1979. The results of
the 30 September 1978 survey are likely to be available by the end of November.
There are some 180 schools with a full-time trained guidance counsellor and a further
16 schools with a full guidance network to provide advice to young people and their
parents. As well, the officers of the Vocational Guidance Service of the Department of
Labour are available to guide and advise. Secondary schools have modified courses
and established new courses for pupils who have returned reluctantly to school this
year. In 1978, additional staffing and other resources were provided at 13 secondary
schools specifically for this purpose, where the courses could not be established within
existing resources. The Department of Education is now asking schools for details of
the additional resources that might be required in 1979. When this information is
available a proposal will be considered by the Government.

Sole-charge Primary Schools-Staffing
(6/10/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: Can he supply
a list of (a) the sole-charge primary schools that will qualify for the new staffing
ratio in 1979; (b) those sole-charge primary schools that will not qualify because
they are contributing schools; (c) the number of schools to which a teacher will be
added but no classroom?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The recently approved
policy, which increases the staffing entitlement of some small full primary schools, has
been effected through the alteration of the staffing schedule that determines the
staffing of primary schools with rolls under 156. The alteration of the schedule affects
full primary schools only and will result for these schools in the entitlement of an
additional staff member at a lesser roll than was previously the case. The new policy
is based on a staffing schedule and not a teacher-pupil ratio as is implied in the
question. It is not possible at this time to provide the lists of schools requested in parts
(a) and (b) of the question, because the determining factor in the implementation of
the policy is the grade of the school, which is determined by education boards and
based on the 30 September 1978 rolls of the schools. At this stage the boards have not
finalised the gradings of schools. The number of sole-charge schools that would have
qualified on the grading returns of 30 September 1977 for an increase in staffing
would have been 29. I do not expect that there would be much variation in this figure
for the next year. The policy to alter the staffing schedule for small full primary
schools was approved on the understanding that no additional expenditure for

Indigenous Forests Policy-Assessment of Effects (6/10/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Forests: Is any assess-
ment planned of the effects of the implementation of the indigenous forests
policy on current forestry operations?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The effects of the
implementation of the indigenous forest policy on current forestry operations are
being assessed continuously. Starting with the selective logging of indigenous forest,
the quality of the operations, costs, roadworks, etc., are closely monitored to see
where improvements might be effected. At strategic places, photographic points have
also been set up recording the condition of the forest after logging and subsequently
photographs of the same area will be taken at intervals to monitor changes in the
forest structure. Older cut-overs are being assessed to establish the degree of
regeneration that has taken place, and, depending on the results of these assessments,
it will be decided whether enrichment planting with indigenous species is warranted.
The Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society, the Wildlife Service, and the Forest
Service are about to study the habitat requirements of the kokako and these will
include the effects of logging on its habitat. The combined effect of price increases in
the higher grades of native timber and the reduced sawlog supply to processing plants
is under scrutiny to ascertain whether the planned effect of higher grades being used
for quality finishing purposes is achieved. Lastly, the possibility of acquiring
outstanding areas of native forest in private ownership by purchase or exchange is
under constant review and acquisitions are effected where funds permit or where
other factors make them possible.
136.
Export Income Loss-British Lamb Market
(6/10/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Agriculture: What
was the estimated loss in export income resulting from our inability to fill the
pre-Christmas lamb market in the United Kingdom last year?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The effects of freezing
works strikes on export earnings are notoriously difficult to estimate. For example, it
is arguable what United Kingdom pre-Christmas 1977 lamb prices would have been
if there had been regular arrivals of shipments of new season's New Zealand lamb at
that time. Undoubtedly these prices would, in such an event, have been lower than
recorded. On the other hand, it should be remembered that United Kingdom lamb
prices have risen since April 1978 to levels substantially above those ruling in the two
months before Christmas 1977. The slower start to the 1977-78 season has resulted in
more lamb being sold at these higher prices than would otherwise have been the case.
It is, therefore, quite possible that any loss in export earnings, resulting from New
Zealand being unable to take full advantage of the United Kingdom pre-Christmas
1977 lamb market, was relatively small or that there was no such loss at all.

Human Rights-Execution of Black South African
(6/10/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: In view of
the statement by the Prime Minister at the United Nations that the international
community cannot ignore the denial of basic human rights, does he intend to
communicate to the South African Government the concern of the New Zealand
Government over the forthcoming execution of a 21-year-old black South African
whose only crime, apparently, was being associated with a liberation movement?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: I assume the
member for Wanganui is referring to the case of Solomon Mahlangu, who is alleged to
have taken part in a terrorist incident in which two innocent bystanders were killed.
It is my understanding that Mahlangu has been convicted on the basis of his
involvement in these killings. According to the information available to me, the trial
has not been criticised by any of the groups within South Africa that monitor the
trials of African dissidents. While the Government abhors the repressive nature of the
apartheid system, we cannot condone acts of terrorism of this nature.

Balance of Payments Deficit
(21/9/78)
Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) to the Minister of Statistics: What
percentage of gross national product did the balance of payments deficit represent as
at 31 March 1973, 1974, 1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): New Zealand had a surplus
on current account for the 1972-73 year of 2.2 percent of gross national product.
Thereafter it faced deficits. The deficit in 1973-74 was 1.3 percent; in 1974-75, 14.5
percent; in 1975-76, 9.3 percent; in 1976-77, 7 percent; and in 1977-78, 5.7 percent.
These percentages are based on the official national income and expenditure
aggregates, except for the 1978 year percentage, which uses estimates prepared by the
New Zealand Institute of Economic Research.
148.
Natural Gas
(21/9/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Is it correct, as
asserted by the energy reporter of the New Zealand Herald in that newspaper on
7 September 1978, that “the New Zealand taxpayer will have to foot a bill of millions
of dollars for massive quantities of natural gas left in the ground through cancellation
of thermal power station projects"?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): No. Any need to advance money to
meet the take-or-pay is not money wasted. It is merely a question of pre-paying for
the gas, and this can be drawn, without further payment, at any time during the
30-year period of the contract. Where any money required to meet any shortfall in the
early years of the take-or-pay might come from would not be decided until the need to
make such an advance was established. The recent decision to provide for Maui gas
to make ammonia-urea and liquid fuels will lessen and may even eliminate the deficit
in take-or-pay.

161.
Deer Farming-Yersinia
(21/9/78)
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Health: Is the diagnosis of
yersinia, an infection contracted from deer, likely to create any difficulty for the deer-
farming industry?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Yersiniosis, which can be caused by
Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, is primarily a zoonotic disease of wild and domesticated
birds and mammals, with man as an accidental host. It occurs throughout the world
and is not associated with any particular species of animal. There is, therefore, no
special danger to those engaged in deer farming. However, it may be that deer in poor
condition and confined on farms in large numbers may give rise to some increase in
the incidence of this disease, but the likelihood of this is directly related to the hygiene
of the farm and its operators.

Infant Mortality Rate
(21/9/78)
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) to the Minister of Health: What was the
recorded infant mortality rate for 1976-the latest year for which data are available—
and how does this compare with other comparable countries?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): New Zealand's infant death rate for 1976
was 14.0 per 1000 live births. This is the lowest ever recorded in New Zealand. By
way of comparison, the latest available rates for some other countries against which
New Zealand customarily measures its performance were: Sweden (1975), 8.3;
Finland (1974), 10.3; Norway (1974), 10.5; Denmark (1974), 10.7; New Zealand
comes in here at 14.0; Canada (1974), 15.0; England and Wales (1975), 16.0; and
Australia (1974), 16.1.

Electoral Enrolment Cards-Porirua
(21/9/78)
Dr WALL (Porirua) to the Minister of Justice: Is he aware that the officer
reputed to act for the electorate officer in the Porirua Post Office refused to give
enrolment cards to a Labour Party official when she requested those cards for the
purpose of canvassing for enrolments, and, if he is aware, would he inform the House
if this action is in accordance with Government policy, and, if not, what does he
intend to do about it?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Justice. "A refusal to provide electoral enrolment cards in response to a bona fide and
reasonable request, as for instance by an official of a political party, is certainly not
part of the Government's policy, nor of the practice of the electoral office. In the
incident referred to by the honourable member a request was made to a staff member
at the Porirua Post Office, at a time when the electorate officer was not present, for a
bulk supply of enrolment cards. The person seeking the bulk supply, I am informed,
gave no indication of her association with a political party, and the request was
wrongly declined on the basis that it could have resulted in adding to the number of
duplicate applications for enrolment that had to be processed. The electorate officer
has been instructed that this policy is not to be followed, and that any person
requiring supplies of cards should be issued with them."

(22/9/78)
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda), on behalf of Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin
Central), to the Minister of Education: When can the Otago Polytechnic Council
expect final approval for its redevelopment programme to be announced?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The Government has decided
that alternative redevelopment plans for Otago Polytechnic are to be investigated
immediately. Because of the falling birth rate, student roll numbers at Dunedin
Teachers College have dropped substantially over the past few years, and the
Government wants to ensure that surplus space at the teachers college is used to the
best advantage. An alternative proposal for meeting the Polytechnic's accommoda-
tion needs is now to be examined by the Department of Education in consultation
with the Polytechnic Council, the Dunedin Teachers College Council, and the
Dunedin City Council. If the Polytechnic were to be rebuilt adjacent to the teachers
college this could allow many facilities such as lecture theatres, student amenities,
and some classrooms to be used to a greater capacity on a joint basis. This proposal
could, if it proved feasible and acceptable, not only reduce the cost of rebuilding the
Polytechnic on the existing site in Stuart Street, but bring distinct educational
advantages steming from the close proximity of the Otago University and the
teachers college

Migration Statistics
(22/9/78)
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North), on behalf of Miss DEWE (Lyttelton), to
the Minister of Immigration: Has he seen a publication entitled Lyttelton '78 issued
by the Labour Party and dated August 1978, and, if so, has he seen a statement in
that which states "New Zealand had a permanent and long-term migration loss of
over 42 000 for the year ended 31 March 1978, and it is expected that this record
figure will be exceeded during the current financial year" and, if so, (i) is this correct,
and, if not, (ii) what are the correct figures; and (iii) can he explain where the Labour
Party may have got the figures quoted?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Immigration. "No, I have not seen the publication referred to, but the

Statistics show that for the year ended 31 March 1978 there was a net outflow,

are a more accurate reflection of the net effect of migration on New Zealand's
population. These show that in the year ended 31 March 1978 there was a loss to
population of 4148 persons. I believe it is fruitless to speculate on how the Labour
Party arrived at the figures quoted by the honourable member."

197.
Nuclear-powered Ships
(22/9/78)
Mr BELL (Gisborne), on behalf of Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua), to the
Minister of Transport: To what degree has marine shipping moved towards nuclear
power as a means of propulsion?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Transport. "There are already more than 200 nuclear-powered warships in
operation, some of which have been in service for more than 20 years. A few nuclear-
powered merchant ships have been built, including an ice breaker, a bulk-ore cargo
carrier, and two general cargo ships. Diesel engines are far and away the most
popular and economic form of machinery in merchant ships, but, as the price of oil
fuel increases and its availability decreases, so other forms of propulsion, including
nuclear energy, could become very economically attractive. Unless a smaller reactor
system than at present envisaged can be developed, however, it is unlikely that more
than about 400 to 500 ships would require means of propulsion of sufficient power to
make nuclear energy economically feasible even if environmental, moral, safety, and
other considerations were satisfied."

202.
Electoral Rolls-Special Votes
(26/9/78)
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Justice: Is it correct that the
checking of the declaration for special votes against the roll during the official count is
usually carried out by an official of the Post Office without the presence of the
returning officer or any scrutineers, and, if so, are any changes in the practice
proposed because of the high probability that many who have actually taken steps to
enrol would not have their names on either roll, yet have received an E2 form?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): There is no basis for the
supposition that anyone who has received an E2 card will not be able to cast a valid
vote, and the suggestion is irresponsible. The Electoral Act 1956-sections 95 and 112
to 115-provides for scrutineers to be appointed by candidates to be present in
polling booths during the scrutiny of the rolls by the returning officer after the poll,
and during the official count by the returning officer, and this includes the counting of
special votes. However, regulation 24 of the Electoral Regulations 1975 provides for
the declarations of special voters to be sent by the returning officer to the electorate
officer-an official of the Post Office-for checking that the special voter is a qualified
registered elector. After checking and endorsement by the electorate officer, the
special voters' declarations are returned to the returning officer for the appropriate
action. This has always been the practice, and there is no proposal for it to be
changed.
203.
Women
(26/9/78)
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Justice How many Acts, or
amendments to Acts, passed during the term of this Government, deal directly with
improving the position of women?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): This Government has passed
several Acts and amendments to Acts, which deal directly with improving the
position of women in our society. The Human Rights Commission Act 1977 prohibits
discrimination on the grounds of sex in a number of fields. The first schedule to that
Act amends various statutes, including the Sale of Liquor Act, by removing
discriminatory provisions. The Matrimonial Property Act 1976 is another obvious
example. The Juries Amendment Act 1976 imposes the same obligation on men and
women in respect of jury service, and the Citzienship Act 1977 gives men and women
the same right to pass on citizenship to their children. Other relevant measures are
the Domicile Act 1976-providing for the separate domicile of married women—and
the Equal Pay Amendment Act 1976. This is not necessarily a complete list, because,
in addition, many Acts benefit women in that they benefit the community as a whole.

Education-Grants to Schools
(26/9/78)
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Education: What
improvements to the system of allocation of grants to schools has been made by this
National Government?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Education. "When the National Government assumed office, I found that
education authorities were not informed of the increased levels of grants applicable
for the current school year in some cases until well into the third term. In 1976 the
Government acknowledged these difficulties in budgeting expenditure, and steps
were taken to determine the new rates of grant for announcement before the next
academic year. As a result, in December 1976 I announced the general level of
increased grants for the 1977 school year, and detailed grants were promulgated early
in the new year. In 1977 I notified not only the level of increase, but also the detailed
rates to controlling authorities before Christmas 1977. There is, I understand, real
appreciation of the early notification of grants under a system that now provides for
sensible budgeting and financial management.”

211.
Overseas Debt
(26/9/78)
Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Finance: What sinking fund
arrangements are in existence to provide for the payment of the outstanding overseas
loan debt, which, according to Budget table No. 13, is $2,446,730,000?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): Table 13 in the 1978
Budget shows total overseas public debt outstanding as at 31 March 1978 to be
$2,446,730,000. The total is made up by 97 loans in the form of direct loans, revolving
credits, and capital equipment credits. Approximately one-third of the direct loans
are subject to sinking fund requirements—that is, repayment of some part of the
outstanding principal is required prior to the date of final maturity. Sinking fund
requirements in fact vary from loan to loan. The majority of capital equipment credits
are also subject to sinking funds. Details of sinking fund provisions as they relate to
individual direct loans can be found in the tables at the back of each year's Budget,
and I am sure the member will refer to those. The general provisions relating to the
repayment of outstanding overseas debt can be found in sections 40 and 87 of the
Public Finance Act 1977.

Truancy
(27/9/78)
Mr N. P. H. JONES (Invercargill) to the Minister of Education: What
practical steps have been taken to deal with truancy, and is he in a position to
comment on their effectiveness to date?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Education. "During the last 2 years my department has developed and
put into practice a comprehensive programme to reduce truancy. It involved
regularly reviewing the level of truancy; issuing a circular that gave guidance to
principals; a national survey of absenteeism; reviews of the teaching programmes for
pupils at risk for truancy and of the procedures used to check attendance and follow
up unexplained absences; and a review of liaison with parents and with other agencies
that have responsibilities in this matter. A survey of education board districts in May
1978 revealed that in the past year truancy has declined in districts that had the
greatest incidence. No increases are evident in any district."

projects, including domiciliary care, family health counselling centres, and health
centres administered by hospital boards. The balance has been allocated to other
community care projects.

Chatham Islands Air Service
(28/9/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Internal Affairs: In
view of the expiry last February of the 10-year contract with Safe Air to
operate the Chatham Islands air service, the strong demand by objectors at the
recent Chatham Islands air services hearing that the service be put out for
tender as it was in 1968, the previous attempts by other operators to secure
Chatham Island rights, and the very much higher level of the new Chatham
fares, will he now agree to the request by Chatham Islanders that tenders be
called?
Mr COMBER (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Internal
Affairs): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Internal Affairs. "No. The requirements
of the Chatham Islands air service call for a special style of aircraft, and the route
involves long over-water flying time and the use of a grass airstrip on the Chatham
Islands. The operator must be able to provide a regular schedule of flights over that
difficult route with an aircraft capable of carrying passengers, mail, and some freight
on each flight. Those requirements have been met very satisfactorily by the present
operator over the past 10 years, and no other prospective operator has demonstrated
a similar capability. The contract with Safe Air Ltd. is therefore being renewed."

QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER
Electoral Rolls-Maori Voters
(29/9/78)
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the
Minister of Justice: Is he aware that staff at the Porirua Post Office have been telling
electors that if they have moved from another Maori electorate into Southern Maori
they are able to choose whether to go on to the Maori roll or the general roll; is this
advice in accordance with section 43B of the Electoral Act; and, if a voter did transfer
from the Maori to the general roll, would his vote be challenged?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I am not aware that any such
advice is being supplied by the Post Office staff at the Porirua Post Office, as the
Porirua electorate officer confirms that it is not. It is possible, however, that an elector
moving to Porirua and filling in a new application for registration as an elector could
be enrolled on the general roll, although previously on a Maori roll, if he did not
supply the name of his electorate. Only the previous address is asked for on the card.
After all, as the honourable member would know, somebody might give a
Christchurch address that could well be in the Christchurch Central electorate in
which he has been enrolled, not the Southern Maori electorate, or vice versa. The
terms of section 43B of the Electoral Act, though difficult to police, are quite clear,
and such a person would not be entitled to be registered on a general roll, and would
therefore not be a qualified voter for that electorate.

teams have been established and in operation for some time. Unfortunately, it has not
yet been possible to secure the services of a doctor for the Christchurch team, but this

Absentee Voters
(29/9/78)
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the
headline "Rowling chases Sydney-siders' election votes" in the Dominion of 22
September, and can he indicate how long a New Zealander, correctly enrolled, can
live in Sydney before he ceases to qualify for a vote?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): A person who has been duly
enrolled for an electoral district ceases to be "ordinarily resident in New Zealand",
and thus ceases to be qualified as an elector, if he has been out of New Zealand
continuously for more than 3 years, unless he or she is a public servant who is outside
New Zealand on official duty, or the spouse or child of such a public servant. This is
the effect of sections 38 and 39 of the Electoral Act.

Regional Development-Hawke's Bay
(4/10/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Local Government: Has he
seen the article in the Hawke's Bay Herald-Tribune of 26 May 1978 in which the Mayor
of Hastings, Mr J. J. O'Connor, describes the provisional scheme for regional
government in Hawke's Bay as unjust and undemocratic, and could he confirm that,
in the provisional scheme for Hawke's Bay, rural votes will be worth as much as three
times a vote cast in an urban area?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): It is incorrect and
misleading to suggest that, in the provisonal scheme for Hawke's Bay, rural votes will
be worth as much as three times a vote cast in urban areas. Under legislation brought
down by the Labour Government as part of the Local Government Act in 1974, the
distribution of membership of united councils is to be made having regard to the
population, rateable value, and area of each constituent district, and such additional
factors as the Local Government Commission considers relevant. It is my
understanding that the provisional scheme for Hawke's Bay has been prepared in
accordance with the law. This does not mean that the present commission may not
vary the weightings attached to each factor when bringing down the final scheme.

295.
Electoral Act-Enrolment Cards
(4/10/78)
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: Are those who tried to vote
or succeeded in voting under section 99(f) of the Electoral Act (now repealed) and
who filled in an application form for registration as an elector, regarded as qualified to
vote under section 99(c) if they are still resident at the same address; and could he say
what was done with the enrolment cards?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Section 99(c) provides that an
individual is qualified to vote if he is qualified to be registered as an elector of the
district and was at the time of the last election duly registered as an elector of the
district. The individuals referred to by the honourable member would not be qualified
to vote under this provision, because they were not “duly registered” at polling day in
1975. Special voters under section 99(f)—as it was-filled in an application form on
election day that did not in itself amount to immediate registration. However, the
individuals referred to by the honourable member would be qualified to vote under
section 99(d) as they would have legally applied for registration since the last election
and before 6 p.m. on writ day. As to the last part of the member's question, cards
filled out by such individuals on polling day at the last election were forwarded to the
appropriate electorate officer and became part of the roll.

307.
Electoral Roll Registration Cards
(4/10/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Justice: Are the application
cards for electoral registration, which apparently constitute the electoral roll, all
centralised in Wellington, and, if so, what method will be used to check special votes
against the roll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The application cards for all
electorates are held in Lower Hutt. At this stage it is intended that special votes will
be checked against the roll in the following manner. First, special votes cast outside a
voter's electoral district will be sent to the appropriate returning officer, who will
check the name of each special voter against his main and supplementary rolls, and, if
that name is found, the vote will be allowed by the returning officer. Secondly, when a
special voter is not found on the main or supplementary rolls, the returning officer
will send the declaration accompanying the special vote to the electorate officer, who
will be holding the application cards of those entitled to apply for registration after
writ day. When the voter's card is held, the electorate officer will return the
declaration to the returning officer endorsed with the word "qualified". The
returning officer will then allow such a vote. Thirdly, if neither of these procedures
enables the vote to be treated as valid, he will forward the declaration to the Chief
Electoral Officer, who will check to see whether an application has been received from
the special voter. In addition, he will check the 1975 roll to see whether the special
voter was on that roll.

310.
Voting Eligibility-Expatriate New Zealanders
(4/10/78)
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
to the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the headline "Rowling chases Sydney-siders'
election votes" in the Dominion of 22 September, and can he indicate what procedures
will be adopted to check the voting eligibility of these expatriate New Zealanders?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have seen the headline
referred to. The same procedures will be adopted this election as in the past. The law
provides, in effect, that a New Zealand elector who has been absent from the country
for more than 3 years is not qualified to vote. The special voting declaration issued to
those voting overseas requires such voters, other than servicemen or public servants,
to declare that they have not been absent from New Zealand for more than 3 years.
These declarations will be forwarded to the Chief Electoral Officer, who is obliged to
ascertain whether a person named in such a declaration is a registered elector or
otherwise qualified to vote under section 99 of the Electoral Act.

332.
Balance of Payments
(5/10/78)
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) to the Minister of Finance: In view
of the beginning of an increase in import ordering, as indicated by the New Zealand
Statistics News Release 78/182, and the increase in the deficit on overseas exchange
transactions revealed in the Reserve Bank press release of 26 September, can he
indicate what plans the Government has to correct New Zealand's balance of
payments problem?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The member refers
to an increase in import ordering. The Government Statistician has projected private
import payments for the year to January 1979. This forecast shows that import
payments will be 5.6 percent lower than in the previous year. Therefore, year on year,
the Government Statistician is actually forecasting a drop in import payments. It is
true that the overseas exchange transactions current account deficit has shown a
slight rise in the month of August. It is well known that it is dangerous to read too
much into the results for any one month and it is more significant to focus on the
annual figures. For the year to August 1978 the deficit is still around half the deficit in
the year to August 1975. The Government has a clear commitment to the control of
the balance of payments deficit. The only long-term solution to our balance of
payments difficulties is to encourage exports. The measures in this year's Budget are
an example of foward-looking policies designed to protect the incomes of exporters.

Airports--Bird Hazard
(5/10/78)
Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West) to the Minister of Transport: What
practical steps are being taken to combat the bird hazard at internal airports?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services) replied: The problem of bird hazards at internal airports is being tackled on
both a short-term and a long-term basis. Short-term control is mainly a programme of
harassment to prevent birds from using an aerodrome as a resting or feeding place.
Long-term bird control involves extended environmental management programmes.
The aim is to remove or modify all features that attract birds to the area. These
features are invariably connected with food sources, such as refuse tips, abattoirs,
food processing plants, and so on.

Pigmeat Ban-New Zealand - Australia
(5/10/78)

fact that in the last 5 years only 1 chopper pig of a total of 47 677 tested for trichinosis
proved to give a positive result-i.e. less than 0.0002 percent-will he reconsider the
ban on the importation of pigmeats from New Zealand into Australia?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The ban is imposed by
the Australian Department of Health, and in spite of repeated representations by
New Zealand authorities at the technical committee on quarantine meeting, no
response has been received from Australia. The ban has been reinforced by the
discovery of Aujeszky's disease in New Zealand pigs. Australia has been fully
informed on the latest position in so far as both trichinosis and Aujeszky's disease are
concerned, but has given no indication when it is likely to lift the ban on live pigs and
pigmeats. At the meeting in February, Australian representatives did say they would
consider the importation of male pigs when their Torrens quarantine station was
completed.

Fishing Regulatory Procedures
(5/10/78)
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he
seen the article in the Evening Post of 28 September 1978 that quotes a counsellor of the
Japanese Fishery Association as saying that New Zealand's regulatory procedures for
fishing were the most complicated in the world and the inefficiency of them without
parallel, and also that the quota of fin fish allocated to Japan is so small that it will


## p. 4399 (#879) ###########################################

6 October
4399
Questions for Oral Answer
make it impossible for Japanese boats to continue their operations, and what steps
has he taken to ensure that this situation does not adversely affect the entry of New
Zealand primary produce to the Japanese market?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied: I have seen
the article in question. New Zealand's regulatory procedures are designed to be
efficient and effective from the point of view of New Zealand requirements, and they
are also generally in accordance with international practice. Furthermore, the
Japanese Government has agreed that its vessels will comply with New Zealand's
regulations in terms of the fisheries agreement now concluded between the two
countries. A fisheries quota for Japan has been set, which is equitable bearing in mind
the extent of the New Zealand resource and the history of Japanese fishing in New
Zealand waters. The article in the Evening Post is not therefore an accurate reflection
of the situation, and there has been no adverse effect on the entry of New Zealand
primary produce to the Japanese market.

against any of the parties to the Cyprus dispute would be helpful in securing the
implementation of the resolutions the United Nations has adopted.
343.
Legislation-Freedom of Speech
(5/10/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Justice: In view of the
comments of the Prime Minister, reported in the Evening Post of 26 September, that
the Government has now completed a comprehensive review of legislation and is
satisfied that our laws are in compliance with the requirements of the international
covenants on political and civil rights, and on economic, social, and cultural rights,
can he indicate whether any of that legislation includes any reference to freedom of
speech?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: In New Zealand,
freedom of speech, like many other basic freedoms, is not conferred by any statute. It
is inherent in the common law, a basic principle of which is that a person is free to say
or write what he pleases subject only to the controls imposed by specific laws.
Obviously there are provisions which qualify absolute freedom of speech-for
example, the law relating to sedition, official secrets, defamation, and indecency. The
International Covenant on Political and Civil Rights itself recognises the need for
such exceptions. Accordingly, it is not necessary for our legislation to refer to freedom
of speech in order to comply-as it does-with the International Covenants on
Human Rights.

370.
Cost of Living Increase
(6/10/78)
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Finance: Is it correct
that during the period in office of the current Government prices have risen more than
in any similar period of a single Government, despite the National Party's 1975
manifesto statement that “National regards the fight against increases in the cost of
living as the most important single issue in economic management"?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: When this
Government assumed office late in 1975 it was confronted with an economy that was
experiencing high and accelerating inflation. This was the legacy of the previous
Government, a problem the National Government could not and did not ignore. It is
a measure of the success of this Government in the economic field that, within a year
of assuming office, inflation had stopped rising and had actually begun to fall. By
November this year it is possible that prices will have risen more during the term of
this Government than in previous ones. The reasons for this are that during our first
year in office the consumer price index was recording price rises that stemmed
directly from actions taken by the Labour Government before November 1975. For
example, increases in the cost of housing are recorded in the consumer price index
from 6 to 9 months after the price rise occurs. Furthermore the Government found it
essential in 1976-77 to eliminate a number of Government subsidies and to adjust
postal, rail and electricity charges so as to ease the burden on the New Zealand
taxpayer of an unduly high Government deficit. A better measure of the performance
of a Government is the trend in prices during its term in office. Under Labour the
trend was upward, while during our term in office the trend has been, and continues
to be, a downward one.

in Auckland in new premises was under investigation. The decision, which was made

by the director, dairy division, and endorsed by the Director-General of the Ministry

372.
Government Spending
(6/10/78)
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of
Finance: Why has he allowed this year's net Government spending to rise to an
estimated 44 percent of the gross national product-the highest ever-despite the
National Party's 1975 manifesto promise that "the growth of Government spending
will be curbed"?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: Net Government
expenditure in 1978-79 as provided in the main and supplementary estimates is 42.8
percent of estimated gross national product. The appropriate proportion of GNP for
Government expenditure varies with the economic conditions prevailing in any year.
At a time of slowing economic activity in the private sector and a slow rate of growth
in GNP, it is to be expected that public sector spending should increase
proportionately to absorb part of those resources that the private sector cannot use.
As the private sector picks up it will reabsorb these resources. This, together with a
growing economy, will result in a falling proportion of Government expenditure to
GNP.

374.
Coastal Shipping
(6/10/78)
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Transport: Why has
he not kept the National Party 1975 manifesto promise to "revive and resuscitate
coastal shipping"?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: The member for
Timaru should understand that to revive and resuscitate coastal shipping the climate
must be right. The essential problem in 1975 was that rail rates had been kept so low
that coastal shipping could not operate without massive subsidy from central
government. The position now, after 3 years of National administration, is that cargo
is being carried between Wellington and Lyttelton on Union Steam Ship Company
vessels without any subsidy and the annual subsidy on the roll on/roll off ship Coastal
Trader has been considerably reduced. In other words, we have created the climate in
which coastal shipping can compete economically with other modes. This is the
climate necessary for its revival.

hours. A further allocation in September 1979 will restore the number of teacher aide
hours to the 1976 level. By February 1979 the equivalent of an additional 84 full-time
teaching positions will have been established in the special education services since
February 1976.

Resources Commission
(6/10/78)
Mr Mac DONELL (Dunedin Central) to the Minister of Regional
Development: Why has he not established a resources commission to make rapid
phased economic assessment of resources on a regional basis, as promised in the 1975
National Party manifesto?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) replied: Assessments of
the resources of many regions have been undertaken during the Government's term of
office. The Government has encouraged and provided financial assistance to regional
development councils to prepare and follow up resources surveys of their regions.

may be taken. Special attention has also been given to a number of other studies,

achieved without creating a new central bureaucracy.

384.
Housing Co-operatives
(6/10/78)
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the
Minister of Housing: Will he detail what has been done to test the feasibility of
housing co-operatives as an alternative to State housing for special categories of
housing needs, such as solo parents, as promised in his Government's 1975 thick
manifesto?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: The feasibility of
housing co-operatives for special categories of housing need, such as solo parents, has
been researched in some depth by the Government. Although there could be
advantages for some solo parents and their children in a type of co-operative housing
arrangement, the research has shown that solo parents have a better opportunity to
make adequate social adjustments if they can be integrated in the community. In this
regard the Housing Corporation has, within its medium-density town houses and
cluster houses, allocated tenancies to solo parents. These units have small curtilages,
and, as such, are eminently suitable for those people less able to maintain a normal-
sized section-they are inexpensive to furnish and are easily maintained.
Furthermore, there are opportunities for co-operative activities such as baby sitting,
care of grounds, etc. This type of accommodation has given the corporation the
opportunity to house a balanced social mix, including solo parents, elderly couples,
and large and small families.

386.
Overseas Aid
(6/10/78)
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Why
has he lowered the proportion of GNP going towards official development assistance,
when the National Party's 1975 manifesto stated that “the National Party . . . will
promote international co-operation in trade, finance and aid, including acceptance of
the target of 1 percent aid"?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The
honourable member will be aware that the Government's strategy for economic
recovery involved the imposition of across-the-board restraints on public sector
expenditure. It was not possible to exempt the annual aid votes for 1976-77 and
1977-78 entirely from this process. In the current financial year it has been possible to
increase the aid vote over the previous year. The effects of these policies are reflected
in the percentage of gross national product devoted to offical development assistance
in each of the last three financial years. New Zealand has reported to the
Development Assistance Committee of the OECD ODA/GNP percentages of 0.41
percent for the 1976 calendar year and 0.39 percent for 1977. The overall averages for
all OECD countries in each of these years were 0.33 percent and 0.31 percent
respectively. Given our especially pressing economic difficulties over the period, these
statistics are a clear indication of the Government's concern to preserve New
Zealand's commitments to international development assistance to the extent
possible. Progress towards the international target of 0.7 percent for ODA transfers
will be determined finally by the rate of New Zealand's economic recovery.

substantial growth in the provision of second-chance education since 1975. Second-
chance education is by no means dependent on the establishment of creches at
education institutions as the question implies. About four-fifths of all secondary
schools-more than 190 in 1978-admit adults to their day classes. The returns as at
March 1978 showed that 2141 adults were so enrolled, of whom 583 were full-time
and 1558 were part-time. About 160 secondary schools offer evening class
programmes, and most if not all offer tuition in secondary school subjects as well as
other non-examinable subjects. In 1977, 8621 adults were so enrolled; 5220 were
studying at School Certificate level, 3177 at University Entrance level, and 224 at a
combination of both these levels. The Correspondence School now teaches more

Questions for Oral Answer
adults than children. In 1978 a total of 9741 adults was enrolled with the
Correspondence School. Of these, 7216 are in examinable courses, virtually all at
secondary level. The combined total enrolments for these second-chance
opportunities are likely to exceed 20 000 for the 1978 year.
The establishment of creches at educational institutions where these are
considered desirable is a matter for the controlling authorities concerned. They are
permitted to use surplus accommodation for creches provided their operation is
financially self-supporting, and many do so. A survey of child care centres in
