404.
School Staff Ratios
(6/10/78)
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: Can he explain
why only the sole-charge full primary country schools are included within the new
staffing ratio for 1979, and indicate how many schools will have to wait until 1980 or
1981 for their new ratio?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The reasons for altering
the staffing schedule applicable to primary schools with rolls under 155 in favour of
full primary but not contributing schools were fourfold. (a) Teachers in contributing
schools are responsible for a more restricted range of classes than are teachers in full
primary schools. (b) Small contributing schools, by virtue of the fact that they
contribute to intermediate schools, area schools, or form I to VII schools are situated
in areas less remote than many small full primary schools. (c) Throughout the
country there are approximately 753 full primary schools in the roll range 9-155 as
against approximately 295 contributing primary schools. (d) In line with its stated
policy, the Government wished to ensure the maximum benefit to the education of
rural children, taking into account the demands of other educational priorities and
the available human and financial resources. Until the 30 September 1979 and
30 September 1980 grading rolls of primary schools become available to officers in the
head office of my department, the exact number of full primary schools that will be
affected in 1980 and 1981 by the recently approved policy that has altered the staffing
schedule of these schools will not be known. However, based on 30 September 1977
grading roll figures, it is expected that approximately 87 schools in the roll range 29 to
90 will receive additional staffing assistance in 1980 and approximately 74 schools in
the roll range 91 to 155 will receive additional staffing assistance in 1981.

Industrial Stoppages
(6/10/78)

question on 5 September 1978, in which he confirmed that there were 1241 industrial
stoppages in the 2 year period ended June 1978, (i) could he indicate for how long
industrial stoppage figures have been kept, and (ii) could he confirm that there is not
one 24-year period in New Zealand's previously recorded history in which more than
1241 industrial stoppages have been recorded?

number of industrial stoppages recorded in the 24-year period ended 30 June 1978 is
the highest number of industrial stoppages recorded in any one 21-year period in the
history of New Zealand's stoppage statistics. Although the frequency of stoppages has
increased over the last 2 years, the annual number of working days lost is beginning
to decrease.

15,682
(6/10/78)
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister of Immigration: In view of the net
migration loss currently being suffered by New Zealand, what steps are being taken
by the Government to assess the skills needed by New Zealand industry and to recruit
those skills, and in which countries is recruitment being undertaken?


## p. 4415 (#895) ###########################################

6 October
4415
Questions for Oral Answer
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: The skills needed by New
Zealand industry are continually being assessed. The occupational priority list, which
contains those occupations determined to be in most urgent and continuing demand
in New Zealand, is based on information from a number of sources, including a
survey of occupational vacancies carried out by the Department of Labour twice a
year. In addition, special consideration is given where an employer is able to
demonstrate a need to recruit from overseas a person with a particular skill that is not
on the occupational priority list. Traditionally we have looked to countries such as the
United Kingdom, Australia, Western European countries, Canada, and the United
States for skilled people. The policy on entry on occupational grounds has, however,
recently been reviewed and widened by Cabinet in an effort to obtain necessary skills.
Cabinet agreed, in principle, that persons from non-traditional source countries who
have skills that are needed in New Zealand may be granted permanent residence on
occupational grounds if the skills they possess are not in demand in their country of
origin, and if it is not possible to obtain the skills from a traditional source country.

Charter Flights, General Motors
(6/10/78)
Mr KIRK (Sydenham) to the Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services: In view of the fact that Noah's Hotel in Christchurch has stated that it
could have accommodated the passengers of the seven Boeing 747 charter flights
arranged by General Motors, as stated in the Christchurch Star of 30 September, thus
contradicting the official reason given for the flights not going to Christchurch—
namely, lack of beds in Christchurch-why did the Government approve of the flights
going to Auckland?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological
Services) replied: I am advised that the seven charter flights were originally
programmed to go to Christchurch until the ground tour organiser was told by
Noah's Hotel that the hotel was "normally booked" and would therefore be unable to
meet the charterers requirement that the 230 persons on each flight be accommodated
under one roof. Suitable accommodation was thereupon sought and obtained in
Auckland. The approval my ministry gave Qantas to operate the charters specifically
authorised the use of Christchurch or Auckland. Therefore if Noah's has now
changed its mind and can persuade the charterer to alter its arrangements by routing
the charters into Christchurch, the necessary landing approvals have already been
given.

(6/10/78)
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of

External Debt
(6/10/78)
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister of Finance: Could he
provide a table listing changes in the external debt for the period 31 March 1978 to
30 September 1978 similar to that contained on pages 76 and 77 of the report of the
Controller and Auditor-General on the Public Accounts (B.1 (Pt.II))?
Rt. HON. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The table referred
to is prepared each year by the Controller and Auditor-General, an officer of
Parliament, not by any of the departments for which I am responsible to Parliament.
The level of external Public Account indebtedness is not made public at dates other
than 31 March each year in any case because: (a) the data would be provisional
because mid-point exchange rates for the purpose of realigning overseas debt in New
Zealand dollar terms usually are struck only once a year, towards the end of the
financial year and, in periods when exchange rates are fluctuating, a table as at some
other date would not reflect a current figure; and (b) only at the end of each financial
year is it possible to ensure that all overseas debt transactions for the year are
allocated in the Public Account.

Absence of Hansard Reporters-19 September
ABSENCE OF HANSARD REPORTERS—19 SEPTEMBER
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): A point of order, Mr Chairman. I notice that the
Hansard reporters are no longer present in the Chamber, and, although we on this side of
the House are naturally concerned, as all members must be, at the physical strain which has
been imposed on them during these long debates, I should like to know whether the debates
are being recorded on tape. If so, the Opposition has no objection, but I would point out that
this is the first time this has happened in all the years I have been in the House.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I appreciate the member's sympathy for
members of the Hansard staff. A few records are being broken if this is the first time the staff
has been unable to keep up with the work. However, the proceedings are being recorded and
copies of speeches will be available as soon as they can be transcribed by the staff available.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I should like an assurance that we can carry on with
a tape recording, and whether there is an obligation upon the Government to supply
Hansard reporters. Otherwise it seems that the proper action is for the Government to
adjourn to a more intelligent hour.
The ACTING CHAIRMAN (Mr Talbot): A very interesting document has just been
handed to me by the Clerk. It is Hansard of 1876, when this happened before and Hansard
reporters were not present. I have not had an opportunity to read this, but I understand the
proceedings of the House were not recorded. There is a statement here by the Speaker that
might be of interest: "I wish it to be clearly understood that if the debates are not now being
reported it cannot be on account of any sanction or order of mine. On the contrary, in
deference to the wishes of the House I gave an assurance that the reporting of the debates
should be proceeded with by the Hansard staff. In pursuance of that promise I gave a distinct
order, taking it upon myself as having either co-ordinate or paramount authority in reference
to the Reporting Debates Committee that the reporters should proceed. Shortly afterwards I
received a letter, which I read to the House, informing me that it was simply impossible for
the reporting staff to report the debates. I am not aware what has been done since, but my
own opinion is that it is the duty of the reporting staff to go on reporting so long as their
power of reporting will enable them to do so. Therefore, the House will distinctly
understand that it is not under my order that the reports are not being taken. I will send to
inquire how it is and why it is that the debates are not being reported." Members should
realise that since those comments were made in 1876 we have made quite an advance; we
now have electronic aids and so forth which enable the debates to be reported.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): It is quite clear from your reading of the report of

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Our Standing Orders require us to do

custody and so on of records. That is what has always happened right back since the first
publication of Hansard—that the proceedings of the House are noted by the Clerk. Whether
they are noted in pen and ink or by typewriter or one of those new-fangled devices that look
so intriguing when one of our Hansard officers uses it, or by tape, it is still, I believe, a
proceeding being noted by the Clerk, and I can see no reason whatsoever to suggest that
there is anything unconstitutional about it. Of course, if there were I have no doubt that the
Opposition would be able to get over this very quickly by adopting a sensible attitude on the
remainder of the supplementary estimates and passing them forthwith instead of hanging

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): There is no dispute as to Standing Order
321. We accept that what applies in the House must apply in the Committee. However, the
Opposition's case, as put by the member for Mangere, rests on a Speaker's ruling, not on the
Standing Orders. We are bound by the Standing Orders, but we can of course refer to
Speakers' rulings for precedents and for interpretation. In response to the concern expressed
by the Opposition as to the constitutional adequacy of our proceedings, I refer the
Committee to Standing Order 59, "Journals of the House": "All proceedings of the House
shall be noted by the Clerk, and shall constitute the Journals of the House." I believe that is
absolutely binding, and, provided the Clerk is present, we would be discharging our
obligations by having him taking a note of the proceedings of the House. When we look at
the Speaker's ruling by Mr Guinness quoted by the member for Mangere, 92/4, we find it is
not a verbatim report of what Mr Speaker Guinness said.

Apparently the Hansard staff of the day were instructed by Mr Speaker that they did not
need to be in the Committee at all times. The question was raised in the House, and the Rt.
Hon. Sir Joseph Ward said, in quite a long argument, "I think the new arrangement is a
mistake and that we should have the Hansard reporters present during the Committee work
in the House." Mr Speaker observed-and this is quite relevant to the suggestions made in
regard to reporting points of order—“I may say that the Hansard reporters only take the
same record as is taken by the clerk of the committee. The discussion on points of order in
Committee are never reported in Hansard. The Rt. Hon. Sir Joseph Ward-"But the
Hansard reporters take amendments to the same extent that the Clerk of the Committee
does. There is no difference" and so on.
It is clear there that it is the function we should be concerned about-that a record is
kept-not that it is kept in a particular way, but that a record is kept. The obligation under
the Standing Orders is that the Clerk shall keep it, and if he keeps it by means of an
electronic device, so be it-provided it is kept. The member for Mangere argued that it is not
possible for members to be satisfied that recordings are being made. We were given an
assurance by an Assistant Clerk that members on this side of the House would be only too
glad to take as a true assurance. And I know no reason why the member for Mangere should
doubt the word of an Assistant Clerk. But I urge you, Sir, to recognise that the Speaker's
ruling 92/4 needs to be read having regard to the circumstances of the day and not so as to
vary Standing Order 59.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I should like to take up the point that the Clerk is
somehow Hansard. I have looked at Erskine May to see what the British experience is, and
there is no evidence of the British system ever having broken down. So I do not think there
has ever been any ruling on that question. But Erskine May at page 254 makes it absolutely
clear that the reporting staff in the British House of Commons is regarded as being not the
Clerk, but the Editor, the Deputy Editor, three Assistant Editors, two Deputy Assistant
Editors, seven senior reporters, 14 reporters, one transcriber assistant supervisor, and 18
transcribers. Perhaps that is why they do not break down. I suggest we are in exactly the
same position. The Editor of Hansard is a named person; we all know who he is. We all
know who the staff are. When previous rulings refer to a Hansard reporter they refer to a
reporter, not to a clerk, and certainly not to a tape recorder. Neither the Clerk nor a tape
recorder can be described as a Hansard reporter. The fact that we have no Hansard reporters
is clearly a breach of the orderliness of the House. It is an obligation on the Government to
have them available. If the Government cannot have them available and cannot get anyone
else we do not have a record that the House can rely upon.
I draw to your attention the fact that the sound system does not pick up everything the
reporters pick up. Even if the tape recording is working—and we have no way of knowing
that it is it does not mean that everybody will be properly reported. We have had a change
since that ruling; the estimates are reported. That is an obligation placed upon Hansard, but
Hansard is not able to carry it out, and therefore it seems to me that the proper course is for
the Government to ask for the leave of the House to proceed. There is no doubt in my mind
that it could proceed, but without leave it is quite improper for the Government to attempt
to continue business. That is the ruling I suggest you should make in line with precedents.
I make one other statement. While it is clear that the Speakers' rulings may not be a
verbatim record of what previous Speakers have said, these Speakers' rulings have been
compiled under the supervision of Speakers, and they came out under the supervision of a
series of Speakers, and the Clerk drew them up with the Speaker at the time; and it was quite
clear at the time when these Standing Orders were drawn up that the Speakers believed it
would be quite improper for the House to try to continue without a Hansard reporter
present. To rule in any other way would seem to be an extraordinary step back from the
provision which in the British House of Commons is quite clear, where the official report of
the Debates House Committee says it is a full report of all speakers alike, a full report being
one which, although not strictly verbatim, is substantially verbatim with repetitions and
redundancies omitted and obvious mistakes corrected, but which on the other hand leaves
out nothing that adds to the meaning of the speech or illustrates the argument. I suggest that
the British House of Commons has not even contemplated the horrific suggestion of the
Government that we can continue without Hansard reporters being here. If we go back to
the British House of Commons rules, you should make a similar ruling, that the idea of
continuing without Hansard reporters just cannot be contemplated.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The member for Auckland Central quoted
